<PB N=v>
<C><B>PREFACE</B></C>
<SHL>
<P><SC>It</SC> is now nearly fifty years since the last so-called Variorum Edition
of Shakespeare, edited by Boswell, (the son of Johnson's biographer,)
was published in twenty-one octavo volumes; and whatever may be
the defects of the notes therein collected, and however much they
may seem to justify the contempt heaped upon &lquo;Shakespearian com-
mentators,&rquo; or be sneered at as &lquo;necessary evils,&rquo; that edition remains
to this day the storehouse whence succeeding editors of Shakespeare
have drawn copious supplies of illustration and criticism. It is
indispensable to a thorough study of Shakespeare&mdash;as necessary to
Shakespeare as Orelli to Horace, or Dissen to Pindar. Not that
an acquaintance with this mass of commentary is essential to the
enjoyment of Shakespeare's plays, or that there may not be even a
very full appreciation of their marvellous beauties as they appear in
the unaided text. A man may be a good Christian without any
knowledge of the commentaries on the Bible, and yet no one ques-
tions their value.
<P>Nevertheless, valuable as the Variorum of 1821 is, it is very far from
supplying the needs of Shakespeare students at the present day. It is
in fact merely rudimentary. In the fifty years that have elapsed since
its publication, Shakespearian criticism has made great progress,
greater in fact than during any other preceding half-century; and,
although in the list of recent editors are found no such world-
renowned names as Pope and Johnson, yet Shakespeare has never had
critics who brought to their task greater learning, keener critical
sagacity and more reverential love than have been shown by his more
modern editors. The student of Shakespeare is no longer offended by
the patronizing tone in which it was the wont to refer to &lquo;our author&rquo;
o<*> &lquo;our poet,&rquo; obscure passages are no longer termed &lquo;nonsense&rquo;
<PB N=vi>
<HE>vi <I>PREFACE.</I></HE>
<P>which &lquo;must be reformed,&rquo; and the cry of &lquo;bad grammar&rquo; is hushed.
The art of writing notes by exclaiming at the &lquo;asinine tastelessness
of preceding critics, so wittily described by Dr. Johnson, is happily
becoming one of the lost arts, and scathing invective over matters
which might seem to &lquo;exercise the wit without engaging the passions,&rquo;
has disappeared before a single desire to make clear what is obscure.
<P>The valuable notes, however, of such editors as Knight, Singer, Col-
lier, Ulrici, Delius, Dyce, Hudson, Staunton, White, Clarke, Keight-
ley, and Halliwell, are to be found only in as many different volumes;
and to gather the comments of these critics on doubtful passages
involves no small amount of labour and much delay. To abridge the
labour and to save the time by collecting these comments after the
manner of a Variorum and presenting them, on the same page, in a
condensed form, in connection with the difficulties which they explain,
is the purpose and plan of the present edition.
<P>A review of the critical labours of preceding editors,
<BQ>
&lquo;Many for many virtues excellent,<LB>
&lquo;None but for some, and yet all different,&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>belongs more properly to the general Preface of all the Plays rather
than to the Preface of a single Play, even if such a review be not,
under any circumstances, impertinent in an edition like the present,
where every editor speaks for himself.
<P>The appearance, in 1863, of the so-called Cambridge Edition created
an era in Shakespearian literature, and put all students of Shakespeare's
text in debt to the learned and laborious editors: Messrs. Glover,
Clark, and Wright.
<P>In the Cambridge Edition, at the foot of every page, is given a
thorough and minute collation of the Quartos and Folios and a
majority of the <I>vari&aelig; lectiones</I> of many modern editors, together with
many conjectural emendations, proposed, but not adopted into any
text&mdash;the result on the part of the editors of very extensive reading.
It is hardly possible to over-estimate the critical and textual value
of such an edition.
<P>The respect, however, wherein the plan of the Cambridge Edition is
<PB N=vii>
<HE><I>PREFACE.</I> vii</HE>
<P>open to improvement&mdash;and I say it with deference&mdash;is that, while it
gives the readings of the old editions, it omits to note the adoption
or rejection of them by the various editors, whereby an important
element in estimating these readings is wanting; however uncouth
a reading may seem at first sight, it ceases to be the &lquo;sophistication&rquo;
of a printer when we learn that men so judicious as Capell or Dyce
had pronounced in its favour; and in disputed passages it is of great
interest to see at a glance on which side lies the weight of authority.
Moreover, by this same defect in the plan of the Cambridge Edition,
credit is not always given to that editor who, from among the ancient
readings, first adopted the text since generally received; and, indeed,
the Cambridge Editors themselves suffer from this omission, when it
happens, as it sometimes does, that their own excellent selection is
passed over uncredited.
<P>It was this omission in the textual notes of the Cambridge Editors
that first led to the present undertaking, which is designed to supply
that want, and at the same time to make a New Variorum, which,
taking the Third Variorum, that of 1821, as a point of departure,
should contain the notes of the editors since that date only; in
other words, to form a supplement to the Third Variorum. But it was
very soon found that the extent to which the notes of the Variorum
enter into the composition of the notes of subsequent editors ren-
dered such a plan impossible. It was therefore decided to prepare a
New Variorum, superseding that of 1821 in so far as it should contain
all the notes in the latter, except such as the united judgments of all
the editors since that date have decided to be valueless, together with
all the original notes of these editors themselves.
<P>Of this edition the First Volume is here presented to the public; and
nothing more remains to be added but an explanation of the plan and
principles upon which it has been formed.
<P><S>First.</S> In the matter of <SC>Text</SC>, I had originally decided, in order to
save printing and space, to adopt the text of some one edition from
which all the variations of the Quartos and Folios and other editions
should be noted, and for this purpose the Cambridge Edition was
selected; but, in consequence of unforeseen obstacles, I altered my
<PB N=viii>
<HE>viii <I>PREFACE.</I></HE>
<P>plan, and have, as a general rule, adopted the reading of a majority
of the ablest editors, but not always: in some cases I have followed
only one editor; and this I have felt at liberty to do, since, in such
an edition as the present, it makes very little difference what text is
printed <I>in extenso,</I> since every other text is also printed with it on the
same page.
<P><S>Secondly.</S> In the textual notes will be found a collation of the Four
Folios, four out of the five Quartos, and the texts of the thirty-five
editions enumerated on p. xvii. Only those readings are noted which
vary from the text; all that are not mentioned agree with it. Students
accustomed to the use of the textual notes in the Cambridge Edition
will not, I think, find any difficulty in understanding mine. Of course
abbreviations were indispensable, but I have endeavoured to make them
as intelligible as possible.
<P>&lquo;<I>The rest</I>&rquo; signifies all the Quartos and Folios other than those speci-
fied: for this abbreviation I am indebted to the Cambridge Edition.
<P>The editors from Rowe to Capell agree far oftener than they dis-
agree; I have therefore employed the sign &lquo;<I>&amp;c.</I>&rquo; to denote Rowe,
Pope, Theobald, Hanmer, Warburton, and Johnson. When one or
two of them are noted as following one reading, the sign &lquo;<I>&amp;c.,</I>&rquo; is
still made to do duty for the others that follow another reading.
<P>As many of the editors have adopted the text of the Variorum, I
have used the abbreviation &lquo;<I>Var.</I>&rquo; to denote the Variorum of 1821,
Rann, Harness, Singer (ed. 1), Campbell, Cornwall and Hazlitt; it
also includes Steevens's edition of 1793. Collier's text, unless other-
wise noted, invariably includes Verplanck's.
<P>When after either of the two latter abbreviations, <I>&amp;c.</I> and <I>Var.,</I>
the name of any editor is included in a parenthesis, it is to be under-
stood that the editor thus distinguished follows, unless otherwise noted,
the same reading as in the text. It is to be borne in mind that this is
the rule only after these abbreviations; when parentheses are elsewhere
employed they designate the editor who first suggested the given
emendation; <I>e. g.,</I> in Act I, scene v, line 92, &lquo;<I>fine</I>] Theob. (Warb.)&rquo;
means that although Theobald's is the first edition in which this
reading is found, instead of the &lquo;sinne&rquo; of the Quartos and Folios,
yet it was Warburton's suggestion. This form of abbreviation I have
<PB N=ix>
<HE><I>PREFACE.</I> ix</HE>
<P>also adopted from the Cambridge Edition, as also the letters F and Q
with inferior numerals to betoken the various Folios and Quartos.
<P>When, after certain readings have been noted as followed by certain
editors, all the rest of the editors adopt the reading of the Variorum,
I have used the abbreviation &lquo;<I>Var. et cet.</I>&rquo; Exceptions are placed in
parentheses; <I>e. g.,</I> I, v, 19, &lquo;<I>You are welcome</I>] Var. et cet. (Knt. Dyce,
Sta. Clarke, Cambr.)&rquo; means that the editors in parenthesis do not
adopt the reading of the Variorum and the rest, but read as in the
text.
<P>Where the Quartos and Folios have a uniform reading different
from the generally accepted modern text, the editor who introduced
the change is specified without giving the list of his predecessors who
followed the ancient reading. <I>E. g.,</I> I, iv, 47, &lquo;<I>our five</I>] Mal. (Wilbra-
&lquo;ham conj.) <I>our fine</I> Qq. Ff. Ulr.&rquo; signifies that Malone, at the sug-
gestion of Wilbraham, first read &lquo;five&rquo; for <I>fine,</I> and that Rowe, Pope,
Theobald, Hanmer, Warburton, Johnson, Capell, and Steevens followed
the old copies; and lastly that Ulrici alone, of editors since Malone,
reverted to the Quartos and Folios.
<P>I have very seldom noted the <I>vari&aelig; lectiones</I> of the First Quarto; it
differs so widely that to do so in every instance in foot-notes is
impossible. I have therefore followed the example of the Cambridge
Edition, and reprinted it entire at the end of the play. When referred
to in the textual notes it is designated as (Q<SUB>1</SUB>).
<P>For the sake of economy in space I have not always recorded the
metrical arrangement of Rowe, who almost invariably follows the
Fourth Folio.
<P>The Manuscript Corrector of Mr Collier's Second Folio I have
uniformly designated by the sign &lquo;<I>Coll.</I> (<I>MS.</I>)&rquo;, and where his emen-
dations have been adopted by subsequent editors I have sometimes
violated the chronological order by placing him the first in the list,&mdash;
before Ulrici, his warmest advocate.
<P>In some other instances also I have placed an editor immediately
after an emendation suggested by him, but adopted by others in edi-
tions which chronologically precede his. <I>E. g.,</I> V, iii, 169, Dyce sug-
gested &lquo;rest,&rquo; for <I>rust</I> in his &lquo;Remarks&rquo;, &amp;c., published in 1844, which
was adopted by three editors before Dyce's own edition appeared in
<PB N=x>
<HE>x <I>PREFACE.</I></HE>
<P>1857. I have nevertheless placed Dyce before the others. In all these
cases the commentary will explain any such apparent irregularity.
<P>When, in recording the <I>vari&aelig; lectiones</I> of the Quartos and Folios, the
point at issue is a matter of punctuation, I have not noted trivial dif-
ferences of spelling, but have followed the spelling of the majority.
<I>E. g.,</I> where attention is called to the period after <I>enough,</I> although the
First and Second Folio have &lquo;inough&rquo; and the Third Folio has
&lquo;enough,&rquo; I have thought it sufficient to record &lquo;<I>inough. F</I><SUB>1</SUB><I>F</I><SUB>2</SUB><I>F</I><SUB>3</SUB>. &rquo;
<P>On the other hand, when it is a matter not of punctuation, but of
words, I have not swelled the space of the notes by giving every
variety of punctuation. <I>E. g.,</I> III, v, 176-178, Theobald, Hanmer
and Warburton are recorded as following Pope in adopting the lines
from the First Quarto, although they differ from him immaterially in
punctuation.
<P>Mere verbal differences in Stage-directions I have not recorded;
where Rowe has &lquo;Ex. Mer. Ben.&rquo; and the text reads &lquo;Exeunt Mercu-
&lquo;tio and Benvolio,&rquo; the whole phrase is credited to Rowe. It shows
little respect for the reader to leave nothing to his intelligence.
<P>As the textual notes in this edition at once invite comparison with
those in the Cambridge Edition, it may not be needless to state briefly
the points of identity and difference.
<P>The collation of the Quartos and Folios is wholly my own, so far as
examining every word in every one of them can make it so. I have
conducted the examination with all the carefulness at my command.
I have not wittingly recorded a single reading in them at second hand,
except in the case of the Fifth Quarto, of which I have only an im-
perfect copy, lacking about seventy lines at the end of the first Act,
and about a hundred and fifty at the end of the fifth; within these
spaces I am indebted to Prof. Mommsen and the Cambridge Editors
for citations of that Quarto. For the collation of the other Quartos
I have used Mr Ashbee's Facsimiles, between which and the readings
recorded in the foot-notes of the Cambridge Edition I have found
about twenty discrepancies, all trifling, and tending to show that the
original copies used by Mr Ashbee and the Cambridge Editors varied.
For instance, in I, v, 115 the Cambridge Edition gives <I>Catulet</I> as the
reading of Q<SUB>3</SUB>, Mr Ashbee's Facsimile has &lquo;Capulet&rquo;; in III, iii, 160
<PB N=xi>
<HE><I>PREFACE.</I> xi</HE>
<P>the Cambridge Edition records <I>learaing</I> in Q<SUB>4</SUB>, the Facsimile has
&lquo;Learning&rquo;; in V, i, 7 the former notes from Q<SUB>4</SUB> <I>dreames that gives,</I> the
latter &lquo;dreame that gives&rquo;; <I>brase</I> of the Cambridge Edition is &lquo;brace&rquo;
in the Facsimile, &amp;c. &amp;c. (It may not be amiss to add that the read-
ings of the Facsimile that vary from the Cambridge Edition have been
kindly verified for me by an eminent Shakespearian collector in Lon-
don, and found to agree with the original copies in the British Museum
and in his own Library.) About the same number of discrepancies
appeared between the original Folios that I have used and those used
by the Cambridge Editors. For instance, the latter note &lquo;<I>mlgh'st</I> F<SUB>4</SUB>&rquo;;
&lquo;<I>stent thou</I> F<SUB>3</SUB>&rquo;; &lquo;<I>saint-seucing</I> F<SUB>2</SUB>&rquo; for &lquo;might'st,&rquo; &lquo;stent thee,&rquo; and
&lquo;saint-seuncing&rquo; in my copies respectively. I do not doubt but that
the Folios used by the Cambridge Editors would in every the smallest
particular sustain the correctness of their notes, so greatly do the old
copies, Quarto and Folio, of the same date, differ, but I mention these
facts solely for the sake of justifying the discretion which I have used
in recording the <I>vari&aelig; lectiones</I> of these ancient copies. I have not
noted manifest misprints in passages about which there never has been
and never can be any difficulty, or such differences of spelling as <I>Wens-
day</I> or <I>Wendsday</I> for Wednesday, <I>Petrucheo</I> for Petruchio, or <I>Catulet</I>
for Capulet; nor have I noted differences of punctuation where the
sense could be in no wise affected. Were there any evidence that
Shakespeare had ever corrected the proof-sheets of this play, or that it
was even printed from his manuscript, every comma should be held
sacred, but when we know that we have to get at Shakespeare ofttimes
through the interpretation of an ignorant compositor, and that copies
of the very same date differ, such minute collation verges on trifling
and caricature. The punctuation adopted by such critics as Dyce, or
Staunton, or the Cambridge Editors appears to me of much higher
authority than that of the Quartos and Folios. Of course the case is
very different in doubtful or disputed passages, where the student
should have before him every aid that the old copies can afford, and
no mispelling nor misprint is too gross, nor punctuation too minute,
to be recorded.
<P>Apart from the distinctive feature of the foot-notes of this edition,
which is, that the different texts are given of over thirty modern edi-
<PB N=xii>
<HE>xii <I>PREFACE.</I></HE>
<P>tions, and apart from the discretion which I have exercised in recording
the collation of the Quartos and Folios, the most noticeable difference
between the textual notes in the present edition and those in the Cam-
bridge Edition is, that I have not noted all the phrases and passages
omitted by Pope, whose edition was not a success in his own day, and
never has been since. His omissions were monstrous and arbitrary,
and where they have not been endorsed by any subsequent editor,
except perhaps Hanmer, I have not noted them. When other editors
have followed his example, the omission is duly recorded.
<P>Wherever I have adopted in the textual notes a <I>varia lectio</I> from
the Cambridge Edition, I have acknowledged it by placing after it
an asterisk.
<P>In the <SC>Commentary</SC> will be found, <I>first,</I> the notes adopted by modern
editors from the Variorum of 1821, and at the end of every note the
names in <I>Italics</I> of all the editors by whom it has been adopted.
<P>Then follow the original notes of the English and German editors.
<P>From all notes I have omitted references simply to the <I>vari&aelig; lec-
tiones</I> of the old copies, except where they were necessary to explain
the substance of the note.
<P>I have also omitted the personalities of editors. One or two of
them have been thoughtlessly retained in the earlier pages of this
volume, before I had made it a stringent rule to exclude them, and
when I had not fully in mind that portion of Dr Johnson's brilliant
preface which the reader will pardon me for quoting, since Shake
speare commentators have so often offended in this respect: &lquo;It is
&lquo;not easy to discover from what cause the acrimony of a scholiast can
&lquo;naturally proceed. The subjects to be discussed by him are of very
&lquo;small importance; they involve neither property nor liberty; nor
&lquo;favour the interest of sect nor party. But whether it be, that <I>small</I>
&lquo;<I>things make mean men proud,</I> and vanity catches small occasions; or
&lquo;that all contrariety of opinion, even in those that can defend it no
&lquo;longer, makes proud men angry; there is often found in comment-
&lquo;aries a spontaneous strain of invective and contempt, more eager and
&lquo;venomous than is vented by the most furious controvertist in poli-
&lquo;tics against those whom he is hired to defame. Perhaps the lightness
<PB N=xiii>
<HE><I>PREFACE.</I> xiii</HE>
<P>&lquo;of the matter may conduce to the vehemence of the agency; when the
&lquo;truth to be investigated is so near to inexistence as to escape atten-
&lquo;tion, its bulk is to be enlarged by rage and exclamation; that to
&lquo;which all would be indifferent in its original state may attract notice
&lquo;when the fate of a name is appended to it. A commentator has indeed
&lquo;great temptation to supply by turbulence what he wants of dignity,
&lquo;to beat his little gold to a spacious surface, to work that to foam
&lquo;which no art or diligence can exalt to spirit.&rquo;
<P>From the German editions those notes only are taken which are
not exclusively designed for a German public. Here and there expla-
nations which I have introduced from this quarter have been drawn, I
apprehend, from the &lquo;depths of German consciousness.&rquo; To save space,
I have not included the names of German editors among those who
have adopted the Variorum notes, nor have I repeated those notes
from the Variorum which only the foreign editors have selected. As
may be very naturally supposed, (although the opposite belief has
pretty generally prevailed in Germany,) the foreign editors are indebted
at every step to the English editors. Lessing revealed Shakespeare
to Germans, but not to Englishmen. Rowe, Pope, Theobald, Hanmer,
Warburton, and Johnson had supplied with their editions the English
demand for the works of him whose supremacy all acknowledged,
before Lessing's powerful voice was raised in the interest of Shake-
speare; and at the very hour that he was writing his <I>Hamburgische
Dramaturgie,</I> Capell was producing, with a laborious care rarely
surpassed, an edition which to this day stands almost unrivalled
for purity of text. In philosophical or &aelig;sthetic criticism on Shake-
speare the Germans have shown themselves eminent, and it has been
a very grateful task to lay before the English reader some of the results
of their keen and refined labours; at no time has the lack of
space been more irksome than when it has compelled me to abridge
or omit much of German criticism that I have been anxious to retain.
Occasionally the demand made by German commentators upon our
admiration a little outruns our ability to meet it, as when, for exam-
ple, Prof. Lemcke of Marburg says:
<P>&lquo;Let us for once lay aside our proverbial modesty, and openly de-
&lquo;clare that it is not the affinity of race, nor the indications in his poetry
<PB N=xiv>
<HE>xiv <I>PREFACE.</I></HE>
<P>&lquo;of a German spirit, which have brought us so close to Shakespeare,
&lquo;but it is that God-given power vouchsafed to us Germans before all
&lquo;other nations, by the grace of which we are enabled to recognize true
&lquo;genius, of whatsoever nation, better than other nations, ofttimes better
&lquo;than its own, and better to enjoy and to appropriate its gifts.<*> We un-
&lquo;derstand and love Shakespeare by virtue of that same German insight
&lquo;which has helped the Italians to understand their Dante, which has
&lquo;helped the Spaniards to arrange their Romances, and which is now
&lquo;and always helping the French to explore the treasures of their me-
&lquo;di&aelig;val literature. We comprehend and love Shakespeare by virtue
&lquo;of that Faust element in us which instinctively recognizes a genius
&lquo;where other nations, with their Wagner eyes, can perceive only a
&lquo;black poodle&mdash;in a word, we comprehend and love Shakespeare
&lquo;because we are undeniably a &ldquo;Nation of Thinkers,&rdquo; as other nations
&lquo;have before now so often been obliged with ill-concealed vexation to
&lquo;acknowledge.&rquo;
<P>Our defence, if any be needed, may safely be left in the hands of
so accomplished a scholar as Prof. Mommsen, whose edition of
Romeo and Juliet will stand as long as Shakespeare is studied, a
monument of critical sagacity, patient toil and microscopic investi-
gation of the text. &lquo;It is assuredly a valuable work,&rquo; says this eminent
scholar, &lquo;to epitomize intelligently the great English commentaries
&lquo;on Shakespeare; here and there by a collation of the old copies we
&lquo;may happily settle some doubtful reading, but it is a perilous game
&lquo;not to confess, under all circumstances, frankly and modestly, that
&lquo;we are wholly dependent on the English; verily we should suffer
&lquo;wreck if with the one hand we accept from them all the means by
&lquo;which we live and breathe, and with the other, by way of thanks.
&lquo;fling scorn and contempt upon their names.&rquo;
<P>I have also introduced here and there into the Commentary, from
nearly fifty different sources, criticisms and notes which seemed too
fragmentary to be inserted in the Appendix, and which might lose
much of their point separated from the passages to which they apply.
Many of these more properly come under the head of Illustrations;
but I was unwilling to separate them from the text for the reason just
<PB N=xv>
<HE><I>PREFACE.</I> xv</HE>
<P>given, and also because I did not wish to introduce another division
in a volume that seems already sufficiently varied.
<P>In the <SC>Appendix</SC> are given, first, certain notes that were too long to
be inserted in the Commentary, and next the various Prefaces of the
different modern editors, digested and divided under separate subjects.
Then follow extracts from English, French, and German critics. Con-
tinually haunted as I have been by the fear of making the volume too
bulky, I have been obliged to make a selection, and in so doing I
decided to give more space to the French and German than to the
English. It must be borne in mind that references to this tragedy
alone, and not to Shakespeare in general, would be appropriate
in this volume. It has given me especial pleasure to lay before the
English reader the extracts from the French: it is but little known,
in this country at least, outside the ranks of Shakespeare students,
how great is the influence which Shakespeare at this hour is exerting
on French literature, and how many and how ardent are his admirers
in that nation.
<P>On p. xviii I have enumerated, in the list of books quoted, some six
or seven volumes, which, judging from their titles only, might seem
to contain matter that should be incorporated in a volume like the
present, but in which nothing has been found either pertinent or avail-
able. They have been included, however, in the list, lest their
absence should imply neglect or oversight on the part of the editor.
It is not to be supposed that the list contains all or nearly all of the
Books, Pamphlets, or Reviews that have been consulted.
<P>In the textual notes will be found the valuable conjectures of Profes-
sor George Allen of the University of Pennsylvania; in the Appendix
is his explanation of the theory on which they are, most of them,
based; no one who has studied Sidney Walker's volumes can fail to be
interested in the development of a law of pronunciation and rhythm
which that acute critic so narrowly missed, and which here, for the
first time, has found an expositor whose name has been for so many
years a synonym, in our city, for accurate and finished scholarship.
<PB N=xvi>
<HE>xvi <I>PREFACE.</I></HE>
<P>Steevens's remark, in the last century, that every new edition of
Shakespeare must be an experiment, is emphatically true of the present
volume, and to suppose that no errors lurk in it would betoken in the
editor a strange degree of folly. It will be preternatural if there be
not many in it. In excuse for the imperfections of my work, I should
doubtless have quoted the Latin proverb, had I not lately noted that
Cotgrave, a contemporary of Shakespeare, considered &lquo;Hvmanum est
&lquo;errare&rquo; as even in his day quite too threadbare to serve as an excuse for
those errors &lquo;such as the malicious and ignorant shall captiously pinch
or fondly point at.&rquo; I shall therefore only say that where errors may
be found, they are not due to any stinted painstaking on my part.
<P>There now only remains to me the pleasant duty of acknowledging
the kind offices that have lightened my labours. My chiefest thanks
are tendered to Professor <SC>Allen</SC>, whose mature judgment, and ripe and
accurate scholarship, have frequently afforded me, while the work was
going through the press, that aid and comfort, which only those can
appreciate who have entered upon the thorny, perilous, and bewilder-
ing path of an editor. To Mr <SC>A. I. Fish</SC>, whose name has been so
long associated in this city with the study of Shakespeare, and who has
for many years been the Dean and the moving spirit of &lquo;The Shak-
spere Society of Philadelphia,&rquo; I owe my warm acknowledgments for
his friendly interest and unfailing sympathy, as well as for the unre-
stricted use of his library where my own was deficient. To Mr <SC>Edwin
Forrest</SC> my sincere thanks are due for the prompt and liberal manner
in which he placed at my service his valuable copies of the Second
and Third Folios. To Mr <SC>Robert F. Smith</SC> I am also indebted for the
loan of Halliwell's Folio Edition. I cannot lay claim to all the trans-
lations in the Appendix. Some of those from the German were made
by my father, and some from the French by my sister, Mrs <SC>A. L.
Wister</SC>, and by one still nearer. The public, who have so often and
so emphatically welcomed other translations from the hands of the
first two, will thus have a proof that certain portions, at least, of this
work are beyond criticism.
<P>H. H. F.

<P><B>Enter Chorus</B>] <SC>Mal.</SC> This I suppose meant only that the prologue was to be
spoken by the same person who personated the Chorus at the end of the first Act.
[<I>Har. Coll. Verp. Huds. White, Hal. Clarke.</I>
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> This was the usual name of the person who spoke the prologues and epi-
logues to the play or to single acts&mdash;a custom derived from those older dramas
which (like the Gorboduc of Lord Sackville and Th. Norton, 1562), modeled on the
antique, adopted the Chorus, and employed it as a Prologue. This Chorus is proba-
bly not Sh.'s, and was therefore omitted by Heminge and Condell.
<P>8. <B>Do</B>] <SC>Coll.</SC> &ldquo;<I>Doth</I>&rdquo; is a grammatical error, not corrected in subsequent
editions.
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> The old reading may be justified in two ways. First of all, Percy, one of
the most thorough scholars in Old English literature, remarks that in Old English
</CC>

<CC>
<P>not only the third person singular but also the third person plural has, in the present
tense, the final syllable <I>eth;</I> and Tollet traces this to the Anglo-Saxon, in which it
is the grammatical rule, corresponding to the Danish-Saxon that has only <I>es</I> instead
of <I>eth.</I> Shakspere thus may have adhered to the Old English form here and there,
where it suited him. He mostly uses it, however (and this is the second reason in
favor of &ldquo;<I>Doth</I>&rdquo;), only where, at all events, it has the force of the singular&mdash;namely,
where the sense is collective, and the plural (as here, &ldquo;overthrows&rdquo;) has essentially
the signification of the singular.
<P><SC>White</SC>. I am not quite sure that the disagreement [of &ldquo;<I>Doth</I>&rdquo;] with the nomi-
native is the result of a misprint or of any other error.
<P>12. <B>two hours</B>] <SC>Del.</SC> This time as the probable duration of one of Sh.'s dramas
occurs also in the Prologue to Hen. VIII:&mdash;&ldquo;may see away their shilling Richly in
two short hours.&rdquo;

<P><B>Stage Direction</B>] <SC>Camb. Edd.</SC> There is no division into Acts and Scenes in the
Quartos, nor any trace of division in the Folios, except the &ldquo;Actus Primus, Sc&aelig;na
Prima&rdquo; at the beginning of the play.
<P>1. <B>carry coals</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> Warburton observes that this was a phrase formerly in
use to signify <I>the bearing of injuries;</I> but, as he gives no instances, I subjoin the
following. Nash in his Have With you to Saffron Walden, 1595, says: &ldquo;We will
<I>bear no coles,</I> I warrant you.&rdquo; Again, in Marston's Antonio and Mellida, second
part, 1602: &ldquo;He has had wrongs; and if I were he I would <I>bear no coles.</I>&rdquo;
Again, in Law Tricks, by John Day, 1608: &ldquo;I'll <I>carry coals</I> an you will, no horns.&rdquo;
In May-Day, by Chapman, 1610 [in <SC>Sing</SC>., 1608]: &ldquo;You must swear by no man's
beard but your own, for that may breed a quarrel; above all things you must <I>carry
no coals.</I>&rdquo; &ldquo;Now, my ancient being a man of an <I>un-coal-carrying</I> spirit,&rdquo; etc.
Again, in Ben Jonson's Every Man out of his Humour: &ldquo;Here comes one that
will <I>carry coals;</I> ergo, will hold my dog.&rdquo; [<I>Cham.</I>] In Hen. V: III, ii, 49: &ldquo;At
Calais they stole a fire-shovel; I knew by that piece of service the men would <I>carry
coals.</I>&rdquo; [<I>Sing. Huds.</I>] Again, in The Malcontent, 1604: &ldquo;Great slaves fear better
than love, born naturally for a <I>coal-basket.</I>&rdquo; [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Percy</SC>. This phrase continued in use to the middle of the last century. In a little
satirical piece of Sir John Birkenhead, entitled Two Centuries [of books] of St.
Paul's Churchyard, etc., published after the death of King Charles I, No. 22, p. 50,
is inserted &ldquo;<I>Fire! fire!</I> a small manual, dedicated to Sir Arthur Haselridge; in
which it is plainly proved by a whole chauldron of Scripture that John Lillburn
will not <I>carry coals.</I>&rdquo; By Dr. Gouge. [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Nares</SC>. The origin of the phrase is this, that in every family the scullions, the
turnspits, the carriers of wood and coals were esteemed the very lowest of menials.
The latter in particular were the <I>servi servorum,</I> the drudges of all the rest. Such
attendants upon the royal households in progresses were jocularly called the &ldquo;black-
guard,&rdquo; and hence the origin of that term. [<I>Sing. Huds.</I>] In most of these cases
charcoal is probably meant.
</CC>

<CC>
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> Upon a passage in Ben Jonson's &ldquo;Every Man out of his Humour,&rdquo; Gifford
has this note: &ldquo;In all great houses, but particularly in the royal residences, there
were a number of mean and dirty dependants whose office it was to attend to the
wood-yard and sculleries, etc. Of these (for in the lowest deep there was a deeper
still), the most forlorn wretches seem to have been selected to carry coals to the
kitchen, halls, etc. To this smutty regiment, who attended the progresses and rode
in the cart with the pots and kettles, which, with every other article of furniture,
were then moved from palace to palace, the people in derision gave the name of
blackguards, a term since become familiar, and never properly explained.&rdquo; [<I>Corn.
Sta. Dyce.</I>] In this passage from Ben Jonson, we find the primary meaning of the
expression&mdash;that of being fit for servile offices; in a subsequent passage we have the
secondary meaning&mdash;that of tamely submitting to an affront. Puntarvolo insults Shift,
who, he supposes, has taken his dog; upon which another character exclaims: &ldquo;Take
heed, Sir Puntarvolo, what you do! he'll bear no coals, I can tell you.&rdquo; Gifford
gives an illustration of this meaning (which is the sense in which Sh. here uses it):
&mdash;&ldquo;the queen was exceedingly well satisfied: saying that you were too like some
body in the world, to whom she is afrayde you are a little kin, to be content to carry
coales at any Frenchman's hand.&rdquo; Secretary Cecyll to Sir Henry Neville, March 2,
1559.
<P><SC>White</SC>. This phrase was euphemistic slang for &ldquo;to put up with an insult.&rdquo;
<P><SC>Dyce</SC>. To submit to any degradation (&ldquo;Il a du feu en la teste. <I>Hee is very
chollericke, furious, or couragious; he will carrie no coales.</I>&rdquo; Cotgrave's <I>Fr. and
Engl. Dict.,</I> sub. &ldquo;Teste&rdquo;). &ldquo;To <I>carry coals,</I> in the sense of tamely putting up
an affront, occurs perpetually in our old writers, both serious and comic.&rdquo; Gifford's
<I>Jonson,</I> vol. ii, p. 169. (In Lyly's <I>Midas,</I> mention is made of &ldquo;one of the Cole
house,&rdquo; sig. <SC>F</SC> 4, ed. 1592&mdash;<I>i. e.,</I> one of the drudges about the palace of Midas.)
<P>2. <B>colliers.</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> A very ancient term of abuse. Twelfth Night, III, iv, 130.
Any person who would <I>bear</I> to be called a <I>collier</I> was said to <I>carry coals.</I> It after-
wards became descriptive of any one who would endure a gibe or flout. So, in
Churchyard's Farewell to the World, 1598: &ldquo;He <I>carried coales</I> that could abide no
gest.&rdquo; [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Halliwell</SC> adds instances from Stephens' Essayes, 1615; Autobiography of Sir
John Bramston, p. 42; Wild's Iter Boreale, 1670, p. 65; Canidia, or the Witches,
1683.
</CC>

<P>what <I>byting of thumbs, to beget quarrels!</I>&rdquo; <I>The Dead Term,</I> 1608. [<I>Sing. Corn.
Knt. Coll. Huds. White, Dyce, Hal. Clarke.</I>
<P><SC>Nares</SC>. The thumb in this action represented a <I>fig,</I> and the whole was equivalent
to a <I>fig for you,</I> or the <I>fico.</I>
<BQ>
Dags and pistols!<LB REND=RIGHT>
<I>To bite his thumb</I> at me!<LB>
Wear I a sword<LB REND=RIGHT>
To see men <I>bite their thumbs?</I><LB>
<I>Randolph, Muses' L. Glass.</I> O. Pl. ix, 220. [<I>Sing.</I><LB>
</BQ>
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> There can be little doubt, we apprehend, that this mode of insult was
originally peculiar to Italy, and was perhaps a mitigated form of the greater insult
of making the fig or fico, that is, thrusting out the thumb in a peculiar manner
between the fingers. Douce has bestowed much laborious investigation upon this
difficult and somewhat worthless subject. The commentators have not distinctly
alluded to what appears to us the identity of biting the thumb and the fico; but the
passage in Lodge's &ldquo;Wits Miserie&rdquo; clearly shows that the customs were one and
the same.
<P><SC>Sing</SC>. The mode in which this contemptuous action was performed is thus
described by Cotgrave, in a passage which has escaped the industry of all the com-
mentators: &ldquo;Faire la nique: to mocke by nodding or lifting up the chinne; or more
properly, to threaten or defie, by putting the thumbe naile into the mouth, and with
a jerke (from the upper teeth) make it to knacke.&rdquo; [<I>Corn. Huds. Dyce, Sta.
Hal. Cham. Clarke.</I>
<P><SC>Hunter</SC>. A trait of Italian manners. Thus Fuller, in his <I>Abel Redivivus,</I> p. 38,
after relating a conversation between Luther and a messenger of Cardinal Cajetan,
says, &ldquo;At this the messenger, <I>after the Italian manner, biting his thumbs,</I> went
away.&rdquo;
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> This contemptuous action, though obsolete in this country, is still in use both
in France and Italy; but Knight is mistaken in supposing it identical with what
is called <I>giving the fico. Biting the thumb</I> is performed by biting the thumb-nail;
or as Cotgrave describes it [as cited by Singer]: The more offensive gesticulation
of <I>giving the fico</I> was by thrusting out the thumb between the forefingers, or putting
it in the mouth so as to swell out the cheek.

<P>custom, on the breaking out of a fray, to call out &ldquo;<I>Clubs! Clubs!</I>&rdquo; to part the com-
batants. So in Tit. And. II, i, 37. [Note on As You Like It, V, ii, 44.] [<I>Sing.</I>
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> The cry of &ldquo;clubs&rdquo; is as thoroughly of English origin as the &ldquo;bite my
thumb&rdquo; is of Italian. Scott has made the cry familiar to us in &ldquo;The Fortunes of
Nigel;&rdquo; and when the citizens of Verona here raise it, we involuntarily think of the
old watch-maker's hatch-door in Fleet Street and Jin Vin and Tunstall darting off
for the affray. &ldquo;The great long club&rdquo; as described by Stow, on the necks of the
London apprentices, was as characteristic as the flat cap of the same quarrelsome
body, in the days of Elizabeth and James. The use by Sh. of home phrases, in the
mouths of foreign characters, was a part of his art. It is the same thing as rendering
Sancho's Spanish proverbs into the corresponding English proverbs, instead of liter-
ally translating them. The cry of clubs by the citizens of Verona expressed an idea
of popular movement, which could not have been conveyed half so emphatically in
a foreign phrase. [<I>Verp. Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Haz.</SC> As we should now say, police.
<P><SC>Hunter</SC>. This word should probably be so printed as to indicate that the citizen
called out, &ldquo;Clubs,&rdquo; an English expression used to part combatants. It may still
sometimes be heard, and occurs in <I>As You Like It,</I> V, ii, 44.
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> Sh., whose wont it is to assimilate the customs of all countries to those of
his own, puts the ancient call to arms of the London 'prentices in the mouth of the
Veronese citizen.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC>. Originally, the cry to call forth the London apprentices, who employed their
clubs to preserve the public peace: sometimes, however, they used those weapons to
raise a disturbance. See Hen. VIII: V, iii.
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. This speech seems to be a collection of exclamations uttered by several
persons rather than the words of one person.
<P>66. <B>bills.</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>. A kind of pike or halbert formerly carried by the English
infantry, and afterwards the usual weapon of watchmen. It is described by Sir Wm.
Temple as giving the most ghastly wounds, which may be imagined by the figures
of bills delineated in Steevens's Shakespeare, vol. ii, p. 316, ed. 1778. Johnson tells
us that these weapons were carried by the watchmen of Lichfield in 1778.
<P>66. <SC>Fairholt</SC>. These long-popular weapons of the foot-soldier were constructed
to thrust at mounted men, or cut and damage their horse-furniture. Sometimes they
were provided with a side-hook to seize a bridle. [<I>Dyce.</I>
<P>66. <B>partisans.</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>. <I>Pertuisan,</I> Old French, a kind of pike or halbert. [<I>Sing.</I>
<P><SC>Fairholt</SC>. It may be described as a sharp two-edged sword placed on the sum-
mit of a staff for the defence of foot-soldiers against cavalry. [<I>Dyce.</I>
<P>67. <B>in his gown.</B>] <SC>Del.</SC> Intimating that he has been disturbed in his night's
rest.

<P><SC>Coleridge</SC> (<I>Lit. Rem.</I> vol. II, p. 151, ed. 1836). With his accustomed judgment,
Shakespeare has begun by placing before us a lively picture of all the impulses of
the play; and as nature ever presents two sides, one for Heraclitus and one for Democ-
ritus, he has, by way of prelude, shown the laughable absurdity of the evil by the
contagion of it reaching the servants, who have so little to do with it, but who are
under the necessity of letting the superfluity of sensorial power fly off through the
escape-valve of wit-combats, and of quarreling with weapons of a sharper edge, all
in humble imitation of their masters. Yet there is a sort of unhired fidelity, an
<I>ourishness</I> about all this, that makes it rest pleasant on one's feelings. All the first
scene, down to the conclusion of the Prince's speech, is a motley dance of all ranks
and ages to one tune, as if the horn of Huon had been playing behind the scenes.
[<I>Huds.</I>

<P>conjugationis prim&aelig;; at <I>I write,</I> imperfectum commune <I>I wrote,</I> et Borealium <I>I
wrate,</I> secund&aelig;. Sic <I>I drive, I drive</I> (<I>i</I> corrept&acirc;), <I>I have driven,</I> impello, prim&aelig;;
at <I>I drive, I drove,</I> aut <I>I drave, I have driven,</I> secund&aelig;. Sedulo autem cavendum
est, ne locum dialectis concedas pr&aelig;terquam communi; aut inter poetas Boreali:
nam nullum fere verbum est quod pro aurium sordibus non deformant.&rdquo;
<P>Hereupon Gil explains that the Pr&aelig;terites in <I>i</I> are more correct, and the others,
secondary forms. In fact <I>writ</I> = <I>scripsi</I> is constantly used in Sh.&mdash;e. g. in this play,
I, iii, 245. Also <I>bid</I> = <I>jussi</I> is the constant form; <I>bad</I> is only found in I, iii, 3, no-
where <I>bade,</I> although our current texts almost always thus write it. We must not
be misled by finding in the F<SUB>1</SUB> as well as in the Q<SUB>5</SUB> of 1 Hen. IV, in the Q<SUB>1</SUB> of Mer.
Wives, and in the Q<SUB>1</SUB> of 3 Hen. VI, the forms <I>droue</I> and <I>draue,</I> for just as here Q<SUB>3</SUB>
suppresses the older and purer form, so it may well have happened oftener; and I
do not mean to affirm that Sh. did not use the forms in <I>a</I> and <I>o.</I> At all events,
there is no apparent reason why we should erase a form found in our best text, and
which then passed, according to a mass of testimony, for the purest; and we should
therefore in future write, &ldquo;A troubled mind <I>drive</I> me to walk abroad.&rdquo;
<P>114. <B>the grove of sycamore.</B>] <SC>Knt.</SC> When Sh. has to deal with descriptions
of natural scenery, he almost invariably localizes himself with the utmost distinct-
ness. He never mistakes the sycamore groves of the south for the birch woods
of the north. In such cases he was not required to employ familiar and conven-
tional images for the sake of presenting an idea more distinctly to his audience than
a rigid adherence to the laws of costume (we employ the word in its large sense of
manners) would have allowed. The grove of sycamore &ldquo;That westward rooteth
from this city's side&rdquo; takes us at once to a scene entirely different from one presented
by Sh.'s own experience. The sycamore is the Oriental plane (little known in
England, though sometimes found), spreading its <I>broad</I> branches&mdash;from which its
name <I>platanus</I>&mdash;to supply the most delightful of shades under the sun of Syria or
Italy. Sh. might have found the sycamore in Chaucer's exquisite tale of the Flower
and the Leaf, where the hedge that
<BQ>
&ldquo;&mdash;&mdash; closed in all&eacute; the green arbere,<LB>
With sycamore was set and eglantere.&rdquo; [<I>Verp.</I><LB>
</BQ>
<P><SC>Del.</SC> The sycamore or wild fig tree Sh. has referred to in Love's Lab. Lost, V,
ii, and in Othello IV, iii, as a tree whose shade is dedicated to dejected lovers.
<P><SC>Beisly</SC>. <I>Sycamore</I> (Acer Pseudo-Platanus), great maple. Miller says, &ldquo;This tree
is wild in Italy, and with us it is vulgarly called the sycamore tree, and by some
&lquo;mock-plane;&rquo; it grows to a great height, and has a clean straight bole, with a
spreading top. It was formerly much planted for walks and avenues. The original
plantations of Vauxhall and Marybone gardens were chiefly of these trees.&rdquo;

<P>Walter Blith recommends the tree as quick growing, rising to gallant shade, and
excellent to make walks and shadow bowers. W. Westmacott, in his &ldquo;Scripture
Herbal,&rdquo; says: &ldquo;Our sycamores are raised more for ornament (they affording a
curious, dark and pleasant shadow), and for their speedy growth, than for any medi-
cal property; yet astrologers regard it as one of Venus her trees, 'tis like to make
her a shady walk, to cool her beauty and prevent sun-burning.&rdquo; Ph. Holland's

<P>120. <B>Which then, etc.</B>] <SC>Coll.</SC> The plain meaning seems to be, that Benvolio,
like Romeo, was indisposed for society, and sought to be most, where most people
were not to be found, being one too many, even when by himself. [<I>Verp.</I>
<P><SC>Del.</SC> [<I>Lexicon,</I> p. 162] This play of antitheses, so truly Shakspearian, betrays the
later touches of the poet's hand. [<I>Ulr.</I>
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> Benvolio means to say that he was in a melancholy state similar to Ro-
meo's, and hence appreciated the mood of the latter by his own, &ldquo;which then most
sought there where mostly nothing is to be found,&rdquo; <I>i. e.</I> which sought the most com-
fort, the most help, in solitude, where it is not to be found. This turning to soli-
tude, he adds, was so strong in him that he was too much for himself, for his own
weary self (for one person), &ldquo;therefore he had pursued his humour,&rdquo; etc. Collier
has with true judgment restored the above reading, but to his explanation of the
second &ldquo;most,&rdquo; as meaning &ldquo;most people,&rdquo; I cannot assent.
<P><SC>Del.</SC> Benvolio measured Romeo's inclinations by his own, which at that time
sought for some solitary spot where other people could not be found, because he him-
self, with his own wearisome <I>I,</I> appeared to be too much company, and followed his
own humour without pursuing Romeo's.
<P><SC>Sing</SC>. (ed. 2). It has been usual to place a comma after &ldquo;sought,&rdquo; but we must
understand: &ldquo;Which then most sought <I>the place</I> least frequented.&rdquo;
<P><SC>Huds</SC>. The meaning evidently is, that his disposition was to be in solitude, as he
could hardly endure even so much company as that of himself. The reading of Q<SUB>1</SUB>
has been strangely preferred by some modern editors.

<P><SC>Knt.</SC> We could scarcely wish to restore the old reading, even if the probability
of a typographical error, <I>same</I> for <I>sunne,</I> were not so obvious. [<I>Dyce.</I>
<P><SC>Sing.</SC> The lines quoted by Mal. from Daniel add great support to Theobald's
emendation. [<I>Corn.</I>
<P><SC>White</SC>. One of Theobald's happiest conjectures.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (&lquo;<I>Remarks,</I>&rquo; &amp;c. 1844, p. 167). Collier, who has taken the trouble to
chronicle a great many wretched conjectures, does not even mention Theobald's
emendation of the present passage&mdash;an emendation that has been adopted by Steev-
ens and by Knight, and which I have not the slightest doubt is the genuine
reading. Both <I>sun</I> and <I>son</I> were very frequently written <I>sunne</I> and <I>sonne,</I> and hence
were often mistaken for other words by the old compositors: See Collier's notes,
vol. v, 347, vi, 555. We also find in early books not a few passages in which
&ldquo;same&rdquo; is a misprint; so in <I>Troilus and Cressida,</I> II, ii, where the right reading is
undoubtedly &ldquo;sieve,&rdquo; the folio has &ldquo;<I>same.</I>&rdquo;
<P>Malone retained &ldquo;same&rdquo; in the present passage with the following note:
<P>&ldquo;In the last Act of this play our poet has evidently imitated the Rosamond of
Daniel; and in the present passage might have remembered the following lines in
one of the sonnets of the same writer, who was then extremely popular. These
lines, whether remembered by our author or not, add such support to Mr. Theobald's
emendation that I should have given it a place in my text, but that the other mode
of expression was not uncommon in Sh.'s time:
<BQ>
&lquo;And whilst thou <I>spread'st</I> unto the rising <I>sunne,</I><LB>
The fairest <I>flower</I> that ever saw the light,<LB>
Now joy thy time, before thy sweet be done.&rquo; <I>Daniel's Sonnets,</I> 1594.<LB>
</BQ>
<P>A similar phraseology to that of my text may be found in Daniel's 14th, 32d, 44th
and 53d sonnets.&rdquo; But the reading in the text receives no confirmation from what
Malone calls the &ldquo;similar phraseology&rdquo; of Daniel; for in every one of the passages
which he refers to it is evident that the words, &ldquo;<I>the same,</I>&rdquo; were forced upon the
poet by the necessity of the rhyme. Besides, Malone ought to have recollected that
though Daniel was often dreadfully flat, Sh. never was.
<P>[The late Mr. <SC>Lettsom</SC>, in a MS. marginal note in the copy of Dyce's &ldquo;Re-
marks,&rdquo; &amp;c., in the present editor's possession, says: &ldquo;Dyce himself, in his 2d ed.
of Peele, vol. ii, p. 8, l. 1, has printed <I>same</I> where the sense requires <I>sunne.</I>&rdquo;]

<P>The reason why <I>same</I> was so often reprinted, no doubt, was that until &ldquo;sun&rdquo; is pro-

<P><SC>Keightley</SC>. The correction of Theobald is so obvious and so natural that I had

<P>148. <B>Enter Romeo</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC>. The old edd. mark his entrance some lines earlier,
just as previously, in the present scene, they make Abraham and Balthasar, and also
Benvolio, enter too soon, and only because they followed the prompter's book, which
had the entrances so set down to show that the performers were to be in readiness
to appear on the stage. Again, in Act II, sc. iii, according to the old edd., Romeo
enters while the Friar has yet several lines of his soliloquy to utter. [Vide &lquo;<I>Re-
marks,</I>&rquo; &amp;c., p. 147.]
<P><SC>Coleridge</SC> (<I>Lit. Rem.,</I> vol. ii, p. 152, ed. 1836). If we are right, from internal
evidence, in pronouncing this one of Sh.'s early dramas, it affords a strong instance
of the fineness of his insight into the nature of the passions that Romeo is already
love-bewildered. The necessity of loving creates an object for itself in man and
woman; and yet there is a difference in this respect between the sexes, though only
to be known by a perception of it. It would have displeased us if Juliet had been
represented as already in love, or as fancying herself so; but no one, I believe, ever
experiences any shock at Romeo's forgetting his Rosaline (who had been a mere
name for the yearning of his youthful imagination) and rushing into his passion for
Juliet. Rosaline was a mere creature of his fancy, and we should remark the boast-
ful positiveness of Romeo in a love of his own making, which is never shown where
love is really near the heart. [<I>Verp. Huds.</I>
<P><SC>White</SC> (vol. i, p. ccxxx). What wonderful psychological knowledge has one of
Sh.'s later critics found in the bringing Romeo upon the scene enamoured of Rosa-
line, to have this passion supplanted by the purer and tenderer one for Juliet!
which, on the contrary, critics of the last century regarded as a great fault in the
amorous Veronese's character. But the truth, which these critics did not know, is,
that in this transfer of affection Sh. merely followed the novel and the poem to
which he went for his plot. There he found the incident of Romeo's earlier love;

<P>165. <B>pathways</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> Romeo laments that love, though blind, should discover

us fast, however much we would gladly escape or be free.&rdquo;

<P>168. <B>Here's much</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>. Romeo is speaking in the riddling mood now
upon him. He means that the fray has much to do with the hate between the rival
houses, yet affects him more, inasmuch as his Rosaline is of the Capulet family; that
what has just passed has had reference to the animosity which divides the two fac-
tions, and has also shown him the anxious affection felt on his account by his father
and Benvolio. To the latter he refers where he says, &ldquo;This love that thou hast
shown,&rdquo; &amp;c.
<P>169. <B>O brawling love</B>] <SC>Farmer</SC>. Every sonneteer characterized Love by con-

<BQ>
&ldquo;Love is a sowre delight, a sugred griefe,<LB>

<P>Turberville makes Reason harangue against it in the same manner:
<BQ>
&ldquo;A fierie frost, a flame that frozen is with ise,<LB>

</BQ>
<P>Immediately from The Romaunt of the Rose:
<BQ>
&ldquo;<I>Loue</I> it is an hateful pees,<LB>

<P>This kind of antithesis was very much to the taste of the Provencal and Italian
poets; perhaps it might be hinted by the Ode of Sappho preserved by Longinus.
Petrarch is full of it:
<BQ>
&ldquo;Pace non trovo e non ho da far guerra;<LB>
E temo, e spero, e ardo, e son un ghiaccio;<LB>

</BQ>
<P>Sir Thomas Wyatt translates this sonnet under the title of &ldquo;<I>Description of the Con-
trarious Passions in a Louer,</I>&rdquo; 1574. [<I>Sing. Knt. Verp. Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Huds.</SC> Such an affected way of speaking not unaptly shows the state of Romeo's
mind; his love is rather self-generated than inspired by any object. As compared
with his style of speech after meeting with Juliet, it serves to mark the difference
between <I>being love-sick</I> and <I>being in love.</I>
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. This is one of the subtle indications given by Sh. that Romeo is not
really in love with Rosaline.

<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2). [Printing 177 and 178 as three lines]. Since printing the text of
this play, I almost regret that I did not retain the usual arrangement. The passage,
however, may be right as it stands, for our early dramatists sometimes introduce
short rhyming lines in the midst of blank-verse dialogues, as in Love's Labour's Lost,
I, i, 126, 127.
<P><SC>Ktly.</SC> I make this insertion, &ldquo;gentle cousin,&rdquo; with confidence, for this is the only
speech in this play beginning with a short line not complementary to the end of a
preceding speech. In our poet's plays of this period, speeches never began with a
short line, unless when complementary, and at no time was the second line of a
couplet short. Lower down (I, v, 63), we have &ldquo;Content thee, <I>gentle coz,</I> let him
alone,&rdquo; where Q<SUB>1</SUB> omits all but &ldquo;let him alone.&rdquo;
<P>182. <B>too much</B>] <SC>Del.</SC> This is to be taken substantively as a compound word.

<P><SC>Del.</SC> <I>Purg'd</I> must be taken in connection with the preceding: when Love has
been purified from the fume of sighs [see l. 126] it becomes a fire, &amp;c. Thus un-
derstood, Johnson's emendation is unnecessary.
<P><SC>Huds.</SC> Johnson's change is a good one, if any were needed. Of course <I>purg'd</I>
is <I>purified.</I>
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> [Notes and Emend. p. 382]. Everybody is aware how a fire sometimes
sparkles in the eyes of those who blow it with their breath: the smoke is first
&ldquo;made&rdquo; by the gentle &ldquo;fume of sighs,&rdquo; and then caused to sparkle by being vio-

<P><SC>White</SC>. Surely the correctors must have failed to see the allusion to the passage
in the Gospels (Matt. iii, 12), &ldquo;whose <I>fan</I> is in his hand, and he will thoroughly
<I>purge</I> his floor.&rdquo; Sh. remembered the &ldquo;fan,&rdquo; and thought of the winnowing that
he had seen at Stratford, where we may be sure they were yet guiltless of the ma-
chine so sacrilegious in the eyes of <I>Mause Headrigg,</I> for raising wind for their ain
particular use by human art, instead of soliciting it by prayer, or waiting patiently
for a dispensation of wind. And doubtless he did not put his less than small Greck
to the task of teaching him that &ldquo;<G>diakaqaipe_i</G>,&rdquo; which is translated &ldquo;purge,&rdquo; refers to
the separation of purity from impurity, or that which is worthless from that which
has worth, by whatever process.

<P>187. <B>preserving</B>] <SC>Ulr.</SC> Sh., in his careless diction, ever delighting in popular
phrases, continually used the active and passive participles, each for the other, as
can be shown by many passages. He here intentionally uses &ldquo;preserving&rdquo; in the
place of &ldquo;preserved,&rdquo; merely for the sake of a play upon words, and to bring out the
contrast with &ldquo;choking gall.&rdquo; Love may be compared to a preserved sweet be-
cause, although against our will, it is kept and cherished.

<P>194. <B>tell me who</B>] <SC>Ktly.</SC> The words &ldquo;she is you love&rdquo; seem evidently to have

<P>203. <B>strong proof</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> As this play was written in the reign of Queen
Elizabeth, I cannot help regarding these speeches of Romeo as an oblique compli-
ment to her majesty, who was not liable to be displeased at hearing her chastity
praised after she was suspected to have lost it, or her beauty commended in the 67th
year of her age, though she never possessed any when she was young. Her decla-
ration that she would continue unmarried increases the probability of the present
supposition. [<I>Har. Sing.</I>

<P>204. <B>unharm'd</B>] <SC>Coll.</SC> (&lquo;<I>Notes and Emend.</I>&rquo;) The alteration required by the
(MS.) is only of a single letter, and by it a much more poetical turn is given to the
thought: She was magically <I>encharmed</I> from love's bow by chastity. Nobody will
deny that &ldquo;unharm'd&rdquo; (changed by Rowe from &ldquo;uncharm'd&rdquo; of Q<SUB>1</SUB>) is compara-
tively flat, poor and insignificant. This emendation cannot be doubted, since it ac-
cords almost exactly with the old copies, and obviously gives the sense of the author
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> Without doubt <I>encharm'd</I> is the right word, and, as it is also the more un-
usual word, was probably changed by the printer into <I>uncharm'd.</I>
<P><SC>White</SC> (&lquo;<I>Sh.'s Scholar</I>&rquo;). Rowe changed <I>uncharm'd</I> to <I>unharm'd.</I> Collier's &ldquo;en-
charm'd&rdquo; is much nearer the original text, and much better in every way. It will
hereafter take a place in the text without a question.
<P>Both <SC>Ulr.</SC> and <SC>Del.</SC> note that <I>unharm'd</I> is the reading of (Q<SUB>1</SUB>).
<P><SC>Huds.</SC> The reading of (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) and F<SUB>1</SUB>&mdash;<I>uncharmed</I>&mdash;gives a sense just the opposite
of that required.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 1). A writer in Blackwood's Maga., Oct. 1853, p. 454, thinks <I>un-
charm'd</I> of Qq and Ff may mean &ldquo;<I>disenchanted</I> from the power of love,&rdquo; &amp;c. I
cannot agree with him. Grant White would not, I apprehend, have said [as above]
if he had recollected that &ldquo;<I>unharm'd</I>&rdquo; is the reading of Q<SUB>1</SUB>, and not, as he, Collier,
and some others state, the conjectural alteration of Rowe.
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). [Repeats substantially the above from his &lquo;<I>Notes and Emend.,</I>&rquo;
and that Rowe altered <I>uncharm'd</I> to <I>unharm'd.</I>]
<P><SC>White</SC>. (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) has &ldquo;<I>'Gainst Cupid's</I> childish bow she lives <I>unharm'd,</I>&rdquo; which seems
a corrupt, or, at least, a much inferior, reading. The repetition of &ldquo;Cupid&rdquo; (avoided
in the later text) is unpleasant; and the use of &ldquo;unharm'd&rdquo; with &ldquo;against&rdquo; is infe-
licitous if not incorrect. If we read &ldquo;'gainst&rdquo; with (Q<SUB>1</SUB>), we might do well to read
&ldquo;she lives <I>encharm'd,</I>&rdquo; with Collier's (MS).
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2). Lettsom has suggested this same reading proposed by White.

<P><SC>Mason</SC>. Romeo means to say that she is poor because she leaves no part of her
store behind her, as with her all beauty will die. [<I>Sing.</I> (ed. 1), <I>Huds. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Mal.</SC> She is <I>rich</I> in beauty; and <I>poor,</I> in this circumstance alone, that with her
beauty will expire. Her <I>store</I> of wealth, which the poet has already said was the
fairness of her person, will not be transmitted to posterity, inasmuch as she will
&ldquo;lead her graces to the grave and leave the world no copy.&rdquo; [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Mal.</SC> also cites Sh.'s 3d Sonnet and Venus and Adonis, 757, 759. [<I>Corn.</I>
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> The meaning of this somewhat complex passage seems to be: She is rich
in the possession of unequalled beauty, but poor, because having devoted herself to
chastity, when she dies her wealth, that is beauty, dies with her. The same conceit
occurs repeatedly in Sh.'s poems:
<BQ>
&ldquo;From fairest creatures we desire increase,<LB>
That thereby <I>beauty's rose might never die.</I>&rdquo; [<I>Sonnet</I> 1.<LB>
&ldquo;Then how, when Nature calls thee to be gone,<LB>
What acceptable audit canst thou leave?<LB>
<I>Thy unus'd beauty must be tomb'd with thee,</I><LB>

</BQ>
<P>See also Sonnets 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 11, 12, 13, and 14.
<P><SC>White</SC>. Romeo means to say that his mistress is only poor in that, at her death,
her store&mdash;<I>i. e.</I> the beauty that she is rich in&mdash;will die with her, and that so her
chief wealth is a possession that she cannot bequeath.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2). &ldquo;The sense required, as is clear from Benvolio's rejoinder, and
even from Malone's note, in which he defends the old reading, is that her beauty
dies with <I>her;</I> but this sense cannot be squeezed out of the old text; therefore
Theobald's conjecture is necessary.&rdquo; <SC>Lettsom</SC>.
<P><SC>Keightley</SC>. The plain meaning of this is that beauty was &ldquo;her store;&rdquo; she had
nothing but it; poor praise indeed from a lover. I would read with Theobald. . . .
The same idea is expressed in the poet's first and following Sonnets: in Venus and
Adonis we have, &ldquo;For he being dead, with him is beauty slain.&rdquo; See also Twelfth
Night, I, v.
<P>212. <B>starved</B>] <SC>Sing.</SC> (ed. 2). All the old copies have <I>sterv'd,</I> which has been

desirable if not necessary. The word occurs in the poem of Romeus and Juliet:

<I>perished,</I> die out.&rdquo;

<P>223. <B>These happy masks</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> <I>I. e.,</I> the masks worn by female spectators
of the play. [<I>Sing.</I> (ed. 1), &ldquo;probably, unless&rdquo; Malone be right. <I>Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Mal.</SC> <I>These</I> happy masks, I believe, means no more than <I>the</I> happy masks. Such
is Tyrwhitt's opinion.
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> It seems scarcely necessary to limit the use of masks to the female specta-
tors of the play. In the Two Gentlemen of Verona we have the &ldquo;sun-expelling
mask.&rdquo; In Love's Labour's Lost the ladies wear masks in the first interview between
the king and the princess: &ldquo;Now fair befall your mask,&rdquo; says Biron to Rosaline.
<P><SC>Del.</SC> Such masks as the ladies of Sh.'s time were wont to wear when they went
out in the street.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2) [in a note on Mea. for Mea. II, iv, 79]. As to &ldquo;<SC>these</SC> <I>black
masks,</I>&rdquo; Tyrwhitt, in his earlier days, conjectured that Sh. alluded to &ldquo;the masks of
the audience when the play was acted at court;&rdquo; but he afterwards repudiated that
most extravagant conjecture. &ldquo;My notion at present,&rdquo; he says, &ldquo;is that the phrase,
<I>these black masks,</I> signifies nothing more than <I>black masks,</I> according to an old idiom
of our language, by which the demonstrative pronoun is put for the prepositive arti-
cle.&rdquo; So we have in the present play [Mea. for Mea.], IV, i, 59: &ldquo;volumes of
report Run with <I>these</I> false and most contrarious quests.&rdquo; And compare Webster,
<I>The Duchess of Malfi,</I> V, ii:
<BQ>
&ldquo;We that are great women of pleasure use to cut off<LB>
<I>These</I> uncertain wishes and unquiet longings<LB>
And in an instant join the sweet delight<LB>
And the pretty excuse together.&rdquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>(I cannot but feel surprised that Tyrwhitt's discarded conjecture, about <I>these masks</I>
meaning the masks of the audience, should have been brought forward by Halliwell
as a probable one, and that he should conceive it to be supported by a passage (to
which he only refers) at the conclusion of Fletcher's <I>Beggar's Bush,</I> where Higgen,
<I>speaking the epilogue,</I> says to the &ldquo;ladies,&rdquo; &ldquo;If you be pleas'd, look cheerly, throw
your eyes Out at your masks.&rdquo;)
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. The masks usually worn, and happy in being privileged to touch the
sweet countenances beneath. &ldquo;These&rdquo; is here used to instance a general obser-
vation.
<P>224. <B>Being black put us</B>] <SC>White</SC>. The old copies, &ldquo;<I>puts</I> us in mind,&rdquo; and, I
have little doubt, correctly; for, aside from other reasons for reading &ldquo;<I>puts,</I>&rdquo; I am
inclined to think that Sh. and his contemporaries regarded &ldquo;being black&rdquo; and not
&ldquo;masks&rdquo; as the nominative to &ldquo;put.&rdquo; I do not, however, feel sufficiently assured
of the point to change the received text.

<P>13. <B>made</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> Puttenham, <I>Art of Poesy,</I> 1589, uses this expression, which
seems to be proverbial, as an instance of a figure which he calls the Rebound:
&ldquo;The maid that <I>soon married</I> is, <I>soon marred</I> is.&rdquo; The jingle between <I>marr'd</I> and
<I>made</I> is likewise frequent among the old writers. So Sidney: &ldquo;Oh! he is marr'd,
that is for others made!&rdquo; Spenser uses it very often. [<I>Sing. Huds. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Sing.</SC> (ed. 2) to the foregoing citations adds:
<BQ>
&ldquo;You're to be <I>marr'd</I> or <I>marryed,</I> as they say,<LB>

<P><SC>White</SC>. In printing Q<SUB>2</SUB> the compositor seems to have been misled by the exist-
ence of a jingling adage similar to that in <I>All's Well,</I> and perhaps by &ldquo;made&rdquo; at
the end of the previous line.
<P>The quibble here (All's Well, II, iii, 315) is just worth noticing because it de-
pends upon the same sound of the <I>a</I> in both words, and the full pronunciation of
the participial <I>ed</I> in both when the play was written. The contraction of the last,
for rhyme's sake, would not destroy the little joke for an ear accustomed to the full
sound of both words.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC>. Sh. has this jingle several times. So in this present play, II, iv, 103, and in
Macbeth II, iii, 28; and, as Paris has used the word &ldquo;<I>made,</I>&rdquo; it appears to me most
natural that Capulet, in his rejoinder, should use &ldquo;<I>made</I>&rdquo; also.

<P>15. <B>lady of my earth</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> A Gallicism: <I>Fille de terre</I> is the French phrase
for an heiress. [<I>Sing. Knt. Huds. Sta. White, Dyce.</I>] <I>Earth</I> in other old plays is
likewise put for <I>lands, i. e.,</I> landed estate. [<I>Sing.</I> (ed. 1), <I>Huds.</I>
<P><SC>M. Mason</SC>. Here <I>earth</I> means <I>corporal part.</I> [<I>Sing.</I> (ed. 1). <I>Sta.</I> &ldquo;it may
be so.&rdquo;
<P><SC>Mal.</SC> Again in this play, II, i, 2. Again, in Sh.'s 146th Sonnet. &ldquo;Poor soul, the
centre of my sinful earth.&rdquo; [<I>Sing. Knt. Sta.</I>
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> That is, she is the hopeful mistress of my world, my life; not, as Steevens
has it, of my landed estate, nor as Knight, with Mason and Malone, thinks, of my
&ldquo;body.&rdquo;
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2). Lettsom suspects that the close of this line is corrupt.
<P><SC>Ktly.</SC> Here a rime is lost in consequence of the first line being in the printer's
mind. There can be little question, I should think, that the original word was not
&ldquo;earth&rdquo; but <I>fee,</I> feud, fief, landed property, as in <I>Knight's fee, in fee,</I> &amp;c., with
which alone &ldquo;lady&rdquo; accords.
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. It is most likely that Capulet intends to include the sense of &ldquo;she is
my sole surviving offspring, in whom I have centred all my hopes.&rdquo;
<P>17. <B>her consent</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> <I>To,</I> in this instance, signifies <I>in comparison with, in
proportion to.</I> [<I>Sing.</I> (ed. 1), <I>Knt.</I>
<P><SC>Del.</SC> This is hardly as Steevens explains it, but it is simply dependent upon &ldquo;a
part&rdquo;&mdash;my will is only a part of her consent, belongs to her consent. The two suc-
ceeding verses more fully explain this meaning.
<P>20. <B>old accustomed</B>] <SC>S. Walker</SC> (&lquo;<I>Crit.</I>&rquo; vol. I, p. 38) cites these words as one
of his examples under <I>Art.</I> II. Passages of Sh. in which a compound epithet or
participle (or a double substantive) has been resolved into two simple epithets or an
adverb and an epithet, &amp;c.
<P>20. <B>feast</B>] <SC>Knt.</SC> In Romeus and Juliet the season of Capulet's feast is winter:
<BQ>
&ldquo;The wery winter's nightes restore the Christmas games,<LB>

Sparth for no cost, the wonted use of banquets to begyn.&rdquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>Sh. had, perhaps, this in his mind when, at the ball, old Capulet cries out, &ldquo;And
quench the fire, the room is grown too hot.&rdquo; But in every other instance the season
is unquestionably summer. &ldquo;The day is hot,&rdquo; says Benvolio. The Friar is up in

<P>25. <B>dark heaven light</B>] <SC>Warb.</SC> This nonsense should be reformed thus: &ldquo;dark
<I>even</I> light,&rdquo; <I>i. e.,</I> When the evening is dark and without stars, these earthly stars
supply their place and light it up. [<I>Knt.</I>
<P><SC>M. Mason</SC>. I propose, &ldquo;dark, <I>heaven's</I> light,&rdquo; <I>i. e. earthly stars</I> that outshine the
stars of heaven and make them appear dark by their own superior brightness. [<I>Knt.
Sing.</I> (ed. 2), &ldquo;an ingenious emendation.&rdquo;
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> It appears unnecessary to alter the original reading, and especially as pas-
sages in the masquerade scene would seem to indicate that the banqueting room
opened into a garden, as &ldquo;Her beauty hangs upon <I>the cheek of night.</I>&rdquo; [<I>Sta.</I>
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> A better reason for abiding by the original text is to consider that the &ldquo;dark
heaven&rdquo; in Sh.'s mind was most probably the <I>Heaven</I> of the stage, hung, as was the
custom during the performance of tragedy, with black.
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. As poetical hyperbole may it not bear the excellent sense of &ldquo;mortal
ladies, brilliant as stars that make night as bright as day?&rdquo;
<P>26. <B>lusty young men</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>. To say, and to say in pompous words, that a
<I>young man shall feel</I> as much in an assembly of beauties <I>as young men feel in the
month of April</I> is surely to waste sound upon a very poor sentiment. I read &ldquo;lusty
<I>yeomen.</I>&rdquo; You shall feel, from the sight and conversation of these ladies, such hopes
of happiness and such pleasure, as the farmer receives from the spring, when the
plenty of the year begins, and the prospect of the harvest fills him with delight.
[<I>Huds.,</I> substantially.

printed by Wynken de Worde, where &ldquo;<I>yonge men</I>&rdquo; occurs four times, it is in each
instance <I>yeomen</I> in Copland's edition printed not many years after. See also Spel-
man's Glossary, <I>voce</I> <SC>Juniores</SC>. It is no less singular, that in a subsequent act of
this very play the old copies should, in two places, read &ldquo;<I>young trees</I>&rdquo; and &ldquo;<I>young
tree,</I>&rdquo; instead of &ldquo;<I>yew-trees</I>&rdquo; and &ldquo;<I>yew-tree.</I>&rdquo; [<I>Sing.</I>

<P>The old folio gives no help. I can offer nothing better than <I>Within your view.</I>
[<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Mal.</SC> There is here an allusion to an old proverbial expression, that <I>one</I> is no
number. So in Decker's Honest Whore, Part II: &ldquo;&mdash;&mdash;to fall to <I>one . . .</I> is to fall
to none, For one no number is.&rdquo; In Sh.'s 136th Sonnet: &ldquo;Among a number <I>one is
reckon'd none.</I>&rdquo; [<I>Sing.</I> (ed. 1), <I>Verp. Huds.</I>
<P><SC>M. Mason</SC>. This passage will not be rendered intelligible by Steevens's conj.,
which is neither sense nor English. The old folio leads us to the right reading,
which I should suppose to have been thus: &ldquo;<I>Whilst on</I> more view of many,&rdquo; &amp;c.
With this alteration the sense is clear, and the deviation from the folio very trifling.
[&ldquo;Only the change of &lquo;ch&rquo; to &lquo;<I>lst,</I>&rquo;&rdquo; adds <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2), who adopts Mason's conj.]
<P><SC>Sing.</SC> (ed. 1). Hear all, see all, and like her most who has the most merit; <I>her,</I>
which, after attentively regarding the many, my daughter being one, may stand
<I>unique</I> in merit, though she may be reckoned nothing, or held in no estimation.
[<I>Huds.</I>] <I>Which</I> is here used for <I>who,</I> a substitution frequent in Sh., as in all the
writers of his time. [<I>Verp.</I>
<P><SC>Del.</SC> (Lexikon). Sh. here uses <I>which</I> in the loose relative connection peculiar to
him, by which the relative pronoun does not refer to a certain antecedent word, but
refers the whole related sentence to the sentence preceding.
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> This explanation [of Delius'] I find as difficult to understand as the words
themselves. Under these circumstances I have turned back to the reading of Q<SUB>1</SUB>,
holding the readings of the other copies for misprints or compositors' sophistications,
and I have allowed myself to introduce an emendation into the text, which, in my
opinion, gives a perfectly clear sense, and can hardly be termed a change of the
text, as it consists only in transposing the first two words. Such a transposition
seems always justifiable where the sense requires it, as misprints of this kind, in the
very negligent printing of all the old edd., are very numerous.
<P><SC>Badham</SC> (&lquo;<I>Cam. Essays,</I>&rquo; 1856). The cause of all this confusion is, that the read-
ing of Q<SUB>1</SUB>, being unintelligible, was altered in the subsequent Qq, and that alteration
was adopted by the folio. The faulty word was left untouched, and the sound parts
were corrupted by the editor of Q<SUB>2</SUB>, who did not see that the right reading was,
&ldquo;such amongst <I>few.</I>&rdquo;
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> Neither reading [of Qq. nor Ff.] affords a clear sense.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 1). The later edd. are not more intelligible than Q<SUB>1</SUB>.
<P><SC>White</SC>. The passage is obscure, elliptical, and debased by a poor conceit; but,
remembering that <I>one</I> used to be regarded as no number, it seems to mean, Such
(<I>i. e.,</I> so high in merit) my daughter may appear; and being one (of those so distin-
guished) may stand, in number, one, though, in reckoning, nothing.

<P>50. <B>plantain leaf</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> This was a blood-stauncher, and was formerly ap-
plied to green wounds. The same thought occurs in Albumazar: &ldquo;Bring a fresh
<I>plantain leaf,</I> I've broke my shin.&rdquo; [<I>Sing. Coll. Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> Of course Sh. did not allude to the tropical fruit-bearing plant, but to the
common plantain of our English marshy grounds and ditches. The plantain was
also considered as a preventive of poison, and to this supposed virtue Romeo first
alludes.
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> Costard calls for it in Love's L. L., III, i, 74.
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> Romeo means, Thy remedy is as excellent for my complaint as a plantain
leaf is for a broken shin. Plantain was used to stop the blood, but not for a fracture
of a bone, to which such a remedy obviously cannot apply. Hence, when Costard,
in L. L. L., calls for a plantain leaf for his broken shin, or a fellow in Ben Jonson's
&ldquo;The Case is Altered,&rdquo; wants it for a broken head, it is, I think, in the same ironical

<P>tense as here. If Romeo, as the English commentators suppose, really considered
plantain a good remedy for a broken bone, his words would have no sense.
<P><SC>Beisly</SC>. (<I>Plantago major</I>) greater plantain. The leaves were, in Sh.'s time, used
to heal fresh wounds, and the village herbalists now use them for the same purpose.
The plant grows near the abodes of men, and commonly by waysides; hence it ob-
tained the common name of &ldquo;way-bread.&rdquo;
<P>Bartholom&aelig;us speaks of it as &ldquo;healing sore wounds, and biting of wood houndes,
and abateth the swelling thereof.&rdquo; And Drayton, in &ldquo;Polyolbion,&rdquo; has &ldquo;Plaintain
for a sore.&rdquo; Knight's note is not correct, as the plant grows on waysides and mostly
in dry places. The water plantain (<I>Alisma plantago</I>) grows in ditches and moist
places, but this is not the plant Sh. alluded to. The figure of the plant given by
Knight is unlike the common plantain.
<P><SC>Cham.</SC> The buck's-horn plantain.
<P>55. <B>Good-den</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>. A mere corruption of <I>good e'en</I> for good evening. This
salutation was used by our ancestors as soon as noon was past, after which time, good
morrow, or good day, was esteemed improper. [<I>Vide post</I> II, iv, 99.] [<I>Dyce.</I>
<P>61. <B>rest you merry</B>] <SC>Del.</SC> He supposes Romeo to be a jester, from whom no
rational answer is to be expected, and is about to leave him.

<P>In The Two Angry Women of Abington, 1599: &ldquo;Fill the pot, hostess, &amp;c., and

both read &ldquo;to fire&rdquo; (or fier). The mere difference of a final <I>s</I> seems not to have
been regarded in rhyme in Sh.'s day, and the reading &ldquo;fires&rdquo; tends to impoverish a
line not over-rich.
