<P>94. <B>lady's love</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>. But the comparison was not to be betwixt the
Love that Romeo's Mistress paid him and the Person of any other young Woman:
but betwixt Romeo's Mistress herself and some other that should be match'd against
her. The Poet, therefore, must certainly have wrote, &ldquo;Your Lady-love.&rdquo;
<P><SC>Heath</SC>. That is, the love you bear to your lady, which, in our language, is com-
monly used for the lady herself. [<I>Sing. Huds. Dyce.</I>
<P><SC>Sing.</SC> Perhaps we should read <I>Your lady love.</I> [<I>Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (&ldquo;<I>Remarks,</I>&rdquo; &amp;c). To me, at least, this explanation (Heath's) is unsatis-
factory: qy. did Sh. write &ldquo;<I>Your</I> lady-love?&rdquo;
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> After all, the misprint may be in the word <I>love,</I> and perhaps instead thereof
we should read <I>look,</I> or <I>laud.</I>
<P><SC>Walker</SC> (&ldquo;<I>Crit.</I>&rdquo; vol. I, p. 255). How can <I>your lady's love</I> mean anything but
<I>your lady's passion for you?</I> which would here be contrary to the fact as well as to
the speaker's meaning. Read your <I>ladie-love;</I> and so I find Dyce suggests.
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> A corruption, I suspect, for &ldquo;lady-love.&rdquo; It was not Romeo's love for
Rosaline, nor hers for him, which was to be poised, but the lady herself, &ldquo;against
some other maid.&rdquo;
<P><SC>White</SC>. It seems as if we should read &ldquo;<I>lady-love</I>&rdquo; here; and this obvious change
has been suggested by Dyce and Singer, and declared absolutely necessary by S.
Walker. But the imperfect and surreptitious (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) has &ldquo;<I>ladyes loue,</I>&rdquo; and the subse-
quent old copies, though printed from another MS., &ldquo;<I>ladies loue.</I>&rdquo; Sh. too, often as
he had opportunity, never used &ldquo;lady-love,&rdquo; if I may trust my memory, or even
Mrs. Clarke's Concordance. And I more than doubt that the compound &ldquo;lady-love&rdquo;
is as old as the time of Sh., although I believe the general opinion is quite the
contrary.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2). I did not know that this was Theobald's reading when I proposed

<P>But it certainly is. Compare Wilson's <I>Coblers Prophesie,</I> 1594: &ldquo;then downe came

<P><SC>Ktly.</SC> This is very oddly expressed, for it was the lady herself, not her love, that
was to be weighed. I doubt if Theobald's phrase was then in use. I read &ldquo;<I>lady
and love,</I>&rdquo; the <I>&amp;</I> of the MS. having been made <I>s</I> by the printer, as it became <I>t</I> in
&ldquo;meant&rdquo; for &ldquo;mean <I>and</I>&rdquo; in All's Well, IV, iii.
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. It is possible that this may mean &ldquo;the small amount of love borne you
by your lady.&rdquo; Romeo has before told Benvolio that &ldquo;she hath forsworn to love,&rdquo;
and it may be that, in Sh.'s elliptical style, the passage means, &ldquo;let there be weighed
the little love your lady bears you against the charms of some other maid,&rdquo; &amp;c.
<P>2. <B>Nurse</B>] <SC>Coleridge</SC> (<I>Lit. Rem.</I> vol. II, p. 152, ed. 1836). The character of
the Nurse is the nearest thing in Sh. to a direct borrowing from mere observation;
and the reason is, that as in infancy and childhood the individual in nature is a
representative of a class&mdash;just as in describing one larch tree you generalize a grove
of them&mdash;so it is nearly as much so in old age. The generalization is done to the
poet's hand. Here you have the garrulity of age strengthened by the feelings of a
long-trusted servant, whose sympathy with the mother's affections gives her privi-
leges and rank in the household. And observe the mode of connection by accident
of time and place, and the childlike fondness of repetition in a second childhood,
and also that happy, humble ducking under, yet constant resurgence against, the
check of her superiors. [<I>Verp. Huds. Sta.</I>
<P>3. <B>lady-bird</B>] <SC>Del.</SC> The nurse does not apply this epithet to Juliet in the insult-
ing sense in which the term is now applied by the vulgar, but sportively, in allusion
to her fluttering hither and thither, and because she will not allow herself to be at
once found when called.

<P>4. <B>God forbid!</B>] <SC>Sta.</SC> An exquisite touch of nature. The old nurse, in her

<P>15. <B>Lammas-tide</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>. <I>Tide</I> for <I>time.</I> It was also scrupulously used by the
Puritans, in composition, instead of the Popish word <I>mass,</I> of which they had a ner-
vous abhorrence. Thus, they said Christ<I>-tide,</I> Hallow<I>-tide,</I> Lamb<I>-tide.</I> Luckily
Whitsuntide was rightly named to their hands.
<P>16. <B>Even</B>] <SC>Knt.</SC> There is not in all Sh. a passage in which the rhythm is more
happily characteristic than in these speeches of the nurse. [<I>Verp.</I>
<P>23. <B>since the earthquake</B>] <SC>Tyrwhitt</SC>. How comes the Nurse to talk of an
earthquake? There is no such circumstance mentioned in any of the novels from
which Sh. drew his story; it therefore seems probable that he had in view the earth-
quake which had really been felt in many parts of England in his own time, viz., on
the 6th of April, 1580. (See Stowe's Chronicle and Gabriel Harvey's Letter in the
Preface to Spenser's Works, ed. 1679.) If so, one may be permitted to conjecture
that this play, or this part of it, at least, was written in 1591, after the 6th of April,
when the <I>eleven years since the earthquake</I> were completed, and not later than the
middle of July, <I>a fortnight and odd days</I> before <I>Lammas-tide.</I> [<I>Sing.,</I> substantially.
<I>Corn.</I>
<P><SC>Mal.</SC> (Vol. II, p. 350). Sh.'s frequent allusions to the manners and events of his
own time have shown me that Tyrwhitt's conj. is not so improbable as I once
thought it. Sh. might have laid the foundation of this play in 1591 and finished it
at a subsequent period. If the earthquake, which happened in England in 1580,
was in his thoughts and induced him to state the earthquake at Verona as happening
on the day when Juliet was <I>weaned,</I> and <I>eleven</I> years before the commencement of
the piece, it has led him into a contradiction; for, according to the Nurse, Juliet was
within a fortnight and odd days of completing her <I>fourteenth</I> year; and yet, accord-

<P>ing to the computation, she could not well be much more than <I>twelve</I> years old.
Whether, indeed, the English earthquake was or was not in his thoughts, the Nurse's
account is inconsistent and contradictory. Perhaps Sh. was more careful to mark
the garrulity than the precision of the old woman; or perhaps he meant this very
incorrectness as a trait of character; or, without having recourse to either of these
suppositions, shall we say that he was here, as in some other places, hasty and inat-
tentive?
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> The principle of dating from an earthquake, or from any other remarkable
phenomenon, is a very obvious one. We have an example as old as the days of the
prophet Amos: &ldquo;The words of Amos, who was among the herdmen of Tekoa,
which he saw concerning Israel, in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the
days of Jeroboam, the son of Joash, king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.&rdquo;
But it is by no means improbable that Sh. might have been acquainted with some
description of the great earthquake which happened at Verona in 1348, when Pe-
trarch was sojourning in that city; and that, with something like historical propriety,
therefore, he made the Nurse date from that event, while at the same time the sup-
posed allusion to the earthquake in England in 1580 would be relished by his au-
dience.
<P><SC>Collier</SC> (ed. 1). In the whole speech of the Nurse there are such discrepancies
as render it impossible to arrive at any definite conclusion, even if we suppose that
Sh. intended a reference to a particular earthquake in England. First, the Nurse
tells us that Juliet was in the course of being weaned; then that she could stand
alone; and, thirdly, that she could run alone. It would have been rather extraordi-
nary if she could not, for even according to the Nurse the child was very nearly
three years old. No fair inference can, therefore, be drawn from the expression,
and we coincide with Malone that the tragedy was probably written towards the
close of 1596.
<P><SC>Hunter</SC> (&ldquo;<I>New Illustr.</I>&rdquo;). It will not be denied that Sh. might make an Italian
in an Italian story allude to an event that occurred in London; but the whole argu-
ment is of the most shadowy kind, and it seems to be entirely destroyed when the
fact is introduced that in 1570 there did occur a most remarkable earthquake in the
neighborhood of Verona, so severe that it destroyed Ferrara, and which would form
long after an epoch in the chronological calculations of the old wives of Lombardy.
When the church of St. Stephen at Ferrara was rebuilt, an inscription was placed
against it, from which we may collect the terrible nature of the visitation:
<P>&ldquo;Cum anno M.D.LXX die XVII Novembris terti&acirc; noctis hor&acirc;, quam maximus terr&aelig; motus
hanc pr&aelig;clarissimam urbem ita conquassasset, ut ejus fortissima m&oelig;nia, munitissimas arces, alta pala-
tia, religiosa templa, sacratas turres, omnesque fere &aelig;des omnino evertisset et prostrasset, una cum
maximo civium damno, atque acerb&acirc; clade.&rdquo;
<P>The order of towers, palaces and temples in this inscription corresponds to the order
in which they occur in the well-known passage in <I>The Tempest.</I> Will this come in
aid of the argument of those who contend that Sh. must, at some period of his life,
have breathed the air of Italy, seen the Italian palaces and witnessed the Italian
customs he has so accurately exhibited?

<P><SC>Sta.</SC> There is a small tract still extant, entitled &ldquo;A coppie of the letter sent from
Ferrara the xxii of November, 1570. Imprinted at London in Paules Churchyarde at
the signe of the Lucrece, by Thomas Purfoote;&rdquo; in which the writer describes &ldquo;the
great and horrible earthquakes, the excessiue and vnrecouerable losses, with the
greate mortalitie and death of people, the ruine and ouerthrowe of an infinite num-
ber of monasteries, pallaces, and other howses, and the destruction of his graces ex-
cellencies castle.&rdquo; The first earthquake was on Thursday, the 11th, at ten at night,
&ldquo;whiche endured the space of an Aue Marie;&rdquo; on the 17th, &ldquo;the earth quaked all
the whole day.&rdquo; In all, &ldquo;the earthquakes are numbered to haue been a hundred
and foure in xl houres.&rdquo;
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. That Sh. alluded to the earthquake of 1580 we think most probable;
but that the allusion particularizes the period when the event occurred in connection
with the writing of the play, we doubt. Sh. would not, we think, thus register a
particular so subject to fluctuation as a date; for what would be an eleven years'
interval when he wrote might become a twelve years' interval when the play was
put upon the stage, and would certainly become an altogether inaccurate interval by
the time the play had been performed during many seasons. It appears to us that
the &ldquo;eleven years&rdquo; in this line is simply a step by which the old Nurse helps herself
to retrace the age of her foster-child.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2). If it be unlikely, as I think it is, that our poet had a view to the
earthquake in his own country during 1580, it is still more unlikely that he should
have alluded to that in Italy during 1570.

<P>26. <B>wormwood</B>] <SC>Halliwell</SC>. &ldquo;Like as when a mother, willing to weane her

thou art growne great inough, and I am with child, my milke is corrupt, it will
make thee sicke;&rquo; yet he is so fond of the breast that he cannot forsake it: but if the
mother put <I>worme-wood or mustard</I> upon the breast, the child sucking it, and feeling
the bitternesse, he quite forsaketh it, without sucking any more: Even so, though
God's Preachers preach unto us, and exhort us to forsake the corrupt milke of the
world and of the flesh, yet we seeme deaf still, and are alwayes backward, untill
God put upon these cursed teates the mustard and worme-wood of afflictions to
weane us.&rdquo;&mdash;<I>Cawdray's Treasurie or Storehouse of Similies,</I> 1600. Also <I>Stephens'
Essayes and Characters,</I> 1615.
<P><SC>Beisly</SC>. Wormwood (<I>Artemisia absinthium</I>) is a well-known plant, native of
Britain, and flowers in Aug. and Sept. It has a nauseous, bitter taste.

<P>72. <B>these years</B>] <SC>Sta.</SC> In the old poem Juliet's age is set down at sixteen; in
Paynter's novel at eighteen. As Sh. makes his heroine only fourteen, if the words
&ldquo;<I>your</I> mother,&rdquo; which is the reading of the old editions, be correct, Lady Capulet
would be eight and twenty; while her husband, having done masking some thirty
years, must be at least threescore. Knight veils the disparity, and perhaps improves
the passage, but we believe without authority.

means a man of puberty, &ldquo;a proper man.&rdquo; &rquo; It seems inconceivable that Dr. Ingleby
should have so grossly misunderstood these words in Romeo and Juliet.
<P>I add a passage which is decisive as to the true meaning of &ldquo;<I>a man of wax:</I>&rdquo;
<BQ>
&ldquo;A sweet face, an exceeding daintie hand;<LB>
<I>A body, were it framed of wax</I><LB>
<I>By all the cunning artists of the world,</I><LB>
<I>It could not better be proportioned.</I>&rdquo;&mdash;<I>Faire Em.,</I> &amp;c., sig. B, ed. 1631<LB>
</BQ>
<P>79. <B>What say you</B>] [This speech <SC>Pope</SC> pronounces &ldquo;ridiculous,&rdquo; and <SC>Steev.</SC>
&ldquo;stuff.&rdquo; <SC>Sing.</SC> repeated Steevens's epithet in (ed. 1), but recalled it in (ed. 2)].
<P><SC>Knight</SC>. This passage furnishes a very remarkable example of the correctness of
the principle laid down in Whiter's very able tract: &ldquo;An Attempt to explain and
illustrate various Passages of Sh. on a new Principle of Criticism, derived from
Locke's Doctrine of the Association of Ideas,&rdquo; wherein the leading doctrine, as ap-
plied to Sh., is, that the exceeding warmth of his imagination often supplied him,
by the power of association, with words, and with ideas, suggested to the mind by a
principle of union unperceived by himself, and independent of the subject to which
they are applied. We readily agree with Whiter that &ldquo;this propensity in the mind
to associate subjects so remote in their meaning, and so heterogeneous in their
nature, must, of necessity, sometimes deceive the ardour of the writer into whimsical
or ridiculous combinations. As the reader, however, is not blinded by this fascinat-
ing principle, which, while it creates the association, conceals likewise its effects,
he is instantly impressed with the quaintness, or the absurdity, of the imagery, and
is inclined to charge the writer with the intention of a foolish quibble or an imperti-
nent allusion.&rdquo; It is in this spirit of a cold and literal criticism, here so well de-
scribed, that Monck Mason pronounces upon the passage before us,&mdash;&ldquo;this ridiculous
speech is full of abstruse quibbles.&rdquo; But the principle of association, as explained
by Whiter, at once reconciles us to the quibbles. The &ldquo;volume&rdquo; of young Paris's
face suggests the &ldquo;beauty's pen,&rdquo; which hath &ldquo;writ&rdquo; there. Then, the obscurities of
the fair &ldquo;volume&rdquo; are written in the &ldquo;margin of his eyes,&rdquo; as comments of ancient
books are always printed in the margin. Lastly, this &ldquo;book of love&rdquo; lacks &ldquo;a
cover;&rdquo; the &ldquo;golden story&rdquo; must be locked with &ldquo;golden clasps.&rdquo; The ingenious
management of the vein of imagery is, at least, as remarkable as its &ldquo;abstruse
quibbles.&rdquo;

<P>83. <B>married lineament</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> Examine how nicely one feature depends
upon another, or accords with another, in order to produce that harmony of the
whole face which seems to be implied in the word <I>content.</I> In <I>Tro. and Cress.</I> we
have &ldquo;the <I>married</I> calm of states,&rdquo; and in the 8th Sonnet the same allusion:
<BQ>
&ldquo;If the true concord of well-tuned sounds,<LB>
By unions <I>married,</I> do offend thine ear.&rdquo;&mdash;[<I>Sing.</I> (ed. 1), <I>Huds.</I><LB>

<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> In my opinion, the prosaic <I>several</I> would be decidedly preferable to the
hyper-poetical and far-fetched &ldquo;<I>married</I>&rdquo; (especially as the thought that the features
were in harmony is distinctly expressed in the next verse), if the whole speech of
Lady Capulet were not so full of plays upon words and strained comparisons. That
Sh. puts in the mouth of Juliet's mother such, so called, Euphuisms is certainly not
without a deep design. She is distinguished by the style and matter of her speech
as a highly cultivated, but in truth an artificial, woman of the world of that day, of
considerable address, but without feeling, without heart or soul, who thinks more
of fashionable elegance of manners, social advantage, &amp;c., than of true inner worth,
and is, therefore, more devoted to the world than to the care and education of her
daughter.
<P><SC>Del.</SC> The epithet, &ldquo;<I>married,</I>&rdquo; anticipates too forcibly the succeeding line. The
blending together, emphasized in the succeeding verse, stands in more marked con-
trast by the use of &ldquo;<I>several</I>&rdquo; than by the use of &ldquo;<I>married.</I>&rdquo;
<P>86. <B>margent</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> The comments on ancient books were always printed in
the margin. So Horatio, in Hamlet, says: &ldquo;I knew you must be edified by the
<I>margent,</I>&rdquo; &amp;c. [<I>Sing. Haz. Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Mal.</SC> So in the Rape of Lucrece:
<BQ>
&ldquo;But she that never cop'd with stranger eyes<LB>
Could pick no meaning from their parling looks,<LB>
Nor read the subtle shining secrecies<LB>
Writ in the glassy <I>margent</I> of such <I>books.</I>&rdquo;&mdash;[<I>Sing. Huds. Sta.</I><LB>
</BQ>
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> Sh. was evidently fond of resembling the face to a book, and having once
arrived at this similitude, the comparison, however odd, of the eyes to the margin
wherein of old the commentary on the text was printed is not altogether unnatural.
This passage, which presents both the primary and subordinate metaphor, is the best
example he has given of this peculiar association of ideas.

<P>3. <B>such prolixity</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>. That is, <I>masks</I> are now out of fashion. That
Sh. was an enemy to these fooleries, appears from his writing none; and that his
plays discredited them is more than probable. [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Steev.</SC> The diversion going forward at present is not a <I>masque</I> but a <I>masquerade.</I>
In Henry VIII, when the king introduces himself to the entertainment given by
Wolsey, he appears, like Romeo and his companions, in a <I>mask,</I> and sends a mes-
senger before to make an apology for his intrusion. This was a custom observed by
those who came uninvited, with a desire to conceal themselves for the sake of
intrigue, or to enjoy the greater freedom of conversation. Their entry on these
occasions was always prefaced by some speech in praise of the beauty of the ladies
or the generosity of the entertainer; and to the <I>prolixity</I> of such introductions allu-
sion is here made. So in Histriomastix, 1610, a man wonders that the <I>maskers</I> come
in &ldquo;so blunt, <I>without device?</I>&rdquo; Of the same kind of masquerading see a specimen
in Timon I, ii, where Cupid precedes a troop of ladies with a speech. [<I>Sing. Huds.
Sta.</I> (subs.) <I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Percy.</SC> Sh. has written a <I>masque</I> in Act IV of The Tempest. It would have
been difficult for Warburton to prove they were discontinued during any period of
Sh.'s life. [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). Sh. ridicules a formal prolix introduction, such as that in Love's
L. L. V, ii, 158.
<P>5. <B>bow of lath</B>] <SC>Douce.</SC> The Tartarian bows, as well as most of those used by
the Asiatic nations, resembled in their form the old Roman or Cupid's bow, such as we
see on medals and bas-reliefs. Sh. used the epithet to distinguish it from the Eng-
lish bow, whose shape is the segment of a circle. [<I>Sing. Knt. Verp. Huds. Hal.</I>

<P><SC>Nares.</SC> At present, in all the midland counties, a boy set to drive the birds away

<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> I should not admit into the text these two lines, found only in (Q<SUB>1</SUB>), and
stricken out afterwards, probably by Sh. himself, were not the printing of the later
eds. so very careless that a couple of lines might easily have fallen out, and did they
not at the same time refer to a custom which certainly excited Sh.'s displeasure, and
consequently might have induced him to intercalate these two verses. . . . &ldquo;Without-
book prologue&rdquo; is doubtless to be taken as one word, and it signifies a prologue not
in the book&mdash;that is, not composed by the poet, but added probably by the manager

the prompter in a weak, mechanical way. That it was not at all unusual for pro-

several passages in Henslow's Diary (edited by J. P. Collier, Lond. 1845, p. 228,
229). For this same reason I believe that the prologue to our tragedy also was not
composed by Sh.

<P>10. <B>measure</B>] <SC>Knt.</SC> This was the courtly dance of the days of Elizabeth, not
so solemn as the pavan&mdash;the &ldquo;doleful pavan,&rdquo; as Davenant calls it,&mdash;in which princes
in their mantles and lawyers in their long robes, and courtly dames with enormous
trains, swept the rushes like the tails of peacocks. From this circumstance came its
name, the pavan&mdash;the dance of the peacock. For a description of the &ldquo;measure,&rdquo;
see &ldquo;Much Ado,&rdquo; II, i, 72. [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> A <I>measure</I> seems originally to have meant any dance the motions of which
kept due time to music: &ldquo;And dancing is a moving all in <I>measure.</I>&rdquo; (<I>Orchestra,</I> by
Sir John Davies, 1622.) In time, however, it obtained a more precise signification,
and was used to denote a movement slow, stately, and sweeping, like the modern
minuet, which appears to be its legitimate successor.
<P>The <I>measures,</I> <SC>Reed</SC> tells us, &lquo;were performed at court, and at public entertain-
ments of the societies of Law and Equity at their halls, on particular occasions. It
was not deemed inconsistent with propriety, even for the gravest persons to join in

was no degrading office. Queen Elizabeth's Gentlemen-Pensioners attended her to
Cambridge, and <I>held torches</I> while a play was acted before her in the Chapel of
King's College, on a Sunday evening. [<I>Sing. Knt. Corn. Huds. Sta. Hal.</I>

<P>36. <B>rushes</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> It was the custom to strew rooms with rushes, before carpets
were in use. See 1 Hen. IV: III, i. [<I>Sing. Coll. Haz. Verp. Huds. Cham.</I>] So
Hentzner, in his Itinerary, speaking of Queen Elizabeth's presence-chamber at

meaning <I>rushes.</I> [<I>Knt.</I>] So in The Dumb Knight, 1633: &lquo;Thou dancest on my
heart, lascivious queen, Even as upon these <I>rushes</I> which thou treadest.&rquo; The <I>stage</I>
was anciently strewn with <I>rushes.</I> In Decker's Gul's Hornbook, 1609: &lquo;&mdash;&mdash; on
the very <I>rushes</I> when the comedy is to daunce.&rquo; [<I>Sing. Huds. Sta. Hal.</I>

in his Hero and Leander: &lquo;She, fearing on the <I>rushes</I> to be flung, Striv'd with re-
doubled strength.&rquo; [<I>Sing. Hal.</I>

<P>42. <B>sir-reverence</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>. A kind of apologetical apostrophe when anything
was said that might be thought filthy or indecent; <I>salv&acirc; reverenti&acirc;.</I> It was con-
tracted into <I>sa'reverence,</I> and thence corrupted into <I>sir</I> or <I>sur-reverence.</I> This word
was considered as a sufficient apology for anything indecorous.
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> Mercutio says he will draw Romeo from the &lquo;mire of this love,&rquo; and uses
parenthetically the ordinary form of apology for speaking so profanely of love.
Gifford has given us a quotation from an old tract on the origin of tobacco which is
exactly in point: &lquo;The time hath been, when, if we did speak of this loathsome
stuff, tobacco, we used to put a &ldquo;Sir reverence&rdquo; before, but we forget our good
manners.&rquo; Elsewhere Gifford says: &lquo;There is much filthy stuff on this simple inter-
jection, of which neither Steevens nor Malone appears to have known the import.&rquo;
(Ben Jonson's Works, vol. vi, p. 149; vol. vii, p. 337.)
<P><SC>White</SC> [<I>Note on</I> Com. of Err. III, ii, 93]. Dromio makes use of the dirtiest
possible comparison: &lquo;for he hath wares that are not worth a save reverence&mdash;<I>nam
merces habet qu&aelig; non merd&acirc; valent.</I>&rquo; <I>Janua Linguarum,</I> 1640, Sig. B 3. And see
Grose's <I>Vulgar Tongue.</I>
<P><SC>Dyce</SC>. In this passage the word is used nearly in the sense which it still retains
among the vulgar.

<P><SC>Sing</SC>. It is applied to superfluous actions in general.

<P>47. <B>five wits</B>] <SC>Ulr.</SC> Plausible as Malone's correction appears at first sight, I
cannot perceive in what sense Mercutio can say that our judgment stands five times
in what we mean, for once in our five wits or our sound human understanding. The
contrary may be far more correctly maintained. &lquo;In our <I>fine</I> wits,&rquo; that is, in our
cultivated, our refined understanding, which clothes everything in fine witty phrases,
gives, on the other hand, a perfectly clear meaning.
<P><SC>Hunter</SC> [<I>New Illust.</I> vol. ii, p. 271. On <I>Lear</I> III, iv]. <I>Five wits</I> were undoubt-
edly the five senses. Thus in Larke's <I>Book of Wisdom:</I> &lquo;And this knowledge de
scendeth and cometh of the <I>five corporal senses and wits</I> of the persons, as the eyes,
understanding, and hearing of the ears, smell of the nose, taste of the mouth,&rquo; and
more plainly in King Henry the Eighth's Primer, 1546: &lquo;My <I>five wits</I> have I fondly
misused and spent, in hearing, seeing, smelling, tasting, and also feeling, which thou
hast given me,&rquo; &amp;c.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC>. &lquo;The <I>wits</I> seem to have been reckoned five by analogy to the five senses,
or the five inlets of ideas&rquo; (<SC>Johnson</SC>): &lquo;From Stephen Hawes's poem called <I>Graunde
Amoure</I> [<I>and La Belle Pucel</I>], ch. xxiv, edit. 1554, it appears that the <I>five wits</I>
were &ldquo;common wit, imagination, fantasy, estimation [<I>i. e.</I> judgment], and memory.&rdquo;
<I>Wit</I> in our author's time was the general term for the intellectual power.&rquo; (<SC>Mal-
one.</SC>) But sundry passages might be adduced from early writers, who considered
the <I>five wits</I> to be the <I>five senses</I> (see, for instance, the passage from the interlude of
The Four Elements cited by Percy on Lear III, iv, apud the Var. Sh., and Hunter's
<I>New Illust.</I>).

<P>53. <B>Queen Mab</B>] <SC>Ktly.</SC> (&lquo;<I>Fairy Mythology,</I>&rquo; vol. ii, p. 135). &lquo;Mab,&rquo; says Voss,
a German translator of Sh., &lquo;is not the Fairy-queen, the same with Titania, as some,
misled by the word <I>queen,</I> have thought. That word in Old English, as in Danish,
designates the female sex.&rquo; True, but where does it or the Danish <I>quinde</I> occur in
the sense of <I>Frau,</I> by which he renders it? The origin of Mab is very uncertain.
Is it a contraction of Habundia, who, Heywood tells us, ruled over the Fairies?
<P><SC>W. J. Thoms</SC> (&lquo;<I>Three Notelets on Sh.,</I>&rquo; 1865). We find the Fairy Queen here in-
vested with the attributes of the Night-mare; and that this arose from no confusion
in Sh.'s mind is clear from the fact that Chaucer has shown us in &lquo;The Wife of
Bath's Tale&rquo; that such connection belonged to the Folk-lore of his times. And the
propriety of this connection is confirmed by an examination of the popular belief
upon the subject as it now exists among the Continental nations. See &lquo;Deutsche
Sagen&rquo; of the Brothers Grimm, vol. i, p. 130. The reader will be surprised to learn
that no earlier instance of Mab being used as the designation of the Fairy Queen
has hitherto been discovered than in this passage, more especially since there can be
no doubt that it is a genuine name learned by Sh. from the Folk-lore of his own
time. (See Brand's Popular Antiquities, vol. iii, p. 218, ed. 1841.)
<P>Looking to the general character given of <I>Dame Abunde,</I> or <I>Habunde,</I> I at one
time felt inclined to answer in the affirmative Keightley's question [<I>ut supra</I>], more
especially since Dame Abonde might have been contracted into Dame Ab, and
thence into Mab. Another derivation may be from <I>Mabel,</I> of which <I>Mab</I> is a com-
mon abbreviation, and respecting which Camden says, &lquo;some will have it to be a
contraction of the Italians from <I>Mabella;</I> that is, my fair daughter, or maid. But,
whereas it is written in deeds <I>Amabilia</I> and <I>Mabilia,</I> I think it cometh from <I>Ama-
bilis,</I> that is, lovable or lovely.&rquo; But further consideration has satisfied me that the
origin of this name Mab is to be found in the Celtic. Beaufort, in his &lquo;Antient To-
pography of Ireland,&rquo; mentions <I>Mabh</I> as the chief of the Irish fairies. In speaking
of the chief of the genii, he says, &lquo;when presiding over the forests and chief of the
<I>Fiodh Rhehe</I>&rquo; (fairies corresponding with the satyrs and elves of the Greeks and
Romans), &lquo;it was denominated <I>Mabh</I> by the Irish, by the Greeks <I>Diana,</I> and by the
Romans <I>Pan.</I>&rquo;
<P>Before meeting with these passages I had satisfied myself of the Celtic origin of
the name of Mab, but upon different grounds; for I saw in this designation a dis-

<P>54. <B>fairies' midwife</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> This does not mean the midwife <I>to</I> the fairies, but
that she was the person <I>among</I> the fairies whose department it was to deliver the
fancies of sleeping men of their dreams, those <I>children of an idle brain.</I> When we
say the <I>king's judges</I> we do not mean persons who are to judge the king, but persons
appointed by him to judge his subjects. [<I>Sing. Verp. Huds. Dyce, Hal.</I>
<P><SC>T. Warton</SC>. Because it was her peculiar employment to steal the new-born babe
in the night, and to leave another in its place. It would clear the appellation to read
the <I>fairy midwife.</I> [<I>Haz. Verp. White, Dyce.</I>
<P><SC>White</SC>. Warburton's reading is very plausible and quite poetical.
<P>55. <B>In shape</B>] <SC>Nicholson</SC> (<I>Notes</I> and <I>Queries,</I> 3d Series, vol. x, p. 163, 1866).
Like an agate-stone in a ring! Surely a strange shape and simile for Queen Mab.
If it be said that <I>shape</I> applies to Queen Mab and her surroundings, and not to her
person only, the answers are, that she herself is the only antecedent mentioned that
in shape is not a shape, and that if it were, it is a more than questionable use of the
word to make it mean equipage when equipage has not been alluded to. Whence,
also, the suggestion, &lquo;on the forefinger of an alderman?&rquo; Read <I>state</I> and all be-
comes clear. At present the words <I>drawn</I> and <I>waggon-spokes</I> break in and turn us
most inartistically from Queen Mab's person to a wholly new idea&mdash;her conveyance.
But with <I>state,</I> Mercutio's words show, from the first, that vision of the Queen in her
state progress which he sees already in his mind's eye, and which he is about to de-
scribe. Instead of an incongruous simile inserted between &lquo;she comes&mdash;drawn,&rquo;
we have &lquo;she comes drawn in state by little atomies,&rquo; where, through the interven-
tion of <I>state,</I> the word <I>drawn</I> applies to the compound idea of herself and her con-
veyance, and prepares us for her &lquo;waggon-spokes.&rquo; Hence, it is that in the first
sketch, or first quarto, while there is mention of waggon-spokes, waggon-cover, traces,
&amp;c., nothing is said of the waggon. Afterwards, the description of the chariot was
evidently given by Mercutio as if it were his, as it was Sh.'s, afterthought evolved
out of the growing luxuriance of his fancy. The after-change also of &lquo;in this sort&rquo;
to &lquo;in this state she gallops,&rquo; is in favour of the previous use of the latter, for Sh.
was fond of such repetitions, and it is one which marks the recurrence to the main
theme after digression into details. Lastly, the comparison is to the agate-ring of
an alderman, because it is the state of a lesser than a Lilliput magnate compared
with that of a large-sized Brobdingnagian, the size of the essential part of the signet
as compared with the whole pomp of a full-blown alderman clad in civic robes and
carried in a cumbrous civic coach.

<P><SC>P. E. Masey</SC> (<I>N. and Q.</I> 3d Ser. vol. x, p. 216). Nicholson is, I think, certainly
wrong. The meaning I apprehend to be: In shape no bigger than the engraved
figures on the agate-stone. The exquisite delicacy which ordinarily characterizes
such a small cameo as is here referred to renders the comparison most appropriate.
Nothing else in the whole range of representative art conveys so perfect an idea of
fairy-like form.
<P>55. <B>agate-stone</B>] <SC>Del.</SC> Sh. has also elsewhere compared diminutive persons to
the little figures cut in relief in agate and set in rings; thus, in 2 K. Hen. IV:
I, ii, 19.
<P><SC>White</SC>. It appears to have been the fashion among civic dignitaries and wealthy
citizens all over Europe to wear on the forefinger or the thumb agate rings cut in
cameo or intaglio. Oftenest in cameo, it would seem, from the not unfrequent com-
parison of children and dwarfish men to &lquo;agates,&rquo; meaning, of course, the figures
cut upon the agate. It would be a matter of some interest in the history of art to
inquire whether these gems were antiques, cinque-cento work, or the production of
contemporary artists.
<P>56. <B>an alderman</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> We may suppose the citizens in Sh.'s time wore this
ornament on the <I>thumb.</I> So Glapthorne, in Wit in a Constable, 1639: &lquo;&mdash;&mdash; and
an <I>alderman</I> as I may say to you, he has no more wit than the rest o' the bench;
and that lies in his <I>thumb-ring.</I>&rquo; [<I>Sing. Hal.</I>
<P>57. <B>atomies</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> An obsolete substitute for <I>atoms.</I> There is likewise a de-

<P>So, as we may see, he was not, and why should a soldier be, afraid of it? In Ma-
lone's quotation from Westward Hoe, we have drinking <I>fathom deep,</I> and it is
apparently drinking healths; but there is nothing about terror in it, and it seems, no
unusual circumstance, to have arisen from the present line. In fine, something must
have been named that was a real object of terror to a soldier; and I know no word
so likely to have been used as <I>trenches,</I> which might easily have been mistaken for
&lquo;healths.&rquo; In that case the metric accent falling on &lquo;five&rquo; would augment the terror.
<P>89. <B>plats the manes</B>] <SC>Douce</SC>. This alludes to a very singular superstition not
yet forgotten in some parts of the country. It was believed that certain malignant
spirits, whose delight was to wander in groves and pleasant places, assumed occa-
sionally the likenesses of women clothed in white; that in this character they some-
times haunted stables in the night-time, carrying in their hands tapers of wax, which
they dropped on the horses' manes, thereby plaiting them in inextricable knots, to
the great annoyance of the poor animals and vexation of their masters. These hags
are mentioned in the works of William of Auvergne, bishop of Paris in the 13th
century. There is a very uncommon old print by Hans Burgmair relating to this
subject. A witch enters the stable with a lighted torch; and previously to the opera-
tion of entangling the horse's mane, practises her enchantment on the groom, who
is lying asleep on his back, and apparently influenced by the nightmare. The <I>Belem-
nites,</I> or elf-stones, were regarded as charms against the last-mentioned disease, and
against evil spirits of all kinds; but the <I>cerauni&aelig;</I> or <I>b&aelig;tuli,</I> and all perforated flint
stones, were not only used for the same purpose, but more particularly for the pro-
tection of horses and other cattle, by suspending them in stables, or tying them
round the necks of the animals. [<I>Knt. Corn. Verp. Huds. Hal.</I>
<P>90. <B>bakes</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>. This superstition seems to have had its rise from the
horrid disease called the <I>Plica Polonica.</I> [<I>Sing. Knt. White, Dyce.</I>
<P><SC>Douce</SC>. The Plica Polonica was supposed to be the operation of wicked elves;
whence the clotted hair was called <I>elf-locks</I> and <I>elf-knots.</I> Thus Edgar talks of
&lquo;<I>elfing</I> all his hair in <I>knots.</I>&rquo; [<I>Knt.</I>] Lodge in his <I>Wits' Miserie,</I> 1599, describing

<P>5-6. <B>court-cupboard</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> Probably what we call the <I>side-board.</I> It is fre-

these tables with their white veils and accomplish the <I>court-cupboard.</I>&rquo; In Chap-
man's Monsieur D'Olive, 1606: &lquo;Here shall stand my <I>court-cupboard</I> with its furni-
ture of plate.&rquo; [<I>Sing. Knt. Coll. Verp. Hal.</I>] And also in his May-Day, 1611:
&lquo;<I>Court-cupboards</I> planted with flaggons, cans, cups, beakers, &amp;c.&rquo; Two of these
<I>court-cupboards</I> are still in Stationers' Hall. [<I>Sing. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Nichols.</SC> The use which to this day is made of them is exactly described in the
quotation from Chapman: to display at public festivals the flaggons and other antique
silver vessels of the Company. [<I>Sing. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Sing.</SC> There is a print in a curious work, entitled <I>Laurea Austriaca,</I> fol. 1627,
representing an entertainment given by James I in 1623, from which the reader will
get a better notion of the <I>court-cupboard</I> than volumes of description would afford.
It was also called a <I>cupboard of plate</I> and a <I>livery cupboard.</I>
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> It appears to have been what we now call a cabinet.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC>. A sort of movable sideboard without doors or drawers, in which was dis-
played the plate of the establishment.
<P><SC>Halliwell</SC>. &lquo;<I>Dressoir,</I> a cupboord; a court-cupboord (without box or drawer),
onely to set plate on.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Cotgrave.</I> [<I>Dyce.</I>
<P>&lquo;John being in London, in a gallant garb passing along, espieth a silver flagon
standing on a <I>court-cupboard,</I> a young gentlewoman being at door, he pretended his
bird flew in; she gave him admittance, he thanked her, but the silver flagon was
never heard of.&rquo; <I>The Witty Jests and Mad Pranks of John Frith,</I> 1673.

<P>Our <I>macaroons</I> are only debased and diminutive <I>marchpanes.</I> [<I>Coll. Verp.
White.</I>
<P><SC>Nares.</SC> The word exists, with little variation, in all European languages; yet its
derivation is uncertain. Skinner says it is &lquo;quasi dicas <I>massa panis, i. e.,</I> a mass of
bread. Lye derives it from the Dutch, in which, besides <I>marcepeyn,</I> which he con-
siders as a corruption, there is <I>massereyn,</I> which means pure bread; but this is not
very satisfactory. In medi&aelig;val Latin they were called <I>martii panes,</I> which gave
occasion to Hermolaus Barbarus to make some inquiry into their origin in a letter to
Cardinal Piccolomini, who had sent some to him as a present.&mdash;<I>Politian's Epistles,</I>
Book xii. Balthasar Bonifacius says that they were named from <I>Marcus</I> Apicius,
the famous epicure: &lquo;Ab hoc Marco, panes saccharo conditi vulgo etiamnum dicun-
tur <I>Marci panes,</I> vel potius ab alio quodam juniore, M. Gavio Apicio, qui sub
Augusto et Tiberio fuit ad omne lux&ucirc;s ingenium mirus, &amp;c.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Fabric. Bibl. Lat.,</I> ed.
Ernest., vol. ii, p. 468. Minshew will have them originally sacred to <I>Mars,</I> and
stamped with a castle, which is nearly the opinion of Hermolaus. Whatever was
the origin of their name, the English receipt-books all show that they were com-
posed of almonds and sugar, compounded and baked. Here is a specimen:
<P><I>To make a marchpane.</I>&mdash;Take two poundes of almonds being blanched, and dryed in a sieve over
the fire, beate them in a stone mortar, and when they bee small mixe them with two pounde of sugar
beeing finely beaten, adding two or three spoonefuls of rosewater, and that will keep your almonds
from oiling; when your paste is beaten fine, drive it thin with a rowling pin, and so lay it on a bottom
of wafers, then raise up a little edge on the side, and so bake it, then yce it with rosewater and sugar,
then put it in the oven againe, and when you see your yce is risen up and drie, then take it out of the
oven and garnish it with prettie conceipts, as birdes and beasts, being cast out of standing moldes. Sticke
long comfits uprig<*>ht in it, cast bisket and carrowaies in it and so serve it; guild it before you serve it:
you may also print of this <I>marchpane</I> paste in your moldes for banqueting dishes. And of this paste
our comfit makers at this day make their letters, knots, armes, escutcheons, beasts, birds and other
fancies.&mdash;<I>Delightes for Ladies,</I> 1608, 12mo. Sign. A 12.
<P>Castles and other figures were often made of <I>marchpane</I> to decorate splendid des-
serts, and were demolished by shooting or throwing sugar-plums at them. Vide
<I>B. and Fl., Faithful Friends,</I> iii, 2, and Taylor's <I>Praise of Hempseed,</I> p. 66.
<P><SC>Hunter.</SC> &lquo;To make a marchpane&rquo; stands in the first place in <I>The Treasury of
Hidden Secrets, commonly called The Good Housewife's Closet of Provision,</I> 1627.
See also, <I>A Hermetical Banquet dressed by a Spagiritical Cook,</I> 1652, p. 102, in
which strange work, in which Sh.'s name is found, we have particular directions for
making marchpane.
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> Evidently the same as our Marcipan, although composed of other ingre-
dients.
<P><SC>Halliwell</SC>. According to Forby, ii, 208, the term was used up to a very recent
period. See Markham's Country Farme, 1616, p. 585; Ben Jonson, ii, 295; Top-
sell's Serpents, p. 165; Warner's Antiq. Culin., p. 103; Harrison's England, p. 167;
Florio, p. 134. &lquo;As to suppresse by message sad, The feast for which they all have
had Their <I>marchpane</I> dream so long.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Songs of the London Prentices,</I> p. 31.

<P>8. <B>Antony! and Potpan</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2). Throughout this scene Potpan is the

<P>24. <B>A hall!</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> This exclamation occurs frequently in old comedies, and
signifies <I>make room.</I> In the comedy of Doctor Dodypoll, 1600: &lquo;Room! room!
<I>a hall! a hall!</I>&rquo; In Ben Jonson's Tale of a Tub: &lquo;&mdash;&mdash; Then cry, <I>a hall! a hall!</I>&rquo;
In an Epithalamium by Christopher Brooke, in England's Helicon, 1614: &lquo;Cry not
<I>a hall, a hall;</I> but chamber-roome;&rquo; and numberless other passages. [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Nares.</SC> As we now say <I>a ring! a ring!</I> So, Marston, Sat. iii: &lquo;A hall! a hall!
Roome for the spheres, the orbs celestiall Will dance Kempe's jigge.&rquo; [<I>Sing. Verp.
Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Verp.</SC> King James, in &lquo;Marmion,&rquo; has made this antiquated phrase familiar.
<P>25. <B>tables</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> Ancient tables were flat leaves joined by hinges and placed

his answer constantly calls him <I>Uncle.</I> And the old Duchess of York, in the same

<P>The repetition of the word <I>beauty,</I> in the next line but one, confirms the emenda-
tion of F<SUB>2</SUB>. [<I>Dyce</I> (ed. 2).
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> Why then, it may be asked, do we depart from our usual principle and
reject an undoubted ancient reading? Because the reading which we give has be-
come familiar, has passed into common use wherever our language is spoken, is
quoted in books as frequently as any of the other examples of Sh.'s exquisite power
of description. Here, it appears to us, is a higher law to be observed than that of
adherence to the ancient copies. It is the same also in I, i, 146.
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 1). We adhere to the authentic, and perfectly intelligible, text, as
contained in every impression during the author's life.
<P><SC>Del.</SC> (&lquo;<I>Lex.</I>&rquo;) Juliet's beauty is only first spoken of in line 45. The boldness of
the simile led the poet to introduce it by &lquo;it seems.&rquo;
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> The reading of F<SUB>2</SUB> is an improvement, although it has no authority, and is
therefore not to be adopted. The succeeding phrase, &lquo;Beauty too rich,&rquo; seems to
demand that a similar word should precede it. On the other hand, it weakens the
otherwise very bold and almost forced image of hanging on the cheek of night.
<P><SC>Corn.</SC> [&lquo;<I>Her beauty</I>&rquo;] is now so consecrated by general approval that it would be
both useless and ungracious to attempt to supersede it. The most rigid sticklers for
the authority of F<SUB>1</SUB> have found it necessary, in very many cases, to prefer the read-
ings of the Qq, and in some comparatively few instances those of F<SUB>2</SUB>. The reason
is this: we know, unfortunately, as far as the matter is susceptible of proof, that
none of Sh.'s plays were published under his own superintendence; we know also,
in reference to all the earlier copies, that typographical errors, stage omissions or
interpolations, the want of regular editing, and other causes, have contributed to
obscure, and, not unfrequently, to destroy the poet's meaning; it is, therefore, in no
irreverent spirit (as is too often inculcated), but rather from a feeling of duty and
gratitude, that even the most cautious commentators have felt themselves compelled
to depart from the principle of taking any one edition as an invariable guide. From
two or three instances selected in the present play from numerous others, merely as
illustrations of the general fact, it will be seen that the reviser, who should in every
case adopt the readings of F<SUB>1</SUB>, would bring upon his devoted head the merited an-
athema of every Shaksperian reader. We have not, however, presumed to vary from
the text without anxious consideration and constant reference to those commentators
who have shown the least disposition to innovate either as to words or versification.
<P><SC>Verp.</SC> So much is gained in poetic beauty by the reading of F<SUB>2</SUB>, and the other
reading is so tame in expression, and so little in Sh.'s manner, whose faults of lan-
guage are never on that side, that it seems quite probable that this was a correction
of the poet's own, obtained from some other MS., altered during the poet's life. It
is, besides, confirmed by the repetition of the word &lquo;beauty&rquo; in line 45.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 1). The reading of F<SUB>2</SUB>, however it may be regarded as an improve-
ment, has not a shadow of a claim to be received into the text.
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). The usual reading of F<SUB>1</SUB> has been tame and poor.

<P><SC>White</SC>. The great gain in poetic beauty by the reading of F<SUB>2</SUB> does not justify a
deviation from the authoritative text, though it may tempt to it. But in this passage
all the old copies come evidently from one source; and in this play, as in some
others, the authority of the folio is impaired, although its authenticity as a whole
cannot be impeached; while in the context there is ground for believing that the
editor of the second folio&mdash;a contemporary of Shakespeare&mdash;restored the true read-
ing. Steevens might have put the case much more strongly; for in line 45 &lquo;beauty&rquo;
is a dependent word, and the clause which begins with it an entirely dependent
clause. Unless &lquo;beauty&rquo; occur in the first clause of the sentence as the apponent of
&lquo;beauty&rquo; in the second, the latter cannot be construed, I will not say according to
grammatical rule and precedent, but so as to preserve that rational coherence of
thought, the necessity of which underlies all grammatical rules, and which Sh., in
his freest style, never violates. Therefore, having this contemporary change of a
reading which, if undisturbed, would leave a unique and derogatory blemish upon
Sh.'s page,&mdash;a change, too, which seems not to <I>add</I> a grace, but to preserve one by
the mere restoration of grammatical integrity to the passage,&mdash;I believe that the elder
copies have in this case, as in some others, but perpetuated an error committed in
the earliest impression, and I adopt the reading of F<SUB>2</SUB>, not upon the authority of that
text, but upon the internal evidence of the context, supported by the inherent merits
of the emendation. All editors of the present century have hitherto deferred to the
authority of the elder copies.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2). The reading of F<SUB>2</SUB> (whencesoever the editor of that folio may have
procured it) is assuredly a great improvement.
<P><SC>Gerald Massey</SC> (&lquo;<I>Sh.'s Sonnets,</I>&rquo; &amp;c., Lond. 1866, p. 470). I fancy that Sh. was
working a good deal from the life and the love of his friends [Southampton's love
for Elizabeth Vernon] when he wrote this play; the Queen's opposition to their mar-
riage standing in the place of that ancient enmity of the two Houses. There is
much of Southampton's character and fate in Romeo the unlucky, doomed to be
crossed in his dearest wishes, whose name was writ in sour Misfortune's book. . . .
There are expressions pointing to the lady of the early Sonnets as being in the poet's
mind when he was thinking of Juliet. A remarkable image in the 27th Sonnet is
also made use of in Romeo's first exclamation on seeing Juliet for the first time.
Considering who the Sonnets were written for, this figure reappears in too pointed a
way not to have some suggestive significance. Looked at in this light, the question
of Juliet, &lquo;Art thou not Romeo and a Montague?&rquo; comes upon us with luminous
force; for the fact is, that Southampton was a Montague by the mother's side, she
being Mary, daughter of Anthony Browne, fair Viscount Montague, which fact calls
to mind what has always seemed a little bit of the Nurse's nonsense in II, iv, 190
[which see].
<P><SC>Clarke.</SC> Inasmuch as the expression of the authentic copies is not only intelligi-
ble, but is one that Sh. has used elsewhere, we feel bound to retain it. In other
passages of description we find &lquo;it seems&rquo; and &lquo;it seem'd&rquo; thus used: Tempest, I,
ii; Lear, IV, iii, and Winter's Tale, V, ii.

<P><SC>Huds.</SC> Minshew calls a <I>princox</I> &lquo;a ripe-headed young boy,&rquo; and derives it from
<I>pr&aelig;cox.</I> The more probable derivation is from <I>prime cock;</I> that is, a <I>cock of prime</I>
courage or spirit; hence applied to a pert, conceited, forward person. In Phaer's
Virgil: &lquo;<I>Fyne princox,</I> fresh of face, furst uttring youth by buds unshorne.&rquo;
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). Skinner says from <I>pr&aelig;cox,</I> but in Richardson's Dict. the ety-
mology given is a <I>prime cock.</I> Florio translates <I>herba da buoi</I> &lquo;a prime-cock boy, a
freshman, a novice.&rquo;
<P><SC>Halliwell</SC>. Brockett has <I>princox</I> as still in use, and <I>princy-cock</I> is given by
Carr, ii, 58. &lquo;If hee bee a little bookish, let him write but the commendation of a
flea, straight begs he the coppie, kissing, hugging, grinning, and smiling, till hee
make the yong <I>princocks</I> as proud as a pecocke.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Lodge's Wits Miserie,</I> 1596.
<P><SC>Coleridge</SC> (<I>Lit. Rem.</I> vol. ii, p. 154). How admirable is the old man's impetu-

<P>a long <I>s. Sin</I> scarcely affords sense, while &lquo;fine&rquo; has a clear meaning. [<I>Verp.

<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> Warburton's correction is needless,&mdash;nay, it disturbs the connection. &lquo;Gentle&rquo;
formerly signified not only &lquo;noble,&rquo; &lquo;distinguished,&rquo; &amp;c., but sometimes also &lquo;pious&rquo;
[<I>fromm</I>] (<I>e. g.</I> 3 Hen VI: I, iv, where &lquo;gentle-hearted&rquo; stands for &lquo;pious-hearted&rquo;).
Romeo says in effect: &lquo;If I by the touch of my unworthy hand profane this shrine
(Altar, Reliquary), it is the pious sin&rquo;&mdash;namely, of the pilgrims, who journey to holy
places for the very purpose of touching the relics, or rather, as was customary, of
kissing them. And following out the same train of thought, he adds that his lips
were therefore ready by a tender kiss to smooth this &lquo;rough&rquo; (unusual, irreverent)
touch. That &lquo;romeo&rquo; in Italian signifies a pilgrim is evident from the last sonnet but
one of Dante's &lquo;Vita nuova.&rquo; It is there remarked that Pilgrims were styled &lquo;Pal-
mieri,&rquo; inasmuch as they came over the sea (of course to Palestine), whence they
brought back Palms. Those on the other hand who went to the tomb of St. James
in Galicia [Santiago de Compostela] were called &lquo;Pelligrini,&rquo; and those who went
to Rome &lquo;Romei.&rquo; My honored friend Blanc, to whom I am indebted for this
information, adds that the later Italian writers do not retain these distinctions.
For instance, Giov. Villani designates by the name of &lquo;romeo&rquo; one who comes from
St. James. Franco Sacchetti and others use this word generally for all pilgrims.
Dante's remark shows us why Romeo chose a pilgrim's mask, and throws light also
upon the &lquo;palmers,&rquo; of whom Juliet speaks; and it proves also that Sh. understood
more Italian than the learned writer in The Quarterly Review, who lately ques-
tioned whether &lquo;<I>romeo</I>&rquo; have the meaning of pilgrim.
<P><SC>Quarterly Rev.</SC> (vol. lxxxi, p. 524, 1847). <I>Romeo</I> is the familiar contraction
of <I>Romualdo,</I> the famous Lombard name, which, though sometimes derived from
the Teutonic, may perhaps have been a corruption of <I>Romulus,</I> but never could have
meant a <I>pilgrim.</I>
<P><SC>Del.</SC> Romeo, in taking Juliet's hand, says, in reference to that hand: If I with
my unworthy hand profane this holy shrine, it is (a sin in truth but) the gentle sin.
If the emendation <I>a gentle sin</I> or <I>the gentlest sin</I> were allowed, there would be no
difficulty in the passage. The idea of the <I>sin</I> is also kept up in the succeeding dia-
logue, and the word <I>sin</I> in line 105 is used in manifest reference to this place.
<P>[Substantially the same note as in Del. &lquo;Lexikon.&rquo;]
<P>95. <B>pilgrim</B>] <SC>Halliwell</SC>. The subjoined engraving, from a sketch by Inigo
Jones, presents us with the Palmer's, or Pilgrim's, dress worn by Romeo in this
scene. It is the usual costume of such personages, consisting of a long loose gown,
or robe, with large sleeves, and a round cape covering the breast and shoulders; a
broad-leafed hat, turned up in front and fastened to the crown by a button, appar-
ently, if it be not intended for a small cockle-shell, the absence of which customary
badge would otherwise be the only remarkable circumstance in the drawing. In
the left hand of the figure is the <I>bourdon,</I> or staff, peculiar to pilgrims. The modern
representatives of Romeo have inaccurately carried a cross. In the text of the play
the only indication of his being in a Pilgrim's habit is derived from Juliet's address-
ing him, &lquo;Good Pilgrim,&rquo; &amp;c. The drawing is therefore most interesting authority

<P>120. <B>banquet</B>] <SC>Nares.</SC> What we now call a dessert was in earlier times often
termed a <I>banquet;</I> and Gifford informs us that the <I>banquet</I> was usually placed in a
separate room, to which the guests removed when they had dined. &lquo;The common
place of <I>banqueting,</I> or eating the dessert,&rquo; the same critic says, &lquo;was the garden-
house or arbour with which almost every dwelling was furnished.&rquo; To this Shallow
alludes in 2 Hen. IV: V, iii, 2. <I>Banquet</I> is often used by Sh., and seems always to
signify a feast as it does now.
<P><SC>Sing.</SC> It was sometimes called a <I>rere-supper.</I> [<I>Huds.</I>] According to Baret,
&lquo;banketting dishes brought at the end of meales were junkettes, tartes, marchpanes.&rquo;
Yet from the same authority it appears that a <I>banquet</I> and a feast were also then
synonymous.
<P><SC>Del.</SC> After the supper, of which the invited guests had already partaken, there
is to follow for the uninvited maskers a collation, which Capulet, with affected
modesty, calls trifling and foolish.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2). When Nares said that Sh. always used <I>banquet</I> to signify a feast
he overlooked <I>Tam. the Shrew,</I> V, ii, 9: &lquo;My banquet is to close our stomachs up

<P><B>Enter Chorus</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>. The use of this Chorus is not easily discovered. It
conduces nothing to the progress of the play, but relates what is already known, or
what the next scene will show; and relates it without adding the improvement of
any moral sentiment. [<I>Sing.</I> (ed. 1).
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> This is one of those &lquo;<I>without-book prologues</I>&rquo; to which reference was made
in I, iv, 7. It is so empty, prosaic, and barren, and so wholly pointless, that in my
opinion it is impossible that it could ever have flowed from Sh.'s pen.
<P>144. <B>gapes</B>] <SC>W. L. Rushton</SC> (&lquo;<I>Sh.'s Testamentary Language,</I>&rquo; 1869, p. 29).
Swinburn's &lquo;<I>Briefe Treatise of Testaments and Last Willes,</I>&rquo; 1590, contains many
uncommon words, or common words having an uncommon sense, which are used by
Sh.&mdash;<I>e. g.,</I> &lquo;the testator is afraid to offende such personnes as doo <I>gape</I> for greater
bequests than they have deserved,&rquo; p. 23. Again, speaking of testaments &lquo;made by
flatterie,&rquo; Swinburn says, p. 243: &lquo;It is an impudent part still to <I>gape</I> and crie upon
the testator.&rquo;

<P>2. <B>dull earth</B>] <SC>Clarke.</SC> Romeo's epithet for his small world of man, the earth-

<P>2. <B>thy centre out</B>] <SC>Del.</SC> Sh. has this same simile elsewhere. In <I>Tro. and

<P><SC>Sing.</SC> (ed. 2). This seems to be one of the many instances of Sh.'s apparent intu-

suggested is of the earth&mdash;symbol of the earthly body&mdash;at its aphelion, or the point
of its orbit most remote from the sun, returning to it again by the force of gravita-
tion to the common centre of gravity.

<I>hortus,</I> but is derived from the Saxon <I>ortyeard,</I> which is itself put for <I>wyrtyeard,</I> a

direct nonsense which was understood in Sh.'s time by all his audience; for this

<P><SC>Knt.</SC> The change of Abraham into Adam is uncalled for. <I>Abraham</I> conveys
another idea than that of Cupid's archery, which is strongly enough conveyed. The
&lquo;Abraham&rquo; Cupid is the cheat&mdash;the &lquo;Abraham man&rquo;&mdash;of our old statutes.
<P><SC>Hunter</SC>. There seems not the smallest reason for substituting &lquo;Adam&rquo; for &lquo;Abra-
ham,&rquo; which, as a nickname of Cupid, has something more of humour about it.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (&lquo;<I>A Few Notes,</I>&rquo; &amp;c., p. 109, 1853). Capell hazarded the strange conjec-
ture that as &lquo;Cophetua was a <I>Jew</I> king of Africa, Sh. might make the Cupid that
struck him a <I>Jew</I> Cupid&rquo; [<I>i. e.,</I> &lquo;Abraham&rquo;]. Notes, &amp;c., vol. ii, P. iv, p. 7. . . .
That Sh. here had an eye to the ballad of <I>King Cophetua and the Beggar-Maid</I> is
certain. But the ballad contains nothing to countenance, in the slightest degree, the
reading &lquo;Adam Cupid.&rquo; In <I>Soliman and Perseda,</I> 1599, we find: &lquo;the eldest
sonne of Pryam, That <I>abraham-</I>coloured Troion?&rquo; Sig. H 3. In Middleton's <I>Blurt,
Master Constable,</I> 1602: &lquo;A goodlie, long, thicke, <I>Abram-</I>colour'd beard.&rquo; Sig. D.
And in Coriolanus, II, iii, according to F<SUB>1</SUB>F<SUB>2</SUB>F<SUB>3</SUB>: &lquo;not that our heads are some
browne, some blacke, some <I>Abram;</I>&rquo;&mdash;there being hardly any reason to doubt that in
these passages &lquo;<I>abraham</I>&rquo; (or &lquo;<I>Abram</I>&rquo;) is a corruption of &lquo;<I>abron</I>&rquo;&mdash;i. e., &lquo;<I>auburn.</I>&rquo;
Is then the right reading in the present line, &lquo;Young <I>abram</I> [or <I>auburn</I>] Cupid,&rquo;
Sh. having used &lquo;<I>abram</I>&rquo; for &lquo;auburn<I>-hair'd,</I>&rquo; as the author of <I>Soliman and Perseda</I>
has used &lquo;<I>abraham-</I>coloured Troion&rquo; for &lquo;Trojan with auburn-coloured <I>hair?</I>&rquo;
Everybody familiar with the Italian poets knows that they term Cupid, as well as
Apollo, &lquo;Il biondo Dio;&rquo; and W. Thomas, in his <I>Principal Rules of the Italian
Grammer,</I> &amp;c., gives &lquo;<I>Biondo,</I> the <I>aberne</I> [i. e., <I>auburn</I>] colour, that is betwene
white and yelow.&rquo; ed. 1567. In <I>The Two Gent.,</I> IV, iv, 194, &lquo;<I>auburn</I>&rquo; means
yellowish.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 1). That here &lquo;Abraham&rquo; is merely a corrupted form of &lquo;<I>auburn</I>&rquo; I
now feel more confident than when I made the foregoing note.
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). This [Dyce's note] is, indeed, to use Mr. Dyce's own strong
words (&lquo;<I>Remarks,</I>&rquo; p. 167), to &lquo;chronicle a wretched conjecture,&rquo; for where, in Eng-
lish, is Cupid called &lquo;<I>auburn</I> Cupid&rquo;?
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2). Mr. Grant White estimates my conjecture very differently,&mdash;he
adopts it.
<P><SC>White</SC>. That &lquo;Abraham&rquo; is a mere error, or, rather, superfluous and mistaken
sophistication of &lquo;abram,&rquo;&mdash;itself one of the numerous modes of spelling &lquo;auburn&rquo;
of old,&mdash;seems undeniable. &lquo;Auburn&rquo; was spelled <I>auburne, auborne, aubrun, aberne,
abron, abrun, abran, abram,</I> and (consequently) sometimes <I>Abraham.</I> See the fol-
lowing instances: &lquo;Her black, browne, <I>auburne,</I> or her yellow hayre.&rquo;&mdash;Drayton's
<I>Moone Calf,</I> p. 164, ed. 1627. &lquo;Light <I>auborne, subflavus.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<I>Baret's Alvearie,</I> 1580.
&lquo;&mdash;&mdash; He's white hair'd, Not wanton white, but such a manly colour Next to an
<I>aubrun.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<I>Two Noble Kinsmen,</I> IV, ii. &lquo;And on his <I>Abron</I> head hore haires peerd
here and there among.&rquo;&mdash;Golding's <I>Ovid,</I> $ol. 157 b., ed. 1587; $ol. 151 b., ed. 1612.
&lquo;They [persons of sanguine temperament] are very hairy; their head is commonly
<I>abran,</I> or amber coloured; so their beards.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Optick Glass of Humours,</I> 1630, p. 116.

<P>The printing of <I>Abraham</I> for <I>Abram</I> was very likely to occur from the fact that the
name of the &lquo;father of the faithful&rquo; occurs in both $orms in <I>Gen.</I> xvii, 5.
<P><SC>Halliwell</SC>. The idea of Adam Cupid in this [Upton's] sense seems forced. The
form [<I>abraham</I> for <I>auburn</I>] is certainly met with in our old writers. &lquo;By the elev-
enth house you can judge of what haire he shall be of, of a browne or <I>Abraham</I>
colour, as the English; of a yellow, as the Dane.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Melton's Astrologaster,</I> 1620.
<P><SC>Ktly.</SC> I incline to the reading, first given by Upton, with an allusion to Adam
Bell, and I think there may be another to Adam, the first man; for Sh. may have
known that in classic mythology Love was the first of beings. There would be
humor, then, in &lquo;young Adam&rquo; denoting the union of youth and age.
<P>14. <B>beggar-maid</B>] <SC>Mal.</SC> The ballad here alluded to is &lquo;King Cophetua and the
Beggar-maid,&rquo; or, as it is called in some old copies, &lquo;The Song of a Beggar and a
King.&rquo; The following stanza Sh. had particularly in view:
<BQ>
&lquo;The <I>blinded</I> boy that <I>shoots</I> so <I>trim,</I><LB>
From heaven down did hie, [&lquo;so high,&rquo; Coll. (ed. 1).]<LB>
He drew a dart and shot at him,<LB>
In place where he did lie.&rquo; [<I>Sing. Coll. Verp. Huds.</I><LB>
</BQ>
<P><SC>Nares</SC>. The song is extant in Percy's Reliques, vol. i, p. 198, and is several times
alluded to by Sh. and others. The name of the fair beggar-maid, according to that
authority, was Zenelophon, but Dr. Percy considered that as a corruption of Penelo-
phon, which is the name in the ballad. . . . It has been conjectured that there was
some old drama on this subject, from which, probably, the bombastic lines spoken
by Ancient Pistol were quoted: 2 Hen. IV: V, iii, 100, 101. The worthy monarch
seems to have been a favorite hero for a rant.
<P><SC>Knight</SC>. This ballad was amongst the most popular of old English ballads, allu-
sions to which were familiar to Sh.'s audience. Upon the authority of learned Mas-
ter &lquo;Moth,&rquo; in Love's Lab. L., I, ii, 114, it was an ancient ballad in Sh.'s day. We
have two versions of this ballad; the one in &lquo;A Collection of Old Ballads&rquo; [&lquo;quoted
by Grey in 1754&rquo; (ed. 2.)], the other in Percy's Reliques. Both of these composi-
tions appear as if they had been &lquo;newly writ o'er&rquo; not long before, or, perhaps, after
Sh.'s time. [A stanza of each is subjoined by Knight.] <SC>Ed.</SC>
<P><SC>Cambr</SC>. Pope was the first commentator who called attention to the ballad which
is alluded to in this passage, and it is remarkable that, with all his partiality for (Q<SUB>1</SUB>),
he did not adopt the reading &lquo;trim,&rquo; found both there and in the ballad. Percy, in a
note to the ballad printed in his <I>Reliques,</I> conjectured that Sh. had written &lquo;trim,&rquo;
not &lquo;true,&rquo; apparently without knowing that the word was found in (Q<SUB>1</SUB>). Capell, in
his note, says that he had retained &lquo;true&rquo; in his text, owing to his not having observed
the authority for the other reading.
<P><SC>Halliwell</SC> gives the ballad at length from Johnson's Crowne Garland of Goulden
Roses, 1612.

<P>18. <B>high forehead</B>] <SC>White</SC> [Note on <I>Two Gent.</I> IV, iv, 198]. &lquo;Forehead&rquo; was

court to the bald-browed Virgin Queen. There are fashions even in beauty.

<P>36. <B>laugh alone</B>] <SC>Knt.</SC> There are two lines here omitted by Steevens, which
Malone restored to the text. The lines are gross, but the grossness is obscure, and
if it were understood, could scarcely be called corrupting. The freedoms of Mer-
cutio arise out of his dramatic character; his exuberant spirit betrays him into levi-
ties which are constantly opposed to the intellectual refinement which rises above
such baser matter. But Pope rejected these lines,&mdash;Pope who, in the Rape of the
Lock, has introduced one couplet, at least, that would have disgraced the age of
Elizabeth. We do not print the two lines of Sh., for they can only interest the ver-
bal critic. But we distinctly record their omission. As far as we have been able to
trace,&mdash;and we have gone through the old eds. with an especial reference to this
matter,&mdash;these two lines constitute the <I>only</I> passage in the original eds. which has
been omitted by modern edd. With this exception there is not a passage in Sh.
which is not reprinted in every ed. except that of Bowdler's. And yet the writer in
Lardner's Cyclop&aelig;dia (Lives of Literary and Scientific Men) has ventured to make
the following assertion: &lquo;<I>Whoever has looked into the original editions of his dramas</I>
will be disgusted with the obscenity of his allusions. They absolutely teem with
the grossest improprieties,&mdash;more gross by far than can be found in any contemporary
dramatist.&rquo; The insinuation that the <I>original</I> editions contain improprieties that are
not to be found in <I>modern editions</I> is difficult to characterize without using expres-
sions that had better be avoided.
<P><SC>Del.</SC> (&lquo;<I>Lexikon</I>&rquo;). These lines, which are perfectly in keeping with Mercutio's
character, and are to be found in all the old eds., have hurt the delicacy of some of
the English critics to such an extent, that the latter have omitted them from the text,
which without them is unintelligible, in order thereby to give them the greater
prominence in their notes.

biographical Poems of Sh.</I>&rquo; p. 215.] <SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>He'd have mistook, and given me a <I>popperin.</I>&rquo; In the Atheist's Tragedy, by Cyril
Turner, 1611, there is much conceit about this pear. I am unable to explain it with
certainty, nor, indeed, does it appear to deserve explanation. Thus much may safely

<P>39. <B>truckle-bed</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>. A small bed made to run under a larger; <I>quasi</I>
trocle-bed, from <I>trochlea,</I> a low wheel or castor. It was generally appropriated to
a servant or attendant of some kind. This bed was the station of the lady's maid,
and of the page, or fool, to a nobleman, and was drawn out at night to the feet of
the principal bed, which was sometimes termed the standing-bed, as in Merry Wives,
IV, v. [<I>Dyce.</I>
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> The furniture of a sleeping-chamber in Sh.'s time consisted of a standing-
bed and a truckle-bed. (See <I>Merry Wives,</I> IV, v, 6.) The former was for the
master, the latter for the servant. It may seem strange, therefore, that Mercutio
should talk of sleeping in the bed of his page; but the next words,&mdash;&lquo;This <I>field-
bed,</I>&rquo;&mdash;will solve the difficulty. The field-bed, in this case, was the ground; but the
field-bed, properly so called, was the travelling-bed,&mdash;the <I>lit de champ,</I>&mdash;called in
old English the &lquo;trussyng-bedde.&rquo; The bed next beyond the luxury of the trussyng
bed was the truckle-bed; and therefore Sh. naturally takes that in preference to the
standing-bed. [<I>Huds. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> Mercutio simply means to say that he himself prefers at night movement
(<I>truckle-</I>beds were provided with rollers) to standing still, and at all events his bad
&lquo;truckle-bed&rquo; to the &lquo;field-bed.&rquo;

<P>weigh the skill shown in justifying him from his inconstancy by making us feel the
difference of his passion. Yet this, too, is a love in, although not merely of, the

<P><SC>Sta.</SC> It has been disputed whether Romeo, overhearing Mercutio's banter, refers
to that, or to his having believed himself, before he saw Juliet, so invincible in his
love for Rosaline, that no other beauty could move him. We feel no doubt that the
allusion is to Mercutio; indeed, the rhyme in <I>found</I> and <I>wound</I> seems purposely
intended to carry on the connection of the speeches; and at this moment Rosaline
is wholly forgotten.
<P><SC>White</SC>. In the Qq and Ff, from the beginning of this Act to the entrance of the
<I>Friar,</I> there is not the slightest implication of a supposed change of scene, but
rather the contrary; and the arrangement in question [Rowe's] seems to have been
the consequence of an assumption that <I>Benvolio's</I> remark (II, i, 5) is made on the
outside of the wall; whereas the text rather implies that the whole of this Act, from
the entrance of <I>Romeo</I> to his exit after his interview with <I>Juliet,</I> passes within
<I>Capulet's</I> garden; for after the stage direction, &lquo;<I>Enter</I> Romeo <I>alone</I>&rquo; (which has a
like particularity in all the old copies), <I>Romeo</I> says, &lquo;Can I go forward while my
heart is <I>here?</I>&rquo;&mdash;not in the street, or outside the wall, but <I>here,</I> in the dwelling-place
of his love, which is before his eyes. After he speaks the next lines, the old copies
(from the absence of scenery) could not direct him to &lquo;climb the wall and leap down
within it;&rquo; but, had he been supposed to do this, some intimation would have been
given that he was to go out of eye-shot of <I>Mer.</I> and <I>Benv.;</I> as, for instance, in
Love's Lab. L., where (IV, iii) <I>Birone</I> is supposed to mount a tree, we have the
direction, &lquo;<I>He steps aside.</I>&rquo; But in the present case nothing of the kind appears, even
in the notably particular indications of (Q<SUB>1</SUB>). Again, <I>Benvolio's</I> remark that <I>Romeo</I>
&lquo;<I>hath hid</I> himself among <I>these trees</I>&rquo; must surely be made within the enclosure where
<I>Romeo</I> is, unless we suppose <I>Benv.</I> able to see farther into a stone wall than most
folk can; while what he previously says about &lquo;<I>this</I> orchard wall&rquo; means merely the
wall of this orchard (as in <I>Romeo's</I> after speech, line 66), and implies no particular
nearness of the barrier. Finally, in QqFf we find that the last line of <I>Benvolio's</I>
last speech and the first of <I>Romeo's</I> soliloquy make a rhyming couplet, and are
printed together without any direction for the entrance of <I>Romeo.</I>
<P>Therefore I have felt obliged to vary from the previous modern arrangement of
this Act, and to make but one Scene of what has been made by other editors two.
It has also been the custom hitherto to direct <I>Juliet</I> to appear before <I>Romeo's</I> excla-
mation at seeing the light. I have a purpose in making him see the light (as he
naturally would) before he sees <I>Juliet,</I> which, to those who share my appreciation
of the passage, will excuse what may seem to others a trifling, if not a needless, change.
<P><SC>Cambr.</SC> As there is no indication in the Qq and Ff of Romeo's entrance here,
it is not impossible that in the old arrangement of the scene the wall was rep-
resented as dividing the stage, so that the audience could see Romeo on one side
and Mercutio on the other. It is clear from the first line of Romeo's speech that he
overhears what Mercutio says; and though we have not altered the usual arrange-
ment, we cannot but feel that there is an awkwardness in thus separating the two
lines of a rhyming couplet.

<P>8. <B>sick and green</B>] <SC>Coll.</SC> [&lquo;<I>Notes and Emend.</I>&rquo;]. &lquo;White and green&rquo; had been
the royal livery in the reign of Henry VIII, but Elizabeth changed it to scarlet and
black; and although motley was the ordinary dress of fools and jesters, it is capable
of proof that, earlier than the time of Sh., the fools and jesters of the court (and
perhaps some others) were still dressed in &lquo;white and green;&rquo; thus it became pro-
verbially the livery of fools. Will Summer (who lived until 1560, and was buried
at Shoreditch on the 15th of June of that year) wore &lquo;white and green,&rquo; and the
circumstance is thus mentioned in &lquo;Certain Edicts of Parliament,&rquo; at the end of the
edition of Sir Thomas Overbury's &lquo;Wife,&rquo; in 1614: &lquo;Item, no fellow shall begin to
argue with a woman, &amp;c., unless he wear <I>white</I> for William and <I>green</I> for Summer&rquo;&mdash;
that is, unless he be a fool like Will Summer. In Fox's &lquo;Acts and Monuments,&rquo; iii,
114, a story is told of a person, who, noticing the colors in which St. John had been
painted by the Papists in St. Paul's, said, &lquo;I hope ye be but a <I>Summer's</I> bird, in that
ye be dressed in <I>white</I> and <I>green.</I>&rquo; Skelton wore &lquo;white and green&rquo; because he was
the royal jester, though he also assumed the rank of laureat. In the time of Sh. it
may have been discontinued as the dress even of court fools, but it may have been
traditionally so considered. [<I>White, Dyce</I> (ed. 2).

<P><I>sick</I> is to be <I>pale</I> in Sh.'s language; thus, &lquo;<I>sicklied</I> o'er with the <I>pale</I> cast of
thought,&rquo; &amp;c. &amp;c.
<P><SC>Del.</SC> The copula here joins what is one substantive idea: green-sickness&mdash;<I>i. e.,</I>
an ailment of languishing young girls.
<P><SC>Sing.</SC> (ed. 2). <I>Sick</I> was caught from the line above.
<P><SC>White</SC>. &lquo;<I>Sicke</I> and greene&rquo;&mdash;a strange combination of <I>colors</I> in a livery, though a
color might be <I>described</I> as sick. But it has hitherto been adopted without question,
I believe, and the variation of texts has remained unnoticed. The compositor ap-
pears to have been confused by a reminiscence of the epithets applied to the moon
in the third line above, and perhaps also by a passing thought of green-sickness
which they suggested, and so repeated the first instead of the second of those epi-
thets. Collier (MS.) offers a violent though specious change, which is made
entirely unnecessary by the reading of (Q<SUB>1</SUB>), and which yet gives an independent
support to that reading. So also does <I>Macbeth,</I> I, vii, 37.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC>. (ed. 2). Whichever epithet [pale or sick] we prefer, there will still be a
slight awkwardness, as both words occur three lines above; but <I>pale</I> is doubtless the
more proper epithet here.
<P>9. <B>cast it off</B>] <SC>White</SC>. We know, from what Romeo says in line 27, that Sh.
imagined Juliet to be at an elevated window or balcony, although no old copy has a
stage-direction to that effect. Our old stage, in spite of its lack of scenery, per-
mitted this scene to be played with a very exact likeness to reality. <I>Juliet</I> could
appear at the window, which opened on the balcony at the back of the stage, draw
the curtain, and, after pausing a few moments, as a girl would naturally do under
the circumstances (during which her lover might, though <I>feeling</I> sure, be unable to
<I>see</I> surely, who it was), step out upon the balcony. And so it doubtless was repre-
sented, and should now be. For this gives a meaning to Romeo's exclamations, &lquo;It
<I>is</I> my lady; O, it <I>is</I> my love!&rquo; which seem somewhat superfluous, to say the least, if
<I>Juliet</I> bolts right out when <I>Romeo's</I> attention is first attracted by the light from her
window, according to modern custom on the stage and the supposition of modern
texts. It is worthy of remark that these exclamations do not appear in (Q<SUB>1</SUB>).

<P>31. <B>lazy-pacing</B>] <SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 1). The origin of the corruption in QqFf possibly
was that in the manuscript from which Q<SUB>2</SUB> was printed &lquo;lazy-pacing&rquo; was written
<I>lazy-pa$$ing,</I> and the compositor misread the two <I>$$</I> for a double <I>f.</I> [<I>White.</I>
<P><SC>White</SC>. &lquo;The lazie <I>puffing</I> cloudes&rquo; affords such picturesque propriety of descrip-
tion that it is only after much hesitation that I adopt the reading of (Q<SUB>1</SUB>), suggestive
as that is; for the lazy puffing clouds are the slow-moving <I>cumuli</I> that puff them-
selves out into swelling breasts of rose-tinted white, and so have seemed to many a
dreamy eye &lquo;the bosom of the air.&rquo; But the epithet &lquo;lazy-pacing,&rquo; aside from its
beauty, has a strong hold in the word &lquo;bestrides,&rquo; which precedes it, and a powerful
auxiliary in a passage of that splendid outpouring of the extravagance of an over-
heated imagination&mdash;Macbeth's soliloquy, as he meditates the murder, where the
same fancy recurs, though fitly varied. (Macbeth I, vii, 21.) And so, although be-
tween two such readings an editor may be somewhat like <I>Captain Macheath</I> between
the two ladies who were so tenderly solicitous as to his fate, the impaired authority
of the folio in this play allows, I think, the more immediate context and the collat-
eral support of another unsuspected passage to decide the doubt.
