<P>39. <B>thyself, though</B>] <SC>Mal.</SC> Thou art, <I>however,</I> says Juliet, a being <I>sui generis,</I>
amiable and perfect, not tainted by the enmity which your family bears to mine.
According to the common punctuation, the adversative particle is used without any
propriety, or rather makes the passage nonsense. <I>Though</I> is again used by Sh. in
Mid-Sum. N. D., III, ii, 343, in the same sense. Again in Tam. the Shrew, III, ii,
26. Again in Henry VIII: II, ii, 84. Other writers frequently use <I>though</I> for <I>how-
ever.</I> Juliet is simply endeavoring to account for Romeo's being amiable and excel-
lent, though he <I>is</I> a Montague. And to prove this she asserts that he merely bears
the name, but has none of the qualities of that House. [<I>Sta. Dyce</I> (ed. 2).
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> Juliet places his personal qualities in opposition to what she thought evil
of his family. [Mr. Knight has this same note in both his first and last editions,
although he has a different punctuation in each.] <SC>Ed.</SC>
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> [After quoting the last two sentences of Malone's note, as above, adds]:
Nothing can be more foreign to her meaning. Her imagination is powerfully ex-
cited by the intelligence she has just received: &lquo;His name is Romeo, and a <I>Mon-
tague!</I>&rquo; In that name she sees an insurmountable impediment to her new-formed
wishes, and in the fancied apostrophe to her lover, she eloquently implores him to
abandon it:

<P>The number of passages in Drayton's &lquo;Heroical Epistles&rquo; almost identical with
lines of Sh. prove that the one must have been indebted to the other. I would
accuse neither of plagiarism. Property was hardly acknowledged in Parnassus at
that time. There might be no deception meant; marginal acknowledgments were
not then appended to plays or poems. It was taken for granted that every writer
availed himself of whatever was to his purpose. These resemblances, however, are
for the most part in those early plays of Sh. which might have been written before
1593, the date, according to Dr. Anderson, of Drayton's &lquo;Heroical Epistles,&rquo; the
style of which throughout, both in the fashion of the language and constitution of
the thought, is more Sh'n than any I am acquainted with. What a pity that none
of Drayton's plays are extant! What they might be in point of plot is hard to say,
but in the <G>le/cis</G> and <G>dia/noia</G> I doubt not they were truly dramatic. The Merry Devil
of Edmonton does not read like him. It has none of the impassioned sententious-
ness of his epistles, which are a kind of monodrame.

<P>108. <B>tips with silver</B>] <SC>Holt White</SC>. This image struck Pope: &lquo;The <I>moonbeam</I>
trembling falls, And <I>tips with silver all</I> the walls.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Imit. of Horace.</I> Again, in the
celebrated simile on the <I>moon</I> at the conclusion of the eighth book of the Iliad:

<P><SC>Verp.</SC> Tom Moore has put it to a profane use in the way of parody, when, alluding

makes it, &lquo;&mdash;&mdash; tip his whiskers' top with red.&rquo;
<P>109. <B>the moon</B>] <SC>Hunter</SC>. This was a commonplace comparison when Sh.
made it, and has been made more commonplace by his successful use of it. Thus
Wilson, in his <I>Rhetorique,</I> chapter on Amplification, &lquo;as in speaking of constancy,
to shew the sun who ever keepeth one course; in speaking of inconstancy, to shew
the moon which keepeth no certain course.&rquo; I have already remarked upon the
resemblance of the moonlit garden of Verona to the moonlit garden of Belmont;
both scenes among the most delicious creations of fancy. At Belmont the silver
light of the moon fell upon a pair not unhappily united; here it falls on an impas-
sioned youth in the hour of his proudest exultation, soon to be followed by deepest
anxieties, misery and death. Such is life!

question.

<P>116. <SC>Coleridge</SC> (&lquo;<I>Lit. Rem.</I>&rquo; vol. ii, p. 154). With love, pure love, there is al-
ways an anxiety for the safety of the object, a disinterestedness by which it is distin-
guished from the counterfeits of its name. Compare this scene with The Tempest,
III, i. I do not know a more wonderful instance of Sh.'s mastery in playing a dis-
tinctly rememberable variation on the same remembered air than in the transporting
love-confessions of Romeo and Juliet and Ferdinand and Miranda. There seems
more passion in the one, and more dignity in the other; yet you feel that the sweet
girlish lingering and busy movement of Juliet, and the calmer and more maidenly
fondness of Miranda, might easily pass into each other. [<I>Knt. Verp. Huds.</I>

<P>153. <B>To-morrow</B>] <SC>Clarke.</SC> Exquisitely has Sh. made Juliet pause not a moment
on the impossible alternative that Romeo &lquo;means&rquo; otherwise than &lquo;well.&rquo; The breath-
less hurry with breathing earnestness in all that Juliet utters during this scene is
marvellously true to the pulsing rapture of a young girl's heart on first learning that
she loves and is beloved.
<P>159. <B>tassel-gentle</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> The <I>tassel</I> or <I>tiercel</I> (for so it should be spelt) is the
male of the <I>gosshawk;</I> so called because it is a <I>tierce</I> or <I>third</I> less than the female.
This is equally true of all birds of prey. This species of hawk had the epithet <I>gentle</I>
annexed to it, from the ease with which it was tamed, and its attachment to man.
[<I>Sing. Coll. Verp. Huds. Sta. Cham.</I>] In the Booke of Falconrye, by George Turber-
ville, Gent., 1575, I find a whole chapter on the <I>falcon-gentle,</I> &amp;c. So in The
Guardian, by Massinger: &lquo;&mdash;&mdash; then for an evening flight, A <I>tiercel-gentle.</I>&rquo; Taylor,
the Water poet, uses the same expression: &lquo;&mdash;&mdash; by casting out the lure, makes the
<I>tassell gentle</I> come to her fist.&rquo; [<I>Cham.</I>] Again in Spenser's Fairy Queen, b. iii,
c. iv: &lquo;Having far off espyde a <I>tassel-gent.</I>&rquo; In Decker's Match me in London,
1631: &lquo;Your <I>tassel-gentle,</I> she's lur'd off and gone.&rquo; [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Mal.</SC> It appears that certain hawks were considered as appropriated to certain
ranks. The <I>tercel-gentle</I> was appropriated to the prince, and thence was chosen by
Juliet as an appellation of her beloved Romeo. In an ancient treatise entitled
&lquo;Hawking, Hunting, and Fishing, with the True Measures of Blowing,&rquo; is the fol-
lowing: &lquo;For a Prince, There is a falcon gentle, and a <I>tercel</I> gentle; and these are
for a prince.&rquo; [Substantially, <I>Sing. Verp. Huds. Sta. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Nares.</SC> This species of hawk was no less commonly termed a <I>falcon-gentle</I>&mdash;so
called, says the Gentleman's Recreation, &lquo;for her familiar, courteous disposition.&rquo;
<P><SC>Sing.</SC> Tardif, in his book of Falconry, says that the tiercel has its name from
being one of three birds usually found in the aerie of a falcon, two of which are
females, and the <I>third</I> a male, hence called <I>tiercelet</I> or the <I>third.</I> [<I>Huds. Sta.
Clarke.</I>
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> The falconer's voice was the voice which the hawk was constrained by

<P>habit to obey. Gervase Markham, in his &lquo;Country Contentments,&rquo; has picturesquely
described the process of training hawks to this obedience, &lquo;by watching and keeping
them from sleep, by a continual carrying of them upon your fist, and by a most
familiar stroking and playing with them, with the wing of a dead fowl, or such like,
and by often gazing and looking them in the face with a loving and gentle counte-
nance.&rquo; A hawk so &lquo;manned&rquo; was brought to the lure &lquo;by easy degrees, and at last
was taught to know the voice and lure so perfectly that, either upon the sound of the
one or the sight of the other, she will presently come in, and be most obedient.&rquo; The
sport with a tassel-gentle is spiritedly described by Massinger:

&lquo;&mdash; Then for an evening flight<LB>
A tiercel-gentle, which I call, my masters,<LB>

by all old copies.
<P>23-30. <SC>Hunter.</SC> The beautiful lines given to the Friar are introduced for the
sake of repose; but in the choice of the topic in these seven lines the Poet seems to
have had a further view. Poison is hereafter to become a main agent in the piece,
and the Poet prepares the audience for the use of poison by familiarizing them, in the
early portion of the play, with the idea, and thus preparing them to witness the use
of it without being so much shocked as they would be were no such preparations
made. This is not the only passage in the earlier scenes in which poison is spoken

<P>of the Friar as one proof of Sh.'s atheism]. The Friar is more of a philosopher

<P>52. <B>physic lies</B>] <SC>M. Mason.</SC> This is one of the passages in which our author
has sacrificed grammar to rhyme.
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> Mason's observation is made in the same spirit in which he calls Romeo's
impassioned language &lquo;quaint jargon.&rquo; Before Sh. was accused of sacrificing gram-
mar, it ought to have been shown that his idiom was essentially different from that
of his predecessors and his contemporaries. [Knight here quotes Percy and Tollet
as cited by Ulrici in the Prologue.] Malone has rightly stated the principle upon
which such idioms, which appear false concords to us, should be corrected; that is,
&lquo;to substitute the modern idiom in all places except where either the metre or rhyme
renders it impossible.&rquo; But to those who can feel the value of a slight sprinkling of
our antique phraseology, it is pleasant to drop upon the instances in which correction
<I>is</I> impossible. We would not part with the exquisite bit of false concord, as we
must now term it, in the last word of the four following lines for all that Sh.'s gram-
mar-correctors have ever written:
<BQ>
&lquo;Hark! hark! the lark at heaven's gate sings,<LB>
And Ph&oelig;bus 'gins arise,<LB>
His steeds to water at those springs<LB>
On chalic'd flowers that lies.&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P><SC>Sing.</SC> Sh. must not be tried by rules which were invented after his time. We
have the same grammatical construction in Venus and Adonis, 1128: &lquo;Where lo!
<I>two lamps</I> burnt out in darkness <I>lies.</I>&rquo; Again in I, iv, 91 of this play.
<P><SC>Delius.</SC> By a Shakespearian license, the singular verb <I>lies</I> follows the plural <I>both
our remedies,</I> not only because the two singular nouns <I>help</I> and <I>physic</I> separate the
verb from its subject, but because the plural, <I>remedies,</I> arose from its connection with
<I>both,</I> and <I>both our remedies</I> is in reality a singular&mdash;the <I>remedy of both of us.</I> Thus
in All's Well, I, iii, &lquo;both our mothers&rquo;&mdash;the mother of both of us. Also in Cymbe-
line, II, ii: &lquo;both your wills&rquo;&mdash;the will of both of you.
<P><SC>White.</SC> The apparent want of grammatical agreement here is the result neither
of ignorance nor oversight. [In a note on Cymbeline, II, iii, 21.] The disagree-
ment in number between &lquo;lies&rquo; and its nominative is not worth all that has been
written about it. A relic of an old usage, it was common enough in Sh.'s day.
</CC>

<P>the expression, &lquo;a white wench's black eye,&rquo; strike us as significant. It seems to us
that in depicting both the characters to whom he has given the name of Rosaline,
Sh. had some special living woman before his mind's eye as their prototype. The
few vivid lines with which he has touched in the sketch of Romeo's Rosaline, un-
seen as she is in the play, accord perfectly with the recurrent delineations and more
elaborated portrait of Biron's Rosaline in &lquo;Love's Lab. L.&rquo; It is a subject of ex-
tremely interesting investigation, for so little is to be gathered of a personal nature
from Sh.'s dramatic writings&mdash;he, like a perfect dramatist, merging self entirely in
the characters he draws&mdash;that every indication, however slight, by which we may
obtain a glimpse of himself or those he knew, is most valuable. Viewed by the
light afforded from Massey's &lquo;<I>Sh.'s Sonnets, &amp;c.,</I>&rquo; the woman who was the original
for the portrait in &lquo;Love's L. L.&rquo; and the sketch here (both of them &lquo;Rosalines&rquo;)
should be Lady Rich: but, however the truth may be with regard to her individual
identity, we have a firm belief that she was an actual woman known to Sh. in the
life.
<P>12. <B>being dared</B>] <SC>Del.</SC> The play upon dare, to venture, and dare, to challenge,
occurs also in 2 Hen. VI: III, ii, 203.
<P>15. <B>pin</B>] <SC>Mal.</SC> The allusion is to archery. The clout or white mark at which
the arrows are directed was fastened by a black <I>pin</I> placed in the centre of it. [<I>Knt.
Coll. Verp. White.</I>] To hit this was the highest ambition of every marksman.
[<I>Huds. Cham.</I>] In No Wit like a Woman's, by Middleton, 1657: &lquo;I'll <I>cleave</I> the
black <I>pin</I> in the midst of the <I>white.</I>&rquo; In Marlowe's Tamburlaine, 1590: &lquo;Our crown,
the <I>pin</I> that thousands seek to <I>cleave.</I>&rquo; [<I>Sing.</I>
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> To <I>cleave the pin</I> was to split the wooden peg which attached the target to
the butt.
<P>16. <B>butt-shaft</B>] <SC>Nares.</SC> A kind of arrow used for shooting at butts; formed
without a barb, so as to stick into the butts, and yet be easily extracted. [<I>Dyce.</I>

<P>18. <B>prince of cats</B>] <SC>Warb.</SC> <I>Tybert</I> is the name given to the <I>cat</I> in &lquo;Reynard
the Fox.&rquo; [<I>Sing. Knt. Coll. Huds. Cham. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Steev.</SC> So in Decker's Satiromastix, 1602: &lquo;tho' you were <I>Tybert,</I> the long-
tail'd prince of cats.&rquo; Again, in Have with You to Saffron Walden, 1598 [cor-
rected to 1596 by Coll. (ed. 1)]: &lquo;not <I>Tibalt</I> prince of <I>cats.</I>&rquo; [<I>Sing. Huds. Cham.
Sta. Hal. Clarke.</I>
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> <I>Tibert, Tybert,</I> or <I>Tybalt</I> are forms of the ancient name <I>Thibault.</I> When
or why the cat was first so called it is, perhaps, hopeless now to inquire. The earliest
instance cited by the commentators is in &lquo;Reynard the Fox&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;Then the King called
for <I>Sir Tibert,</I> the cat, and said to him, <I>Sir Tibert,</I> you shall go to Reynard,&rquo; &amp;c.,
ch. vi; and the association was evidently not uncommon, for Jonson speaks of <I>cats</I>
as <I>tiberts.</I>
<P>19. <B>compliments</B>] <SC>Johnson.</SC> [in note on Love's Lab. L., I, i, quoted by <SC>Dyce</SC>
<I>in loc.</I>]. <I>Compliment,</I> in Sh.'s time, did not signify, at least did not only signify,
verbal civility, or phrases of courtesy; but, according to its original meaning, the
trappings or ornamental appendages of a character; in the same manner, and on the
same principles of speech, with <I>accomplishment. Complement</I> is, as Armado well
expresses it, <I>the varnish of a complete man.</I> A <I>captain</I> of compliments is a com-
plete master of all the laws of ceremony, the principal man in the doctrine of
punctilio.
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> One versed in punctilios, of <I>point-de-vice</I> manners,&mdash;a formalist. &lquo;He walks
most commonly with a clove or pick-tooth in his mouth; he is the very mint of com-
pliment; all his behaviors are printed; his face is another volume of essays; and
his beard is an Aristarchus.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ben Jonson's</SC> <I>Cynthia's Revels</I> (Gifford's ed.), vol ii,
p. 264.
<P>20. <B>prick-song</B>] <SC>Nares.</SC> Music written down, sometimes, more particularly,
music in parts, from the points or dots with which it is noted down. See Hawkins,
ii, 243. Hence the nightingale's song, being more regularly musical than any other,
was often termed <I>prick-song.</I> When opposed to plain song it meant counter-point,
as distinguished from mere melody.
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> Music pricked or noted down, so as to read according to rule, in contradis-
tinction to music learnt by the ear or sung from memory. [<I>Verp. Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> [quotes Chappell's &lquo;Popular Music of the Olden Time,&rquo; &amp;c., vol. i, p. 51,
note, ed. 2]: &lquo;harmony written or pricked down, in opposition to plain-song,
where the descant rested with the will of the singer.&rquo;

<P>22. <B>duellist</B>] <SC>Knt.</SC> George Wither, in his obsequies upon the death of Prince
Henry, thus introduces Britannia lamenting: &lquo;Alas! who now shall grace my tourna-
ments, Or honour me with deeds of chivalrie?&rquo; The tournaments and the chivalrie
were then, however, but &lquo;an insubstantial pageant faded.&rquo; Men had learnt to
revenge their private wrongs without the paraphernalia of heralds and warders. In
the old chivalrous times, they might suppress any outbreak of hatred or passion, and
cherish their malice against each other until it could be legally gratified; so that,
according to the phrase of Richard C&oelig;ur-de-Lion, in his ordinance for permitting
tournaments, &lquo;the peace of our land be not broken, nor justice hindred, nor damage
done to our forests.&rquo; The private contests of two knights were a violation of the
laws of chivalry. Chaucer has a remarkable exemplification of this in his &lquo;Knight's
Tale,&rquo; where the Duke, coming to the plain, saw Arcite and Palamon fighting like
two bulls, and says:
<BQ>
&lquo;But telleth me what mistere men ye been,<LB>
That be so hardy for to fighten here<LB>
Withouten any judge or other officer,<LB>
As though it were in list&eacute;s really&rquo; (royally).<LB>
</BQ>
<P>That duels were frequent in England in the reign of Elizabeth, we might collect, if
there were no other evidence, from Sh. alone. The matter had been reduced to a
science. The degrees in quarreling were called the causes; and these have been
most happily ridiculed by Sh. in As You Like It, V, iv, 63-77. When Touchstone
alludes to &lquo;the book,&rquo; he refers to the works of Saviolo and Caranza, who laid down
laws for the duello. The wit of Sh. is the best commentary upon the philosophy of
Montaigne: &lquo;Inquire why that man hazards his life and honour upon the fortune of
his rapier and dagger; let him acquaint you with the occasion of the quarrel, he
cannot do it without blushing, 'tis so idle and frivolous.&rquo;&mdash;(<I>Essays,</I> book iii, ch. 10.)
But philosophy and wit were equally unavailing to put down the quarrelsome spirit
of the times; and Henry IV of France in vain declared all duellists guilty of l&egrave;se-
majest&eacute;, and punishable by death; and James I of England as vainly denounced
them in the Star-Chamber. The practice of duelling went on with us till the civil
wars came to merge private quarrels in public ones. Burton, in his &lquo;Anatomy of
Melancholy,&rquo; has a bitter satire against the nobility, when he says, they are &lquo;like our
modern Frenchmen, that had rather lose a pound of blood in a single combat than
a drop of sweat in any honest labour.&rquo;

<P>duellists, and one who understands the whole science of quarreling, and will tell

Huds.</I>] Tybalt could not pretend to be the head of his family, as both Capulet and
Romeo barred his claim to that elevation.
<P><SC>Mal.</SC> We find the same expression in Fletcher's Women Pleas'd: &lquo;a gentleman's
gone then; A gentleman of the first house; there's the end of't.&rquo; [<I>Sta.</I>
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> Mercutio's mockery is not directed against the practice of duelling in the
abstract, for he appears to be almost as pugnacious as the fiery Tybalt himself. He
is ridiculing the professors and <I>alumni</I> of those academies established in London
during the latter part of the 16th century for the study of &lquo;The Noble Science of
Defence,&rquo; as it was called,&mdash;a class who appear to have prided themselves on the
punctilious observance of certain forms and an affected diction, which had been
rendered fashionable by the treatises of Saviolo [&lquo;<I>Practise of the Duello,</I>&rquo; Vinc.
Saviolo, 1595] and Caranza. The most obvious meaning of the words, &lquo;A gentle-
man of the very first house,&rquo; appears to be that Tybalt was a gentleman-scholar &lquo;of
the very first house&rquo; or school of fencing of the greatest teacher existing at the
period. In George Silver's <I>Paradoxes of Defence,</I> Lond., 1599, it is stated that
there were three &lquo;Italian Teachers of Offence;&rquo; the first of whom was Signior Rocco,
who had come into England thirty years before. &lquo;He disbursed a great summe of
mony for the lease of a house in Warwicke-lane, which he called his colledge, for
he thought it a great disgrace for him to keepe a fence-schoole, he being then
thought to be the only famous maister of the arte of armes in the whole world.&rquo; &lquo;He
taught none commonly under twentie, forty, fifty or an hundred pounds.&rquo; To be,
therefore, a gentleman of such a house as this, was really &lquo;a very ribband in the cap
of youth.&rquo; In the same tract occurs a curious illustration of another expression in
the same speech of <I>Mercutio:</I> &lquo;the very butcher of a silk button.&rquo; &lquo;One Austen
Bagger, a verie tall gentleman of his handes,&rquo; resolved to encounter Signior Rocco,
and went to another house which he had in the Blackfriars, &lquo;and called to him in
this manner: &ldquo;Signior Rocco, thou that art thought to be the only cunning man in
the world with thy weapons; <I>thou that takest upon thee to hit anie Englishman with
a thrust upon anie button . . .</I> I am come to fight with thee.&rdquo;&rquo; To Warburton's
explanation Steevens objects that both Capulet and Romeo preceded Tybalt in gene-
alogical rank; but the truth is that neither of them at all interfered with such claim.
Romeo was of the house of Capulet only by marriage with Juliet; and in the list
of persons represented in the tragedy, Tybalt is called <I>Nephew to Lady Capulet.</I>
The real heraldical reference, if that be the genuine sense of the passage, appears to
have been quite overlooked. When the bearing of armorial ensigns became reduced
to a science, a series of differences was instituted, the more readily to distinguish
between the arms borne by the several sons and descendants of the same family, and
to show their order and consanguinity. They consisted of six small figures, called
a label, crescent, mullet, martlet, annulet, and fleur-de-lis, which were always to be
placed in the most prominent part of the coat-armour. These signs, borne singly,
were for the sons of the original ancestors, who constituted that which heralds

<P>The <I>passado,</I> more properly <I>passata,</I> meant a step forward or aside in fencing: &lquo;If

<P>29. <B>grandsire</B>] <SC>Warb.</SC> Humourously apostrophizing his ancestors, whose sober

<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> I think that he applied this title to his friend, <I>Benvolio,</I> on account of the

<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. This appears to be addressed to Benvolio, partly in raillery of his staid

<P>36. <B>marry, she had a better love to be-rhyme her</B>] <SC>Ulr.</SC> I have enclosed

<P><SC>Gerald Massey</SC> (&lquo;<I>Sh. Sonnets,</I>&rquo; &amp;c., p. 473). Supposing my theory to be correct,
the perfection of the banter here,&mdash;as between Sh. and Southampton,&mdash;would lie in
an allusion unperceived by the audience, but well known to poet and patron as re-
lating to the Sonnets which were then being written. This would be no more than
his making public allusion to the Sonnets, as work in hand, when he dedicated the
poem of &lquo;Lucrece.&rquo; Besides, Sh. may be the original of Mercutio (see Ben Jonson's
description of his liveliness); he may even be playing the part on the stage to Bur-
bage's Romeo, and the joke at his own and his friend's expense would be greatly
heightened by an arch look at Southampton sitting on the stage in &lquo;the Lord's
places, on the very rushes where the comedy is to dance.&rquo; Many things would be
conveyed to the initiated friends by the Poet's humour thus slyly playing bo-peep
from behind the dramatic mask.
<P>39. <B>grey eye</B>] <SC>Mal.</SC> He means to allow that Thisbe had a very fine eye, for it
appears that a grey eye was in Sh.'s time thought eminently beautiful. This may
seem strange to those who are not conversant with ancient phraseology; but a <I>grey
eye</I> undoubtedly meant what we now denominate a <I>blue</I> eye. [<I>Corn.</I>] Thus in
Venus and Adonis: &lquo;Her two <I>blue</I> windows faintly she upheaveth,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> the win-
dows or lids of her <I>blue</I> eyes. In the very same poem the eyes of Venus are termed
grey: &lquo;Mine eyes are <I>grey</I> and bright, and quick in turning.&rquo; [Subs. <I>Sing. Knt.
Verp. Huds.</I>

<P>44. <B>slip</B>] <SC>Reed</SC>. &lquo;And therefore he went and got him certain <I>slips</I> which are

<P><SC>Halliwell</SC>. Nash, in his Life of Jacke Wilton, 1594, has the following passage:
&lquo;Aie me, shee was but a <I>counterfeit slip,</I> for she not only gave me the slip,&rquo; &amp;c. &lquo;Is
he not fond then which a slip receaves For currant money?&rquo;&mdash;<I>Skialetheia or a
Shadowe of Truth,</I> 1598.
<P>48. <B>to bow in the hams</B>] <SC>Ulr.</SC> <I>Ham</I> is the kneepan, which in polite obeisance
(as in kneeling) was bent outwardly. &lquo;To bow <I>in</I> the hams,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> to bend the knee
inwardly, is expressive of the opposite, namely, of impoliteness. But <I>Ham</I> signifies
also the thigh, and what Mercutio's indecent tongue means &lquo;by bending in the ham&rquo;
cannot be doubtful.

<P>when Warwick says, &lquo;Sweet King! the bishop hath a <I>kindly gird,</I>&rquo; he does not
mean, as it has been interpreted, &lquo;a reproof meant in kindness,&rquo; but an <I>apposite</I>
reproof, a reproof in <I>kind.</I> This sense of the word is very clearly shown in a pass-
age in Middleton's play, &lquo;The Mayor of Queenborough,&rquo; III, iii, where Vortigern,
having discovered the trick of Hengist in cutting the hide into <I>thongs,</I> tells him his
castle shall be called <I>Thong</I> Castle; to which the latter replies: &lquo;there your grace
quites me <I>kindly.</I>&rquo;
<P><SC>White</SC>. That is, in kind; your reply was of a piece with my speech.
<P>55. <B>pump well flowered</B>] <SC>Johns</SC>. Here is a vein of wit too thin to be easily
found. The fundamental idea is, that Romeo wore <I>pinked</I> pumps,&mdash;that is, punched
in holes with figures. [<I>Sing. Corn. Huds. Dyce, Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Steev.</SC> See the shoes of the morris-dancers in the plate [from Tollet's painted
window, where the figures marked 4 and 10 have pinked shoes] at the conclusion
of 1 Hen. IV. [Var., vol. xvi.] [<I>Dyce.</I>] It was the custom to wear ribbons in
the shoes, formed into the shape of roses or of any other flowers. [<I>Knt.</I>] So in
<I>The Masque of Flowers,</I> acted by the Gentlemen of Gray's-Inn, 1614: &lquo;Every
masker's <I>pump</I> was fasten'd with a <I>flower</I> suitable to his cap.&rquo; [<I>Sing. Corn. Verp.
Huds. Hal. Clarke.</I>
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> Neither flowers, nor ribbons in the shape of flowers, were worn on &lquo;pumps&rquo;
(that is, dancing-shoes, or shoes in general), as the English commentators assert,&mdash;
the passage adduced in proof of it by Steevens does not show what it purports to
do,&mdash;but Romeo continues to pun on the word <I>pink,</I> a point [<I>spitze</I>], a flower, and
says, in effect: if <I>pink</I> is for flower, then my shoes&mdash;which were then worn very
pointed [<I>zugespitzt</I>]&mdash;&lquo;are well flowered.&rquo;
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> The idea seems to be,&mdash;my shoe or <I>pump,</I> being <I>pinked</I> or punched with
holes, is well <I>flowered.</I> There may be also a latent allusion to the custom referred
to by Steevens.
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. These ornaments are still used for women's shoes, and called &lquo;rosettes.&rquo;
<P>59. <B>single-soled</B>] <SC>Mal.</SC> It formerly signified <I>mean</I> or <I>contemptible;</I> and that is
one of the senses in which it is used here. In Holinshed's <I>Ireland,</I> p. 23: &lquo;which
was not unlikely, considering that a <I>meane</I> tower might serve such <I>single-soale</I> kings
as were at those daies in Ireland.&rquo;

<P><SC>Sing.</SC> Malone and Steevens have made strange work with their conjectures on the
meaning of <I>single-soled.</I> I have shown (vol. v, p. 270, note 20) that <I>single</I> meant
<I>simple,</I> silly. <I>Single-soled</I> had also the same meaning: &lquo;He is a good <I>sengyll soule,</I>
and can do no harm; est doli nescius non simplex.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Horman's Vulgaria.</I> The
&lquo;<I>single soule</I> kings,&rquo; the &lquo;<I>single sole</I> fidler,&rquo; and the &lquo;<I>single soal'd</I> gentlewoman,&rquo; were
all <I>simple</I> persons. It sometimes was synonymous with <SC>threadbare</SC>, <I>coarse spun,</I>
and this is its meaning here. The worthy Cotgrave explains, &lquo;Monsieur de trois au
boisseau et de trois &agrave; un &eacute;p&eacute;e: a threadbare, coarse-spun, <I>single-soled</I> gentleman.&rquo;
[<I>Huds. White, Dyce, Hal.</I>

Singer quotes the very same words), the reprint of Hall's &lquo;Satires&rquo; in 1824 is wrong,
for there &lquo;excite&rquo; is printed <I>incite:</I> the meaning is nearly the same, and we are only
anxious to be accurate, not having at hand any original copy of Hall's &lquo;Satires.&rquo;

<P>63. <B>wild-goose chase</B>] <SC>Holt White</SC>. One kind of horse-race, which resem-

started together, and whichever rider could get the lead, the other was obliged to
follow him over whatever ground the foremost jockey chose to go. [<I>Huds.</I>] That
horse which could distance the other won the race. See Chambers's <I>Dict.,</I> article
<SC>Chase</SC>. This barbarous sport is enumerated by Burton, in his Anatomy of Melan-
choly, as a recreation much in vogue in his time among gentlemen: &lquo;Riding of great
horses, running at ring, tilts and turnaments, horse-races, <I>wild-goose</I> chases, are the dis-
ports of great men.&rquo;&mdash;P. 266, ed. 1632, fol. [<I>Sing. Huds. Sta. White, Dyce, Hal.</I>

<P>91. <B>Enter Nurse . . . . smock</B>] <SC>Ulrici.</SC> I cannot see why Romeo should not
add &lquo;A sail, a sail!&rquo; by way of explaining his exclamation, &lquo;Here's goodly gear!&rquo;
At all events, the words that follow, &lquo;Two, two,&rquo; &amp;c., are far more appropriate from
Mercutio than from Benvolio.
<P><SC>White</SC>. Especially does the surreptitious 4to [(Q<SUB>1</SUB>)] appear to err (yet since
Malone's time&mdash;1790&mdash;it has hitherto been universally followed) in assigning that
most Mercutian exclamation, &lquo;Two, two; a shirt and a smock!&rquo; to the taciturn, cor-
rect, and commonplace <I>Benvolio.</I> It should be observed, too, that in this Scene,
both before and after the entrance of the <I>Nurse, Romeo</I> is in a very lively mood, and
rivals Mercutio in the brisk encounter of empty words; but <I>Benvolio</I> is not moved
from his usual quiet and decorum.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2). Mr. Grant White objects to the words &lquo;Two, two; a shirt and a
smock&rquo; being assigned to the taciturn, correct, and commonplace Benvolio, yet in his
note on the speech which presently follows, &lquo;she will indite him to some supper,&rquo; he
observes that &lquo;Benvolio can be slyly ironical.&rquo;
<P>94. <B>My fan</B>] <SC>Farmer</SC>. The business of Peter carrying the <I>Nurse's fan</I> seems

mistress must have one to carry her cloake and hood, another her <I>fanne.</I>&rquo; [<I>Sing.
Huds. Hal. Clarke.</I>
<P><SC>Steev.</SC> Again in Love's Lab. L., IV, i, 147. [<I>Sing. Huds. Clarke.</I>
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> [gives at the end of the Act a picture of the kind of fan which Peter had to
bear, and says]: It does not appear, therefore, quite so ridiculous, when we look
at the size of the machine, to believe that the Nurse should have a servant to
bear it.
<P><SC>Dr. F. T. Vischer</SC> (&lquo;<I>Aesthetik,</I>&rquo; &amp;c., 1857, vol. iii, p. 1201). When the Nurse
enters in all her finery, and begins, &lquo;Peter, my fan,&rquo; it must be a very stupid reader
who does not have instantly before him, in all essential features, the picture of the
silly old creature, faithful but vulgar, talkative but secretive, as full of vanity as of
wrinkles, tricked out in her ribbons, as, with bridling gait and nose upturned, she
affects the fine lady.

<P>96. <B>fairer of the two</B>] <SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 1). Some modern edd. have here adopted
the reading of no old copy, but have compounded a text out of several.
<P><SC>Huds.</SC> Divers modern eds. have compounded a third reading out of the two
[in (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) and Q<SUB>2</SUB>], which is hardly allowable anywhere, and something worse than
useless here, even if it were allowable.
<P>98. <B>God ye good den</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> That is, God give you a good even. The first
of these contractions is common among the ancient comic writers. So in R. Brome's
Northern Lass, 1633: <I>God you good even,</I> sir. [<I>Sing. Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Nares.</SC> This salutation was used by our ancestors as soon as noon was past, after
which time good morrow, or good day, was esteemed improper. [<I>Dyce.</I>
<P>99. <B>good den?</B>] <SC>Knt.</SC> Sh. had here English manners in his eye. The Italian
custom of commencing the day half an hour after sunset, and reckoning through the
twenty-four hours, is inconsistent with such a division of time as this.
<P><SC>Nares</SC>. <I>Good den</I> is a mere corruption of <I>good e'en</I> for good evening.
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> <I>Den</I> is probably derived from <I>day-even;</I> the two words were made into
one, because, according to the way of reckoning time in those days, <I>even</I> began im-
mediately after noon.
<P>101. <B>prick of noon</B>] <SC>Amner</SC> [the pseudonym of Steevens]. This hath already
occurred in 3 Hen. VI: I, iv: &lquo;And made an evening at the <I>noon-tide prick.</I>&rquo;
<I>Prick</I> meaneth <I>point&mdash;i. e.,</I> punctum, a note of distinction in writing, a stop. So in
Timothy Bright's <I>Characterie, or an Arte of Shorte, &amp;c., Writing by Characters,</I>
1588: &lquo;If the worde, by reason of tence, ende in ed, as I loved, then make a <I>prick</I>
in the character of the word, on the left side.&rquo; [<I>Sing. Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Dyce</SC>. That is, the point of noon, with a quibble.
<P>102. <B>Out . . . you</B>] <SC>Ulr.</SC> The indignant reply of the Nurse shows that Mercutio
must have meant something more than that it would soon be noon. &lquo;Noon&rquo; some-
times also signifies the middle of the night&mdash;<I>e. g.,</I> &lquo;the night advancing to her noon,&rquo;
or (in Dryden) &lquo;at the noon of night he saw,&rquo; &amp;c. Mercutio means therefore to say
that the looks of the Nurse point to the late evening (of her life), indeed even to the
midnight (perhaps also with an obscene allusion), and he probably indicated this
allusion by a gesture of his hand towards her bosom, on which account Schlegel
very well translates: &lquo;Your stomacher points to sundown.&rquo;

<P>130. <B>merchant</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> This term, which was, and still is, frequently applied
to the lowest sort of dealers, seems to have been used in contradistinction to <I>gentle-
man.</I> The term <I>chap,</I> i. e., <I>chapman,</I> a word of the same import with <I>merchant</I> in
its less respectable sense, is still in use among the vulgar as a general denomination
for any person of whom they mean to speak with freedom or disrespect. In Church-
yard's <I>Chance,</I> 1580: &lquo;What <I>saucie merchaunt</I> speaketh now, saied Venus in her
rage.&rquo; [<I>Sing. Sta.</I>
<P><SC>Douce.</SC> <I>Whetstone,</I> in his <I>Mirour for magestrates of cyties,</I> 1584, speaking of the
usurious practices of the citizens of London who attended the gaming-houses for the
purpose of supplying the gentlemen players with money, has the following: &lquo;The
extremity of these mens dealings hath beene and is so cruell as there is a natural
malice generally impressed in the hearts of the gentlemen of England towards the
citizens of London, insomuch as if they odiously name a man, they foorthwith call
him a <I>trimme merchaunt.</I> In like despight the citizen calleth every rascall a <I>joly
gentleman.</I> And truly this mortall envie betweene these two woorthie estates was
first engendred of the cruell usage of covetous merchaunts in hard bargaines gotten
of gentlemen, and nourished with malitious words and revenges taken of both par-
ties.&rquo; [<I>Knt. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Dyce</SC>. Compare, in <I>The Faire Maide of Bristow,</I> 1605, &lquo;What [s]ausie mer-
chant have you got there?&rquo; Sig. B. ii.
<P><SC>White</SC>. Sometimes used of old in the derogatory sense now attached to &lquo;huckster.
<P><SC>Halliwell</SC>. Barnaby Rich, in his New Description of Ireland, 1610, p. 69,
speaking of the shop-keepers of Dublin, says: &lquo;The trade that they commonly use
is but to London; from thence they do furnish themselves with all sortes of wares
for their shoppes, for shipping they have none belonging to the towne that is worth
the speaking of, yet they will bee called merchanttes; and hee that hath but a bar-
rell of salt or a barre or two of iron, in his shop, is called a merchant; he that doth
but sel earthen pottes and pannes, sope, otmeale, trenchers, and such other like
trash, is no lesse than a merchant: there bee shopkeepers in Dublin that all the
warres they are able to shewe are not worth a poore English pedlar's packe, and yet
all these bee merchantes.&rquo;

<P><SC>Douce</SC>. The word seems to have been deemed unworthy of a place in our early
dictionaries, and was probably coined in the mint of the slang or canting crew. It
savours strongly of the halter, and appears to have signified a low kind of knavish
waggery. From some other words of similar import it may derive illustration.
Thus a <I>rope-rype</I> is defined in Hul&aelig;t's <I>Abecedarium</I> to be &lquo;an ungracious waghalter,
<I>nequam;</I>&rquo; and in Minshew's dictionary, &lquo;one ripe for a rope, or for whom the gal-
lowes grones.&rquo; A <I>roper</I> has nearly the same definition in the English vocabulary at
the end of Thomasii <I>Dictionarium,</I> 1615; but the word occasionally denoted a crafty
fellow, or one who would practise a fraud against another (for which he might de-
serve hanging). So in the book of blasing of arms or coat-armour, ascribed to
Dame Juliana Berners, the author says, &lquo;which crosse I saw but late in tharmes of a
noble man; the which in very dede was sometyme <I>a crafty man, a roper,</I> as he him-
self sayd,&rquo; sig. Aij. b. <I>Roper</I> had also another sense, which, though rather foreign
to the present purpose, is so quaintly expressed in one of our old dictionaries that
the insertion of it will doubtless be excused: &lquo;Roper, <I>restio,</I> is he that looketh in at
John Roper's window by translation, he that hangeth himselfe.&rquo;&mdash;Hul&aelig;t's <I>Abceda-
rium</I> Anglico-Latinum, 1552, fo.
<P><SC>Nares</SC>. The same as roguery, well deserving of a rope.
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> Churchyard, in his &lquo;Choice&rquo; (Sign. Cc iii), uses <I>roperipe</I> as an adjective:
&lquo;But gallows lucke and <I>roperipe</I> happe.&rquo;
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> That is, <I>ribaldry.</I>
<P><SC>White</SC>. &lquo;Ropery,&rquo; &lquo;rope ripe&rquo; and &lquo;rope-tricks&rquo; were all used with humourous
reference to acts deemed worthy of hempen expiation; and these, in Sh.'s time, in-
cluded almost every violation of public order or the laws of property.
<P>138. <B>flirt-gills</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>. An arbitrary transposition of the compound word <I>gill-
flirt,</I> that is, a <I>flirting-gill,</I> a woman of light behavior. The <I>gilly-flower,</I> from the
resemblance of its name to the word <I>gill-flirt,</I> was considered as an emblem of false-
hood. <I>Gill</I> was a current and familiar term for a female. As in the proverb, &lquo;Every
Jack must have his <I>Gill,</I>&rquo; Ray says it ought to be written <I>Jyll,</I> being a familiar sub-
stitute for <I>Julia</I> or <I>Juliana. Gill,</I> however, may be safely written, for from Juli-
ana was derived the popular name <I>Gillian,</I> as well as <I>Gillet</I> from Julietta, either of
which would supply the abbreviation <I>Gill.</I>
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> The meaning of <I>flirt-gills</I> is not far to seek. It implied, like <I>fiz-gig,</I> an-
other term of the same age, a <I>wild, flirting, romping wench.</I>

where we may suppose the exercise of this weapon was taught. Green, in his Quip
for an Upstart Courtier, describes &lquo;an ill-favoured knave, who wore by his side a
<I>skeine</I> like a brewer's bung-knife.&rquo; <I>Skein</I> is the Irish word for a <I>knife.</I> [<I>Sing.</I>
(ed. 1), <I>Corn. Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Douce.</SC> The objection to these interpretations is, that the Nurse could not very
well compare herself with characters which it is presumed would scarcely be found
among females of any description. One commentator [M. Mason] thinks that she
uses <I>skains-mates</I> for <I>kins-mates,</I> but the existence of such a term may be questioned.
Besides, the Nurse blunders only in the use of less obvious words. The following
conjecture is therefore offered, but not with entire confidence in its propriety. It
will be recollected that there are <I>skeins of thread,</I> so that the good nurse may perhaps
mean nothing more than <I>sempstresses,</I> a word not always used in the most honorable
acceptation. She had before stated that she was &lquo;none of his flirt-gills.&rquo; [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Warner.</SC> I rather take it to mean one who assists in winding off a skein of silk,
for it must be done by two; and I am told these are at this time, among the weavers
in Spital-fields, looked upon as the lowest kind of people. [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Nares</SC>. A companion of some sort, from the term <I>mate;</I> but Mercutio and the
Nurse could not well be <I>mates,</I> either in <I>sword</I> play or in winding <I>skains</I> of silk.
I am inclined to think that the old lady means &lquo;roaring or swaggering companions.&rquo;
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 1). <I>Skene</I> is used by many writers of the time. R. Armin, in his
&lquo;Nest of Ninnies,&rquo; 1608 (reprinted by the Sh. Society), has this passage: &lquo;If I do
stick in the bogs, help me out&mdash;not with your good <I>skene</I> head me.&rquo;
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (&lquo;<I>Remarks,</I>&rquo; &amp;c.). This interpretation [Collier's approval of Malone] can-
not be right, because the Nurse is evidently speaking of Mercutio's <I>female</I> compan-
ions. The meaning of <I>skains-mates</I> (if not a misprint, which I suspect it is) remains
to be discovered. [<I>Sing.</I> (ed. 2), subs.
<P><SC>Huds.</SC> [Malone's interpretation and Dyce's objection quoted]. We do not quite
see how this should be decisive.
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). [Dyce's remark quoted that <I>female</I> associates are alluded to]. Just
the contrary; for she has already referred to his female companions as &lquo;flirt-gills.&rquo;
She means that she is no companion of his, whether female or not.
<P><SC>Walker</SC>. Read &lquo;<I>scurvy-</I>mates;&rquo; see context. Scurvy, in the old plays, is written
indiscriminately with an <I>sc</I> or an <I>sk,</I> a <I>y</I> or an <I>ie;</I> see this very passage. <I>Skuruie</I>
might easily be mistaken for <I>skaines</I> by an eye like that of a printer; perhaps, too,
the intrusive final <I>s</I> (Art. xxxviii) may have crept in here; though there is no need
of calling in its assistance.
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> This has been a sore puzzle to all the commentators. The difficulty, after
all, proves of easy solution. The word <I>skain,</I> I am told by a Kentishman, was for-
merly a familiar term in parts of Kent to express what we now call a <I>scape-grace</I> or

<P>178. <B>Is your,</B> &amp;c.] <SC>Mommsen</SC> (&lquo;<I>Proleg.,</I>&rquo; p. 144). Sh. does not by any means
follow Marlowe's convenient custom of giving all the lesser speeches in prose. We
find Mercutio, for example, from the beginning of this scene, designedly made to
speak in prose, while Benvolio, the graver character, first uses blank verse, then, from
line 9 on, falling into the tone of Mercutio, and also speaking in prose. The second
speech of Mercutio, line 4, is at best only half rhythmical. At the end of this scene,
when the jesting speeches end, Romeo uses verse again, the Nurse comes in with
prose, Romeo keeps on in verse, and now the Nurse falls partly into it, rises to a
trivial rhyming proverb (which she turns upside down), but soon falls back into her
prosaic tattle. In like manner in III, i, we find prose and verse alternating, accord-
ing as the more elevated, or the more common, tone is meant to preponderate. It
is indeed very doubtful, in my judgment, whether Romeo's speech, III, i, 80-84,
was not meant as prose.
<P>180. <B>I warrant</B>] <SC>White</SC>. One of the modernizations of F<SUB>2</SUB> was the addition
of the pronoun &lquo;<I>I,</I>&rquo; in which it has been universally followed hitherto. The elision
was common in Sh.'s day and long after. [<I>Dyce</I> (ed. 2).

<P>188. <B>rosemary</B>] <SC>Mal.</SC> Rosemary, being conceived to have the power of strength-

and (for this reason, probably,) was worn at weddings. [<I>Corn.</I>] So in a <I>Handfull
of Pleasant Delites,</I> &amp;c., 1584: &lquo;<I>Rosemary</I> is for <I>remembrance,</I> Betweene us daie
and night.&rquo; Again, in our author's Hamlet, IV, v, 175. That rosemary was much
used at weddings, appears from many passages in the old plays. So in The Noble
Spanish Soldier, 1634: &lquo;I meet few but are stuck with a <I>rosemary;</I> every one ask'd
me who was to be <I>married?</I>&rquo; Again, in The Wit of a Woman, 1604: &lquo;Wine and
cakes, and <I>rosemary</I> and <I>nosegaies?</I> What, a <I>wedding?</I>&rquo; [<I>Hal.</I>

Juliet has &lquo;the prettiest sententious of it.&rquo; [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Dyce</SC>. It was used both at weddings and at funerals. [Compare note on IV,
v, 79.]

<P>Warburton has quoted a verse from Lucilius that does not exist. The verse really is:
Irritata canis quod, homo quam, planiu' dicit. It alludes, indeed, to the letter R,
but does not introduce it. Persius also says: Sonat h&aelig;c de nare canina litera.
[<I>Sta.</I>] But the idea has been taken up in all ages, and must have been very familiar
in Sh.'s time, or he would not have put it into the mouth of the old Nurse, whom
the context shows to be unable to spell. Sh. would find it in the commonest books
of his time. His friend Jonson's Grammar was not published perhaps in his life-
time; but he might have heard from him, in conversation, that &lquo;R is <I>the dog's letter,</I>
and hurreth in the sound.&rquo; Or he might have studied the curious rebus in the
Alchemist (ii, 6) on Abel Drugger's name.
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> In Holland's translation of Plutarch's Morals: &lquo;a dog is, by nature, fell and
quarrelsome, given to <I>arre</I> and war upon a very small occasion.&rquo;
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 1). The meaning of this passage seems to have been hitherto mistaken,
owing to &lquo;thee&rquo; in the old copies (as was often the case) having been misprinted <I>the.</I>
The Nurse means to ask, &lquo;how can R, which is the dog's name, be <I>for thee?</I>&rquo; And
she answers herself, &lquo;No; I know Romeo begins with some other letter.&rquo; The
modern text has usually followed the suggestion of Tyrwhitt; but no change is neces-
sary beyond the mere alteration of <I>the</I> to &lquo;thee.&rquo; It is singular that this trifling
change should not have been suggested before [&lquo;long ago&rquo; (ed. 2)]. [<I>Verp.</I>
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (&lquo;<I>Remarks,</I>&rquo; &amp;c., p. 171). Collier is not aware that the &lquo;trifling change&rquo;
which he has made here was not only proposed by Warburton, but, at his suggestion,
inserted in the text by Theobald. I think it quite wrong; &lquo;R <I>is</I> for thee?&rquo; being by
no means a simple or natural mode of putting the question. The strong probability
is, that the word &lquo;dog&rquo; (as Tyrwhitt conjectured) has dropt out from the text.
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> It is to me very doubtful whether the foregoing emendation [Warburton's]
is the true one or not, for the reason that the Nurse has always hitherto addressed
Romeo as &lquo;you;&rquo; and the sudden transition to the &lquo;Thou&rquo; appears wholly purpose-
less. I am more inclined to suspect a misprint in &lquo;no,&rquo; and instead thereof would
read &lquo;dog,&rquo; as Tyrwhitt conjectures; but then drop the &lquo;no&rquo; before which Tyrwhitt
inserts &lquo;dog.&rquo;
<P><SC>Del.</SC> Ritson's emendation, which only changes the punctuation of the old text, is
the most plausible.
<P><SC>White</SC>. Collier more reasonably supposes that &lquo;the&rquo; was printed for &lquo;thee,&rquo; which
often happened.

which is quoted with various corruptions by Nonius Marcellus, Charisius, and Donatus
on Terence, and which Joseph Scaliger amended thus: &lquo;Irritata canes quod, homo
qu&agrave;m, planiu&rquo; dicit' (&lquo;canes&rquo; being the nom. sing. fem.); and Persius has &lquo;Sonat hic
de nare canina Litera,&rquo; sat. i, 109. Ben Jonson, in his <I>English Grammar,</I> says that
R &lquo;Is the <I>dog's</I> letter, and hurreth in the sound; the tongue striking the inner palate

<P>with a trembling about the teeth.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Works,</I> vol. ix, p. 281, ed. Gifford; and various
passages to the same effect might be cited from our early authors.
<P><SC>Gerald Massey</SC> (&lquo;<I>Sh.'s Sonnets,</I>&rquo; &amp;c., London, 1866, p. 471). Now, here is more
meant than meets the eye. The Nurse is being used. There is something that she
does not quite fathom, yet her lady does. She is prettily wise over a pleasant con-
ceit. Romeo understands it, too, if we may judge by his judicious answer. The
Nurse, however, knows there is <I>another letter</I> involved. There is a name that
begins with a different letter to the one sounded; but this name is not in the Play,
therefore it cannot be Rosemary, which the Nurse knows does not begin with an
&lquo;R.&rquo; Name and letter have to do with Romeo; the lady sees how, but the Nurse,
who started to tell the lover a good joke about Juliet's playing with his name, is
puzzled in the midst of it; can't make it out exactly, but it's a capital joke, and it
would do his heart good to see how it pleases the lady, who is learned in the matter,
though she, the Nurse, be no scholar! We shall find a meaning for the first time
if Southampton be the original of Romeo, and make sense of the Nurse's nonsense
by supposing, as we well may, that here is an <I>aside</I> on the part of the Poet to his
friends, and that the name which begins with <I>another letter</I> than the one first
sounded is Wriothesley! This bit of Sh.'s fun has perplexed his commentators most
amusingly; their hunt after the Dog and the &lquo;dog's letter R&rquo; being the best fun of all.
The only &lquo;dog&rquo; in the Nurse's mind is that &lquo;mocker&rquo; of herself, the audacious lover
of her young lady. Romeo has put her out of reckoning by saying &lquo;both with an
R.&rquo; And the Nurse, with the familiarity of an old household favorite, and a chuckle
of her amorous old heart, says: &lquo;Ah you dog, you, &ldquo;R&rdquo; is for &ldquo;Rosemary&rdquo; and
also for&mdash;<I>no, there's some other letter,</I> and my lady knows all about it;&rquo; only she says
this half to herself, as she tries to catch the missing meaning of her speech, the very
point of her story. &lquo;Rosemary&rquo; is merely the herb of that name. &lquo;<I>That's</I> for
remembrance&rquo; with Juliet, not for the name of a dog! The second Dog is Tyr-
whitt's, not Sh.'s. In the present instance the Poet is using the Nurse for the amuse-
ment of his friends, just as he uses Mrs. Quickly and Dogberry for ours; that is, by
making ignorance a dark reflector of light for us; causing them to hit the mark of
his meaning for us whilst missing it for themselves; thus we are flattered and they
are befooled.
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. We think that the Nurse is made to say &lquo;the dog's name&rquo; instead of &lquo;the
dog's letter,&rquo; partly because Sh. has a mode of using a popularly known phrase and
giving it a touch of his own peculiar fashion, partly because it gives an effect of
blunder and confusion to the old woman's diction here, and partly because the word
&lquo;name&rquo; thus introduced forms the antecedent to &lquo;it&rquo; in the next clause of the sen-
tence: &lquo;I know <I>it</I> begins with some other letter&rquo;&mdash;meaning &lquo;the name I am thinking
of,&mdash;Romeo.&rquo;

<P>197. <B>my fan</B>] <SC>Del.</SC> (<I>Lexikon</I>). Sh., having once before made the public laugh
over Peter and the fan, in revising the play, struck out the repetition of the joke.
But the edd. cannot thus resign him, and therefore bring him to light again out
of (Q<SUB>1</SUB>).
<P><SC>Dyce</SC>. The fans used by ladies in Sh.'s time consisted generally of ostrich or
other feathers stuck into handles, which were sometimes very costly, being made of
silver, gold, or ivory inlaid: &lquo;In the Sidney Papers, published by Collins, a fan is
presented to Queen Elizabeth for a New-Year's gift, the handle of which was studded
with diamonds.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>T. Warton</SC>.
<P>4. <B>be thoughts</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> Sh. seems to have thought the idea, contained in the
corresponding lines in (Q<SUB>1</SUB>), too valuable to be lost. He has therefore inserted it in
Romeo's first speech to the Apothecary in V, i, 64, 65. [<I>Sing.</I>
<P>6. <B>back shadows</B>] <SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). Juliet is probably referring to the rapid manner
in which the sun's light drives back the shadows in which the hills are involved.
Here, perhaps, the (MS.) misheard &lquo;back,&rquo; and wrote <I>black</I> in his margin in
consequence.

<P>16. <B>many feign</B>] <SC>Coll.</SC> (&lquo;<I>Notes and Emend.,</I>&rquo; &amp;c., ed. 2, 1853). There must be
something wrong here; why should &lquo;old folks feign as dead?&rquo; Feign is spelt
&lquo;faine,&rquo; and it turns out to be a misprint for <I>seeme</I> (the long <I>s</I> being in fault), and the
three lines are thus reduced to two in the (MS.):
<BQ>
&lquo;And his to me; but old folks <I>seem</I> as dead;<LB>
Unwieldy, slow, heavy and <I>dull</I> as lead.&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>There appears very little fitness in saying that old folks are &lquo;pale as lead;&rquo; for though
the epithet in itself is intelligible enough, to state that old folks are &lquo;dull as lead&rquo; is
far more applicable to Juliet's complaint.
<P><SC>White</SC>. Hitherto &lquo;faine&rquo; has been accepted as a spelling of &lquo;feign,&rquo; though with
a universally-expressed opinion that the passage was corrupt. But is it not clear
that &lquo;<I>many faine</I>&rquo; is a misprint of &lquo;<I>marry, fare</I>&rquo;<I>?</I> [<I>Dyce</I> (ed. 2).
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2). But &lquo;fare&rquo; has no propriety here. (Qy., had the MS. &lquo;moue yfaith&rquo;
(&lquo;move i' faith&rquo;), which was corrupted into &lquo;<I>many fain</I>&rquo;?)
<P><SC>Ktly.</SC> &lquo;Many faine&rquo; is nonsense; for &lquo;many&rquo; <I>marry</I> has been proposed, and I
adopt it, reading <I>fare</I> (to go, to move along, a Spenserian term) for &lquo;faine.&rquo; In Cor.
ii, 2, we have again <I>ain</I> for <I>ar.</I> For &lquo;pale&rquo; we should probably read <I>dull.</I> See
Timon, II, i, 228. We have elsewhere (Merc. of Ven., II, vii, 8) &lquo;<I>dull</I> lead.&rquo; More-
over, lead is not pale, and the Nurse would seem to have been rather a jolly, rubi-
cund sort of woman. If <I>fare</I> be the right reading, it would almost require <I>dull.</I>
On the other hand we have in Chaucer (Tr. and Cr., ii): &lquo;With asshen <I>pale as lede,</I>&rquo;
and (Dream) &lquo;That <I>pale</I> he wax as any <I>lede.</I>&rquo;

<P>26. <B>ache</B>] <SC>S. Walker</SC>. (&lquo;<I>Vers.</I>&rquo; p. 117). <SC>Ache, Aches</SC> (the noun substantive),

Ado, &amp;c., III, iv, with the var. notes, vol. vii, p. 99. Was it not also pronounced
<I>atch?</I> (Compare <I>bake</I> and <I>batch,</I> &amp;c.) Was the word pronounced both ways? I
believe that the verb was uniformly <I>ake.</I> It is at least frequently, if not always, so
printed; and in some places the pronunciation is established by the metre or other-
wise. Instances of the spelling <I>ake</I> in the Folio.&mdash;Rom. and Jul. [the present line,
and line 47]; Coriolanus, III, i, 108, also II, ii, 152; Timon, III, v, 96; Tempest,
III, iii, 2. [For proofs drawn from the metre and from plays on words from other
poets, vide ad loc. p. 119.] <SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>mainder, lines 1026-1033, 1044, 1045, 1050, 1051 of (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) will, I think, hardly be

<P>9. <B>violent ends</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (&lquo;<I>Vers.,</I>&rquo; &amp;c., p. 138) cites this line as an instance of

<P>14. <B>love moderately</B>] <SC>Vischer</SC> (&lquo;<I>Aesthetik, oder Wissenschaft des Sch&ouml;nen,</I>&rquo; 1857,
vol. iii, p. 1124). In the view of Gervinus, who traces the tragical end throughout
to the excess of violent passion, there is a species of tragedy which does not merely
illustrate character, but which contains no truth of universal interest beyond the
lesson that teaches the duty of moderation, a lesson which, as an abstract proposition
of morality, can never be the basis of any great poetic work. Accordingly, Gervinus
preaches moderation to Romeo&mdash;very properly, doubtless; Friar Lawrence does so
too. But had Romeo minded the lesson, there would have been no impassioned
youth, nor would Love have been represented in the Drama in all its power, its infin-
itude. At another time one may bethink himself that there are other things besides
Love in the world,&mdash;reflection, duty,&mdash;but here and now the divinity of Love is the
thing; this it is that is to be represented, an ideal passion. Even here there is,

<P><SC>Nares</SC>. From the French, <I>gossampine,</I> the cotton tree, which is from <I>gossipium;</I>
properly, therefore, cotton wool. Also any light downy matter, such as the flying
seeds of thistles and other plants. Now used not unfrequently to signify the long,
floating cobwebs seen in fine weather in the air.
<P><SC>Holt White</SC>. It is formed from the collected webs of flying spiders, and during
calm weather in autumn, sometimes falls in amazing quantities. [<I>Sing.</I>
<P><SC>Sing</SC>. [Note on <I>Lear,</I> IV, vi, 49]. Some think it the down of plants; others the
vapour arising from boggy or marshy ground in warm weather. The etymon of this
word, which has puzzled the lexicographers, is said to be <I>summer goose</I> or <I>summer
gauze;</I> hence &lquo;gauze o' the summer,&rquo; its well-known name in the north. See <I>Hor&aelig;
Moment&aelig; Craven&aelig;, or the Craven Dialect Exemplified,</I> 1824, 8vo, p. 79.

<P>30. <B>conceit</B>] <SC>Mal.</SC> It here means <I>imagination.</I> [<I>Sing.</I>] So in The Rape of
Lucrece: &lquo;&mdash;&mdash; which the <I>conceited</I> painter drew,&rquo; &amp;c. [<I>Sta.</I>
<P><SC>Craik</SC> [&lquo;<I>Eng. of Sh.,</I>&rquo; p. 135]. To <I>conceit</I> is another form of our still familiar to
<I>conceive.</I> And the noun <I>conceit,</I> which survives with a limited meaning (the con-
ception of a man by himself, which is so apt to be one of over-estimation), is also
frequent in Sh. with the sense, nearly, of what we now call <I>conception,</I> in general.
Sometimes it is used in a sense which might almost be said to be the opposite of
what it now means; as when Juliet [in this passage] employs it as the term to denote
her all-absorbing affection for Romeo; or as when Gratiano, in the Mer. of Ven., I, i,
90, speaks of a sort of men who
<BQ>
&lquo;do a wilful stillness entertain,<LB REND=RIGHT>
With purpose to be dress'd in an opinion<LB>
Of wisdom, gravity, profound conceit&rquo;&mdash;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>that is, deep thought. So, again, when Rosaline, in Love's Lab., II, i, 72, speaking of
Biron, describes his &lquo;fair tongue&rquo; as &lquo;conceit's expositor,&rquo; all that she means is, that
speech is the expounder of thought. The scriptural expression, still in familiar use,
&lquo;wise in his own conceit,&rquo; means merely wise in his own thought, or in his own eyes,
as we are told in the margin the Hebrew literally signifies. In the New Testament,
where we have &lquo;in their own conceits,&rquo; the Greek is simply <G>rap) e(auto_is</G> (in or with
themselves).

<P>47. <B>Or reason</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC>. A mistake occasioned by the &lquo;<I>Or</I>&rquo; which commences the
next line.
<P><SC>White</SC>. Benvolio presents a triple alternative: either to withdraw to a private
place, or to discuss the matter quietly where they were, or else to part company; and
it is supremely in character that on such an occasion he should perceive and suggest
all these methods of avoiding public scandal.
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. It is more likely that Benvolio should recommend his friends to retire
and talk over their grievances coolly, than that he should offer them three alter-
natives.

<P>58. <B>appertaining rage To</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (&lquo;<I>Crit.,</I>&rquo; vol. i, p. 162) [cites this as a
peculiar construction with the adjective]; that is, <I>rage appertaining to.</I>
<P>63. <B>injured</B>] <SC>Mommsen</SC>. The old and especially more correct form, <I>injuried</I>
(cf. Nares, ed. Halliw. s. v), is to be preferred, used as it is here in manifest reference
to the preceding substantive, and with a thoroughly denominative application. No
one seems to have noticed it; all adopt the more common form, <I>injured,</I> of (Q<SUB>1</SUB>)
and Q<SUB>3</SUB>, or rather the <I>injur'd</I> of F<SUB>1</SUB>. In the beginning of the seventeenth century,
the old form had already vanished, and was frequently omitted from older pieces by
the printers. Yet it is found undoubtedly a few times in Lyly (before 1584), Mar-
lowe (before 1586), and Heywood (before 1604). See Dyce in Marl. I, p. 19. The
latter learned commentator, as well as all the others, failed to notice it in this passage,
where it is an interesting archaism.
<P>69. <B>A la stoccata</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> <I>Stoccata</I> is the Italian term for a thrust or stab with
a rapier. [<I>Sing. Knt. Verp. Huds. Sta.</I>
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> Mercutio uses <I>la stoccata</I> as one word, and places before it the indefinite
article <I>a.</I> He intends to say: &lquo;Only a well-directed thrust carries away this shame-
ful submission.&rquo; Schlegel's translation is here incorrect.
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. Mercutio jocosely gives this term as a title for Tybalt.
<P>72. <B>king of cats</B>] <SC>Mal.</SC> Alluding to his name. [<I>Sing. Ulr. Del. Huds.</I>

<P>74. <B>dry-beat</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>. That is, <I>severely beat.</I> Dry in the sense of &lquo;hard,&rquo;
&lquo;severe,&rquo; comes indirectly from <I>drien,</I> an ancient verb for endure or suffer, and the
Scottish and old English verb to &lquo;dree,&rquo; which has the same meaning. Lord Bacon,
and Butler in his &lquo;Hudibras,&rquo; use the word in this sense. Also it is in Com. of Err.
II, ii, 64.
<P>75. <B>pilcher</B>] <SC>Warb.</SC> We should read <I>pilche,</I> which signifies a cloak or coat of
skins, meaning the scabbard. [<I>Sing. Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Steev.</SC> This explanation is, I believe, just. Nash, in Pierce Pennyless, 1595,
speaks of a carman in a leather <I>pilche.</I> [<I>Sing.</I> (ed. 1), <I>Huds. Clarke.</I>] Again, in
Decker's Satiromastix, 1602: &lquo;I'll beat five pounds out of his leather <I>pilch.</I>&rquo; Again,
&lquo;Thou hast forgot how thou ambled'st in a leather <I>pilch,</I> by a play-waggon in the
highway, and took'st mad Jeronimo's part, to get service among the mimicks.&rquo; It
appears from this passage that Ben Jonson acted the part of <I>Hieronimo</I> in the Span-
ish tragedy, the speech being addressed to <I>Horace,</I> under which character old <I>Ben</I>
is ridiculed. [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Nares</SC>. A scabbard [<I>Knt.</I>] from <I>pylche,</I> a skin-coat, Saxon. See Skinner.
<P><SC>Sing</SC>. (ed. 2). There has been a vain attempt to make <I>Pilcher</I> signify a leathern
sheath, because a Pilch meant a leathern coat or pelt. It is quite evident that in
this jocose, bantering speech Mercutio substitutes <I>Pitcher</I> for <I>Scabbard.</I> The poet
was familiar with the proverb &lquo;Pitchers have ears,&rquo; of which he has twice availed
himself. The <I>ears,</I> as every one knows, are the <I>handles,</I> which have since been
called the <I>lugs; pitcher</I> was suggested by the play upon the word <I>ears,</I> which is here
used for <I>hilts</I> in the plural, according to the usage of the poet's time. [<I>Sta.</I>
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> A <I>pilch</I> was the name for some outer garment made of leather [&lquo;Pierce Pen-
niless,&rquo; 1592, cited], and the word might be applied suitably enough for the leathern
sheath of a rapier. Perhaps we should read, &lquo;out of his pilch, sir,&rquo; &amp;c.
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). No other instance has been adduced of the use of this word in
this way in any other author. [<I>Verp. White.</I>] Very likely the last syllable was
accidentally added by the printer, and that Mercutio said, &lquo;Pluck your sword out of
his <I>pilch.</I>&rquo; [<I>Ulr.</I>
<P><SC>Dyce.</SC> A scabbard, a sheath.
<P><SC>Ktly.</SC> I think the right word is <I>pilche,</I> a leathern coat. In V, i, 202, the sheath
of a dagger is termed its house.

<P>129. <B>fortune's fool</B>] <SC>Johns</SC>. I am always running in the way of evil fortune
<I>like</I> the Fool in the play. &lquo;Thou art death's fool,&rquo; in Meas, for Meas. [<I>Sing. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Douce</SC>. There is certainly no allusion to any <I>play.</I> Sh. is very fond of alluding
to the <I>mockery</I> of fortune. Thus we have, &lquo;Ye fools of fortune.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Tim. of Athens.</I>
&lquo;I am the natural fool of fortune.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Lear.</I> In the last passage a pointed allusion is
made to the <I>idiot fool.</I> Sir J. Suckling uses the same expression in his play of <I>The
Goblins;</I> and Hamlet speaks of &lquo;the fools of nature,&rquo; precisely in the same sense.
[<I>Sing. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Sing.</SC> In Julius C&aelig;sar the expression is, &lquo;He is but fortune's knave.&rquo; [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> I am the sport of fortune.
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. It has reference to the &lquo;fool&rquo; in the old mysteries, moralities, or dra-
matic shows, who is represented as the perpetual object of pursuit, mockery, and
disaster.

<P>170. <B>false</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>. The charge of falsehood on Benvolio, though produced
at hazard, is very just. The author, who seems to intend the character of Benvolio
as good, meant, perhaps, to show how the best minds, in a state of faction and dis-
cord, are detorted to criminal partiality. [<I>Sing. Knt. Corn. Verp. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> There is a slight particle of untruth in Benvolio's statement, which, to a
certain degree, justifies this charge of Lady Capulet. Tybalt was bent on quarrel-
ling with Romeo, but Mercutio forced on his own quarrel with Tybalt. Dr. John-
son's remark upon this circumstance is worthy of his character as a moralist.
<P>182. <B>My blood</B>] <SC>S. Walker</SC>. That is, <I>my kinsman; sanguis meus.</I>
<P>185. <B>I will</B>] <SC>Momm.</SC> Q<SUB>2</SUB> has <I>It,</I> referring to <I>blood,</I>&mdash;compare Gen. iv. 10, <I>the
voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto Me from the ground,</I>&mdash;to me this interpreta
tion is very beautiful.

<P>190. <B>Mercy but murders</B>] <SC>Mal.</SC> So in Hale's Memorials: &lquo;When I find
myself swayed to mercy, let me remember likewise that there is a mercy due to the
country.&rquo; [<I>Sing. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Mal.</SC> So in Stubbes's Anatomie of Abuses, 2d part: &lquo;And yet let the Prince be
sure of this, to answere at the day of judgment before the tribunall seate of God for
all the offences that the partie pardoned shall commit at any time of his life after.
For if the Prince had cutte him off when the lawe had passed on him, that evill had
not been committed. To this purpose I remember I have heard a certeine pretie
apothegue [apothegme] uttered by a jester to a king. The king had pardoned one
of his subjectes that had committed murther, who, being pardoned, committed the
like offence againe, and by meanes was pardoned the second time also, and yet filling
up the measure of his iniquitie, killed the third, and being brought before the king,
the king being verie sorie, asked him why he had killed three men, to whom his
jester, standing by, replied, saieing, No (O King) he killed but the first, and thou
hast killed the other two; for if thou hadst hanged him up at the first, the other two
had not beene killed; therefore thou hast killed them, and shall answere for their
bloud. Which thing being heard, the king hanged him up straightway, as he very
well deserved.&rquo; [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). In F<SUB>1</SUB> is another of the places in which the old printers confounded
&ldquo;but&rdquo; and <I>not.</I>
<P><B>Scene II.</B>] <SC>Hartley Coleridge</SC> (&lquo;<I>Essays,</I>&rquo; &amp;c., vol. ii, p. 197). That the con-
ceits in this scene are suitable to tragedy I cannot maintain; but they have a smack
of nature. The mind, surprised by sorrow in the midst of playful delights, will not
immediately change its tune. The confusion of feelings will produce an antic blend-
ing of thoughts, a dance of death.

<P>10. <B>civil</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>. That is, <I>grave, decently solemn.</I> [<I>Sing. Huds.</I>
<P>14. <B>Hood . . . . bating</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> These are terms of falconry. An <I>unmanned</I>
hawk is one that is not brought to endure company. <I>Bating</I> is fluttering with the
wings as striving to fly away. [<I>Sing. Coll. Verp. Huds. White, Cham.</I>
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> To <I>man</I> a hawk was to accustom her to the falconer who trained her.
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> The hood was the cap with which the hawk was usually hoodwinked. An
<I>unmann'd</I> hawk was one not sufficiently trained to be familiar with her keeper, and
such birds commonly fluttered and beat their wings violently in efforts to escape.
See also Tam. of Shr., IV, i, 206.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC>. The hawk was <I>hooded</I> till let fly at the game.
<P><SC>Nares</SC>. To <I>bate,</I> probably from <I>battre,</I> Fr. It is a natural action with birds, after
bathing, to shake the moisture from their wings; also when desirous of their food, or
prey. The true meaning of the word is beautifully exemplified in the following pas-
sage from Bacon: &lquo;Wherein (viz., in matters of business) I would to God that I
were hooded, that I saw less; or that I could perform more; for now I am like a
hawk that <I>bates,</I> when I see occasion of service; but cannot fly because I am ty'd
to another's fist.&rquo;
<P><SC>Dyce</SC>. &lquo;<I>Bate,</I> Bateing or Bateth, is when the Hawk fluttereth with her Wings
either from Pearch or Fist, as it were striveing to get away; also it is taken for her
striving with her Prey, and not forsaking it till it be overcome.&rquo;&mdash;R. Holme's
<I>Academy of Armory and Blazon,</I> B. ii, c. xi, p. 238.
<P>15. <B>strange</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>. That is, <I>reserved, retiring.</I>
<P>15. <B>grown</B>] <SC>Coll</SC>. (ed. 1). Rowe's change was scarcely necessary.
<P><SC>Keightley</SC>. Rowe was probably right. Still, when we consider the joyous per-
turbation of Juliet's mind, there may be an asyndeton, and she may be speaking <I>allo
staccato.</I>

<P>45. <B>but &lquo;I,&rquo;</B>] <SC>Theob.</SC> At Sh.'s time of day the affirmative adverb <I>Ay</I> was gene-
rally written <I>I:</I> and by this means it both becomes a vowel, and answers in sound
to <I>Eye,</I> upon which the conceit turns in the second line. [Substantially, <I>Mal. Sing.
Knt. Corn. Verp. Coll. Huds. Sta. White, Dyce.</I>
<P><SC>Corn.</SC> The edd. have here thought it necessary to retain the old spelling [<I>I</I> for
<I>ay</I>]. We have, however, ventured to deviate from this unsightly practice, conceiving
that there is sufficient similarity between the sounds of &lquo;ay&rquo; and &lquo;I&rquo; to point out the
intended quibble. This is one of the trivial passages which we easily persuade our-
selves have, by some accident or impertinence, been foisted into the genuine text.
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). &lquo;That bare vowel&rquo; it is obviously necessary to retain here; but
elsewhere we adopt the modern form.
<P><SC>White</SC>. It has been necessary to retain the simple vowel <I>I</I> twice in this passage.

<P><I>Errors,</I> III, vii, p. 126. Many fables were current respecting it. In the first place,
it was supposed to have so deadly an eye as to kill by the very look.&mdash;<I>Twelfth N.,</I>
III, iv, 215. But there was a still further refinement, that if the cockatrice first saw
the person, he killed him by it; but if the animal was first seen, he died. They
were supposed to be able to penetrate steel by pecking it. <I>Cockatrice</I> was also a
current name for a loose woman; probably from the fascination of the eye.
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> [To these citations adds]: 3 Hen. VI: III, ii, 187.
<P>53. <B>God save the mark</B>] <SC>Knt.</SC> The commentators leave the expression in Its
original obscurity. May we venture a conjecture? The <I>mark</I> which persons who
are unable to write are required to make, instead of their signature, is in the form
of a <I>cross;</I> but anciently the use of this mark was not confined to illiterate persons,
for amongst the Saxons the mark of the cross, as an attestation of the good faith of
the person signing, was required to be attached to the signature of those who could
write, and to stand in the place of the signature of those who could not write. (See
Blackstone's Commentaries.) The ancient use of the mark was universal; and the
word <I>mark</I> was, we believe, thus taken to signify the <I>cross. God save the mark</I> was,
therefore, a form of ejaculation approaching to the character of an oath; in the same
manner as assertions were made emphatic by the addition of &lquo;by the rood,&rquo; or, &lquo;by
the holy rood.&rquo;
<P><SC>White</SC>. (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) has &lquo;God save the <I>sample!</I>&rquo; May we conclude from this that, in the
other phrase, &lquo;mark&rquo; means such a mark as is made with a needle upon a sampler?
<P><SC>Dyce</SC>. The origin and meaning of the exclamation are alike obscure.
<P>56. <B>gore blood</B>] <SC>Forby.</SC> That is, clotted, congealed blood. The words sepa-

East-Anglian nurse say on a like occasion. Or, perhaps &lquo;all of a <I>gore,</I>&rquo; or &lquo;all of a
<I>gore of blood.</I>&rquo; [<I>Hal.</I>

<P>69. <B>Romeo banished</B>] <SC>Heraud</SC> (&lquo;<I>Sh.'s Inner Life,</I>&rquo; 1865, p. 61). It must
have struck every reader that both Romeo and Juliet's excessive lamentations
for his banishment from Verona rather want motive. Why could not Juliet have
gone with him? and, by so doing, have prevented the after evils, which originate
solely in their apparently needless separation. Brooke's poem supplies the hiatus.
Juliet there supplicates her lover for his permission to be his companion in exile.
But he gives her the reasons why this cannot be:

tives,&mdash;the verbs more especially, I think, in the form of the past participle,&mdash;which,
though at present they are accented on the latter syllable exclusively, have, in our
old poets, an accent,&mdash;though of course an unequal one,&mdash;on both syllables; the
principal one being shifted <I>ad libitum</I> from the one syllable to the other.

<P>21. <B>&lquo;banished&rquo;</B>] <SC>Del.</SC> (&lquo;<I>Lex.</I>&rquo;). The repetition of the same word at the end of
several successive lines is in Sh.'s style; and those edd. who adopt &lquo;banishment&rquo;
from (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) sacrifice to their own grammatical precision a perfectly Shaksperian inac-
curacy of speeeh, originating in Romeo's passion.
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> Romeo in his wild agony retains the word, which Lorenzo had just used,
and which evokes the outpouring of his rage, with the obstinacy of passion, and uses
the hated word even where the calm speech of every-day life would certainly say
&lquo;banishment.&rquo;
<P>26. <B>rush'd</B>] <SC>Ktly.</SC> Would not <I>push'd</I> be better? As in Hen. V: I, i, 5:

<P><SC>Steevens</SC> (1773) reads:
<BQ>
&lquo;Flies may do this, when I from this must fly;<LB>
They are free men, but I am banish'd.<LB>
And say'st thou yet, that exile is not death?<LB>

</BQ>
<P>In his note on the passage, in the edition of 1778, he conjectured that the line &lquo;But
Romeo . . . banished&rquo; should be inserted after &lquo;their own kisses sin;&rquo; an arrange-
ment which was adopted by <SC>Malone</SC>, and by Steevens himself in his ed. of 1793.
Capell suggests that the lines he retains &lquo;were second thoughts of the poet's, and
their original was meant for expunction.&rquo; This may possibly be true, but we have
adopted the reading given in our text because it retains, without manifest absurdity,
lines which are all undoubtedly Sh.'s. [So far the Cambridge Editors.]
<P><SC>Variorum</SC> of 1821, <SC>Har. Sing.</SC> (ed. 1), <SC>Camp. Corn.</SC> and <SC>Delius</SC> follow Steev-
ens of 1793.
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 1) [also <SC>Verp. Ulr.</SC>]. We follow Q<SUB>2</SUB> and Q<SUB>3</SUB>. In F<SUB>1</SUB> the impassioned
repetition of &lquo;Flies may do this, but I from this must fly,&rquo; was, it would seem, not
allowed for, and that and the following line were, therefore, as we think, unneces-
sarily omitted.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> [&lquo;<I>Remarks,</I>&rquo; &amp;c.]. Collier supposes that Sh. would make Romeo utter <I>the
very same conceit twice over in the course of a few lines.</I> The repetition is nothing
more than one of the innumerable <I>vari&aelig; lectiones</I> of this tragedy. The line &lquo;But
Romeo may not,&rquo; &amp;c., is quite out of place. In such a passage as this, where hideous
confusion has arisen from the various readings, it is absolutely necessary that an
editor should do his endeavor to rectify that confusion: he should neither jumble
two texts together, nor slavishly follow one particular text.
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> As it is characteristic of passion to delight in a repetition of the same words
while indulging in a variety and abundance of images and conceits, I should have
omitted these lines [41, 42], which contain a repetition of the same conceit merely,
if F<SUB>1</SUB> had also omitted the preceding line, &lquo;But Romeo may not.&rquo; If these lines be
retained, which continue the simile of flies, the two following are, in my opinion,
also necessary. Either the latter have been omitted, or the former retained through
oversight.
<P><SC>Hazlitt</SC> omits lines 40-42, <I>But....banished.</I>
<P><SC>Hudson, Dyce, Chambers, Keightley</SC> adopt F<SUB>1</SUB> and transpose the line &lquo;But
Romeo may not,&rquo; &amp;c., to follow &lquo;Still blush, as thinking,&rquo; &amp;c.
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> [adopts F<SUB>1</SUB> and transposes &lquo;But Romeo,&rquo; &amp;c., to follow &lquo;This may flies do,&rquo;
&amp;c.] Capell rightly conjectures that the author's first draft of this passage was left
standing in the MS., and so got printed with the after version.
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2) [adds to his former note]: There is manifestly some confusion in
the text, but as by leaving out the lines we might exclude something which Sh. at
