<P><SC>Del.</SC> (&lquo;<I>Lex.</I>&rquo;) Throughout this scene, as well as in the scenes that follow, Sh.
represents the readiness of the Friar to act, in contrast to the vain wailings of Romeo
and the Nurse. The Friar, therefore, instead of joining in the lamentations of the
others, would be much more likely to repress them.
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> It is far from being out of character for the Nurse to interlard her talk
with some few grand, high-sounding phrases, which she had caught up in her

is also sustained by the word <I>predicament,</I> which only half and half applies here,
inasmuch as it only exceptionally, and under certain circumstances, signifies the

<P>132. <B>powder</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> The ancient English soldiers, using <I>match-</I>locks instead

<BQ>

</BQ>
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> That flint-locks were in use in Sh.'s middle age a passage in Hen. V: II, i,
55, shows. So that this reference here to a match-lock seems to me another proof
that this tragedy belongs to the earlier pieces of Sh., and was written probably six or
eight years before Henry V (1599).

<P><SC>Knt.</SC> To understand these directions we must refer to the construction of the old
theatres. &lquo;Towards the rear of the stage,&rquo; says Malone, &lquo;there appears to have
been a balcony or upper stage, the platform of which was probably eight or nine feet
from the ground. I suppose it was supported by pillars. Hence, in many of our
old plays, part of the dialogue was spoken, and, in front of it, curtains likewise were
hung, so as occasionally to conceal the persons in it from the audience. At each
side of this balcony was a box very inconveniently situated, sometimes called the
<I>private box.</I> In these boxes, which were at a lower price, some persons sate, either
from economy or singularity.&rquo; The balcony probably served a variety of purposes.
Malone says, &lquo;When the citizens of Angiers are to appear on the walls of their
town, and young Arthur to leap from the battlements, I suppose our ancestors were
contented with seeing them in the balcony already described, or perhaps a few
boards tacked together and painted so as to resemble the rude discolored walls of
an old town, behind which a platform might have been placed near the top, on
which the citizens stood.&rquo; It appears to us probable that even in these cases the
balcony served for the platform, and that a few painted boards in front supplied the
illusion of wall and tower. There was still another use of the balcony. Accord-
ing to Malone, when a play was exhibited within a play, as in Hamlet, the court, or
audience, before whom the interlude was performed, sate in the balcony. [<I>Hal.</I>]
We prefix a representation of the old stage with its balcony engraved in the title-
page to Alabaster's Latin Tragedy of Roxana, 1632.
<P><SC>Verplanck</SC>. The scene in the Poet's eye was doubtless the large and massy pro-
jecting balcony before one or more windows, common in Italian palaces and not
unfrequent in Gothic civil architecture. The <I>loggia,</I> an open gallery, or high ter-
race, communicating with the upper apartments of a palace, is a common feature of
Palladian architecture, and would also be well adapted to such a scene.
<P><SC>White</SC>. The place meant is plainly the very same in which <I>Romeo</I> surprises
<I>Juliet</I> confessing to herself her love for him; but in this edition the stage-directions
have been conformed to the poet's imagination of the scene.
<P>4. <B>Nightly</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> This is not merely a poetical supposition. It is said of the
nightingale that, if undisturbed, she sits and sings upon the same tree for many
weeks together. [<SC>Singer</SC> adds: As almost all birds sing only during the period of
incubation, this may be accounted for; the male bird sings near where the female
is sitting.] What Eustathius, however, has observed relative to a <I>fig-tree</I> mentioned
by Homer in his 12th Odyssey, may be applied to the passage before us: &lquo;These
particularities, which seem of no consequence, have a very good effect in poetry, as
they give the relation an air of truth and probability. For what can induce a poet
to mention such a tree if the tree were not there in reality?&rquo; [<I>Sta.</I>
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> In the description of the garden in Chaucer's translation of the &lquo;Romaunt
of the Rose,&rquo; the pomegranate is first mentioned amongst the fruit-trees. The
&lquo;orchard of pomegranates with pleasant fruits&rquo; was one of the beautiful objects de-
scribed by Solomon in his Canticles. Amongst the fruit-bearing trees, the pome-
granate is in some respects the most beautiful; and therefore, in the south of Europe

<P>and in the East, it has become the chief ornament of the garden. But where did
Sh. find that the nightingale haunted the pomegranate tree, pouring forth her song
from the same bough week after week? Doubtless in some of the old travels with
which he was familiar. Chaucer puts his nightingale &lquo;in a fresh green laurel tree;&rquo;
but the preference of the nightingale for the pomegranate is unquestionable. &lquo;The
nightingale sings from the pomegranate groves in the day time,&rquo; says Russel in his
account of Aleppo. A friend, whose observations as a traveller are as acute as his
descriptions are graphic and forcible, informs us that throughout his journeys in the
East he never heard such a choir of nightingales as in a row of pomegranate trees
that skirt the road from Smyrna to Boudjia. In the truth of details such as these
the genius of Sh. is as much exhibited as in his wonderful powers of generalization.
[<I>Huds. Sta.</I>
<P>6. <B>the lark</B>] <SC>Knt.</SC> Sh.'s power of describing natural objects is unequalled in this
beautiful scene, which, as we think, was amongst his very early productions. The
Venus and Adonis, published in 1593, is also full of this power. Compare the fol-
lowing passage with the description of morning in the scene before us:
<BQ>

<P>9. <B>Night's candles are</B>] <SC>Blakeway</SC>. Thus Sophocles:
<BQ>
&mdash;&mdash; <G>a)/kpas nukto\s, h(ni/x' e(/srepoi</G><LB>
<G>*aamrth=pes ou)ke/t' h)=|qon.</G>&mdash;Ajax, 285. <I>[Sing.</I><LB>

<P><SC>Sta.</SC> [thus translates]: &lquo;At dead of night, What time the evening tapers had ex-
pired.&rquo; But Sh. certainly meant the stars, while Sophocles seems only to have
thought of the less poetical lamps of earth.
<P><SC>Jeffrey</SC> (Edin. Rev., Aug. 1817). If the advocates for the grand style object to
this expression, we shall not stop to defend it; but to us it seems equally beautiful,
as it is obvious and natural, to a person coming out of a lighted chamber into the
pale dawn. The word candle, we admit, is rather homely in modern language,
while lamp is sufficiently dignified for poetry. The moon hangs her silver lamp on
high in every school-boy's copy of verses; and she could not be called the candle
of heaven without manifest absurdity. Such are the caprices of usage. Yet we
like the passage before us much better as it is than if the candles were changed into
lamps. If we should read, &lquo;The lamps of heaven are quenched,&rquo; or &lquo;wax dim,&rquo; the
whole charm of the expression would be lost&mdash;our fancies would no longer be re-
called to the privacy of that dim-lighted chamber which the lovers were so reluc-
tantly leaving.

<P><SC>Dyce</SC>. (&lquo;<I>Strictures,</I>&rquo; &amp;c., 1859, p. 165). I really cannot see any objection to the

<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. &lquo;Cynthia&rquo; is one of the names of Diana (from Mount Cynthus, where

<P>29. <B>division</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>. To make divisions in music is to run a simple strain into
a great variety of shorter notes to the same modulation. [<I>Dyce.</I>
<P><SC>Sing.</SC> A <I>division,</I> in music, is a <I>variation of melody</I> upon some given funda
mental harmony. See 1 Hen. IV: III, i, 210: &lquo;Sung by a fair queen in a sum-
mer's bower, With ravishing <I>division</I> to her lute.&rquo; This verse, Stephen Weston
observes, might serve for a translation of a line in Horace: &lquo;&mdash;&mdash;grataque feminis
Imbelli cithara carmina <I>divides.</I>&rquo; [<I>Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> A number of quick notes sung to one syllable; a kind of warbling, which
prevailed in vocal music till rather recently. [<I>Verp.</I>] Handel, governed by custom
rather than by his own better taste, introduces divisions into many of his airs and
choruses. [<I>Hal.</I>] Steevens, in his note on this word, mistakes the meaning
entirely.
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> It is what we now term <I>variation;</I> where, instead of one note, two, three
or more notes are sung to one syllable or to one chord. [<I>White,</I> subs.

<P>34. <B>hunts-up</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> The tune anciently played to wake and collect the

feather'd sylvans sing.&rquo; [<I>Sing. Huds. White, Clarke.</I>
<P><SC>Ritson</SC> Puttenham, in his Art of English Poesy, 1589, speaking of one Gray,
says: &lquo;What good estimation did he grow into with King Henry [the Eighth] . . .
for making certaine merry ballads, whereof one chiefly was &lquo;<I>The Hunte is up, the
Hunte is up.</I>&rquo; [<I>Sing. Knt. Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Mal.</SC> It also signified a morning song to a new-married woman, the day after her
marriage, and is certainly used here in that sense. See Cotgrave's Dict., s. v.
Resveil. [<I>Sing. Huds. Clarke.</I>

similar title.

<I>Morning Song,</I> for a new-married wife.&rquo; See <SC>W. Chappell</SC>, <I>Popular Music of the

<P><SC>Halliwell</SC>. The hunts-up was a tune played on the horn, under the windows of
sportsmen, very early in the morning. Hence the term was applied to any noise of
an awakening or alarming nature. &lquo;A hunt is up or musike plaid under one's
window in a morning.&rquo;&mdash;Florio, p. 304. &lquo;<I>Resveil,</I> a hunts-up, or morning song for
a new-married wife the day after the marriage.&rquo;&mdash;Cotgrave. &lquo;<I>Hunsup,</I> a clamour, a
turbulent outcry.&rquo;&mdash;Craven Gl. Mr. W. H. Black discovered a document in the
Rolls-house, from which it appeared that a song of <I>the Hunt's up</I> was known as
early as 1536, when information was sent to the council against one John Hogon,
who, &lquo;with a crowd or a fyddyll,&rquo; sung a song, with some political allusions, to that
tune. Some of the words are given in the information:
<BQ>
&lquo;The hunt is up, the hunt is up, &amp;c.<LB>
The Masters of Arte and Doctours of Dyvynyte<LB>
Have brought this realme ought of good unyt&eacute;.<LB>
Thre nobyll men have take this to stay,<LB>
My Lords of Norff. Lorde of Surrey,<LB>
And my Lorde of Shrewsbyrry;<LB>
The Duke of Suff. myght have made Inglond mery.&rquo;<LB>

it to &lquo;ah;&rquo; for which perhaps it was intended.
<P><SC>White</SC>. Perhaps &lquo;<I>ay</I>&rquo; is a misprint for &lquo;my.&rquo; The reading of (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) has the advan-
tage of ridding the line of the awkward and unpoetic word &lquo;husband,&rquo; which is in
no sense, except legally, a counterpart to &lquo;wife.&rquo; But in the word &lquo;friend&rquo; there was
not that anticlimax in Sh.'s time that there is now. &lquo;Friend&rquo; was then used to
express the dearest possible relation, even between the sexes. It frequently occurs
in that sense in the poem <I>Romeus and Juliet;</I> and in the very passage which is
here dramatized, <I>Juliet,</I> in her distress that <I>Romeo</I> will neither remain with her, nor
let her go with him, exclaims (and Sh. seems to have remembered it):

<P>53. <B>ill-divining soul</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> This miserable prescience of futurity I have
always regarded as a circumstance particularly beautiful. The same kind of warning
from the mind, Romeo seems to have been conscious of, on his going to the enter-
tainment at the house of Capulet. [<I>Sing. Huds. Sta.</I>
<P><SC>Mal.</SC> So in Venus and Adonis:
<BQ>
&lquo;The thought of it doth make my faint heart bleed;<LB>
And fear doth teach it <I>divination;</I><LB>
<I>I prophesy thy death.</I>&rquo; <SD>[Knt.</SD><LB>
</BQ>
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> Coleridge has some remarks upon Richard II: II, ii, 10, which we may
properly quote here: &lquo;Mark in this scene Sh.'s gentleness in touching the tender
superstitions, the <I>terr&aelig; incognit&aelig;</I> of presentiments, in the human mind; and how
sharp a line of distinction he commonly draws between these obscure forecastings
of general experience in each individual, and the vulgar errors of mere tradition.
Indeed, it may be taken once for all as the truth that Sh., in the absolute universality
of his genius, always reverences whatever arises out of our moral nature. He never
profanes his muse with a contemptuous reasoning away of the genuine and general,
however unaccountable, feelings of mankind.&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;<I>Lit. Rem.,</I>&rquo; vol. ii, p. 174. Sh. has
exhibited the feeling under three different aspects in this play. When Romeo utters
his presentiment before going to the masquerade, he is under the influence of his
habitual melancholy,&mdash;the sentiment of unrequited love, which colours all his
imagination with a gloomy foreshadowing of coming events. In the passage before
us, when Juliet sees her husband &lquo;As one dead in the bottom of a tomb,&rquo; we have
&lquo;the fear&rquo; which doth &lquo;teach&rquo; her heart &lquo;divination.&rquo; But Romeo in Act V has a
presentiment directly contrary to the approaching catastrophe; and this arises out of
his &lquo;unaccustomed&rquo; animal spirits. All these states of mind are common to the
imagination deeply stirred by passionate emotions. Nothing in all Sh.'s philosophy
appears to us finer than the deceiving nature of Romeo's presages in the last Act as
compared with the true-divining fears of Juliet.

<P>58. <B>Dry sorrow</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>. The belief that grieving exhausts the blood and
impairs the health is more than once alluded to by Sh. See Mid. N.'s D., III, ii, 97.
<P>66. <B>Enter Lady Capulet</B>] <SC>Mrs. Jameson</SC>. In the dialogue between Juliet and
her parents, and in the scenes with the Nurse, we seem to have before us the whole
of her previous education and habits; we see her, on the one hand, kept in severe
subjection by her austere parents, and, on the other, fondled and spoiled by a foolish
old nurse&mdash;a situation perfectly accordant with the manners of the time. Then
Lady Capulet comes sweeping by, with her train of velvet, her black hood, her fan
and rosary&mdash;the very <I>beau-ideal</I> of a proud Italian matron of the fifteenth century,
whose offer to poison Romeo, in revenge for the death of Tybalt, stamps her with
one very characteristic trait of the age and the country. Yet she loves her daugh-
ter, and there is a touch of remorseful tenderness in her lamentations over her which
adds to our impression of the timid softness of Juliet and the harsh subjection in
which she has been kept. [<I>Verp.</I>
<P>66. <B>procures</B>] <SC>Warb.</SC> <I>Procures</I> for <I>brings.</I> [<I>Sing.</I>

<P>75. <B>Feeling</B>] <SC>Mommsen</SC>. Suppose Sh. has for once committed a metrical error
(<I>bonus dormitat Homerus</I>), what harm is there if a critic correct the same? Which
shows a higher estimate of Sh., and of the nature of poetic forms in general,
the critic who corrects here and there an error which Sh. himself perhaps over-
looked, or he who attributes to the poet many hundreds of halting verses? I think
the latter shows more reverence for the Printing Offices of the 16th and 17th centu-
ries than for the art of the great poet. This respect for the printers is as false as it
is convenient.
<P>80. <B>asunder</B>] <SC>Ktly.</SC> I have placed a (!) at the end of this line; for Juliet is
evidently speaking here in the ambiguous manner of her subsequent speeches. She
means an indicative, but wishes her mother to understand her in the optative mood.
The editors of the last century, not understanding this, have, without any authority,
changed &lquo;be&rquo; to <I>are.</I> I should be inclined to make an <I>Aside</I> of &lquo;I do with all my
heart,&rquo; as she pretends to plan his death.
<P>80. <B>he be</B>] <SC>Mommsen</SC>. <I>Be</I> in consonance with <I>he</I> is very frequent in Sh. instead
of <I>are.</I>

<P>In this arbitrary change he is followed, as usual, by Hanmer, except that the latter

<P>84. <B>Ay, madam</B>] <SC>Johns</SC>. Juliet's equivocations are rather too artful for a mind
disturbed by the loss of a new lover. [<I>Sing. Clarke.</I>
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. It appears to us that, on the contrary, the evasions of speech here used
by the young girl-wife are precisely those that a mind, suddenly and sharply awakened
from previous inactivity, by desperate love and grief, into self-conscious strength,
would instinctively use. Especially are they exactly the sort of shifts and quibbles
that a nature rendered timid by stinted intercourse with her kind, and by communion
limited to the innocent confidences made by one of her age in the confessional, is
prone to resort to, when first left to itself in difficulties of situation and abrupt
encounter with life's perplexities. The Italian-born-and-bred Juliet is made by our
author to speak and act with wonderful truth to her southern self. The miracle is
how he, who could draw the courageous and direct-hearted Helena, the noble-
minded Portia, the transparent-souled Imogen, could so thoroughly divine and so
naturally depict the manner in which the two Italian girl-wives, Juliet and Desde-
mona, speak and act in accordance with their southern birth and breeding. He has
drawn them exquisitely gentle, charming, winning, but he has given them the gen-
tleness that blights into timidity, instead of the gentleness that blossoms into moral
courage, and has shown how it brings fatal results. The wonder beyond this is,
how, with all his faithful denotement of the underlying defect in their characters, he
has yet contrived to make the more beautiful portions of their characters so ineffably
lovely, so prevailingly and saliently attractive.
<P>86. <B>We will have vengeance</B>] <SC>Hartley Coleridge</SC> (&lquo;<I>Essays,</I>&rquo; &amp;c., vol. ii,
p. 197). The perfect <I>nonchalance</I> with which this horrid proposition is uttered by a
respectable matron proves how familiar were the minds and ears of our virtuous
ancestors to deeds at which their demoralized posterity would thrill with horror. It
might, however, be Sh.'s art to make the old Capulets unamiable, that our sympathy
with Juliet might be the less distracted by disapprobation of her disobedience.
Capulet's speech is about the worst that Sh. ever wrote. But for a model of parental
rebuke and paternal despotism, I recommend the old gent's behavior to his daughter
throughout the scene. Sh. must have intended to show the vulgarity of rage; and
true it is, a man in a passion is never a gentleman&mdash;much less is a woman a lady.
There may be noble anger, as in Brutus; but then it must be just, and not exceed
the bounds of self-possession. Even Brutus forgets himself a little when irritated by
the intrusion of the men.
</CC>

<P>110. <B>in happy time</B>] <SC>Johns</SC>. <I>A la bonne heure.</I> This phrase was interjected
when the hearer was not quite so well pleased as the speaker. [<I>Sing. Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Sing.</SC> Bishop Lowth uses it in his Letter to Warburton, p. 101: &lquo;And may I not
hope then for the honour of your lordship's animadversions? <I>In good time:</I> when
the candid examiner understands Latin a little better, and when your lordship has a
competent knowledge of Hebrew.&rquo; [<I>Clarke.</I>
<P>113. <B>The County Paris</B>] <SC>Farmer</SC>. It is remarked that &lquo;Paris, though in one
place called <I>Earl,</I> is most commonly styled the <I>Countie</I> in this play. Sh. seems to
have preferred, for some reason or other, the <I>Italian Comte</I> to our <I>Count;</I> perhaps
he took it from the old English novel, from which he is said to have taken his plot.&rquo;
He certainly did so; Paris is there first styled <I>a young Earle,</I> and afterwards <I>Counte,
Countee, County,</I> according to the unsettled orthography of the time. [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Sing.</SC> <I>County</I> or <I>countie</I> was the usual term for an earl in Sh.'s time. [<I>Sta.</I>]
Paris is in this play first styled a <I>young earle.</I> [<I>Huds.</I>] So Baret, &lquo;a <I>countie,</I> or an
<I>earle,</I> comes, un comte,&rquo; and &lquo;a <I>countie</I> or <I>earldome,</I> comitatus.&rquo;
<P>120. <B>I swear</B>] <SC>Coll.</SC> [&lquo;<I>Notes and Emend.</I>&rquo;]. This is erased, perhaps, as not
adding to the force of Juliet's expression, hardly consistent with the delicacy of her
character, and certainly destructive of the measure.
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> But her mother's announcement has manifestly excited Juliet to the highest
pitch, as is shown by the imprudent abruptness and obstinacy with which she op-
poses the wishes of her parents, and which could only make bad worse. She con-
stantly displays a temper as passionate and as easily enkindled as Romeo's. In
such a state of excitement words could easily escape her which she would not use

<P>122. <B>These are news indeed</B>] <SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). These words indicate the sur-

well worthy of being considered.

read the passage, as it stands in the old copies, without perceiving that Juliet's excla-
mation has reference to what her mother has said a little before, &lquo;But now I'll tell
thee <I>joyful tidings,</I> girl.&rquo;
<P>125. <B>the air doth drizzle dew</B>] <SC>Mal.</SC> The reading of Q<SUB>2</SUB>Q<SUB>3</SUB>Ff is philosophically
true, and perhaps ought to be preferred. I suspected, when this note was written,
that <I>earth</I> was the poet's word, and a line in the Rape of Lucrece strongly supports
that reading: &lquo;But as the <I>earth</I> doth <I>weep</I> the <I>sun being set.</I>&rquo; [<I>Sing. Huds. Sta.
Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Steev.</SC> When our author in A Mid. Sum. N. D. says: &lquo;And when she [the
moon] weeps, <I>weeps</I> every little flower,&rquo; he only means that every little flower is
moistened with dew, as if with tears, and not that the flower itself <I>drizzles dew.</I>
This passage sufficiently explains how the <I>earth,</I> in the quotation from the Rape of
Lucrece, may be said to <I>weep.</I> [<I>Sing. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Ritson</SC>. That Sh. thought it was the <I>air</I> and not the <I>earth</I> that <I>drizzled dew,</I> is
evident from other passages. So in King John: &lquo;Before the <I>dew</I> of evening <I>fall.</I>&rquo;
[<I>Sing.</I>
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 1). Malone fully justifies &lquo;<I>earth</I>&rquo; (though he prints <I>air</I>) by the line
from Sh.'s Lucrece.
<P><SC>Huds.</SC> This is scientifically true; poetically, it would seem better to read <I>air</I> in-
stead of <I>earth.</I>
<P><SC>Dyce.</SC> As to the passage from our author's <I>Lucrece,</I> Steevens showed long ago
that it did <I>not</I> &lquo;justify&rquo; (what, indeed, could?) such an utter absurdity as &lquo;the <SC>earth
drizzling</SC> dew.&rquo;

<P><SC>White</SC>. The absurd reading &lquo;earth&rquo; is probably the result of a confusion produced
by the old pronunciation of &lquo;earth,&rquo; <I>airth,</I> which has survived in New England.
The variations in old <I>Capulet's</I> speech in (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) seem not due to the manner in which
that text was obtained; and in that case are interesting because they show the
manner in which Sh. worked over an idea.
<P><SC>Ktly.</SC> To talk of the earth drizzling dew appears, no doubt, to be absurd; but
expressions as incongruous occur in these plays, and we have in Lucrece, &lquo;But
as,&rquo; &amp;c.
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. It must be borne in mind that in each of these passages [cited by other
edd. to sustain &lquo;<I>earth</I>&rquo;] the earth is poetically represented as being <I>wet</I> with dew,
rather than <I>shedding</I> dew; whereas the expression &lquo;drizzle,&rquo; in the text, denotes the
<I>dropping</I> of dew in the same way that Sh. indicates it where he says, Before the <I>dew</I>
of evening <I>fall.&mdash;K. John,</I> II, i, 285.
<P>126. <B>brother's son</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>. Probably here used for &lquo;brother-in-law's son,&rquo; as
Lady Capulet says in the first scene of the present act, &lquo;Tybalt, my cousin! Oh <I>my
brother's child!</I>&rquo;
<P>128. <B>a conduit</B>] <SC>Mal.</SC> The same image occurs more than once in the old poem
of Romeus and Juliet: &lquo;His sighes are stopt, and stopped are the <I>conduits</I> of his
teares.&rquo; [<I>Sing. Huds.</I>
<P>140. <B>take me with you</B>] <SC>Huds.</SC> Let me understand you. [<I>Sta. Clarke.</I>] Like
the Greek phrase, &lquo;Let me go along with you.&rquo;

<P>141. <B>how! . . . none?</B>] <SC>Mommsen</SC>. This is one sentence, and equivalent to
&lquo;What do you mean by that, that she will none?&rquo; which is much more characteristic
of the violent Capulet than the tame and disjointed &lquo;How? Will she none?&rquo;
<P>144. <B>her bridegroom</B>] <SC>Mommsen</SC>. Q<SUB>2</SUB> has here the noteworthy reading <I>Bride.</I>
I must leave it undecided whether or not this is also to be found elsewhere, but will
call attention to the fact that <I>bride</I> is also in our language dialectic for <I>bridegroom,</I>
although Grimm (Dt. W&ouml;rterb, ii, p. 332) considers it as a transferring of the idea.
It was also Middle High German. Compare M&uuml;ller Mhd. W&ouml;rterb., p. 273 f, where
a passage is cited from Gotfrit in reference to Christ as the spiritual Bridegroom:
&lquo;Vil maniges reinen herzen tr&ucirc;t, Vil maniger reinen megde <I>br&ucirc;t.</I>&rquo; There is, in
addition, the metrical reason that, in this play, supernumerary syllables [<I>der kling-
ende Ausgang</I>] are comparatively rare, and almost wholly confined to light final
syllables. I therefore consider it better to disregard the sophistications of the com-
positor of Q<SUB>3</SUB>.
<P>147. <B>is meant love</B>] <SC>Knt.</SC> That is, meant <I>as</I> love.

<P>152. <B>fettle</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>. To go intently upon any business. Certainly an English word,
being acknowledged by our old dictionary-makers. Phillips has &lquo;to <I>fettle to,</I> to go
about, or enter upon a business.&rquo; Kersey, as usual, copies him. Coles has, &lquo;to <I>fettle,
se accingere ad aliquid, aggredior.</I>&rquo; Of uncertain derivation, though it seems like a
corruption of <I>settle.</I> It was, probably, always a familiar, undignified word, and still
exists as a provincial term. Ray speaks of it as in common use in the north, and
defines it, &lquo;to set or go about anything, to dress or prepare.&rquo; The only old author
hitherto quoted for it is Hall, <I>Satires,</I> B. iv, sat. 6: &lquo;But sells his team, and <I>fettleth</I>
to the warre&rquo; [cited by <I>Staunton, Keightley</I>]. I can add Sylvester: &lquo;They to their
long hard journey <I>fettling</I> them, Leaving Samaria and Jerusalem.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Maiden's Blush</I>
[cited by <I>Keightley</I>]. Swift also used it in his Directions to Servants. See Todd.
In the Glossary to Tim Bobbin, we have <I>fettle,</I> explained as a substantive by &lquo;dress,
case, condition.&rquo;
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> To <I>fettle</I> means to <I>prepare,</I> to <I>make ready:</I> &lquo;When the sheriffe saw
Little John bend his bow, He <I>fettled</I> him to be gone.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Percy's</SC> <I>Reliques,</I> i, 92,
ed. 1767. The word does not occur again in our author, and, curiously enough, it
has been overlooked in this passage by every editor from Rowe downwards.
<P><SC>White</SC>. The misprint is so very easy, and both words are so well adapted to the
passage, that there may be some doubt as to what Sh. wrote. But the weight of
authority is in favor of &lquo;fettle.&rquo;
<P><SC>Ktly.</SC> I cannot conceive why the editors all read <I>settle</I> for &lquo;<I>fettle.</I>&rquo;
<P>156. <B>tallow-face</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> Such was the indelicacy of the age of Sh. that
authors were not contented only to employ these terms of abuse in their own original
performances, but even felt no reluctance to introduce them in their versions of the
most chaste and elegant of the Greek or Roman poets. Stanyhurst, the translator
of Virgil, 1582, makes Dido call &AElig;neas <I>hedge-brat, cullion</I> and <I>tar-breech</I> in the
course of one speech. [<I>Huds.</I>] Nay, in the Interlude of The Repentance of
Mary Magdalene, 1567, Mary Magdalene says to one of her attendants: &lquo;<I>Horeson,</I>
I beshrowe your heart, are you here?&rquo; [<I>Sing.</I>
<P><SC>White</SC>. It is intended, of course, that Capulet should be vituperative; but the
terms which he uses did not excite the disgust in Sh.'s time that they do now. &lquo;Car-
cass&rquo; and &lquo;carrion,&rquo; and even kindred words that we do not now write or speak,

<P>were then used without indecency. The ideas and things which they express are
talked about and ever must be; it is only the words that have degraded in process
of time. This is the general tendency of language; it is very rarely that words are
raised permanently from a lower to a higher grade of usage.
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. Even in these coarsely abusive terms with which the irate old man loads
his daughter, how well the dramatist contrives to paint and set before our imagina-
tion the pale face of Juliet, white with suppressed feeling, and almost livid under
the momentary impulse to throw herself at her father's feet and confess all.
<P>158, 159. <B>Hear . . . . wretch</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>. We here see the root of Juliet's pre-
varication; irrational violence if she attempt to offer remonstrance instead of blind
obedience, or if she think for a moment of honest avowal. This is the way to con-
vert original candour of disposition into timid misprision of truth, and artlessness
into artfulness.

or <I>hindling,</I> diminutive of <I>hind.</I> It was applied to women as well as men.

<P>180. <B>train'd</B>] <SC>Ulr.</SC> I prefer &lquo;<I>allied,</I>&rquo; because it follows almost of necessity, from

<P>180. <B>nobly trained</B>] <SC>Mommsen</SC>. This [<I>liand</I> of Q<SUB>2</SUB>] might be metrically toler-
ated, but it might be that Capulet, having described Paris as a gentleman <I>of noble
parentage,</I> should go on to enumerate several other of his qualities, and then once
more speak of him as <I>nobly allied,</I> which would be simply iterating what he had
just said, as <I>e. g.</I> in Marlowe, ii, p. 212: &lquo;His name is Spenser; he is <I>well allied.</I>&rquo;
Rhetorical pleonasms&mdash;like &lquo;The spring, the head, the fountain of your blood&rquo;&mdash;
Macb., II, iii, 103; &lquo;Being with his presence glutted, gorg'd and full&rquo;&mdash;1 Hen. IV:
III, ii, 84; &lquo;Uncapable of pity, void and empty From any dram of pity&rquo;&mdash;Mer. of Ven.,
IV, i, 5&mdash;would prove nothing in this passage, where various different features are
introduced. Therefore most of the later edd. have adopted <I>nobly train'd.</I> But by
<I>liand</I> might have been meant <I>lined,</I> an orthography which, it is true, I have not
met with elsewhere, but which is at times found in the case of <I>ire,</I> thus <I>intierly</I> for
<I>entirely, wiars</I> for <I>wires</I> (in How to Choose a Good Wife from a Bad, 1608, 4to);
<I>fier, hier, squier</I> not seldom for <I>fire, hire, squire;</I> just as the reverse is often found,
<I>lide, tride</I> for <I>lied, tried,</I> &amp;c. Then too <I>nobly lined</I> might refer to his purse; although
<I>loin'd</I> would suit <I>youthful</I> better, and the rude style of the speaker. The spelling
<I>ryall</I> for <I>royal</I> is to be found in Heywood. Perchance, can <I>gryans, lians</I> be found,
as a kind of drawling, for <I>groins, loins,</I> like <I>quire</I> for <I>choir?</I> Until it can be proved
by examples which of the two words is meant, we must fall back upon the conclu-
sion that <I>allied</I> is assuredly corrupt.

<P>184. <B>mammet</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>. A puppet, or doll; a diminutive of <I>mam.</I> &lquo;Quasi dicat
parvam matrem, seu matronulam.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Minshew.</I> &lquo;<I>Mammets,</I> puppets, icuncul&aelig;.&rquo;&mdash;
<I>Coles.</I> &lquo;Icuncul&aelig;&mdash;<I>mammets</I> or puppets that goe by devises of wyer or strings, as
though they had life and moving.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Abr. Fleming's Nomencl.,</I> p. 308. [<I>Sing.</I>] It
has been supposed to be a corruption of <I>movement.</I> Often used as a jocular term of
reproach to young women [this passage cited]. It was sometimes written <I>maumet.</I>
Holinshed also speaks of &lquo;<I>mawmets</I> and idols.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Hist. of Eng.,</I> p. 108. Ruddiman,
in the Glossary to Douglas's Virgil, favours the derivation from Mahomet in <I>Maw-
mentis.</I>
<P><SC>Dyce.</SC> That <I>mammet</I> here means &lquo;puppet&rquo; (used as a term of reproach) is certain
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. In Archbishop Trench's admirable book &lquo;On the Study of Words,&rquo; he
traces the origin of this word to &lquo;Mahomet;&rquo; because the religion of the Arabian
prophet was synonymous, in the minds of English Christians, with idolatry, it being
forgotten that the most characteristic feature and chief glory of Mahometanism is its
protest against all idol-worship whatever. From this original error and injustice
arose the habit of applying the word &lquo;mammet&rquo; (a corruption of &lquo;Mahomet&rquo;) not
only to idols or religious images, but to dolls and puppets. [The substance of
Trench's remarks is to be found in the Var. notes on 1 Hen. IV: II, iii, 95.] <SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>184. <B>her fortune's tender</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>. &lquo;In the moment when good fortune pre-

<P>220. <B>not so green</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> Perhaps Chaucer has given to Emetrius, in The
Knight's Tale, eyes of the same colour: &lquo;His nose was high, his eyin bright <I>citryn:</I>&rquo;
<I>i. e.,</I> the hue of an unripe lemon or citron. Again, in The Two Noble Kinsmen,
by Fletcher and Sh., V, i: &lquo;&mdash;&mdash; oh vouchsafe With that thy rare <I>green</I> eye,&rquo; &amp;c.
[<I>Huds.</I>] I may add that Arthur Hall (the most ignorant and absurd of all the
translators of Homer), in the fourth Iliad, 1581, calls Minerva &lquo;The <I>greene</I> eide
Goddese.&rquo; [<I>Sing.</I>
<P><SC>Douce</SC>. Besides the authorities already produced in favor of <I>green</I> eyes, and
which show the impropriety of Hanmer's alteration to <I>keen,</I> a hundred others might,
if necessary, be given. The early French poets are extremely fond of alluding to
them under the title of <I>yeux vers,</I> which Mons. Le Grand has in vain attempted to
convert into <I>yeux vairs,</I> or grey eyes. It must be confessed that the scarcity, if not
total absence, of such eyes in modern times might well have excited the doubts of
the above intelligent and agreeable writer. For this let naturalists, if they can,
account. It is certain that green eyes were found among the ancients. Plautus thus
alludes to them in his <I>Curculio:</I> &lquo;Qui hic est homo Cum collativo ventre, atque
oculis <I>herbeis?</I>&rquo; Lord Verulam says, &lquo;Great eyes with a <I>green circle</I> between the
white and the white of the eye signify long life.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Hist. of Life and Death,</I> p. 124.
Villa Real, a Portuguese, has written a treatise in praise of them, and they are even
said to exist now among his countrymen. See Pinkerton's Geography, vol. i, p.
556. [<I>Sing. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). These citations unquestionably establish the point.
<P><SC>Huds.</SC> Lord Bacon says that &lquo;eyes somewhat large, and the circles of them in-
clined to <I>greenness,</I> are signs of long life.&rquo; [<I>Clarke.</I>
<P><SC>Dyce.</SC> &lquo;<I>Green eyes</I> were considered as peculiarly beautiful. . . . The Spanish
writers are peculiarly enthusiastic in the praise of green eyes. So Cervantes, in his
novel <I>El Zeloso Estreme&ntilde;o:</I> &ldquo;Ay que ojos tan grandes y tan rasgados! y por el siglo
de mi madre, que son <I>verdes,</I> que no parecen sino que son de esmeraldas.&rdquo;&rquo; (<SC>Weber</SC>).
Gifford, after observing that he has &lquo;seen many Norwegian seamen with eyes of this
hue, which were invariably quick, keen, and glancing,&rquo; and that the expression
&lquo;<I>green eyes</I>&rquo; is common in our early poets, cites the following Sonnet by Drummond
of Hawthornden:

<P><SC>White</SC>. Of all the varieties of the orange-colored eye (usually called black,
hazel, or brown), that which at a distance appears very dark, but which, when
clearly seen, is found to be of an olive-green tint, is perhaps the brightest and most
beautiful.
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. The brilliant touch of green visible in very light hazel eyes, and which
gives wonderful clearness and animation to their look, has been admiringly denoted
by various poets from time immemorial.
<P>222-225. <B>second match . . . him</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>. This sentence presents a point of
study in Sh.'s method of using relative words in a sentence; &lquo;<I>it</I>&rquo; refers to &lquo;second
match;&rquo; then &lquo;first&rquo; relates to &lquo;match;&rquo; then &lquo;<I>he</I>&rquo; and &lquo;<I>him</I>&rquo; relate to &lquo;first.&rquo;
<P>225. <B>living here</B>] <SC>Johns</SC>. Hanmer reads,&mdash;as living <I>hence</I>&mdash;that is, at a distance,

<P>3. <B>I am nothing slow</B>] <SC>Johns</SC>. His haste shall not be abated by my slowness.

import the reverse of this, and seem rather to mean, <I>I am not backward in restrain-

tation extorted a meaning from the words which they do not at first present; and

<P>hence his proposed alteration; but Sh. must answer for his own peculiarities. See

<P><SC>Sing</SC>. Sh. has hastily fallen into similar inadvertencies elsewhere.
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> The meaning is obvious as it stands: &lquo;I am nothing slow (so as), to slack
his haste.&rquo;
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> Sh.'s marvellous power of condensation sometimes renders his meaning
obscure. In this instance, the sense appears to be, &lquo;and I am not slow <I>in my own
preparations for the wedding, to give him any reason</I> to slacken his hasty proceed-
ings.&rquo; [<I>Dyce</I> (ed. 2).

means, obviously, is, I have no wish that he should lessen his haste. The (Q<SUB>1</SUB>)
makes the speech the very reverse.
<P><SC>Ktly.</SC> Collier's (MS.) mistakes the sense. &lquo;To&rquo; is, so as to, that I should.
Editors have not understood it.
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. There are remarkably few instances of elliptical diction in the present
play. It is a form that Sh. used but sparingly in his earlier dramas, whereas, in his
latter ones, it occurs perpetually. As his habit of writing and facility of expression
increased, so his power of condensed and inclusive phraseology strengthened; while
his own taste and judgment made him ever more and more exercise it as a skill in
itself and productive of the most vigorous effect.
<P>7. <B>talk'd</B>] <SC>Mommsen</SC>. By &lquo;<I>talk'd</I>&rquo; the meaning is wholly changed. Paris does
not here wish to give to the Friar, as an excuse for his uncertainty concerning
Juliet's mind, that, owing to her grief for Tybalt, he had been unable to talk befit-
tingly with her about love, but he simply explains, by this grief, Juliet's silence and
reserve in his own favour; this was the only reason why he received from her so few
words of love. Since this interpretation gives throughout a clear meaning&mdash;for
that Paris does not positively know how Juliet is minded does not preclude the con-
viction on his part that the expression of her love is alone wanting,&mdash;since it renders
more graceful the connection with what follows, in so far as Julia, silent about love,
is his sorrowing Venus, and since <I>I have talk</I> could have been more easily corrupted
into <I>I have talk'd</I> than the reverse, we abide by the old reading.
<P>10. <B>so much sway</B>] <SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). There seems much reason in the emenda
tion of the (MS.).

<P>38. <B>evening mass</B>] <SC>Ritson</SC>. Juliet means <I>vespers.</I> There is no such thing as
<I>evening mass.</I> [<I>Huds. White.</I>] &lquo;<I>Masses,</I>&rquo; as Fynes Moryson observes, &lquo;are only sung
in the morning, and when the priests are fasting.&rquo; [<I>Sing.</I>] So, likewise, in The
Boke of Thenseygnemente and Techynge that the Knight of the Toure made to his
Doughters, translated and printed by Caxton: &lquo;And they of the parysshe told the
preest that it was past <I>none,</I> and therefor he durst not synge masse, and so they hadde
no masse that daye.&rquo; [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> It is strange that Sh., who on other occasions has shown a competent know-
ledge of the doctrines and usages of the Roman Catholic Church, should have fallen
into this error. The celebration of mass, as is well known, can only take place in
the forenoon.
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. The word &lquo;mass&rquo; is here employed in the general sense of &lquo;service,&rquo;
&lquo;office,&rquo; &lquo;prayer;&rquo; while, on the contrary, the Italians usually apply their word <I>fun-
zione</I> to &lquo;high mass&rquo; only, though in strictness it means &lquo;divine service&rquo; generally.
<P>45. <B>past cure</B>] <SC>Del.</SC> So in Love's Lab. L., V, ii, 28.
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> This change from <I>care</I> to <I>cure</I> is not only needless, but even objectionable.
<I>Past cure</I> is the same as <I>past help,</I> and therefore only a weak repetition of the same
thought. &lquo;Past all hope, past all care or effort (for escape), past all help,&rquo; perfectly
expresses the desperate position and mood in which Juliet finds herself.
</CC>

<P>54. <B>this knife</B>] <SC>White</SC>. The ladies of Sh.'s day customarily wore knives at their
girdles.
<P>57. <B>the label</B>] <SC>Mal.</SC> The seals of deeds in our author's time were not impressed
on the parchment itself on which the deed was written, but were appended on dis-
tinct slips or labels affixed to the deed. Hence, in Rich. II: V, ii, 56, the Duke
of York discovers, by the depending seal, a covenant into which his son, the Duke
of Aumerle, had entered: &lquo;What seal is that which <I>hangs</I> without thy bosom?&rquo;
[<I>Sing. Corn. Verp. Huds. Sta. Dyce, Clarke, Hal.</I>
<P>60. <B>Therefore out of</B>] This line is cited by <SC>S. Walker</SC> (&lquo;<I>Crit.</I>&rquo; vol. ii, p. 173)
as an instance of the peculiar accentuation of the preposition &lquo;<I>of.</I>&rquo;
<P>63. <B>the umpire</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>. That is, this knife shall decide the struggle between
me and my distresses. [<I>Sing.</I>
<P>64. <B>the commission</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>. <I>Commission</I> is for <I>authority</I> or <I>power.</I> [<I>Sing.</I>
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> I do not think that <I>commission</I> stands here, as Johnson says, for &lquo;authority,&rquo;
or &lquo;power,&rquo; but is used in its ordinary sense. Juliet says in effect: this knife shall
decide that which the commission [<I>die Vollmacht</I>] that thy age and thy art give thee&mdash;
the commission, namely, to appoint an umpire&mdash;could not bring to an honourable
issue.
<P>66. <B>Be not so long</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>. The constraint, with sparing speech, visible in
Juliet when with her parents, as contrasted with her free outpouring flow of words
when she is with her lover, her father-confessor, or her nurse&mdash;when, in short, she
is her natural self and at perfect ease&mdash;is true to characteristic delineation. The
young girl, the very young girl, the girl brought up as Juliet has been reared, the
youthful southern maiden, lives and breathes in every line by which Sh. has set her
before us.
</CC>

<P>69. <B>as desperate</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>. It is interesting to observe how different is the style
here, in one of Sh.'s earlier written plays, from the style in his later ones. The
repetition of the word &lquo;desperate,&rquo; the precision of statement in this comparison, is
utterly contrary to the conciseness, the elliptical condensedness, which we find in the
comparisons from Sh.'s hand at a later date.
<P>69. <B>an execution</B>] <SC>S. Walker</SC>. I suspect <I>an</I> is an interpolation. (Vol. i, p.
269, <SC>Art.</SC> xl: &lquo;Metre affected by the pronunciation of <I>ion</I> final.&rquo;)
<P>76. <B>And if</B>] <SC>Del.</SC> According to the punctuation of (Q<SUB>1</SUB>)Qq, which puts a stop
at the end of the preceding sentence, &lquo;<I>And if</I>&rquo; should here be read as &lquo;<I>An</I> if.&rquo;
<P>78. <B>yonder tower</B>] <SC>Ulr.</SC> But I cannot perceive why Juliet must designate a
particular, actual tower, since all that follows is purely imaginary, the tasks of hor-
ror which her imagination conjured up. And besides, the expression, &lquo;Bid me leap
from any (no matter how high) tower&rquo; is more vigorous than &lquo;from that tower there.&rquo;
<P><SC>White</SC>. &lquo;Yonder&rquo; has been almost universally followed hitherto as the more
poetic reading. But the passage was evidently rewritten on the revision of the play,
as will be seen by comparison with the earliest text, which will give the reader a
fair notion of the nature and extent of the variations between the two versions in
this part of the play, all of which cannot be noticed. It is difficult to see why one
word of the revised version should be rejected while all the others are accepted.
</CC>

<P><SC>Knt.</SC> In the adaptation of Bandello's tale in Painter's &lquo;Palace of Pleasure&rquo; we
have, &lquo;they will judge you to be dead, and, according to the custom of our city, you

of this custom; but Sh. saw how beautifully it accorded with the conduct of his
story, and he therefore emphatically repeats it in the directions of the Friar after
Juliet's supposed death: IV, v, 79. Ancient customs survive when they are built
upon the unaltering parts of national character, and have connection with unalter-
able local circumstances. Juliet was carried to her tomb as the maids and matrons
of Italy are still carried:

<P>110. <B>on the bier</B>] <SC>Knt.</SC> The editors [in omitting the line from QqFf] have
here gone far beyond their office; nor can we understand why the more particular
working out of the idea in the next two lines should have given them offence. &lquo;Be
borne&rquo; means &lquo;<I>to</I> be borne.&rquo;
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (&lquo;<I>Remarks,</I>&rquo; &amp;c., p. 174). The line [of the QqFf] is a various lection of
the two lines [111, 112]. I apprehend that Knight would search the poetry of
England in vain for another example of such an ellipsis as &lquo;Be borne&rquo; for <I>to be
borne.</I> When Beaumont and Fletcher imitated the passage in <I>The Knight of Malta,</I>
IV, i, they were content with <I>one reading.</I>
<P><SC>Lettsom</SC> [marginal MS. note on the above in the present editor's copy]. Very
true. These various lections, like those in Love's Lab. L., seem to have originated
in transcribing from Sh.'s foul copies.
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> The hypothesis that the line &lquo;Be borne,&rquo; &amp;c., retained its place in the MS.
only through an oversight of Sh. when he revised the piece (about 1598), supposes
that the printer of Q<SUB>2</SUB> had before him Sh.'s own handwriting, which is very improb-
able. At all events, it is unscholarly upon such an hypothesis to omit the line alto-
gether. For although it is not to be denied that it seems superfluous, yet it may be
quite easily conformed to the construction, if Knight's explanation of the ellipsis be
correct.
<P><SC>Cambr.</SC> We have [here] omitted a line which occurs in all the Quartos, except
the first, and all the Folios, because it could not be retained without absolute detri-

<P>shillings; and the cook, fifteen shillings. The relative scale of estimation for

Ben Jonson has described a master cook in his gorgeous style:
<BQ>
&lquo;A master cook! why, he's a man of men<LB>
For a professor; he designs, he draws,<LB>
He paints, he carves, he builds, he fortifies,<LB>
Makes citadels of curious fowl and fish.<LB>
Some he dry-ditches, some motes round with broths,<LB>
Mounts marrow-bones, cuts fifty angled custards,<LB>

<P>Capulet is evidently a man of ostentation; but his ostentation, as is most generally
the case, is covered with a thin veil of affected indifference. In Act I he says to his
guests: &lquo;We have a trifling, foolish banquet toward.&rquo; In Act III, when he settles
the day of Paris's marriage, he just hints: &lquo;We'll keep no great ado&mdash;a friend or
two.&rquo; But Sh. knew that these indications of the &lquo;pride which apes humility&rquo; were
not inconsistent with the &lquo;twenty cooks&rquo;&mdash;the regret that &lquo;We shall be much unfur-
nished for this time,&rquo; and the solicitude expressed in &lquo;Look to the baked meats, good
Angelica.&rquo; Steevens turns up his nose aristocratically at Sh. for imputing &lquo;to an
Italian nobleman and his lady all the petty solicitudes of a private house, concerning
a provincial entertainment;&rquo; and he adds, very grandly: &lquo;To such a bustle our
author might have been witness at home; but the like anxieties could not well have
occurred in the family of Capulet.&rquo; Steevens had not well read the history of society,
either in Italy or in England, to have fallen into the error of believing that the great
were exempt from such &lquo;anxieties.&rquo; The baron's lady overlooked the baron's kitchen
from her private chamber; and the still-room and the spicery not unfrequently occu-
pied a large portion of her attention. [<I>Verp. Huds.</I>

<P>14. <B>harlotry</B>] <SC>Del.</SC> Sh. has also elsewhere used this abstract for the concrete

<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). It is used both as an adjective and substantive. In 1 Hen. IV:

<P>16. <B>gadding</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> The primitive sense of this word was to straggle from
house to house, and collect money, under pretence of singing carols to the Blessed
Virgin. See T. Warton's note on Milton's Lycidas, v. 40.
<P><SC>Douce</SC>. Steevens's derivation seems too refined. Warton's authority is an old
register at Gadderston, in these words: &lquo;Receyvid at the <I>gadyng</I> with Saynte Mary
songe at Crismas.&rquo; If the original were attentively examined, it would perhaps turn
out that the word in question has some mark of contraction over it, which would
convert it into <I>gaderyng&mdash;i. e.,</I> gathering or collecting money, and not simply <I>going
about from house to house,</I> according to Warton's explanation.

<P>39. <B>near night</B>] <SC>Mal.</SC> In III, v, Romeo parted from his bride at daybreak on

<P>desires Capulet to go with him at once, and Montague to come to him &lquo;this after-

which indicates that the Prince's charge had just been given to both of them, and
shortly after speaks of the festival at his house &lquo;this night.&rquo; At this festival Romeo
sees Juliet when she speaks of sending to him &lquo;to-morrow;&rquo; and on that &lquo;morrow&rquo;

Tybalt kills Mercutio, and during which scene Romeo's words, &lquo;Tybalt, that <I>an hour</I>
hath been my kinsman,&rquo; show that the then time is the afternoon of the same day.
The Friar, at the close of Scene iii of that Act bids Romeo &lquo;good night;&rquo; and in the
next scene, Paris, in reply to Capulet's inquiry, &lquo;What day is this?&rquo; replies, &lquo;<I>Monday,</I>
my lord.&rquo; This, by the way, denotes that the &lquo;old accustomed feast&rquo; of the Capu-
lets, according to a usual practice in Catholic countries, was celebrated on a Sunday
evening. In Scene v of Act III comes the parting of the lovers at the dawn of
Tuesday, and when, at the close of the scene, Juliet says she shall repair to Friar
Laurence&rquo; cell. Act IV commences with her appearance there, thus carrying on the
action during the same day, Tuesday. But the effect of long time is introduced by
the mention of &lquo;<I>evening</I> mass,&rquo; and by the Friar's detailed directions and reference to
&lquo;to-morrow's night;&rquo; so that when the mind has been prepared by the change of
scene, by Capulet's anxious preparations for the wedding, and by Juliet's return to
filial submission, there seems no violence done to the imagination by Lady Capulet's
remarking, &lquo;'Tis now near night.&rquo; Nay, it is one of Sh.'s expedients in dramatic
time for bringing on the period of the catastrophe; for Juliet retires to her own room
with the intention of selecting wedding attire for the next morning, which her father
has said shall be that of the marriage, anticipating it by a whole day&mdash;Wednesday
instead of Thursday&mdash;thus naturally preparing for the immediate sequence of the
incidents in the remainder of Act IV.

<P>23. <B>Lie thou there</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> It appears, from several passages in our old plays,
that knives were formerly part of the accoutrements of a bride, and everything
<I>behoveful</I> for Juliet's <I>state</I> had just been left with her. So in Decker's Match Me in
London, 1631: &lquo;See at my girdle hang my <I>wedding knives!</I>&rquo; Again, in King
Edward III, 1599: &lquo;Here at my side do hang my <I>wedding</I> knives.&rquo; Again:
&lquo;&mdash;&mdash; there was a maid named, &amp;c.&mdash;She tooke <I>one of her knives</I> that was some
halfe a foote long,&rquo; &amp;c. &amp;c. &lquo;And it was found in all respects like to <I>the other
that was in her sheath.</I>&rquo;&mdash;Goulart's Admirable Histories, 1607, pp. 176, 178. In
Sidney's Arcadia, b. iii, we are likewise informed that Amphialus &lquo;in his crest car-
ried Philoclea's <I>knives,</I> the only token of her forced favour.&rquo; [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Mal.</SC> In order to account for Juliet's having a dagger, it is not necessary to have
recourse to the ancient accoutrements of brides, how prevalent soever the custom
may have been; for Juliet appears to have furnished herself with this instrument
immediately after her father and mother had threatened to force her to marry Paris:
&lquo;If all else fail, myself have power to die.&rquo; Accordingly, in the very next scene,
when she is at the Friar's cell, and before she could have been furnished with any
of the apparatus of a bride (not having then consented to marry the count), she
says: &lquo;'Twixt me and my extremes this bloody knife shall,&rquo; &amp;c. [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Boswell</SC>. Gifford, in a note on Jonson's Staple of News, informs us that in Sh.'s
time &lquo;daggers, or, as they were more commonly called, knives, were worn at all
times by every woman in England.&rquo; [<SC>Sing</SC>. finishes the sentence]: &lquo;Whether they
were so worn in Italy, Sh., I believe, never inquired, and I cannot tell.&rquo; [<I>Coll.
Verp. Huds. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). It certainly was the case.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC>. (ed. 2). &lquo;The omission of &ldquo;knife&rdquo; is peculiarly awkward, as Juliet has
been addressing the vial just before.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>W. N. Lettsom</SC>.

<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> If it be assumed that Juliet, or rather Sh., wishes to thrust aside utterly
the suspicion which comes up in her mind, then this line is absolutely necessary.
But it may fairly be asked whether this were the intention of the poet. It was
emphatically so according to the text of (Q<SUB>1</SUB>). On the other hand, the enlarging and
revising which the whole monologue received in the &lquo;corrected, augmented, and
amended&rquo; edition of Q<SUB>2</SUB> consists precisely herein that Sh. brings forward far more
strongly and impressively than in (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) the doubts, the apprehensions, and horror
which seize Juliet's soul at the sight of the vial which she must drain, and this is
done manifestly to place in clearer light the loftiness of her resolve and the depth
of her love and fidelity. With this in view it would clearly be very little to the
purpose to represent the suspicion aroused against Laurence as wholly allayed. On
the contrary, it must remain, even if it amounts to only a dubious apprehension.

<P>43. <B>Lies festering</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> To <I>fester</I> is to corrupt. So, in King Edward III,
1599: &lquo;Lilies that <I>fester</I> smell far worse than weeds.&rquo; This line likewise occurs in
the 94th Sonnet of Sh. The play of Edward III has been ascribed to him. [<I>Sing.</I>
<P>45. <B>is it not like</B>] <SC>Del.</SC> This repeats the previous question, &lquo;Is it not very
like,&rquo; without completing the sentence to which &lquo;the horrible conceit&rquo; is the subject&mdash;
a Shakespearian anacoluthon which here marks Juliet's excitement.
<P>47. <B>mandrakes</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> The mandrake (says Thomas Newton in his Herball
of the Bible, 1587) has been idly represented as &lquo;a creature having life and engen-
dered under the earth of the seed of some dead person, who hath beene convicted
and put to death for some felonie or murther; and that they had the same in such
dampish and funerall places, where the said convicted persons were buried,&rquo; &amp;c.
[<I>Sing. Huds. Hal. Clarke.</I>] In Webster's Duchess of Malfy, 1623: &lquo;I have this
night dug up a <I>mandrake,</I> And am <I>grown mad</I> with it.&rquo; Again, in the Atheist's
Tiagedy, 1611: &lquo;The <I>cries of mandrakes</I> never touch'd the ear With more sad
horror.&rquo; In A Christian turn'd Turk, 1612: &lquo;I'll rather give an ear to the black
<I>shrieks</I> Of <I>mandrakes,</I>&rquo; &amp;c. In Aristippus or the Jovial Philosopher: &lquo;This is the
mandrake's voice that undoes me.&rquo; [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Nares</SC>. The English name of Mandragoras. An inferior degree of animal life
was attributed to it, and it was commonly supposed that when torn from the ground
it uttered groans of so pernicious a nature that the person who committed the vio-
lence went mad or died. To escape that danger it was recommended to tie one
end of a string to the plant and the other to a dog, upon whom the fatal groan
would then discharge its full malignity. See Bulleine's <I>Bulwarke of Defence
against Sicknesse,</I> p. 41. These strange notions arose, probably, from the little less
fanciful comparison of the root to the human figure, strengthened, doubtless, in
England by the accidental circumstance of <I>man</I> being the first syllable of the word.
The ancients, however, made the same comparison of its form:
<BQ>
&lquo;Quamvis <I>semihominis,</I> vesano gramine f&oelig;ta,<LB>
Mandragor&aelig; pariat flores.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Columella, de l. Hort.,</I> v, 19.<LB>
</BQ>
<P>The white mandrake, which they called the male, was that whose root bore this
resemblance. Lyte says of it, &lquo;The roote is great and white, not muche unlyke a
radishe roote divided into two or three partes and sometimes growing one upon
another, almost lyke the legges and thighes of a man.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Transl. of Dodoens,</I> p. 437.
It is supposed to cause death, in 2 Hen. VI: III, ii, 310. A very diminutive or
grotesque figure was often compared to a mandrake; that is, to the root, as above
described. So in 2 Hen. IV: I, ii, 17. It was sometimes considered as an emblem

<P><B>Stage-direction</B>] <SC>Coll.</SC> The &lquo;curtains&rquo; were &lquo;the traverse,&rquo; as it was called, at
the back of the stage.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (&lquo;<I>Life of Sh.</I>&rquo; p. 42, ed. 2). At the third <I>sounding,</I> or flourish of trumpets,
the exhibition began. The curtain, which concealed the stage from the audience,
was then drawn, opening in the middle and running upon iron rods. Other cur-
tains, called <I>traverses,</I> were used as a substitute for scenes. At the back of the
stage was a balcony, the platform of which was raised about eight or nine feet from
the ground; it served as a window, gallery, or upper chamber; from it a portion of
the dialogue was sometimes spoken, and in front of it curtains were suspended to
conceal, if necessary, those who occupied it from the audience. The internal roof
of the stage, either painted blue or adorned with drapery of that colour, was termed
<I>the heavens.</I> The stage was generally strewed with rushes, but on extraordinary
occasions was matted. We have reason to believe that when tragedies were per-
formed it was hung with black. Movable painted scenery there was none:
<BQ>

No pencil's aid as yet had dar'd supply,<LB>

<P>2. <B>dates</B>] <SC>Beisly</SC>. Dr. Moffet, in &lquo;Health Improvement,&rquo; says of dates: &lquo;They
are usually put into stewed broths, mince-pies and restorative cullices, as though
they were of great and wholesome nourishment.&rquo; William Turner does not speak
so favorably of them, &lquo;as they fill the stomach full of wind, and are hurtful to them
that are disposed to the tooth-ache. Wherefore our sweete-lipped Londoners and
wanton courtiers do not wysely to suffer so many dates to be put into their pyes and
other meats, to the great charge of their purses, and to no less undoing of the health
of their bodies.&rquo; In Westmacott's &lquo;Scripture Herbal&rquo; it is said of dates &lquo;that astrolo-
gers have given them to Mars, perhaps to please the lady Venus with.&rquo; In Sylves-
ter's &lquo;Dubartas&rquo; the date and olive are noticed as aiding appetite. Gerarde notices
the Quince, and says &lquo;the marmalad or cotiniat of quinces is good and profitable to
strengthen the stomach, that it may retain and keep the meat therein, until it be per-
fectly digested.&rquo;

<P>an hour later: &lquo;Well, 'tis <I>nine</I> o'clock, 'tis time to ring the <I>curfew.</I>&rquo;&mdash;O. Pl, v. 292.
By [this] passage in Romeo and Juliet it seems that the bell which was commonly
used for that purpose obtained in time the name of the <I>curfew-bell,</I> and was so called
whenever it rung on any occasion. . . . At the regular time it probably was called
simply the <I>curfew;</I> at others, if it was known that the same bell was used, it might
be said, as above, that the <I>curfew-bell</I> had rung.
<P><SC>Ritson</SC>. The <I>curfew-bell</I> is universally rung at <I>eight</I> or <I>nine</I> o'clock at night;
generally according to the season. The term is here used with peculiar impropriety,
as it is not believed that <I>any</I> bell was ever rung so early as <I>three</I> in the morning.
The derivation of <I>curfeu</I> is well known; but it is a mere vulgar error that the insti-
tution was a badge of slavery imposed by the Norman Conqueror. To <I>put out the
fire</I> became necessary only because it was time to go to bed. And if the curfew
commanded all fires to be extinguished, the morning bell ordered them to be
lighted again. In short, the ringing of these two bells was a manifest and essential
service to people who had scarcely any other means of measuring their time. [<I>Cham.</I>
<P><SC>Mitford</SC> (&lquo;<I>Gent. Mag.,</I>&rquo; 1845, p. 579). Sh. does not mean that the bell rang for
curfew, but that the <I>same bell which was used for the curfew was now rung as the
morning bell.</I>
<P><SC>Del.</SC> In all other passages Sh. uses <I>curfew</I> in its own proper signification. And
yet (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) has: The curfew-bell hath rung, 'tis four o'clock.
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> It is very unlikely that it should be rung as early as three o'clock in the
morning; and old Capulet in his flurrying officiousness only imagines that he has
heard it.
<P><SC>White</SC>. An error inexplicable to me. The curfew-bell was rung at eight in the
evening. It is still rung at nine in New England, though within the last ten years
the custom has been rapidly disappearing. Sh. elsewhere (Meas. for Meas., IV, ii,
78, and Lear III, iv, 21) uses &lquo;curfew&rquo; correctly.
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. Inasmuch as the same bell was used for ringing the last thing at night
and the first thing in the morning, it is probable that what is here familiarly called
&lquo;the curfew-bell,&rquo; means, more strictly speaking, &lquo;the matin-bell.&rquo;
<P>5. <B>Look to the baked meats</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> Sh. has here imputed to an Italian
nobleman and his lady all the petty solicitudes of a private house concerning a pro-

home; but the like anxieties could not well have occurred in the family of Capulet,
whose wife, if <I>Angelica</I> be her name, is here directed to perform the office of a
housekeeper. [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Mal.</SC> Such were the simple manners of our poet's time that, without doubt, in
many families much superior to Sh.'s, the lady of the house gave directions concern-
ing the baked meats. [<I>Hal.</I>

<P>6. <B>cot-quean</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>. Probably a <I>cock-quean</I>&mdash;that is a male <I>quean,</I> a man
who troubles himself with female affairs. It continued long in use in this sense, and
is quoted by Addison, who compares a woman meddling with state affairs to a man
interfering in female business, a <I>cot-quean,</I> adding, &lquo;Each of the sexes should keep
within its bounds.&rquo; It seems to have meant, also, a hen-pecked husband, which
suits the same derivation. [<I>Verp. Huds.</I>] In the following passage it means <I>mas-
culine hussy.</I> It is spoken by Ovid, as Jupiter, to Julia, as Juno: &lquo;We tell thee
thou angerest us, <I>cot-quean;</I> and we will thunder thee in pieces for thy <I>col-
queanity.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<I>B. Jons., Poetaster,</I> IV, iii. [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Hunter</SC>. A <I>cot-quean</I> is the wife of a faithless husband, and not, as Johnson, who
knew little of the language of Sh.'s time, explains it, &lquo;a man who busies himself
about kitchen affairs.&rquo; It occurs twice in Golding's translation of the Story of
Tereus. The Nurse is speaking to Lady Capulet, and the word calls forth all the
conversation which follows about jealousy. Authorities for this being the true sense
might be produced in abundance.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (&lquo;<I>Few Notes,</I>&rquo; p. 113). But Golding, in the passage to which Hunter refers, has
<I>cuc-queane,</I> which is a distinct word from <I>cot-quean,</I> though they are sometimes con-
founded by early writers,&mdash;a <I>cuc-quean</I> (<I>cuck quean,</I> or <I>cock quean</I>) meaning a she-
cuckold; a <I>cot-quean,</I> a man who busies himself too much in women's affairs. [Sub-
stantially, <I>Sing.</I> (ed. 2), <I>Coll.</I> (ed. 2).] In Fletcher's <I>Love's Care,</I> Act II, Sc. ii,

<P><SC>Hunter</SC>. (&lquo;<I>A Few Words in Reply,</I>&rquo; &amp;c., 1853, p. 19). Finding &lquo;cutquean&rquo; in

with Dyce, and others, in thinking that the &lquo;cotquean&rquo; of the Nurse does mean &lquo;a
man that busies himself in women's affairs,&rquo; and that the whole of what the Nurse
says is addressed to Capulet. The jealous-hood, which might appear naturally
enough to arise out of the use of such a word as that which the Nurse used, seems to
have an origin later in the dialogue.
<P><SC>Sing</SC>. (ed. 2). That a <I>cot-quean</I> signified a man who troubled himself with female
affairs, what has since been called a <I>molly-coddle,</I> as well as a hen-pecked husband,
is quite certain. Thus, Hall in his Sixth Satire, b. iv:
<BQ>
&lquo;And make a drudge of their uxorious mate,<LB>
Who like a <I>cot-quean</I> freezeth at the rock.&rquo;<LB>

<P>It is probably derived from the Fr., <I>coquine.</I>
<P><SC>White</SC>. As late as the beginning of the last century, a man given to prying into
women's matters was called a cot-quean. See <I>Vanbrugh's Confederacy</I> (1705),
Act II: &lquo;<I>Money-trap.</I> You won't take it amiss if I should ask you a few questions?
&mdash;<I>Flippanta.</I> What's this Cot-quean going to pry into now?&rquo; And in the Craven
dialect a man fond of cooking for himself is called a cot.

<P>6. <B>set up his rest</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> This expression, frequently employed by the old
dramatic writers, is taken from the manner of firing the harquebuss, which was so
heavy that a supporter, called a rest, was fixed in the ground before the piece was
levelled to take aim. Decker, in Old Fortunatus, 1600: &lquo;&mdash;&mdash; set your heart at
rest, for I have <I>set up my rest,</I> that unless you can run swifter than a hart,&rquo; &amp;c. Also
in B. and Fl.'s Elder Brother: &lquo;&mdash;&mdash; My <I>rest is up,</I> Nor will I go less.&rquo; Again in
the Roaring Girl, 1611: &lquo;Like a musket on a <I>rest.</I>&rquo; See Montfaucon's Monarchie
Fran&ccedil;oise, tom. v, pl. 48. [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Reed</SC>. It is, however, oftener employed with reference to the <I>game at primero,</I>
in which it was one of the terms then in use. In the second instance above quoted
it is certainly so. See Dodsley's Collection of Old Plays, vol. x, p. 364, edit. 1780,
where several instances are brought together. [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>M. Mason</SC>. It means that the gamester has determined what stake he would play
for. In the passage from Fletcher's Elder Brother, where Eustace says, &lquo;<I>My rest is
up,</I> and I will go no less,&rquo; he means to say, <I>my stake is laid,</I> and I will not play for
a smaller. The same phrase very frequently occurs in the plays of B. and Fl. It
is also used by Lord Clarendon in his History, as well as in the old comedy of Sup-
poses, 1587. [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Boswell</SC>. Nash quibbles upon this word in his Terrors of the Night: &lquo;You that
are married and have wives of your owne, and yet hold too nere frendship with your
neighbours, <I>set up your rests,</I> that the Night will be an il neighbour to <I>your rest,</I> and
that you shall have as little peace of mind as the rest.&rquo; [<I>Sing. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Nares</SC>. A metaphor from the game of primero, meaning, to stand upon the cards
you have in your hand in hopes that they may prove better than your adversary.
Hence to make up your mind, to be determined. It is fully explained in an epigram
of Sir J. Harington's, where Marcus, a foolish gamester, is described as standing at
first upon small games and consequently losing; but still losing, by the fraud of his
antagonists, even when he grew more wary. Hence we may see how erroneous was
one of Steevens' explanations of this phrase. I say <I>one,</I> for he has given the right
in other places. A <I>rest</I> was, in fact, an appendage to every matchlock gun, not
particularly the harquebuss, because the soldier could not manage his match without
it. There was, therefore, such a <I>rest,</I> but that was not the allusion. [<I>Sta.</I> sub-
stantially.
<P><SC>Sing</SC>. (ed. 1) [Note on All's Well, II, i, 138]. This word furnished many other
proverbial expressions among the Italians, one of which is to be found in the Ciriffo
Calvanco of Luca Pulci: &lquo;<I>Fa del suo resto,</I>&rquo; to adventure all. &lquo;<I>Haver fatto del resto,</I>&rquo;
to have lost all or have nothing to <I>rest</I> upon. &lquo;<I>Riserbar il Resto,</I>&rquo; to reserve one's
<I>rest,</I> to be wary and circumspect, &amp;c., &amp;c. All authorities are decisive upon the
derivation of this word from Primero, as Nares has amply shown. . . . In Spanish
too, &lquo;<I>Echar el resto,</I>&rquo; <I>to set or lay up one's rest,</I> has the same origin and figurative
meaning&mdash;to adventure all, <I>to be determined.</I> We shall now, it is to be hoped, hear
no more of <I>musket rests,</I> &amp;c., in explanation of this phrase.
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 1). A figurative expression apparently derived from the mode of firing

<P>the heavy harquebuss by placing the barrel upon a rest or support. The phrase was
applied in a variety of ways, generally indicating determination; as at the game of
Primero, a person who had staked all the money he meant to risk at once was said
to have &lquo;set up his rest.&rquo; It was in constant use.
<P><SC>Huds.</SC> The same as to <I>make up one's mind.</I> Launcelot (Mer. of Ven. II, ii, 110)
has a similar quibble. See also Com. of Errors, IV, iii, 27.
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2) [Note on All's Well, II, i, 138]. This expression is not derived
from Primero or any other game of cards, but originally from musketry. . . . Dyce,
in his Beaumont and Fletcher, always refers it to some game and not to its true
original. We say this in spite of Gifford.&mdash;<I>Ben Jonson,</I> vol. i, p. 107.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2). This phrase, meaning that the speaker is perfectly determined on
a thing, is &lquo;a metaphor taken from play, where the highest stake the parties were
disposed to venture was called <I>the rest.</I> To appropriate this term to any particular
game, as is sometimes done, is extremely incorrect.&rquo;&mdash;Gifford's note on <I>Massinger's
Works,</I> vol. ii, p. 21, ed. 1813.
<P><SC>Ktly.</SC> (&lquo;<I>N. and Qu.</I>&rquo; 2d Ser. vol. xii, p. 65, 1861). I have more than once re-
marked the slender acquaintance with the language and literature of Spain shown
by our Shakespearian critics, and the present is an instance, and a strong one, of the
truth of my observation. <I>set up rest,</I> they all tell us, belonged to the game of Pri-
mero, which was derived from Spain. Now the dictionary of the Spanish Academy
defines <I>Resto</I> in these words (the reader must excuse my quoting Spanish): &lquo;En los
juegos de envite es aquella cantitad que separa el jugador del demas dinero para
jugar y envidar;&rquo; and <I>Echar el resto</I> (set up the rest), &lquo;En el juego donde hai
envites envidar con todo el caudal que uno tiene delante y de que hace su resto.&rquo;
<I>Envidar</I> and <I>envite,</I> I may here observe, come from the Latin verb <I>invito,</I> and
signify challenge, wager, bet&mdash;a sense in which the Italians also use their verb <I>invi-
tare,</I> and which is also to be found in the French <I>&agrave; l'envi</I> and our own <I>vie. Rest,</I>
then, is a Spanish term which was adopted along with the Spanish name of the game
<I>Primero</I> (properly <I>Primera</I>), or <I>Qu&iacute;nola,</I> a term also in use; just as when the Span-
ish game of <I>Ombre</I> came into England it brought in its train <I>Basto, Spadilla, Ma-
nilla</I> (<I>Malilla</I>), <I>Matador.</I> Another term which came with <I>Primero</I> was <I>flush,</I> the
Spanish <I>flux,</I> the sibilant, as usual, taking the place of the guttural. It is plain
that the <I>rest</I> was different from the stake, and was what we term a bet. It may be
finally observed that <I>set up</I> was equivalent to <I>lay down,</I> and arose from the piling up
of the money ventured, and that we still use <I>set</I> and <I>lay</I> with an ellipse in each case
of the preposition. <I>Set up rest</I> soon came to be used in a general sense, as meaning
make up one's mind, resolve on&mdash;a sense in which it occurs more than once in Sh.
The same seems to have been the case in Spanish.
<P><SC>Ktly.</SC> (&lquo;<I>N. and Qu.</I>&rquo; 2d Ser. vol. xii, p. 451, 1861). It has struck me as being
rather strange that our forefathers, when they got the game of Primero from Spain,
did not render <I>echar el resto</I> literally, &lquo;Put or lay down the rest.&rquo; I believe the
reason was that they had the phrase <I>set up rest</I> already, but in its military sense, and
so they frugally made it do double duty. Steevens was not altogether wrong in his
derivation of this phrase.

<P>have introduced an extraordinary corruption here by reading &lquo;life <I>leaving.</I>&rquo; Every

reason for changing &lquo;living&rquo; to <I>leaving.</I> Capulet says that death is his heir&mdash;that he
will die and leave death all he has&mdash;viz., &lquo;life, living,&rquo; and everything else. Malone

<P><SC>Sta.</SC> Most of the modern editors follow Capell, whose change is uncalled for;

distinction between <I>life</I> and <I>living</I> in the &lquo;Merc. of Ven.,&rquo; V, i, 286, where Antonio,
whose life had been saved by Portia, says: &lquo;Sweet lady, you have given me <I>life</I> and

<P>65. <B>Peace,</B> &amp;c.] <SC>Birch</SC> (&lquo;<I>Philosophy and Religion of Sh.</I>&rquo;). The Friar employs
the language of religion equivocally, or gives a meaning to it in words, which, from
the occasion, proves false. When Juliet is merely sleeping from the effects of a
draught given to her by himself, he addresses the consolations of religion to her
family as though she were dead. He calls the grief of her relatives on this occasion
&lquo;reason's merriment,&rquo; and foregoes the character of a priest when she is really dead.
<P>65. <B>lives</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2). Here too <SC>Lettsom</SC> would alter &lquo;<I>lives</I>&rquo; to &lquo;lies&rquo; (<I>Live</I>
and <I>lie,</I> as we have already seen, were frequently confounded by transcribers and
printers).

<P>76. <B>she is well</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>. One of several allusions in Sh. to the conventional
mode of saying of the dead that they are &lquo;well.&rquo; See Wint. T., V, i, 30.
<P>79. <B>rosemary</B>] <SC>Douce</SC>. This plant was used in various ways at funerals. Being
an evergreen, it was regarded as an emblem of immortality. In an obituary kept
by Mr. Smith, preserved in the British Museum, is the following: &lquo;Jan<SUP>y</SUP>. 2, 1671.
Mr. Cornelius Bee bookseller in Little Britain died; buried Jan. 4. at Great St.
Bartholomew's without a sermon, without wine or wafers, only gloves and <I>ros-
mary.</I>&rquo; And Gay, when describing Blouzelinda's funeral, records that &lquo;Sprigg'd
rosemary the lads and lasses bore.&rquo;
<P><SC>Nares</SC>. It was carried at funerals, probably, for its odour, and as a token of re-
membrance of the deceased; noticed as late as the time of Gay, in his Pastoral Dirge.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC>. This plant was formerly supposed to strengthen the memory:
<BQ>
&lquo;He from his lasse him lauander hath sent,<LB>
Shewing her loue, and doth requitall craue;<LB>

<P>80. <B>as the custom is</B>] <SC>Hunter</SC>. &lquo;The burials are so strange both in Venice
and all other cities, towns, and parishes of Italy, that they differ not only from Eng-
land but from all other nations whatever in Christendom. For they carry the corse
to church with face, hands, and feet all naked, and wearing the same apparel that
the person wore lately before it died, or that which it craved to be buried in; which
apparel is interred together with their bodies.&rquo;&mdash;Coryat, <I>Crudities,</I> vol. ii, p. 27.
[<I>Sta.</I>
<P>81. <B>In all</B>] <SC>Ulr.</SC> According to the text that I have followed, the emphasis falls
on &lquo;as the custom is;&rquo; that is to say, the Friar recommends them (for everything
depends on it) to inter Juliet on that selfsame day on an open bier, &amp;c. He only
casually adds &lquo;and in her best array,&rquo; which, although, to be sure, it was the custom,
was of no special importance either to him or in itself. If the reading, &lquo;<I>In all her
best array,</I>&rquo; be adopted, and a comma be placed after &lquo;<I>is,</I>&rquo; all the emphasis will be
thrown upon this wholly indifferent circumstance, which injures the sense of the
speech.
