<P>100. <B>Musicians</B>] <SC>Coleridge</SC> (&lquo;<I>Lit. Rem.,</I>&rquo; vol. ii, p. 157). As the audience
know that Juliet is not dead, this scene is perhaps excusable. But it is a strong
warning to minor dramatists not to introduce at one time many separate characters
agitated by one and the same circumstance. It is difficult to understand what effect,
whether that of pity or of laughter, Sh. meant to produce;&mdash;the occasion and the
characteristic speeches are so little in harmony! For example, what the Nurse says
is excellently suited to the Nurse's character, but grotesquely unsuited to the occa-
sion. [<I>Verp. Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Knt.</SC> Rightly understood, this scene requires no apology. It was the custom of
our ancient theatre to introduce, in the irregular pauses of a play that stood in place
of a division into acts, some short diversion, such as a song, a dance, or the extem-
pore buffoonery of a clown. At this point of Romeo and Juliet there is a natural
pause in the action, and at this point such an interlude would, probably, have been
presented, whether Sh. had written one or not. The stage-direction in Q<SUB>2</SUB> puts this
matter beyond a doubt. That direction says, &lquo;Enter Will Kempe,&rquo; and the dialogue
immediately begins between Peter and the musicians. Will Kempe was the Liston
of his day, and was as great a popular favourite as Tarleton had been before him.
It was wise, therefore, in Sh. to find some business for Will Kempe, that should not
be entirely out of harmony with the great business of his play. This scene of the
musicians is very short, and, regarded as a necessary part of the routine of the
ancient stage, is excellently managed. Nothing can be more naturally exhibited
than the indifference of hirelings, without attachment, to a family scene of grief.
Peter and the musicians bandy jokes; and, although the musicians think Peter a
&lquo;pestilent knave,&rquo; perhaps for his inopportune sallies, they are ready enough to look
after their own gratification, even amidst the sorrow which they see around them.
A wedding or a burial is the same to them. &lquo;Come, we'll in here&mdash;tarry for the
mourners, and stay dinner.&rquo; So Sh. read the course of the world&mdash;and it is not
much changed. The quotation beginning, &lquo;When griping grief the heart doth
wound,&rquo; is from a short poem in <I>The Paradise of Daintie Deuises,</I> by Richard
Edwards, master of the children of the chapel to Queen Elizabeth. This was set as
a four-part song by Adrian Batten, organist of St. Paul's in the reign of Charles I,
and is thus printed, but without any name, in Hawkins's History of Music, vol. v.
The question of Peter, &lquo;Why silver sound, why music with her silver sound?&rquo; is
happily enough explained by Percy: &lquo;This ridicule is not so much levelled at the
song itself (which, for the time it was written, is not inelegant) as at those forced and
unnatural explanations often given by us painful editors and expositors of ancient
</CC>

<P>authors.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Reliques,</I> vol. i. Had Sh. a presentiment of what he was to receive at
the hands of his own commentators?
<P><SC>Huds.</SC> It seems not unlikely that this part of the scene was written on purpose
for Kempe to display his talents in, as there could hardly be any other reason for
such a piece of buffoonery.
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. But to our minds the intention was to show how grief and gaiety, pathos
and absurdity, sorrow and jesting, elbow each other in life's crowd; how the calami-
ties of existence fall heavily upon the souls of some, while others, standing close
beside the grievers, feel no jot of suffering or sympathy. Far from the want of har-
mony that has been found here, we feel it to be one of those passing discords that
produce richest and fullest effect of harmonious contrivance. The Nurse's heartless-
ness in bidding Juliet renounce Romeo for Paris, from her selfish desire to secure
her snug place, with its comforts of good feeding, store of <I>aqua-vit&aelig;,</I> a footboy to
wait upon her nurse-ship, &amp;c. &amp;c., is in strict keeping with the footboy's callous eager-
ness to have his &lquo;merry dump&rquo; played to him while the musicians are conveniently
in the house, though in the very hour of his young lady's sudden death; and the
musicians' loitering to bandy jokes with the footboy, secure their pay, and get a
good dinner, all combine to form the most perfect harmony in dramatic composition.
<P>[This scene between Peter and the Musicians is transposed, in Edwin Booth's
Acting copy, to I, v, 13.] <SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>Arraignment of Paris, 1584, after the shepherds have sung an elegiac hymn over
the hearse of Colin, Venus says to Paris:
<BQ>
&lquo;&mdash;&mdash;How cheers my lovely boy after this <I>dump</I> of woe?<LB REND=RIGHT>
<S>Paris.</S> Such <I>dumps,</I> sweet lady, as bin these, are deadly <I>dumps</I> to prove.&rquo; [<I>Sta. Hal.</I><LB>
</BQ>
<P><SC>Ritson</SC>. <I>Dumps</I> were heavy mournful tunes; possibly, indeed, any sort of move-
ments were once so called. Hence <I>doleful dumps,</I> deep sorrow, or grievous afflic-
tion as in the less ancient ballad of Chevy Chase. It is still said of a person uncom-
monly sad, that he is in the <I>dumps.</I> In a MS. of Hen. VIII's time is a tune for
the cittern or guitar, entitled, &lquo;My lady Careys <I>dompe;</I>&rquo; there is also &lquo;The duke
of Sommersettes <I>dompe;</I>&rquo; as we now say, &lquo;Lady Coventry's <I>minuet,</I>&rquo; &amp;c. &lquo;If thou
wert not some blockish and senseless dolt, thou wouldest never laugh when I sung a
heavy mixt-Lydian tune, or a note to a <I>dumpe</I> or dolefull dittie.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Plutarch's Morals,
by Holland,</I> 1602, p. 61. [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Reed</SC>. At the end of The Secretaries Studie, by Thomas Gainsford, Esq., 1616,
is a long poem of forty-seven stanzas, and called A Dumpe or Passion. [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Nares</SC>. Formerly the received term for a melancholy strain in music. A <I>merry
dump</I> in this passage is evidently a purposed absurdity suited to the character of the
speaker. Stafford Smith gave to Steevens the music (without words) of a <I>dump</I>
which he had discovered in an old MS. A dump appears also to have been a kind
of dance. <I>Dumps,</I> for sorrow, was not always a burlesque expression. It was even
used in the sense of elegy. Davies, of Hereford, has a singular poem in that style,
entitled &lquo;A <I>Dump</I> upon the Death of the most noble Henrie Earle of Pembrooke.&rquo;
[<I>Sing. Knt.</I> (ed. 2) (substantially), <I>Dyce.</I>
<P><SC>Sing</SC>. That it was a sad or dismal strain, perhaps sometimes for the sake of con-
trast and effect mixed up with livelier airs, appears from Cavendish's Metrical
Visions, p. 17:
<BQ>
&lquo;What is now left to helpe me in this case?<LB>
Nothing at all but <I>dompe in the dance,</I><LB>
Among deade men to tryppe on the trace.&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 1). See Chappell's &lquo;National English Airs,&rquo; vol. ii, p. 137. [<I>Verp.</I>
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> Master Peter's &lquo;<I>merry</I> dump&rquo; was a purposed contradiction in terms.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC>. Chappell remarks: &lquo;A dump was a slow dance. <I>Queen Mary's Dump</I> is
one of the tunes in William Ballet's Lute Book, and <I>My Lady Carey's Dompe</I> is
printed in Stafford Smith's <I>Musica Antiqua,</I> ii, 470, from a MS. in the British
Museum, temp. Henry VIII.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Popular Music,</I> &amp;c., vol. i, p. 210, (ed. 2).
<P><SC>White</SC>. &lquo;Dump&rquo; conveyed no ludicrous impression in Sh.'s day, though here it
serves a comic purpose.

<P>110. <B>gleek</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> To <I>gleek</I> is to <I>scoff,</I> taken from an ancient game at cards
called <I>gleek.</I> So in Turberville's translation of Ovid's Epistle from Dido to &AElig;neas:
&lquo;By manly mart to purchase prayse, And <I>give his foes the gleeke.</I>&rquo; Again, in the
argument to the same translator's version of Hermione to Orestes: &lquo;Orestes <I>gave</I>
Achylles' sonne <I>the gleeke.</I>&rquo; [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Ritson</SC>. The use of this cant term is nowhere explained, and, in all probability,
cannot, at this distance of time, be recovered. <I>To gleek,</I> however, signified to put
a joke or trick upon a person, perhaps to <I>jest</I> according to the coarse humour of that
age. [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Douce</SC>. In some of the notes on this word it has been supposed to be connected
with the card game of gleek; but it was not recollected that the Saxon language
supplied the term <I>Glig,</I> ludibrium, and doubtless a corresponding verb. Thus <I>glee</I>
signifies <I>mirth, jocularity;</I> and <I>gleeman,</I> or <I>gligman,</I> a minstrel or <I>joculator. Gleek</I>
was, therefore, used to express a stronger sort of joke, a <I>scoffing.</I> It does not appear
that the phrase <I>to give the gleek</I> was ever introduced in the above game, which was
borrowed by us from the French, and derived from an original of very different
import from the word in question. . . . <I>To give the minstrel</I> is no more than a pun-
ning phrase for <I>giving the gleek.</I> Minstrels and jesters were anciently called <I>gleek-
men</I> or <I>gligmen.</I> [<I>Dyce, Sing. Huds. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Nares</SC>. <I>To give the gleek</I> meant to pass a jest upon, to make a person ridiculous.
<I>To give the minstrel,</I> which follows, has no such meaning. Peter only means, &lquo;I
will call you minstrel and so treat you,&rquo; to which the musician replies, &lquo;Then I will
give you the <I>serving creature,</I>&rquo; as a personal retort in kind. [<I>Sing. Dyce.</I>
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> <I>To give the gleek,</I> a phrase borrowed from the old game of cards called
<I>gleek,</I> signified to <I>flout or scorn</I> any one, and, as a <I>gleekman</I> or <I>gligman</I> was a name
for a minstrel, we get a notion of the quibble meant. A similar <I>equivoque</I> is, no
doubt, intended in &lquo;the serving creature,&rquo; but the allusion is yet to be discovered.
<P><SC>White</SC>. The allusion to the glee-man or gligmon is obvious. Not so, however,
the double meaning in the musician's reply, unless <I>Peter</I> means that he will apply
the term &lquo;minstrel&rquo; reproachfully, and the musician that he will retort by calling
<I>Peter</I> the servant to the minstrel.
<P>111. <B>the minstrel</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> From the following entry on the books of the Sta-
tioner's Company, in the year 1560, it appears that the hire of a <I>parson</I> was cheaper
than that of a <I>minstrel</I> or a <I>cook.</I> [See note on IV, ii, 2. <SC>Ed.</SC>] [<I>Hal.</I>
<P>113. <B>dagger</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>. Even in so slight a touch as this Sh. gives token of his
sleepless attention to consistency and the production of dramatic verity in effect.
Peter is thus shown to wear a knife or dagger about him, which he draws upon the
slightest occasion of threat, whether made in joke or in earnest; and this serves to
make more natural the point of Juliet's wearing a dagger.

<P>114. <B>crotchets</B>] <SC>Ulr.</SC> A crotchet (so called because its shape is like that of a
crook) is a quarter-note, and also a whim. Peter, therefore, intends to say, &lquo;I will
not endure your whims, your refusal to play,&rquo; but says, in effect, &lquo;I will play no
quarter-notes (but whole ones) on your pates.&rquo;
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. An instance of Sh.'s using a familiarly known phrase, and varying it
with one of his own introduced words. The effect is given of the then well-known
phrase, &lquo;I'll not carry coals,&rquo; meaning, &lquo;I'll not put up with insults;&rquo; while, by
introducing the word &lquo;crotchets,&rquo; the joke is made doubly applicable to the rallying
musician, in the sense of those musical symbols of notes denominated &lquo;crotchets,&rquo;
and those whimsies of banter sometimes jocosely so called.
<P>114. <B>re you, and fa you</B>] <SC>Knt.</SC> <I>Re</I> and <I>fa</I> are the syllables or names given in
solmization, or sol-faing, to the sounds D and F in the musical scale. [<I>Verp. Sta.
Ulr.</I>
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> &lquo;To ray&rquo; also means &lquo;to sift,&rquo; (<I>sieben</I>) and &lquo;to fey&rquo; is &lquo;to cleanse out&rquo; (<I>schl&auml;m-
men</I>), both of which words are pronounced exactly like Re and Fa. Herein lies
the wit of Peter.
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> The pun on <I>note</I> is self-evident, and the word appears to have been a favor-
ite one to play upon, for Sh. has used it with a double meaning at least a score
of times.
<P>119. <B>Have . . . my wit</B>] <SC>Del.</SC> Beware of my wit. [<I>Ulr.</I>
<P>122. <B>griping grief</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> The epithet <I>griping</I> was by no means likely to

gil's &AElig;neid, makes the hero say: &lquo;New <I>gripes</I> of dred then pearse our trembling
brestes.&rquo; [<I>Clarke.</I>]
<P><SC>Sir John Hawkins</SC>.

<P><SC>Mommsen</SC>. <I>Pretie</I> of (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) looks like an error of the ear, for <I>pretty</I> by no means
suits the context. Peter does not intend to praise, and irony would be out of place.
<I>Prat'ee</I> is formed like <I>Look'ee, hark'ee, think'ee. Prates</I> is a misprint in Q<SUB>2</SUB> of an
unusual dialectic word, just like <I>pardons</I> for <I>perdona,</I> II, iv, 30. The other old

<I>pretty,</I> which a majority of the later English edd. prefer.
<P>128. <B>Rebeck</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> An instrument with three strings, which is mentioned by
several of the old writers. <I>Rebeck, rebecquin.</I> See Menage, in v. <I>Rebec.</I> So in
B. and Fl.'s Knight of the Burning Pestle: &lquo;'Tis present death for these fidlers to
tune their <I>rebecks</I> before the great Turk's grace.&rquo; So in England's Helicon, 1600, is
The Shepherd Arsilius, his Song to his <I>Rebeck,</I> by Bar. Young. [<I>Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Mal.</SC> It is mentioned by Milton as an instrument of mirth: &lquo;When the merry
bells ring round And the jocund <I>rebecks</I> sound.&rquo; [<I>Sing. Huds. Sta. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Nares</SC>. An instrument of music, having catgut strings, and played with a bow,
but originally with only two strings, then with three, till it was exalted into the more
perfect violin, with four strings. It is thought to be the same with <I>ribible,</I> being a
Moorish instrument, and in that language called <I>reheb.</I> Thence it passed into Italy,
where it became <I>ribeca</I> or <I>ribeba,</I> whence our English word. See Hawkins's Hist.
of Music, II, p. 86.
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> It is frequently noticed by old writers: &lquo;He turned his <I>rebeck</I> to a mournful
note.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Drayton,</I> ed. 11.

<P>139. <B>Jack</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC>. A common term of contempt and reproach (fellow, knave,

<P>1. <B>truth</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> If I may repose any confidence in the flattering visions of the

<P><SC>Knt.</SC> It is not difficult to see the growth of that philosophical spirit in Sh. which

<P>The interpretation of dreams was one of the most important functions of the sooth-
sayer. The word can hardly need gloss or explanation of any kind. The reading
of F<SUB>1</SUB> is quite incomprehensible; for what is the &lquo;truth of sleep&rquo;? But although
&lquo;truth&rquo; could not be a misprint for &lquo;eye,&rquo; it might very easily be printed for &lquo;<I>$</I>ooth&rquo;
for &lquo;<I>$</I>outh,&rquo; as it was commonly written), either through mistake of eye or ear. And
there is a connection of ideas between the presaging &lquo;eye of sleep&rquo; and the &lquo;sooth
of sleep&rquo; in dreams, by which we can detect the correcting hand of the poet, or the
confused memory of the procurer of (Q<SUB>1</SUB>), and which is not traceable between &lquo;eye&rquo;
and &lquo;truth.&rquo; For, even according to ancient usage, &lquo;sooth&rquo; and &lquo;truth&rquo; were not
absolute synonyms. &lquo;Sooth&rquo; was a promising, forward-looking, or a sweet, pleasant
truth; and in this shade of difference is the affinity between the reading of (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) and
that of this corrected text. <I>Pericles,</I> I, ii, 44, in a passage unmistakably Sh.'s, fur-
nishes at once a comment upon this reading and a confirmation of it:
<BQ>
&lquo;When Signior <I>Sooth,</I> here, does proclaim a peace,<LB>
He flatters you, makes war upon your life.&rquo;<LB>

<P><SC>Mommsen</SC>, in his chapter on the value of Collier's (MS.), enumerates certain cor-
rections, of which this is one, and, remarking that all these corrections are intelli-
gent, questions whether any one could affirm with confidence that Sh. could not have
written thus. &lquo;Are not the recollections of the stage a sort of authority?&rquo; he asks,
and ought we not to believe that the (MS.), who goes to work in such a brief and
decided manner, was guided for the most part by a distinct recollection of the acted
play?

<P><SC>The Cornhill Magazine</SC> (<I>October,</I> 1866, p. 453). The essence of a genuine

tragic. As it was, the presentiment did all in its power. It warned him of some-
thing good, and he refused to believe it. You cannot blame your guide for mislead-

<P>37. <B>an apothecary</B>] <SC>Knt.</SC> The criticism of the French school has not spared

<P>&lquo;It may not be improper to produce the following glaring instance of the absurdity of introducing
long and minute descriptions into tragedy. When Romeo receives the dreadful and unexpected news
of Juliet's death, this fond husband, in an agony of grief, immediately resolves to poison himself. But
his sorrow is interrupted while he gives us an exact picture of the apothecary-shop, where he intends
to purchase the poison. I appeal to those who know anything of the human heart, whether Romeo,
in this distressful situation, could have leisure to think of the alligator, empty boxes, and bladders, and
other furniture of this beggarly shop, and to point them out so distinctly to the audience. The descrip-
tion is, indeed, very lively and natural, but very improperly put into the mouth of a person agitated
with such passion as Romeo is represented to be.&rquo;
<P>The criticism of Warton, ingenious as it may appear, and true as applied to many
&lquo;long and minute descriptions in tragedy,&rquo; is here based upon a wrong principle.
He says that Romeo, in his distressful situation, had not &lquo;leisure&rquo; to think of the
furniture of the apothecary's shop. What then had he leisure to do? Had he leis-

<P>ure to run off into declamations against fate and into tedious apostrophes and gen-
eralizations, as a less skilful artist than Sh. would have made him indulge in? From
the moment he had said, &lquo;Well, Juliet, I will lie with thee to-night, Let's see for means,&rquo;
the apothecary's shop became to him the object of the most intense interest. Great
passions, when they have shaped themselves into firm resolves, attach the most dis-
tinct importance to the minutest objects connected with the execution of their pur-
pose. He had seen the apothecary's shop in his placid moments as an object of
curiosity. He had hastily looked at the tortoise and the alligator, the empty boxes
and the earthen pots; and he had looked at the tattered weed and overwhelming
brows of their needy owner. But he had also said, when he first saw these things:
<BQ>
&lquo;An if a man did need a poison now,<LB>
Whose sale is present death in Mantua,<LB>
Here lives a caitiff wretch would sell it him.&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>When he <I>did</I> need a poison, all these documents of the misery that was to serve
him, came with a double intensity upon his vision. The shaping of these things into
words was not for the audience. It was not to introduce a &lquo;long and minute descrip-
tion into tragedy&rquo; that had no foundation in the workings of nature. It was the
very cunning of nature which produced this description. Mischief was, indeed,
swift to enter into the thoughts of the desperate man. But the mind once made up,
it took a perverse pleasure in going over every circumstance that had suggested the
means of mischief. All other thoughts had passed out of Romeo's mind. He had
nothing left but to die; and everything connected with the means of his death was
seized upon by his imagination with an energy that could only find relief in words.
Sh. has exhibited the same knowledge of nature in his sad and solemn poem of
&lquo;The Rape of Lucrece,&rquo; where the injured wife, having resolved to wipe out her
stain by death,
<BQ>
&lquo;&mdash;&mdash;calls to mind where hangs a piece<LB>
Of skilfull painting, made for Priam's Troy.&rquo;&mdash;1366, 7.<LB>
</BQ>
<P>She sees in that painting some fancied resemblance to her own position, and spends
the heavy hours till her husband arrives in its contemplation [1496-8]. It was the
intense interest in his own resolve which made Romeo so minutely describe his
apothecary. But that stage past, came the <I>abstraction</I> of his sorrow:
<BQ>
&lquo;What said my man, when my betossed soul<LB>
Did not attend him, as we rode? I think<LB>
He told me Paris should have married Juliet.&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>Juliet was dead, and what mattered it to his &lquo;betossed soul&rquo; who she should have
married? &lquo;Well, Juliet, I will lie with thee to-night&rquo; was the sole thought that
made him remember an &lquo;apothecary,&rquo; and treat what his servant said as a &lquo;dream.&rquo;
Who but Sh. could have given us the key to these subtle and delicate workings of
the human heart?

<P>40. <B>Culling of</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&lquo;<I>Shakespearian Grammar,</I>&rquo; P. 170, (ed. 3) 1870). <I>Of</I>
naturally followed a verbal noun. In many cases we should call the verbal noun a
participle, and the <I>of</I> has become unintelligible to us, because of the omission of the
prepositional &lquo;a,&rquo; &lquo;in,&rquo; or &lquo;on.&rquo; Thus &lquo;(<I>a-</I>) culling of,&rquo; &amp;c.
<P>41. <B>Sharp misery</B>] <SC>Mal.</SC> See Sackville's description of Misery in his Induc-
tion: &lquo;His <I>face was leane,</I> and some deal pinde away; And eke <I>his hands consumed
to the bone.</I>&rquo; [<I>Sing.</I>
<P>43. <B>An alligator stuff'd</B>] <SC>Mal.</SC> It appears from Nashe's Have With You to
Saffron Walden, 1596, that a stuffed alligator, in Sh.'s time, made part of the furni-
ture of an apothecary's shop. &lquo;He made&rquo; (says Nashe) &lquo;an anatomie of a rat, and
after hanged her over his head, instead of an <I>apothecary's</I> crocodile or <I>dried alli-
gator.</I>&rquo; [<I>Sing. Huds. Sta. Clarke, Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Steev.</SC> I was many years ago assured that, formerly, when an apothecary first
engaged with his druggist, he was gratuitously furnished by him with these articles
of show, which were then imported for that use only. I have met with the alligator,
tortoise, &amp;c., hanging up in the shop of an ancient apothecary at Limehouse, as well
as in places more remote from our metropolis. See Hogarth, Marriage &agrave; la Mode,
plate iii. It may be remarked, however, that the apothecaries dismissed their alli-
gators, &amp;c., some time before the physicians were willing to part with their amber-
headed canes and solemn periwigs. [<I>Sing. Hal.</I>
<P><SC>Douce</SC>. This word was probably introduced into the language by some of our
early voyagers to the Spanish or Portuguese settlements in the newly-discovered
world. They would hear the Spaniards discoursing of the animal by the name of
<I>el lagarto,</I> or the lizard&mdash;Lat., <I>lacerta;</I> and on their return home they would inform
their countrymen that this sort of crocodile was called an <I>alligator.</I>
<P><SC>Halliwell</SC>. Mr. Fairholt sends me this note: &lquo;Romeo's description of the shop
of the poor apothecary may be accepted as minutely accurate, for it was customary
with his class &ldquo;to make a show,&rdquo; according to their means. Rows of drug-bottles
in Majolica, highly decorated by painting, filled their shelves, and are now among
the most coveted articles to collectors of &ldquo;Raffaelle-ware.&rdquo; The apothecary's shop
was then (as it is now in Italy) the rendezvous for idlers and elderly gossips; hence
the proprietor made the best display he could of his own position. Dried fishes and
marine monsters were suspended from the ceiling; &ldquo;an alligator stuff'd&rdquo; was the
most coveted and indispensable of all; and we rarely meet with any representation
of the shop of the humblest medical practitioner without one. In Dutch art they
abound. Our cut represents that of a village barber-surgeon after one of Teniers
best pictures.&rquo;

<P>46. <B>Green earthen pots</B>] <SC>Halliwell</SC>. The manufacture of green earthen pots
was carried on in England in Sh.'s time, as appears from the following curious letter,
written in August, 1594, from Sir Julius C&aelig;sar to Sir William Moore: &lquo;After my
hartie comendacions, &amp;c., Wheras in tymes past the bearer hereof hath had out of
the parke of Farnham, belonging to the Bishopprick of Winchester, certaine white
clay for the making of grene potts usually drunk in by the gentlemen of the Temple;
and nowe understandinge of some restraint thereof, and that you (amongst others)
are authorized there in divers respects during the vacancye of the said Busshoppricke;
my request therefore unto you is, and the rather for that I am a member of the said
house, that you would in favour of us all permytt the bearer hereof to digge and
carie awaye so muche of the said claye as by him shalbe thought sufficient for the
furnishinge of the said house with grene potts as aforesaid, paying as he hath here-
tofore for the same. In accomplishement whereof, myself, with the whole societie,
shall acknowledge ourselves muche beholden unto you, and shalbe readie to requite
you, at all tymes hereafter, with the like pleasure. And so I bid you moste hartelie
farewell.&rquo;

<P>50. <B>An if</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (<I>Shakespearian Grammar,</I> 1869, Art. 37). This particle
[An = if] has been derived from <I>an,</I> the imperative of <I>anan,</I> to grant. But the word
is generally written <I>and</I> in Early English (Stratmann), and frequently in Elizabethan
authors. . . . The true explanation appears to be that the hypothesis, the <I>if,</I> is
expressed not by the <I>and,</I> but by the subjunctive, and that <I>and</I> merely means <I>with
the addition of, plus,</I> just as <I>but</I> means <I>leaving out,</I> or <I>minus. . . .</I> Latterly, the
subjunctive, falling into disuse, was felt to be too weak unaided to express the
hypothesis; and the same tendency which introduced &lquo;more better,&rquo; &lquo;most unkind-
est,&rquo; &amp;c., superseded <I>and</I> by <I>and if, an if</I> and <I>if.</I> There is nothing remarkable in
the change of <I>and</I> into <I>an. And,</I> even in its ordinary sense, is often written <I>an</I> in
Early English. (See Halliwell.)
<P>51. <B>Mantua</B>] <SC>Knt.</SC> Sir Walter Raleigh, in his &lquo;Discourse of Tenures,&rquo; says:
&lquo;By the laws of Spain and Portugal it is not lawful to sell poison.&rquo; A similar law,
if we are rightly informed, prevailed in Italy. There is no such law in our own
statute-book; and the circumstance is a remarkable exemplification of the difference
between English and continental manners.

<P>70. <B>starveth in</B>] <SC>Ritson</SC>. Need and oppression cannot, properly, be said to
<I>starve</I> in his eyes, though <I>starved famine</I> may be allowed to dwell in his cheeks.
[<I>Sing. Dyce.</I>
<P><SC>Mal.</SC> The word <I>starved</I> in (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) shows that <I>starveth</I> is right. [<I>Dyce</I> (ed. 2).
<P><SC>Sing</SC>. The alteration, in Otway's version, is so slight that it well merits adoption.
Ritson's observation is just.
<P><SC>Verp.</SC> [(Q<SUB>1</SUB>) quoted]. Certainly very good lines, which might very well keep their
place, if the author had chosen it, but we have no right with Steevens and the ordi-
nary text to make an entire new reading by piecing together the two. Otway's em-
endation is a poetical and probable emendation. Yet the original phrase, though
harsh, is powerful and expressive, and not to be thrown out on mere conjecture.
The singular verb <I>starveth,</I> with the two nouns, was not a grammatical error accord-
ing to old English usage when both nominatives, as here, made up one compound
idea. Unless, therefore, we choose to erase all the peculiarities of ancient idiom,
there is no reason to adopt Pope's double emendation. [<I>Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> That this genuinely Shakespearian, boldly poetic expression [&lquo;starveth in&rquo;]
is preferable to all other attempts at emendation, seems to me indubitable.
<P><SC>Huds.</SC> As it stands, the expression conveys a strong sense, though it will hardly
bear analyzing.
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). Some modern editors, without any other authority than that of
Otway in his Caius Marius, read &lquo;<I>stareth.</I>&rquo;
<P><SC>Sta.</SC> Although Otway's reading has been adopted by several of the modern
editors, and is perhaps preferable to the other, I have not felt justified in departing
from the old text.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2) [Ritson's criticism quoted with approval]. Otway was the first to
substitute &lquo;<I>stareth</I>&rquo; for the corruption &lquo;starveth&rquo;&mdash;Otway being endowed with common
sense as well as with genius.
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. As well might Ritson object that contempt and beggary cannot strictly
be said to hang upon his back. These are among the bold licenses of expression
that poets take, and which are full of poetic significance to poetic minds, while
affording trouble and perplexity to literal scanners.

<P>5. <B>Going to find</B>] <SC>Knt.</SC> Friar Laurence and his associates must be supposed to
belong to the Franciscan order of friars. In his kindliness, his learning, and his
inclination to mix with and, perhaps, control the affairs of the world, he is no unapt
representative of one of this distinguished order in their best days. Warton, in his
History of English Poetry, has described the learning, the magnificence, and the
prodigious influence of this remarkable body. Friar Laurence was able to give to
Romeo &lquo;Adversity's sweet milk&mdash;philosophy.&rquo; He was to Romeo &lquo;a divine, a
ghostly confessor, A sin-absolver, and my friend professed;&rquo; but he was yet of the
world. He married Romeo and his mistress, partly to gratify their love, and partly
to secure his influence in the reconciliation of their families. Warton says the Fran-
ciscans &lquo;managed the machines of every important operation or event, both in the
religious and political world.&rquo;
<P><SC>Mal.</SC> So in Romeus and Juliet:
<BQ>
&lquo;Apace our frier John to Mantua him hyes;<LB>
And, for because in Italy it is a wonted gyse<LB>
That friers in the towne should seeldome walke alone,<LB>
But of theyr covent ay <I>should be accompanide with one</I><LB>
<I>Of his profession,</I> straight a house he fyndeth out,<LB>
In mynde to take some frier with him, to walke the towne about.&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>Our author, having occasion for Friar John, has here departed from the poem,
and supposed the pestilence to rage at Verona, instead of Mantua. [<I>Sing. Huds.
Knt.</I>

p. 448. [<I>Sing. Huds. Sta. Hal.</I>

implied particular; &lquo;a messenger&rquo; allowing to be implied, in the word &lquo;they,&rquo; those
who would not undertake to bear a message for fear of infection.
<P>18. <B>nice</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> <I>I. e.,</I> was not written on a trivial or idle subject. [<I>Sing. Huds.
Knt. Coll. White.</I>] The learned editor [Tyrwhitt] of Chaucer's Canterbury Tales,
1775, observes that H. Stephens informs us that <I>nice</I> was the old French word for
<I>niais,</I> one of the synonyms of <I>sot.</I>
<P><SC>Del.</SC> Compare, in this same sense, &lquo;How nice the quarrel was,&rquo; III, i, 150. [<I>Sta.
Coll.</I> (ed. 2).
<P><SC>White</SC>. To be nice is to be particular in small things.

<P><B>A churchyard,</B> &amp;c.] <SC>Hunter</SC>. It is clear that Sh., or some writer whom he
followed, had in mind the churchyard of Saint Mary the Old in Verona, and the
monument of the Scaligers which stood in it. We have nothing in England which
corresponds to this scene, and no monument or vault in which scenes such as this
could be exhibited. Coryat, who could often be worse spared than a better man,
writes thus:
<P>&lquo;I saw the monuments of two of the noble Scaligers of Verona in a little churchyard adjoining to the
church called Maria Antiqua; the fairest whereof is that of Mastinus Scaliger, standing at one corner
of the churchyard, which is such an exceeding sumptuous mausoleum that I saw not the like in Italy.
The other monument is that of Canis Grandi, or Magnus Scaliger, which stood within another corner
of the same churchyard, right opposite unto this.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Crudities,</I> vol. ii, p. 114.
<P><SC>Sing.</SC> (ed. 2). The Lovers are said to have been buried in the Sotterr&aacute;neo of
Fermo Maggiore, belonging to an order of Franciscans. The monastery was burnt
down some years since, and a sarcophagus, said to be that of Juliet, was removed
from the ruins, and is still shown at Verona. [<I>White.</I>

<P><SC>Steev.</SC> Ben Jonson uses the word <I>dear</I> in the same sense in <I>Catiline,</I> Act I:

<P><SC>Singer</SC> [Note on Twelfth Night, V, i, 74: &lquo;in terms so bloody and so <I>dear</I>&rquo;].
Tooke has so admirably accounted for the epithet <I>dear</I> applied by our ancient writers
to any object which excites a sensation of <I>hurt, pain,</I> and consequently of <I>anxiety,
solicitude, care, earnestness,</I> that I shall extract it as the best comment upon the
<I>apparently</I> opposite uses of the word in our great poet: &lquo;<I>Dearth</I> is the third person
singular of the English (from the Anglo-Saxon verb <I>Derian,</I> nocere, l&aelig;dere), <I>to
dere.</I> It means some or any season, weather, or other cause, which <I>dereth, i. e.,</I>
maketh <I>dear,</I> hurteth, or doth mischief. The English verb <I>to dere</I> was formerly in
common use.&rquo; He then produces about twenty examples, the last from Hamlet
[I, ii, 182]: &lquo;Would I had met my <I>dearest</I> foe in heaven,&rquo; &amp;c. Tooke continues:
&lquo;Johnson and Malone, who trusted to <I>their</I> Latin to explain <I>his</I> (Sh.'s) English, for
<I>deer</I> and <I>deerest</I> would have us read <I>dire</I> and <I>direst;</I> not knowing that Dere and
Deriend mean <I>hurt</I> and <I>hurting, mischief</I> and <I>mischievous;</I> and that their Latin
<I>dirus</I> is from our Anglo-Saxon Dere, which they would expunge.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Epea Pteroenta,</I>
vol. ii, p. 409. A most pertinent illustration of Tooke's etymology has occurred to
me in a MS. poem by Richard Rolle the Hermit of Hampole:
<BQ>
&lquo;Bot flatering lele and loselry,<LB>
Is grete <I>chepe</I> in thair courtes namly,<LB>
The most <I>derthe</I> of any, that is<LB>
Aboute tham there, is sothfastnes.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Spec. Vit&aelig;.</I><LB>
</BQ>
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> [quotes the foregoing and adds]: See, too, Richardson's <I>Dict.,</I> where
Tooke's explanation of <I>dear</I> is given as the true one.
<P><SC>Caldecott</SC> [Note on &lquo;my dearest foe,&rquo; Hamlet I, ii, 182]. Throughout Sh., and
all the poets of his and a much later day, we find this epithet applied to the person
or thing which, for or against us, excites the liveliest and strongest interest. It is
used variously, indefinitely, and metaphorically to express the warmest feelings of the
soul; its nearest, most intimate, home and heart-felt emotions: and here, no doubt,
though, as everywhere else, more directly interpreted, signifying &lquo;veriest, extremest,&rquo;
must by consequence and figuratively import &lquo;bitterest, deadliest, most mortal.&rquo; As
extremes are said, in a certain sense, to approximate, and are in many respects alike
or the same, so this word is made, in a certain sense, to carry with it an union of
the fiercest opposites: it is made to signify the extremes of love and hatred. It may
be said to be equivalent generally to <I>very,</I> and to import &lquo;the excess, the utmost, the
superlative&rquo; of that, whatever it may be, to which it is applied. But to suppose, with
Tooke (<I>Divers. of Purley,</I> ii, 409), that in <I>all</I> cases <I>dear</I> must at that time have
meant &lquo;injurious,&rquo; as being derived from the Saxon verb <I>dere,</I> to hurt, is perfectly
absurd. Dr. Johnson's derivation of the word, as used in this place, from the Latin
<I>dirus,</I> is doubtless ridiculous enough; but Tooke has not produced a single instance
of it, <I>i. e.,</I> of the adjective, in the sense upon which he insists, except, as he pre-
tends, from our author, &amp;c. [<I>Dyce.</I>
<P><SC>Craik</SC> [&lquo;<I>The English of Sh.</I>&rquo; p. 237: &lquo;Shall it not grieve thee, dearer than thy
death?&rquo;&mdash;Jul. C&aelig;s., III, i, 196]. Horne Tooke (&lquo;<I>Div. of Purley,</I>&rquo; 612, &amp;c.) makes

<P>a plausible case in favour of <I>dear</I> being derived from the ancient verb <I>derian,</I> to
hurt, to annoy, and of its proper meaning being, therefore, injurious or hateful.
His notion seems to be that from this <I>derian</I> we have <I>dearth,</I> meaning properly that
sort of injury that is done by the weather, and that, a usual consequence of dearth
being to make the produce of the earth high-priced, the adjective <I>dear</I> has thence
taken its common meaning of precious. This is not all distinctly asserted, but
what of it may not be explicitly set forth is supposed and implied. It is, however,
against an explanation which has been generally accepted, that there is no appear-
ance of connection between <I>derian</I> and the contemporary word answering to <I>dear</I>
in the sense of high-priced, precious, beloved, which is <I>deore, d&uacute;re,</I> or <I>d&yacute;re,</I> and is
evidently from the same root, not with <I>derian,</I> but with <I>de<*>ran</I> or <I>d&yacute;ran,</I> to hold
dear, to love. There is no doubt about the existence of an old English verb <I>dere,</I>
meaning to hurt, the unquestionable representative of the original <I>derian.</I> Thus in
Chaucer (<I>C. T.</I> 1824), Theseus says to Palamon and Arcite, in the Knight's Tale:
<BQ>
&lquo;And ye shul bothe anon unto me swere<LB>
That never mo ye shul my contree <I>dere,</I><LB>
Ne maken werre upon me night ne day,<LB>
But ben my frendes in alle that ye may.&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>But perhaps we can get most easily and naturally at the sense which <I>dear</I> sometimes
assumes by supposing that the notion properly involved in it of love, having first
become generalized into that of a strong affection of any kind, had thence passed
on into that of such an emotion the very reverse of love. We seem to have it in
the intermediate sense in such instances as the following:
<BQ>
&lquo;Some <I>dear</I> cause<LB REND=RIGHT>
Will in concealment wrap me up awhile.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Lear,</I> IV, iii, 53.<LB>
</BQ>
<P>[The present line cited.] And even when Hamlet speaks of his &lquo;<I>dearest</I> foe,&rquo; or
when Celia remarks to Rosalind, in <I>As You Like It,</I> I, iii, 31, &lquo;My father hated his
[Orlando's] father <I>dearly,</I>&rquo; the word need not be understood as implying more than
strong or passionate emotion. [<I>Dyce.</I>

<P>47. <B>Stage-direction</B>] <SC>Malone</SC> (&lquo;<I>Hist. of English Stage,</I>&rquo; p. 90). Though un-
doubtedly Sh.'s company were furnished with some wooden fabrick sufficiently re-
sembling a tomb, for which they must have had occasion in several plays, yet some
doubt may be entertained whether any exhibition of Juliet's monument was given
on the stage. Romeo, perhaps, only opened with his mattock one of the stage trap-
doors (which might have represented a tomb-stone), by which he descended to a
vault beneath the stage, where Juliet was deposited. Juliet, however, after her re-
covery, speaks and dies upon the stage. If, therefore, the exhibition was such as I
have supposed, Romeo must have brought her up in his arms from the vault beneath
the stage, after he had killed Paris.

<P>84. <B>a lantern</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> This may not here signify an enclosure for a lighted
candle, but a <I>louvre,</I> or what in ancient records is styled <I>lanternium, i. e.</I> a spa-
cious round or octagonal turret full of windows, by means of which cathedrals, and
sometimes halls, are illuminated. See the beautiful lantern at Ely Minster. [<I>Sta.
Dyce.</I>] The same word, in the same sense, occurs in Churchyard's Siege of Edin-
brough Castle: &lquo;This lofty seat and <I>lantern</I> of that land.&rquo; Again in Holland's trans.
Pliny's Natural History, b. 35, chap. 12: &lquo;&mdash;&mdash; hence came the <I>louvers</I> and <I>lan-
ternes</I> reared over the roofes of temples,&rquo; &amp;c. [<I>Sing. Verp. Huds.</I>
<P><SC>White</SC>. In the ancient kitchens and halls the louvre was the only exit for the
smoke and heated air of the apartment. See the following passage from the old
romance, <I>Thomas of Reading:</I> &lquo;And with that he caused his Men to take him pres-
ently, and to bind him Hand and Foot. Which being done, they drew him vp in a
Basket into the Smoky Louer of the Hall, and there did let him hang, &amp;c. And in
such a heate was hee driuen with drawing him vp, that he was faine to cast off his
Gownes, his Coates and two paire of his Stockings,&rquo; &amp;c.&mdash;Sig. F, ed. 1632.

<P><SC>Nares</SC>. The state-room in a palace, where the sovereign usually appears. Hence
used also for any grand state-room. [<I>Sta.</I>
<P><SC>Hunter</SC>. It is here used for &lquo;presence-chamber,&rquo; the hall of audience, the most
splendid apartment of a royal palace. &lquo;The next chamber within it, which is the
presence, very fair.&rquo;&mdash;Coryat, <I>Crudities,</I> vol. i, p. 32. A longer quotation may be
excused for the rareness of the source from whence it comes, and the curious theatri-

from London, January 5th, 1608, says: &lquo;The Marquess goes forward at court the
twelfth day, though I doubt the new room will be scant ready. All the holidays
there were Plays, but with so little concourse of strangers that they say they wanted
company. The King was very earnest to have one on Christmas Night, though, as
I take it, He and the Prince received sacrament that day; but the Lords told him
that it was not the fashion, which answer pleased him not a whit, but said, &ldquo;What
do you tell me of the fashion? I will make it a fashion.&rdquo; Yesterday he dined in
the <I>Presence,</I> in great pomp, with his rich cupboards of plate, the one of gold, the
other that of the House of Burgundy, pawned to Queen Elizabeth by the States of
Brabant, and hath seldom been seen abroad, being exceeding massy, fair, and sump-
tuous. I could learn no reason of this extraordinary bravery, but that he would
shew himself in glory to certain Scots that were never here before, as they say there
be many lately come, and that the Court is full of new and strange faces.&rquo;&mdash;From a
copy of the Original in the State Paper Office. It shows us something of the splen-
dour of a Presence contrasting with the dark and dismal sepulchral vault.

<P>87. <B>by a dead man</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>. This fine license of poetic anticipation, by which
Romeo, resolved to die, speaks already of himself as &lquo;a dead man,&rquo; is stigmatized by
Steevens as one of &lquo;those miserable conceits with which our author too frequently
counteracts his own pathos.&rquo; (!) That the genuine poet, John Keats, thought very
differently of this striking idea is testified by his having introduced its twin thought
into his poem of &lquo;Isabella,&rquo; where stanza xxvii begins:
<BQ>
&lquo;So the two brothers and <I>their murder'd man</I><LB>
Rode past fair Florence,&rquo; &amp;c.<LB>
</BQ>
<P>88, 120. <B>How oft . . . I die</B>] <SC>Coleridge</SC> (&lquo;<I>Lit. Rem.,</I>&rquo; vol. ii, p. 158). Here,
here, is the master example how beauty can at once increase and modify passion.
<P>90. <B>A lightning</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> This idea occurs frequently in old dramas. So in
the Second Part of The Downfall of Robert, Earl of Huntington, 1601: &lquo;I thought
it was <I>a lightening before death.</I>&rquo; [<I>Sing. Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> The commentators have wholly misunderstood this passage. Romeo simply
wishes to say: &lquo;To other men at the point of death such a bright, clear moment is
often granted; how different is the last moment that is granted to me!&rquo;
<P><SC>Del.</SC> Romeo asks himself how he can characterize the sight which the now
opened tomb discloses as such a <I>lightening.</I>
<P>90. <B>lightning before death</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>. A proverbial phrase, partly deduced from
observation of some extraordinary effort of nature, often made in sick persons just
before death; and partly from a superstitious notion of an ominous and preternatural
mirth, supposed to come on at that period, without any ostensible reason. [<I>Dyce.</I>
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. The mingling here of words and images full of light and colour with
the murky gray of the sepulchral vault and the darkness of the midnight church-
yard, the blending of these images of beauty and tenderness with the deep gloom
of the speaker's inmost heart, form a poetical and metaphysical picture unequalled
in its kind.
<P><SC>Cham.</SC> We may note Byron's remark, that even the scaffold echoes with jests:
&lquo;In Sir Thomas More, for instance, on the scaffold, and Anne Boleyn in the Tower,
when grasping her neck, she remarked that it &ldquo;was too slender to trouble the heads-
man much.&rdquo; During one part of the French Revolution it became a fashion to
leave some <I>mot</I> as a legacy; and the quantity of facetious last words spoken during
that period would form a melancholy jest-book of a considerable size!&rquo;&mdash;<I>Note to The
Corsair.</I>

<P>101. <B>Forgive me, cousin</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>. Inexpressibly beautiful and moving is this
gentleness of Romeo's in his death hour. His yearning to be at peace with his foe,
his beseeching pardon of him and calling him kinsman in token of final atonement,
his forbearance and even magnanimity towards Paris, his words of closing consid-
eration and kindly farewell to his faithful Balthasar, all combine to crown Romeo as
the prince of youthful gentlemen and lovers.

<P>102, 103. <B>shall I . . . amorous</B>] <SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 1). Romeo first asserts that he will

<P>106. <B>I still will</B>] <SC>Sta.</SC> [Note on Mer. of Ven., I, i, 136]. <I>Still,</I> that is, <I>always,
ever.</I> This signification of the word is frequent in Sh., although no commentator.
that I remember, has noticed it.
<P><SC>Abbott</SC> (&lquo;<I>Sh.'n Grammar</I>&rquo; (ed. 3), 1870, p. 69). <I>Still</I> is used for <I>constantly,</I> in
accordance with the derivation of the word &lquo;quiet,&rquo; &lquo;unmoved.&rquo; It is now used only
in the sense of &lquo;even now,&rquo; &lquo;even then.&rquo; The connection between &lquo;during all time
up to the present&rquo; and &lquo;even at the present&rquo; is natural, and both meanings are easily
derived from the radical meaning &lquo;without moving from its place.&rquo; Compare the
different meanings of <I>dum, donec,</I> <G>e(/ws</G>, &amp;c. Thus in Ham. II, ii, 42; Tr. and Cres.
IV, v, 195; Oth. I, iii, 147; Tit. And. III, ii, 44; Rich. III: IV, iii, 229.
<P>107. <B>palace</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> In The Second Maiden's Tragedy (an old MS. in the
library of the Marquis of Lansdowne) monuments are styled &lquo;the <I>palaces</I> of death.&rquo;
[<I>Sing.</I>
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. By these few words&mdash;a concentrated amalgamation of richest splendours
with dunnest obscurity&mdash;the poet brings his grandly-blended imagery in this speech
to a fitting climax.

<P>though I am well aware that the word <I>bitterly</I> [I, iv, 108] was suggested to the

<P>137. <B>yew-tree</B>] <SC>Ulr.</SC> The majority of the edd. here read &lquo;yew-tree&rquo; on the sup-
position that Balthasar is speaking of the same trees of which the County Paris had
previously thought (V, iii, 3). Nevertheless, as I have before observed, it can
scarcely have been Sh.'s intention to represent Balthasar and the County's Page as
sleeping under the same tree&mdash;which would be almost comic in its by-play&mdash;and
that he has therefore probably been obliged to represent the trees as different. There
is consequently no sufficient reason to make any change here.
<P>138. <B>I dreamt</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> This is one of the touches of nature that would have
escaped the hand of any painter less attentive to it than Sh. What happens to a
person under the manifest influence of fear will seem to him, when he is recovered
from it, like a dream. [<I>Sta.</I>] Homer, book 8th, represents Rhesus dying fast
asleep, and, as it were, beholding his enemy plunging a sword into his bosom. Eus-
tathius and Dacier both applaud this image as very natural; for a man in such a
condition, says Pope, awakes no further than to see confusedly what environs him,
and to think it not a reality but a vision. [<I>Verp. Huds.</I>] Let me add that this
passage appears to have been imitated by Quintus Calaber, xiii, 125:

<P>143. <B>To lie</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (<I>Sh.'n Grammar,</I> 1870 (ed. 3), p. 256). <I>To</I> was originally
used not with the infinitive but with the gerund in <I>-e,</I> and, like the Latin &lquo;<I>ad</I>&rquo; with
the gerund, denoted a purpose. Thus &lquo;<I>to</I> love&rquo; was originally &lquo;<I>to</I> lovene,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> &lquo;<I>to</I>
(or <I>toward</I>) loving&rquo; (ad amandum). Gradually, as <I>to</I> superseded the proper infini-
tival inflection, <I>to</I> was used in other and more indefinite senses, &lquo;for,&rquo; &lquo;about,&rquo; &lquo;in,&rquo;
&lquo;as regards,&rquo; and, in a word, for any form of the gerund as well as for the infinitive.
This gerundive use of the infinitive is common after the verb &lquo;to mean.&rquo;&mdash;Ant. and
Cleo. IV, i, 34.

<P>152. <B>unnatural sleep</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> The sleep of Juliet was <I>unnatural,</I> being brought
on by drugs. [<I>Del.</I>
<P><SC>Del.</SC> In connection with <I>death</I> and <I>contagion</I> it means, perhaps, more probably

<P>155. <B>Thy husband . . . dead</B>] <SC>Mal.</SC> Sh. has been arraigned for departing from
the Italian novel, in making Romeo die before Juliet awakes, and thus losing a
happy opportunity of introducing an affecting scene. But he undoubtedly had never
read the Italian novel, or any <I>literal</I> translation of it, and was misled by the poem
of Romeus and Juliet, which departs from the Italian story in this regard. [<I>Sing.
Huds.</I>
<P><SC>Sing.</SC> Schlegel remarks that &lquo;the poet seems to have hit upon what was best.
There is a measure of agitation, beyond which all that is superadded becomes tor-
ture, or glides off ineffectually from the already saturated mind. In case of the cruel
reunion of the lovers for an instant, Romeo's remorse for his over-hasty self-murder,
Juliet's despair over her deceitful hope, at first cherished, then annihilated, that she
was at the goal of her wishes, must have deviated into caricatures. Nobody surely
doubts that Sh. was able to represent these with suitable force; but here everything
soothing was welcome in order that we may not be frightened out of the melancholy,
to which we willingly resign ourselves, by too painful discords. Why should we
heap still more upon accident, that is already so guilty? Wherefore shall not the
tortured Romeo quietly &lquo;Shake the yoke of inauspicious stars From his world-
wearied flesh?&rquo; He holds his beloved in his arms, and, dying, cheers himself with
a vision of everlasting marriage. She also seeks death, in a kiss, upon his lips.
These last moments must belong unparticipated to tenderness, that we may hold fast
to the thought, that love lives, although the lovers perish. [<I>Verp. Huds.</I>

<P>169. <B>there rest</B>] <SC>Steev.</SC> The alteration from <I>rest</I> in (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) to <I>rust</I> in Q<SUB>2</SUB> was
probably made by Sh. when he introduced the words, &lquo;This is thy <I>sheath.</I>&rquo;
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> [&lquo;<I>Remarks,</I>&rquo; &amp;c. p. 177]. &lquo;<I>Rest</I>&rquo; appears to me the more natural expression:
at such a moment the thoughts of Juliet were not likely to wander away to the
<I>future rusting</I> of the dagger; she only wishes it, by <I>resting</I> in her bosom as in its
sheath, to give her instant death. [<I>Huds. Coll.</I> (ed. 2).
<P><SC>Lettsom</SC>. True. [MS. marginal note in the present editor's copy of the above.]
<P><SC>White</SC> (&lquo;<I>Shaks. Scholar</I>&rquo;). &lquo;There <I>rust</I>&rquo; is an obvious misprint for &lquo;There <I>rest.</I>&rquo;
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 1). I believe &lquo;rust&rquo; to be a decided error. Steevens's remark [as
above] I do not understand.
<P><SC>Huds.</SC> Dyce is surely right.
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). <I>Rust</I> is altered to &lquo;rest&rquo; in the (MS.), which word we, on all ac-
counts, prefer. [Dyce quoted.] It may be added that if short-hand were employed
in the original publication of this play, the words &lquo;rest&rquo; and <I>rust</I> would be spelt
with the same letters.
<P><SC>White</SC>. When I was green in judgment, I hastily agreed that &lquo;rust&rquo; is a misprint.
<I>Juliet's</I> thoughts do not, as Dyce says, wander: they go forward, though not to the
literal end. Her imagination is excited, and, looking beyond her suicidal act, she
sees her dead <I>Romeo's</I> dagger, which would otherwise rust in its sheath, rusting in
her heart; and, with fierce and amorous joy, she cries, &lquo;<I>This</I> is thy sheath; <I>there</I>
rust and let me die.&rquo;
<P><SC>Clarke</SC>. The expression, &lquo;Oh, <I>happy</I> dagger,&rquo; though meaning, &lquo;Oh, happily-
found dagger!&rquo; &lquo;opportune dagger!&rquo; yet conveys an included sense that is in keep-
ing with the word &lquo;rest,&rquo; which also affords antithetical effect with &lquo;let me <I>die.</I>&rquo;
Poetically calling her bosom the &lquo;sheath&rquo; to Romeo's dagger, &lquo;rest&rquo; seems more in
harmony than &lquo;rust&rquo; with the image presented.
<P>[The Tragedy here ends in Booth's Acting Copy.] <SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>intransitively might be permissible, but it is a very venturesome conjecture to put the
full form <I>mis-sheath&egrave;d,</I> as in the Imperfect, because Sh. almost always syncopated it.
The only instance in this play (IV, v, 84) is <I>ordain&egrave;d,</I> in Spenserian style, and this too
in a place where Q<SUB>2</SUB> has close by some gross misprints. On the other hand, it is
manifestly incorrect, for the sake of the <I>is</I> of Q<SUB>3</SUB>, to throw out the new Nominative
<I>it</I> transmitted from (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) through Q<SUB>2</SUB>, and so urgently required by the construction.
(Pope properly felt this.) The error in Q<SUB>2</SUB> therefore does not consist in having the
syncopated form instead of the full one,&mdash;this would be a most excessively rare error
for Q<SUB>2</SUB>,&mdash;but in the omission of the little word <I>is</I> after <I>it</I> and before <I>mis.</I> Since Sh.
in his (earlier) plays occasionally places the paroxytone accent on the words com-
pounded with <I>mis, for, con, be</I> [numerous examples are here given by the learned
commentator. <SC>Ed.</SC>], there can be no doubt, I think, that we must not write <I>it's
mis-sheathed,</I> but <I>it is mis-sheath'd.</I>

<P>215. <B>mouth of outrage</B>] <SC>Coll.</SC> (&lquo;<I>Notes and Emend.</I>&rquo; &amp;c. p. 394). Perhaps
&lquo;outrage&rquo; is to be taken in the general sense of disturbance; but the (MS.) gives
the word differently. The necessity for the change is not very apparent; but, never-
theless, Lady Capulet has exclaimed on entering: [lines 190-192.]
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> I consider this change as one which the (MS.) made out of whole cloth:
he might have thought that &lquo;outrage&rquo; was too strong a phrase to apply to what old
Montague has just said. This is certainly true; but on the other hand, the &lquo;mouth
of <I>outcry</I>&rquo; is sheer tautology, and is besides a very strong expression, as it is scarcely
to be assumed that old Montague had really &lquo;shrieked out.&rquo; At all events, the em<*>
endation, if it be one, is unimportant.
<P><SC>Sing.</SC> (ed. 2). A plausible conjecture, but change seems hardly necessary.
<P><SC>Huds.</SC> It is not easy to see what business <I>outrage</I> can have in such a place.

precisely the same signification as in the present passage:
<BQ>
&lquo;&mdash;&mdash;Are you not asham'd,<LB REND=RIGHT>

To trouble and disturb the king and us?&rquo;<LB>

<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 1). It is worth notice that Johnson (<I>Dict.</I> sub. &lquo;<I>Outrage</I>&rquo;) has cited a

used for mere commotion.&rquo; [Collier's &lquo;very specious&rquo; change cited.]
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). The reading &lquo;<I>outrage</I>&rquo; (as constantly misprinted) is almost non
sense, and Lady Capulet has spoken just before of the &lquo;open outcry&rquo; which had
aroused her. The mouth of this &lquo;open outcry&rquo; the Prince wished to be sealed.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2). Thus in a play written long after Sh.'s days, Settle's <I>Female Pre-

<P>228. <B>I will be brief</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>. It is much to be lamented that the poet did not

<P><SC>Mal.</SC> Sh. was led into this uninteresting narrative by following Romeus and
Juliet too closely. [<I>Sing. Verp.</I>
<P><SC>Steev.</SC> In the poem the bodies of the dead are removed to a public scaffold, and
from that elevation is the Friar's narrative delivered. The same circumstance is
introduced in Hamlet. [<I>Sing. Verp. Coll.</I> (ed. 2).
<P><SC>Ulr.</SC> Johnson and Malone think that Sh. committed an &aelig;sthetic blunder in here
following Brooke's poem. But they do not reflect that without this &lquo;narrative&rquo; all
that follows, most especially the reconciliation of the Capulets and Montagues over
the corpses of their children, the victims of their hate, would be lost, and thereby
the tragedy be robbed of one of its profoundest and most exquisite elements. (Com-
pare <I>Shakespeare's Dramatic Art,</I> p. 359.) It is, moreover, interesting to note
that in the (Q<SUB>1</SUB>), where the text is everywhere shorter and more scanty, this narra-
tive, which had to be compressed into the smallest possible compass, is even longer
than it is in the later editions.
<P><SC>White</SC>. In the two versions of this tragedy this speech differs little in thought
and nothing in purpose, but greatly in language. In the earlier it is much the
poorer, and with a poverty of expression which is not Sh.'s at any period of his life.
I believe it to have been patched up from memory or imperfect notes by an inferior
hand. Notice in this speech in (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) the idioms &lquo;whereas&rquo; and &lquo;for to,&rquo; which Sh.
seems so sedulously to have avoided, and which, it should be observed, are found in
all the surreptitious and mutilated versions of his plays, and disappear in the
authentic eds.

<P>246. <B>as this</B>] <SC>Allen</SC> (&lquo;<I>Notes on The Tempest. Minutes of the Sh. Soc. of
Phila.,</I>&rquo; 1866, p. 12. Temp. I, ii, 70, &lquo;as, at that time&rquo;). By removing the comma
we get an expression precisely equivalent to the <I>as-at-this-time</I> in the Prayer-Book
Collect for Christmas, which (thirty odd years ago) I settled in my mind (against
the commentators) must be a more or less precise and emphatic <I>now.</I> I considered,
namely, that <I>at-this-time</I> was simply equal to <I>now;</I> that <I>as-</I>at-this-time was equal to
<I>as-now</I> or <I>now-as;</I> and that <I>now-as</I> would be one of the correlatives of the recog-
nized <I>whenas.</I> It was easy enough to go further and say, that <I>as-at-</I>that<I>-time</I> would
be equal to <I>as-then</I> or <I>then-as,</I> and that <I>then-as</I> would be the other correlative of
<I>whenas.</I> I did not, indeed, imagine that either <I>now-as</I> and <I>then-as,</I> or <I>as-now</I> and
<I>as-then,</I> could be found in any of our old <I>authors,</I> but Johnson taught me that <I>as how</I>
was used by so late a writer as Addison, and I remembered that the exact equivalent
of <I>as then</I> was current in German, under the form of <I>alsdann.</I> There was reason
to believe, therefore, that more such adverbial forms, with <I>as</I> prefixed or suffixed&mdash;
perhaps, even, systems of <I>correlatives</I> with <I>as</I> (analogous to <I>whereby</I> and <I>thereby,</I>
&amp;c.)&mdash;once existed in the old colloquial language of both England and Germany.
Turning to the <I>Deutsches W&ouml;rterbuch</I> of the brothers Grimm, I not only found
(vol. i, p. 258<I>a</I>) that <I>als</I> (= <I>as</I>) was used with such Adverbs as <I>yesterday, to-day,
to-morrow,</I> &amp;c., in Opitz and other old authors, and to this day (vol. i, p. 247<I>a</I>) in
the spoken language of the Rhine and Main lands, but also perceived that a similar
use of <I>as</I> in English was known to these German philologists. Verifying this state-
ment, I met in Chaucer's <I>Legende of Goode Women</I> (so admirably edited by Prof.
Corson), &lquo;This thoghte hire was felicite <I>as here</I>&rquo; (2587), &lquo;us nedeth trewely Nothing
<I>as now</I>&rquo; (1491), &lquo;<I>As-in-that-poynt . . .</I> Thou folwest him certayn&rquo; (2547), and &lquo;<I>as-in-
love</I> trusteth no man but me&rquo; (2568). Professor Corson's MS. <I>Select Glossary of La
Mort d'Arthur</I> (kindly lent me) furnishes seventeen examples, including not only
<I>as at this time</I> and <I>as at that time, as to-night</I> and <I>as to-morrow,</I> but also <I>as at bed
and at board.</I> In the Paston Letters (Bohn's ed., vol. ii, p. 156), the Duke of Nor-
folk writes that &lquo;the King would have set forth <I>as upon Monday;</I>&rquo; and in the Homily
for Good Friday (near the beginning) we have &lquo;<I>as</I> about this time.&rquo; <I>As then</I> occurs
also in Jeremy Taylor's &lquo;Sermon on the Marriage-Ring:&rquo; &lquo;because <I>as then</I> it was,
when they were to flie.&rquo; Nor is the passage in The Temp. absolutely the only one in
which Shakespeare so uses <I>as:</I> in Meas. for Meas., V, i, 70, Isabella declares Lucio
to have been &lquo;<I>as then</I> the messenger;&rquo; in Sonn. xlvi, &lquo;The clear eye's moiety and
the dear heart's part&rquo; is determined &lquo;<I>as thus;</I>&rquo; and the reading of F<SUB>1</SUB> in Twelfth
Night, II, ii, 33, may stand, if we consider &lquo;such as&rquo; to be a composite form equiva-

<P>lent to &lquo;precisely such:&rquo; &lquo;Alas! our <I>frailty</I> is the cause, not we; For <I>such-as</I> we
are <I>made,</I> if such we <I>be.</I>&rquo;
<P><SC>Abbott</SC> (&lquo;<I>Shakespearian Grammar,</I>&rquo; 1870, p. 79). <I>As</I> is apparently used redun-
dantly with definitions of time (as <G>w(s</G> is used in Greek with respect to motion). It
is said by Halliwell to be an Eastern Counties' phrase: &lquo;This is my birthday, <I>as</I> this
very day Was Cassius born.&rquo;&mdash;Jul. C&aelig;s., V, i, 72; Meas. for Meas., V, i, 74. The
<I>as</I> in the first example may be intended to qualify the statement that Cassius was
born on &lquo;this very day,&rquo; which is not literally true, <I>as</I> meaning &lquo;<I>as</I> I may say.&rquo;
Here, and in our Collect for Christmas Day, &lquo;<I>as</I> at this time to be born,&rquo; <I>as</I> seems
appropriate to an <I>anniversary.</I> In the second example the meaning of &lquo;<I>as</I> then&rquo;
is not so clear. Perhaps it means &lquo;<I>as far as regards</I> that occasion.&rquo; Compare
<BQ>
&lquo;Yet God at last<LB REND=RIGHT>
To Satan, first in sin, his doom applied,<LB>
Though in mysterious terms, judged <I>as then best.</I>&rquo;&mdash;Milton, P. L., x, 173,<LB>
</BQ>
<P>where &lquo;<I>as</I> then&rquo; seems to mean &lquo;for the present.&rquo; So &lquo;as yet&rquo; means &lquo;<I>as far as
regards</I> time up to the present time.&rquo; So in German, &lquo;<I>als</I> dann&rquo; means &lquo;then,&rquo; and
&lquo;als&rquo; is applied to other temporal adverbs. <I>As</I> in Early English was often prefixed
to dates: &lquo;<I>As</I> in the year of grace,&rquo; &amp;c. &lquo;<I>As</I> now&rquo; is often used in Chaucer and
earlier writers for &lquo;as regards now,&rquo; &lquo;for the present:&rquo; &lquo;But al that thing I must <I>as</I>
now forbere.&rquo;&mdash;Chauc., <I>Knights Tale,</I> 27. In Rom. and Jul., V, iii, 246, <I>as</I> perhaps
means &lquo;<I>as</I> (he did come).&rquo;

<P>272. <B>in post</B>] <SC>Ulr.</SC> Sh. uses this phrase frequently and in different connections,

<P>274. <B>This letter,</B> &amp;c.] <SC>S. Walker</SC> (&lquo;<I>Vers.,</I>&rquo; p. 67) cites this line as an instance
of the frequent contraction into one syllable of certain classes of words, the greater
part of them composed of two short syllables. This takes place chiefly when they
are followed by a vowel, or when placed in monosyllabic places in the line.
<P>275. <B>letter he</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&lquo;<I>Sh.</I>&rquo;<I>n Grammar</I> (ed. 3), 1870, p. 346). <I>Er, el,</I> and
<I>le</I> final are dropped or softened, especially before vowels or silent <I>h.</I> The syllable
<I>er,</I> as in <I>letter,</I> is easily interchangeable with <I>re,</I> as <I>lettre.</I> In Old English, &lquo;bettre&rquo;
is found for &lquo;better.&rquo; Thus words frequently drop or soften <I>-er;</I> and in like manner
<I>-el</I> and <I>le,</I> especially before a vowel or <I>h</I> in the next word.

<PB N=299>
<HE><SC>act v, sc.</SC> iii.] <I>ROMEO AND JULIET.</I> 299</HE>
<P>The scenes are busy and various, the incidents numerous and important, the catas-
trophe irresistibly affecting, and the process of the action carried on with such prob-
ability, at least with such congruity to popular opinions, as tragedy requires.
<P>Here is one of the few attempts of Sh. to exhibit the conversation of gentlemen,
to represent the airy sprightliness of juvenile elegance. Dryden mentions a tradi-
tion, which might easily reach his time, of a declaration made by Sh., that <I>he was
obliged to kill Mercutio in the third Act, lest he should have been killed by him.</I> Yet
he thinks him <I>no such formidable person but that he might have lived through the
play, and died in his bed,</I> without danger to the poet. Dryden well knew, had he
been in quest of truth, in a pointed sentence, that more regard is commonly had to
the words than the thought, and that it is very seldom to be rigorously understood.
Mercutio's wit, gaiety, and courage will always procure him friends that wish him a
longer life: but his death is not precipitated, he has lived out the time allotted him
in the construction of the play; nor do I doubt the ability of Sh. to have continued
his existence, though some of his sallies are perhaps out of the reach of Dryden,
whose genius was not very fertile of merriment, nor ductile to humour, but acute,
argumentative, comprehensive, and sublime.
<P>The Nurse is one of the characters in which the author delighted: he has, with
great subtility of distinction, drawn her at once loquacious and secret, obsequious
and insolent, trusty and dishonest.
<P>His comic scenes are happily wrought, but his pathetic strains are always polluted
with some unexpected depravations. His persons, however distressed, <I>have a con-
ceit left them in their misery&mdash;a miserable conceit.</I>
<P><SC>Steevens</SC>. This last quotation of Dr. Johnson's is also found in the Preface to
Dryden's Fables: &lquo;Just <I>John Littlewit</I> in <I>Bartholomew Fair,</I> who had a conceit
(as he tells you) left him in his misery; a miserable conceit.&rquo;
<P><SC>Singer</SC>. This last remark of Dr. Johnson's has been answered at length, and, as
I think, satisfactorily, by A. W. Schlegel in a detailed criticism of this tragedy, pub-
lished in the <I>Horen,</I> a journal conducted by Schiller in 1794-1795, and made acces-
sible to the English reader in Ollier's Literary Miscellany, Part I. In his Lectures
on Dramatic Literature (vol. ii, p. 135, Eng. trans.) will be found some further sen-
sible remarks upon the &lquo;conceits&rquo; here stigmatized. It should be remembered that
<I>playing on words</I> was a very favorite species of wit combat with our ancestors.
&lquo;With children, as well as nations of the most simple manners, a great inclination
to playing on words is often displayed [they cannot therefore be both <I>puerile</I> and
<I>unnatural.</I> If the first charge is founded the second cannot be so]. In <I>Homer</I> we
find several examples: the <I>Books of Moses,</I> the oldest written memorial of the primi-
tive world, are, it is well known, full of them. On the other hand, poets of a very
cultivated taste, or orators like Cicero, have delighted in them. Whoever in Richard
the Second is disgusted with the affecting play of words of the dying John of Gaunt
on his own name, let him remember that the same thing occurs in the Ajax of
Sophocles.
<P><SC>Coleridge</SC> (&lquo;<I>Lit. Rem.</I>&rquo; vol. ii, p. 77). The stage in Sh.'s time was a naked room
with a blanket for a curtain; but he made it a field for monarchs. That law of
unity which has its foundations, not in the factitious necessity of custom, but in
nature itself, the unity of feeling, is everywhere and at all times observed by Sh. in
his plays. Read Romeo and Juliet; all is youth and spring; youth with its follies,
its virtues, its precipitancies; spring with its odours, its flowers, and its transiency;
it is one and the same feeling that commences, goes through, and ends the play.
<PB N=300>
<HE>300 <I>ROMEO AND JULIET.</I> [<SC>act v, sc.</SC> iii</HE>
<P>The old men, the Capulets and the Montagues, are not common old men; they have
an eagerness, a heartiness, a vehemence, the effect of spring; with Romeo, his
change of passion, his sudden marriage, and his rash death are all the effects of
youth; whilst in Juliet love has all that is tender and melancholy in the nightingale,
all that is voluptuous in the rose, with whatever is sweet in the freshness of spring;
but it ends with a long, deep sigh like the last breeze of the Italian evening. This
unity of feeling and character pervades every drama of Sh.
<P><SC>Schlegel</SC>. Whatever is most intoxicating in the odour of a southern spring, lan-
guishing in the song of the nightingale, or voluptuous in the first opening of the
rose, is breathed into this poem. But even more rapidly than the earliest blossoms
of youth and beauty decay, it hurries on from the first timidly-bold declaration of
love and modest return to the most unlimited passion, to an irrevocable union: then,
amidst alternating storms of rapture and despair, to the death of the two lovers, who
still appear enviable as their love survives them, and as by their death they have
obtained a triumph over every separating power. The sweetest and the bitterest,
love and hatred, festivity and dark forebodings, tender embraces and sepulchres, the
fulness of life and self-annihilation, are all here brought close to each other; and
all these contrasts are so blended, in the harmonious and beautiful work, into a unity
of impression that the echo which the whole leaves behind in the mind resembles a
single but endless sigh.
<P><SC>Hazlitt</SC>. This description [of Schlegel's] is true, and yet it does not come up to
our idea of the play. For if it has the sweetness of the rose, it has its freshness
too; if it has the languor of the nightingale's song, it has also its giddy transport;
if it has the softness of a southern spring, it is as glowing and as bright. There is
nothing of a sickly, sentimental cast. Romeo and Juliet are in love but they are
not love-sick. Everything speaks the very soul of pleasure, the high and healthy
pulse of the passions: the heart beats and the blood circulates and mantles through-
out. Their courtship is not an insipid interchange of sentiments lip-deep, learnt at
second-hand from poems and plays&mdash;made up of beauties of the most shadowy
kind, of &lquo;fancies wan,&rquo; of evanescent smiles and sighs that breathe not, of delicacy
that shrinks from the touch, and feebleness that scarce supports itself, an elaborate
vacuity of thought, and an artificial dearth of sense, spirit, truth, and nature! It is
the reverse of all this. It is Sh. all over, and Sh. when he was young.
<P><SC>Hartley Coleridge</SC>. (&lquo;<I>Essays,</I>&rquo; &amp;c., vol. ii, p. 198). There is something hasty
and inconsiderate in these last scenes. Perhaps no human genius can grapple with
such aggregated disaster. Words cannot express the horror of such judicial calami-
ties which overswell the capacity of conscious grief, and must needs produce mad-
ness or stupefaction, or, likely enough, demoniac scorn and laughter. The recon-
ciliation of the parents seems to me more moral than natural. I doubt if real hatred
is ever cured. As for the golden statues, they are not so good a monument as the
sweetbriars growing from the common grave of hapless lovers in so many old ballads.
Garrick has certainly deepened and humanized the pathos by making Juliet awake
before Romeo dies, which I believe is according to the original story.
<P><SC>Chambers</SC>. Byron, in one of his letters to Moore, says: Of the truth of Juliet's
story they (the Veronese) seem tenacious to a degree,&mdash;insisting on the fact, giving
a date (1303), and showing a tomb. It is a plain, open, and partly decayed sar-
cophagus, with withered leaves in it, in a wild and desolate conventual garden, once
a cemetery, now ruined to the very graves. The situation struck me as very appro-
priate to the legend, being blighted as their love.
<PB N=301>
<P>[<SC>In</SC> the following Reprint of the Quarto of 1597 I have adhered with the most
scrupulous exactness to Mr Ashbee's Facsimile of 1866, executed under the super-
vision of Mr Halliwell.
<P>At the foot of each page will be found some of the results of a thorough colla-
tion of Steevens's, Mommsen's, and the Cambridge Editors' Reprints. To give all
the <I>vari&aelig; lectiones</I> would be both tedious and unprofitable. Steevens, for instance,
utterly disregards the use of capital letters except for proper names. Throughout
the play I can remember but one exception; namely, &lquo;Lent&rquo; in line 932. Not even
upon a Saint does he bestow this dignity. In his stage-directions proper names are
almost uniformly printed in Roman letters, and in this respect he is as uniformly fol-
lowed by Prof. Mommsen. He furthermore separates words which are printed as
one in the original, and unites words which are sometimes printed as two, <I>e. g., shal
be</I> for &lquo;shalbe,&rquo; and <I>asleepe</I> for &lquo;a sleepe.&rquo;
<P>The most noteworthy discrepancy in Prof. Mommsen's Reprint is the omission of
two entire consecutive lines.
<P>In the Reprint of the Cambridge Edition I have noted only about fifty variations
from Mr Halliwell's Facsimile; the majority of them are very trifling, and consist
chiefly in the use of a period for a comma, or the reverse. To distinguish these two
marks of punctuation in the thick, heavy printing of the Quarto is often a matter of
much doubt, and although the Cambridge Editors are as likely to be correct as Mr
Ashbee, I am bound to follow the Facsimile. I have not noted the running together
of separate words, because it happens to be a point upon which, in many cases, two
persons might disagree even with the same copy before them. In John Danter's
printing-office there seems to have been a plentiful lack of &lquo;spaces;&rquo; many a line
being printed as one unbroken word.
<P>In short, only those <I>vari&aelig; lectiones</I> are given which seem to indicate that the
original copies from which the three Reprints were made vary one from another.
<P>Whenever the characters on the stage retire, and their places are taken by others,
the Cambridge Editors indicate the change in the margin by a series of Scenes,
from I to XXII, and they number the lines with reference to these Scenes.
<P><S>S.</S> stands for Steevens's Reprint, 1766; <I>M.</I> stands for Mommsen's, 1859; <I>C.</I> repre-
sents the Cambridge Edition, 1865.] <SC>Ed.</SC>
