<C>APPENDIX</C>
<SHL>
<C><I>That runaway's eyes may wink, and Romeo</I>&mdash;III, ii, 6, p. 166.</C>
<P><SC>Warburton</SC> (1747). Macbeth (III, ii, 46) invokes night much in the same
strain: &lquo;Come, seeling night, <I>Scarf</I> up the tender <I>eye</I> of pitiful <I>day,</I>&rquo; &amp;c. So Juliet
would have night's darkness obscure the great eye of the day&mdash;the <I>sun</I>&mdash;whom con-
sidering as Ph&oelig;bus, drawn in his car with <I>fiery-footed</I> steeds, she very properly calls,
with regard to the swiftness of his course, the <I>runaway.</I> In like manner Sh. speaks
of the night in the Mer. of Ven. (II, vi, 47): &lquo;For the close <I>night</I> doth play the
<I>run-away.</I>&rquo; [<I>Theobald, Johnson.</I>
<P><SC>Johnson</SC> (1765). I am not satisfied with this emendation, yet have nothing better
to propose.
<P><SC>Heath</SC> (&lquo;<I>Revisal of Sh.'s Text,</I>&rquo; 1765, p. 512). By the <I>run-away</I> Warburton un-
derstands the sun himself. But besides that the sun had been already sufficiently
invoked, and is absent as soon as night comes; besides that the runaway is at any
time a very strange and quaint appellation for the sun, it is singularly improper in
this passage. Juliet had just before complained of the sun's tedious slowness in
finishing his course, and therefore it is very unlikely she should in the same breath
call him a <I>run-away.</I> I think it not improbable that the poet wrote &lquo;That <I>Rumour's</I>
eyes may wink,&rquo; &amp;c.
<P><SC>Steevens</SC> (1773). Yet Sh., who has introduced this personage (Rumour) by way
of Prologue-speaker to one of his historical plays, has only described her as <I>painted</I>
full of tongues.
<P><SC>Steevens</SC> (1778). The construction of this passage, however elliptical or per-
verse, I believe to be as follows: &lquo;May that run-away's eyes wink!&rquo; or &lquo;That run-
away's eyes, may (they) wink!&rquo; These ellipses are common in Spenser: and <I>that</I>
for <I>oh! that,</I> is not uncommon, as Dr. Farmer observes in a note on the first scene
of Winter's Tale. So in Ant. and Cleop. III, vi, 40. Juliet first wishes for the
absence of the sun, and then invokes the night to spread its curtain close around the
world. Next recollecting that the night would seem short to her, she speaks of it
as of a <I>run-away</I> whose flight she would wish to retard, and whose eyes she would
blind lest they should make discoveries. The <I>eyes of night</I> are the stars so called
in Mid Sum. N. D. In the Fair Maid of the Exchange, 1607, night is spoken of as
in the Mer. of Ven.: &lquo;The night hath played the swift-foot <I>run-away.</I>&rquo; Romeo was
<PB N=368>
<HE>368 <I>APPENDIX.</I></HE>
<P>not expected by Juliet till the sun was gone, and therefore it was of no consequence
to her that any eyes should wink but those of night; for, as Ben Jonson says in
Sejanus, &lquo;&mdash;&mdash; night hath many eyes, Whereof, though most do sleep, yet some are
spies.&rquo;
<P><SC>Blackstone</SC> (in Johns. and Steev. ed. 1785). <I>That</I> seems not to be the optative
adverb <I>utinam,</I> but the pronoun <I>ista.</I> These lines contain no wish, but a reason for
Juliet's preceding wish for the approach of <I>cloudy</I> night; for in such a night there
may be no starlight to discover our stolen pleasures: &lquo;That run-away eyes <I>may</I>
wink.&rquo;
<P><SC>Monk Mason</SC> (&lquo;<I>Comments,</I>&rquo; &amp;c. 1785, p. 367). The omission of the article proves
that the word, whatever the meaning of it may be, was intended for a proper name.
Though I am not so fond as Warburton of making Sh. speak French, I believe that
here he uses a French word with an English termination, and have little doubt that
we ought to read &lquo;that <I>Renomy's</I> eyes,&rquo; &amp;c. <I>Renomm&eacute;e</I> is the French word for
<I>Rumour,</I> and is thus described by Boileau in his Lutrin:
<BQ>
&lquo;Cependant cet oiseau qui prone les merveilles,<LB>
Ce monstre compos&eacute; de bouches et d'oreilles,<LB>
Qui sans cesse volant de climats en climats<LB>
Dit partout ce qu'il scait, et ce qu'il ne scait pas,<LB>
La Renomm&eacute;e enfin,&rquo; &amp;c.<LB>
</BQ>
<P>The words <I>untalk'd of</I> and <I>unseen</I> confirm this conjecture.
<P><SC>Rann</SC> (1786). That no bright star may discover our stolen pleasures.
<P><SC>Seymour</SC> (&lquo;<I>Remarks,</I>&rquo; &amp;c. 1805, vol. ii, p. 406). Romeo I take to be the run-
away, <I>i. e.,</I> the person that is to come and run away with Juliet, and she would have
him post to her on the wings of love with such celerity as to be blind to every obsta-
cle and invisible to every eye; that Romeo is he whose eyes are to wink, and is,
of consequence, the runaway, seems partly implied in what follows: &lquo;if love <I>be
blind,</I>&rquo; &amp;c.
<P><SC>Capel Lofft</SC> [cited in Seymour's &lquo;<I>Remarks</I>&rquo;]. Is it not possible that Fame or
Rumour, with all its vigilant eyes, may be intended?
<P><SC>Douce</SC> (&lquo;<I>Illustrations,</I>&rquo; &amp;c. 1807). Whoever attentively reads over Juliet's speech
will be inclined to think, or even be satisfied, that the whole <I>tenor</I> of it is <I>optative.</I>
As to calling night a <I>run-away,</I> one might surely ask how it can possibly be so
termed in <I>an abstract point of view.</I> Is it a greater fugitive than the morning, the
noon, or the evening? Steevens lays great stress on Sh.'s having before called the
night a <I>run-away</I> in the Mer. of Ven. But there it was already far advanced, and
might therefore with great propriety be said to <I>play the run-away;</I> here it was not
begun. The same remark applies to the other passage cited by Steevens from The
Fair Maid of the Exchange. Can this <I>run-away</I> be Juliet herself? She who had
just been secretly married to the enemy of her parents might, with some propriety,
be termed a <I>run-away from her duty;</I> but she had not abandoned her native pu-
dency. She therefore invokes the night to veil those rites which she was about to
perform, and to bring her Romeo to her arms in darkness and in silence. The lines
that immediately follow may be thought to favour this interpretation; and the whole
scene may possibly recall to the reader the beautiful story of Cupid and Psyche.
<P><SC>Becket</SC> (&lquo;<I>Sh. Himself Again,</I>&rquo; 1815, p. 214). I would read &lquo;That <I>runagate's</I>
eyes,&rquo; &amp;c., which must be understood as follows: &lquo;Let the eyes of runagates, rebels,
or love-apostates be shut, so that there may be no opposition, no hindrance to the
completion of my wishes.&rquo; It will be admitted, I think, that change is necessary&mdash;
<PB N=369>
<HE><I>RUNAWAY'S EYES.</I> 369</HE>
<P>that something, in short, should be substituted for &lquo;runaway;&rquo; and it may be farther
acknowledged, perhaps, that I have fallen on the proper term.
<P><SC>Zachary Jackson</SC> (&lquo;<I>Sh.'s Genius Justified,</I>&rquo; p. 421, 1819). According to the
orthography of Sh.'s time, the transposition of a single letter gives the original
word, and produces so clear a meaning that neither the Greek of Judge Blackstone
nor the laboured elucidations of the other commentators are necessary. Our great
Poet wrote, &lquo;That unawares eyes may wink,&rquo; &amp;c. Juliet invokes night to mantle
the world in darkness, that by a heavy atmosphere sleep may steal unawares upon
the eyelids of those who would obstruct her pleasures. What can possibly be more
simple? Now see how the error originated. The old mode of spelling <I>unawares</I>
was <I>unawayrs:</I> the word had what printers term a literal error; that is, such as an
<I>o</I> for an <I>r;</I> in the correcting of which, having taken out the <I>o,</I> the compositor
placed the <I>r</I> at the beginning of the word, and thus turned <I>unawayrs</I> to <I>runaways.</I>
<P><SC>Knight</SC> (1838, ed. 1). This passage has been a perpetual source of contention
to the commentators. . . . After all this learning there comes an unlearned com-
positor, Zachary Jackson, and sets the matter straight. <I>Run-aways</I> is a misprint for
<I>unawares.</I> We have not the least hesitation in adopting Jackson's reading; and
we have the authority of a very clever article in Blackwood's Magazine (July, 1819)
for a general testimony to the value of Jackson's book, and the equally valuable
authority of a most accomplished friend, who called our attention to this particular
reading as settled by the common sense of the printer.
<P><SC>Cornwall</SC>. The most probable solution is that which supposes Sh. to have meant
by &lquo;runaway&rquo; the night, and by its eyes the stars. Zachary Jackson's alteration gives
a prosaic flatness to the phrase, which, to say nothing of other objections, alone con-
vinces us that it is not the true reading.
<P><SC>Collier</SC> (ed. 1). Zachary Jackson has shown that <I>run-aways</I> was in all proba-
bility a misprint for &lquo;unawares.&rquo;
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> [&lquo;<I>Remarks,</I>&rquo; &amp;c., 1844]. I cannot allow that the reading in this passage has
been &lquo;settled&rquo; by Jackson (about the value of whose book I think very differently
from Knight and the writer in Blackwood). I do not believe that Sh. would have
used such an expression as &lquo;that <I>unawares</I> eyes may wink.&rquo; That &lquo;ways&rquo; (the last
syllable of &lquo;run-aways&rquo;) ought to be &lquo;<I>Days</I>&rquo; I feel next to certain; but what word
originally preceded it I do not pretend to determine:
<BQ>
<CURL>
<I>rude</I><LB>
That<I>?</I><LB>
<I>soon</I><LB>
</CURL>
<I>Day's</I> eyes may wink, and Romeo&mdash;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>Compare Macbeth, III, ii, 46. The passages in our early poets about Night spread
ing her curtains, and Day closing her eyes, are numerous. So in Drayton:
<BQ>
&lquo;The sullen <I>Night</I> hath her black <I>Curtaines spred;</I><LB>
Lowring <I>the Day</I> hath tarried vp so long,<LB>
<I>Whose faire eyes closing</I> softly steales to bed,&rquo; &amp;c.<LB>
<I>Barons Warres,</I> p. 111, st. 17, ed. 8vo.<LB REND=RIGHT>
</BQ>
<P>(This stanza is very different in the folio ed.) [<SC>Mr. Lettsom's MS.</SC> marginal note.
&lquo;My ed., 1605, is the same as this.&rquo; <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P><SC>Mitford</SC> (in the <I>Gent. Mag.,</I> June 1845, p. 580). It strikes us as rather singular
that not one out of the whole body of the commentators has hit on the real mean-
ing, or seen how the corruption of the text was created. The right reading we take
to be &lquo;That <I>Luna's</I> eye,&rquo; &amp;c. When the L of <I>Luna</I> was changed into R and made
&lquo;<I>Runa,</I>&rquo; then the sense was entirely lost, and, to give at least some meaning to the
word, it was made &lquo;<I>Run-away.</I>&rquo; The corruption stood thus:
<PB N=370>
<HE>370 <I>APPENDIX.</I></HE>
<P>That <I>Luna's</I> eye. That <I>Runa's</I> eye. That <I>Runa-way's</I> eye.
Almost all Latin or foreign words are corrupted in the old eds., and there was no
learning in the printers to set them right. We have the same expression in Pericles,
II, v, 11: &lquo;This by <I>the eye of Cynthia</I> hath she vowed.&rquo; We trust that this emen-
dation will at once approve itself to the understanding of all our readers, except of
those who, having <I>positively</I> engaged themselves to stand by a particular reading,
will be reluctant to confess their error; and that it may supersede at once those
former readings which have arisen from typographical blunders, and with which the
commentators themselves have been obliged to acknowledge their dissatisfaction.
<P><SC>Rev. N. J. Halpin</SC> (&lquo;<I>The Bridal Runaway,</I>&rquo; Sh. Soc. Papers, vol. ii, p. 14,
1845). The source of the obscurity in these words which misleads us is that the
commentators have not sought the meaning of the terms and figures of the passage
in <I>the peculiar species of poetry</I> to which it belongs. They have, in fact, failed to
observe that the character and language of this soliloquy are purely <SC>Hymeneal</SC>.
Now, as every distinct class of poetry, whether the Anacreontic, the Pindaric, the
pastoral, or the elegy, has each not only a subject and a mythology <I>sui generis,</I> but
a suit of imagery and diction appropriate to itself, in which particular words and
figures bear a meaning modified and restricted by the nature of the composition: in
the same manner and degree is hymeneal, or epithalamic, poetry distinguished from
every other species by its own range of sentiments and its conventional phraseology.
<P>There will be no difficulty, I suppose, in conceding this; nor should I shrink from
the task of sustaining, by the usual method of demonstration,<SUP>*</SUP> my view of the par-
ticular class to which this soliloquy belongs were the subject other than it is, or had
we to deal with the literature of a period more refined and delicate. There is not
a line in it which it would not be easy to parallel with others harmonizing with it
altogether in sentiment, and, to a very great extent, in imagery and diction,<SUP>&dagger;</SUP>
extracted from the hymeneal poetry of contemporary writers. . . . This premised, I
proceed with my task.
<P>The first thing remarkable on the surface of the soliloquy is the frequent and
varied invocation of Night. For brevity sake I forbear to illustrate with correspond-
ing quotations from the contemporary poets the peculiar imagery so lavishly bestowed
on this mythological personage. But a reference to the class of poems in question
will, in this respect also, furnish abundant evidence that in the composition of this
piece the mind of Sh. was saturated with the images of hymeneal poetry, which he
has here accumulated <I>not without design.</I>
<P>I must also observe that the structure, no less than the spirit, of the soliloquy is
distinctly hymeneal. &lquo;This poem,&rquo; quoth Ben Jonson, speaking of the Epithala-
mion, &lquo;had for the most part <I>versum intercalarem,</I> or <I>carmen am&oelig;b&aelig;um;</I> and that
not always one but ofttimes varied, and sometimes neglected in the same song.&rquo;<SUP>&ddager;</SUP>
It was, in fact, the custom of the epithalamic poets to close every stanza, or division,
with a <I>refrein,</I> which, running on some leading image, or some harmonious combi-
<FHL>
<NOTE>* Namely, by the collation of parallel passages, words, phrases, and sentiments, of which process one

<P>nation of words, was, with more or less variation, repeated, sometimes at fixed. and

<P>Juliet's soliloquy is constructed on the same intercalary principle. Four several
invocations to Night [lines 5, 10, 17, 20], more or less varied, occur at intervals
more or less regular, and realize Jonson's description of the structure of this species
of poem. In short, as it appears to me, this soliloquy differs in nothing from the
legitimate epithalamion but as blank verse differs from the rhymed stanza.
<P>It is now time that we advert to the passage in which the &lquo;run-away&rquo; makes his
appearance.
<P>In the mythology of the nuptial poem it might be expected that Cupid would play
no unimportant <I>r&ocirc;le.</I> And here one might make a cheap parade of erudition at no
more cost of study than turning to the authorities quoted by Ben Jonson; but I shall
rest content with the authority of the great hierophant himself. From him we find
the part of Cupid on those occasions to have been peculiar and restricted. Hymen
had, of course, a more distinguished office; nor did he resign his ministry till, at
the door of the bridal chamber, he surrendered it to his brother. Up to this point
Cupid, by concealment or flight, usually contrived to be absent; but there it was his
duty (accompanied by a crowd of Loves and Sports) to receive the married couple.
Thus in the Hue and Cry, when about to elope for the <I>second</I> time, he whispers his
light-winged brethren:
<BQ>
&lquo;I may not stay;<LB REND=RIGHT>
Hymen's presence bids away,<LB>
'Tis already at his sight;<LB>
He can give you further light,<LB>
You, my Sports, may here abide,<LB>
<I>'Till I call to light the bride.</I>&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>It was his part to illuminate the bride-chamber, and his lights were generally his
own eyes and those of his sportive co-mates, kindled at the brilliancy of the bride's:
<BQ>
&lquo;See, a thousand Cupids fly<LB>
To light their tapers at the bride's bright eye.&rquo;<SUP>*</SUP><LB>

<P>calls &lquo;run-away,&rquo; may &lquo;wink&rquo; in order that Romeo's visit may be &lquo;untalked-of and
unseen.&rquo; Who is this? In the hymeneal system, none could be present with the
&lquo;lovers&rquo; in the bridal chamber except Cupid, by whose eyes it was supposed to be
illuminated. But Juliet does not want their light; partly, because &lquo;Lovers can see
by their own beauties,&rquo; but chiefly, that the interview may be &lquo;untalked-of and
unseen.&rquo;
<P>Is <SC>Cupid</SC>, then, the &lquo;runaway,&rquo; the Love (in the correlative) which has eyes and
can see? So far, it is, at least, very probable. The <I>sobriquet,</I> by which I suppose him
here designated, is founded on his mythical character, and was familiar, in one form
or another, to the Greek poets, who endued him with properties, and to the English,
as well as the Latin, who adopted their inventions. The characteristic alluded to, is
his notorious propensity to <I>running away</I> from his mother. To this notion are to
be referred the numberless medallions, pictures, and stories in which he is represented
as captured, imprisoned, caged, fettered, and with his wings bound, crossed behind
his back, or clipped with scissors, to prevent his escape. In reference to this trait,
he is called by the Greeks <G>dpareth\s; dpareti/das</G>; by the Latins, fugitivus, profugus,
vagus; by the English, truant, deserter, wanderer, vagrant, vagabond, runagate, and
why not, <I>runaway,</I> the exact translation of the Greek epithets? &lquo;Small Latin and
less Greek&rquo; had surely sufficed for the construction, if copied, or the coincidence, if
original, of a title so obvious and appropriate. The characteristic was familiar and
popular in the classico-romantic days of Queen Elizabeth. It furnishes the ma-
chinery of two of Lylie's court comedies, and in both the etymology of the English
synonym is distinctly suggested. &lquo;Whilst I truant from my mother,&rquo; quoth Cupid,
&lquo;I will use some tyranny in these woods, and so shall their exercise in foolish love
be my excuse for <I>running away.</I>&rquo;<SUP>*</SUP> &lquo;As for you, Sir Boy,&rquo; exclaims Venus, &lquo;I will
teach you to <I>run away.</I> You shall be stripped from top to toe, and whipped with
nettles, not roses.&rquo;<SUP>&dagger;</SUP> We lay no stress, however, on those suggestive phrases; nor
need we, for the word itself, in its compound form, is used as a synonym for Cupid
by Thomas Heywood, in that scene of his Mask of Love's Mistress, where Venus,
aided by Pan, discovers the fugitive in Vulcan's smithy:
<BQ>
&lquo;<S>Pan.</S> This way he ran with shackles on his heels,<LB>
And said he would to Vulcan. O, but see<LB>
Where he stands cogging with him.<LB>
<S>Venus.</S> Now, you <I>Runaway!</I><SUP>&ddager;</SUP><LB>
You disobedient&mdash;thou unhappy wag&mdash;<LB>

</BQ>
<P>I am bound, however, to show, not merely the use of the particular word in English
poetry as a synonym for Cupid, but its use <I>as such</I> in poetry professedly hymeneal.
Let us, then, turn again to the Hue and Cry of Ben Jonson; and there, in an ode
poorly paraphrased from the <G>*)epws *dpareth\s</G> of Moschus, we shall find the very term
applied in the very sense required. Cupid had, as usual, on the approach of the
nuptials, absconded. Distressed at his absence, Venus commissions the Graces to
&lquo;proclaim reward to her that brings him in;&rquo; whereupon the first Grace, addressing
the ladies of the Court, exclaims:
<BQ>
&lquo;Beauties, have you seen this toy<LB>
Called Love&mdash;a little boy,<LB>

<P>I believe that there can be no doubt that this <SC>Run-away</SC> is the &lquo;Run-away&rquo; of Juliet's
soliloquy. Their part in the hymeneal ceremony is the same; they are both <I>Run-
aways;</I> both are to be found at the proper time in the bride-chamber; and the office
of both is to give light in the room. If Sh.'s Run-away have eyes, so has the
original of Moschus; and if Jonson's be blind, it is doubtful whether Sh.'s is not in
the same predicament.
<P>But how, if the &lquo;winking Cupid&rquo; were, in those days, a familiar object in the bridal
chamber, emblematic of secresy and silence, and if Sh. himself should have placed
him there, a second time, to preserve the <I>arcana</I> of another clandestine marriage?
The evidence of such a fact would, I presume, be conclusive. Let us then turn to
&lquo;Cymbeline,&rquo; where the marriage of Imogen was, like Juliet's, clandestine, and the
interviews between the bride and bride-groom, in like manner, stolen and secret;
and there we shall find, amongst the furniture of the bride's apartment, &lquo;two <I>wink-
ing Cupids</I> Of silver.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Cymbeline</I> II, iv, 89. I have already shown that &lquo;Runaway&rquo;
was what we would now-a-days call a <I>pet</I> name for Cupid; that Cupid, in the hyme-
neal imagery, was a necessary attendant in the bridal chamber; and I have now
produced him (or rather an image representing himself and his functions) winking
at the rites of a clandestine marriage. There can scarcely be a doubt, I think, that
the &lquo;winking Cupid&rquo; of Imogen's bed-chamber and the <I>winking Runaway</I> of Juliet's
are, if not identical, sons of the same mother. From what I can gather of the
hymeneal mythology, it appears to me as if Cupid's presence in the bride-chamber
was in <I>all</I> cases necessary, as signifying the love between the parties; but that in
cases of clandestine marriage he was required to &lquo;wink,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> neither to see, nor to
give light, in order that the secret interviews of the lovers might be &lquo;untalked-of
and unseen.&rquo;
<P>And now, assuming this interpretation established, we arrive at the full hymeneal
meaning of the passage; which appears to be this: Secrecy is essential to our safety.
Let the day, therefore, depart, and let Night spread her curtain around, and let not
Cupid discharge his ministry of lighting up the bride-chamber.<SUP>&dagger;</SUP> If (as painted by
some) he have eyes, let them wink&mdash;<I>i. e.,</I> be darkened; for we have need of dark-
ness, that the interview, being invisible, may be untalked of; and we have no need
of light, because lovers can see by their own beauties. If, however, (as depicted by
others,) he be blind, it is all as it should be; his blindness agrees with that dark-
ness, for the sake of which the presence of night is so desirable.<SUP>&ddager;</SUP>
<P>In the ninth line, therefore, love should be printed Love.
<P>And now it may be asked, how comes Juliet so conversant with the topics and
diction of this class of poetry; and why, on this occasion, does she pour out her heart
in its language?

<P>In answer to the first, we may observe, that the nuptial pageant had at that time
become popular in England. &lquo;The worthy custom,&rquo; says Ben Jonson, &lquo;of honouring
worthy marriages with those noble solemnities, hath of late years advanced itself
frequently with us to the reputation no less of our Court than Nobles; expressing
besides (through the difficulties of expense and travel, with the cheerfulness of
undertaking) a most real affection in the personators to those for whose sake they
would sustain those persons.&rquo;<SUP>*</SUP> Although the scene lies in Italy, yet Sh. gives to
every country the manners of his own, and has given proof of the habitual occurrence
of such festivities, by celebrating with the nuptial mask the marriage of some of his
heroines.<SUP>&dagger;</SUP>
<P>From the prevalence of the practice, then, it is to be assumed that Juliet had wit-
nessed the bridal ceremonies of many of her young companions, and, like other
noble persons of the day, &lquo;expressed a most real affection&rquo; to the parties by taking a
character in the mask. Thus might she have caught up the topics and language
appropriated to this species of poetry; and hence may be inferred her familiarity
with thoughts and expressions not likely in any other way to have obtained entrance
into the mind of an innocent and unsophisticated girl of fourteen years of age.
<P>And why (in the second place) does she harp upon this string on the present
occasion?
<P>Alas, poor Juliet! who is there that, in the concomitant circumstances, does not
see the reason? It is her bridal day, but a bridal without its triumphs.

hymeneal mask. No troops of friends led her to the church, nor followed her to
the banquet. No father&mdash;no mother&mdash;gave away her hand. No minstrel sung her
nuptial hymn; and the hour that should conduct her all glorious to the bride-chamber
finds her alone, unfriended, without countenance, without sympathy. Is it any
wonder, then, that the absence of those festive rites, which, under happier auspices,
would have given splendour to her nuptials, should recall them to her imagination,

<P>and&mdash;with the vision&mdash;bring vividly to her memory the sentiments appropriated to
such occasions, and the very turn of expression which they had habitually acquired?
Nay, is it not of the very essence of our nature, that, pacing that solitary chamber,
while the twilight was thickening into darkness, and the growing silence left the
throbbings of her heart audible, she should brood over the impassioned imagery of
the Bridal Song, and give it a half-unconscious utterance? Poor Juliet! She had
nobody to sing this song for her. It bursts spontaneously from her own lips.
<P>I cannot but think that this view invests the passage with a melancholy charm,
unsurpassed in its pathos by any situation in the whole range of the drama, except
perhaps that of Iphigenia at the sacrificial altar. It is scarcely possible, indeed, that
it can ever again awaken emotions so intense as it must have kindled in the days of
Elizabeth and James; because its language does not call up in our minds the same
associations as in the minds of our ancestors. The Hymeneal Masque has vanished
from our customs, and its idiom has become a dead letter. To us the language is
not a suggestion, but a study; to them it was fraught with a peculiar significance,
and every image was coupled with an every-day reality. The very opening lines&mdash;
so essentially epithalamic&mdash;must have conjured up, to an auditory in whose ears the
phraseology was as &lquo;familiar as household words,&rquo; &lquo;the whole pride, pomp, and cir-
cumstance&rquo; of honoured wedlock; and they would have instinctively imagined the
magnificent and joyous solemnities that should have blessed the union of the only
daughter of the rich and noble Capulet with the only son of the no less noble and
wealthy Montague. But what was the scene before their eyes? Where was the
bridal escort? where the assembled friends of &lquo;both their houses&rquo;? where the crowd
of gay and gallant youths who should have homaged the beauty of the bride&mdash;and
where, oh where, the maidens that were her fellows to bear her company? Of all
the customary pageant, but one solitary figure&mdash;the figure of the bride herself&mdash;is to
be seen. All is solitude and darkness and silence. But one sound breaks the
unnatural stillness&mdash;the voice of that sweet, lonely girl, who&mdash;like the young bird
timidly practising, in the unfrequented shade, the remembered song of its kindred&mdash;
&lquo;sits darkling&rquo; in her sequestered bower, and eases her impassioned heart in snatches
of <I>remembered song,</I> which in <I>her</I> mind, too, are associated with her situation.
<P>And what a song it is!&mdash;sweet as the nightingale's that &lquo;nightly sings on yon
pomegranate tree;&rquo; and ardent as, when in Eden,
<BQ>
&lquo;the amorous bird of night<LB REND=RIGHT>
Sung Spousal; and bid haste the evening Star<LB>
On his hill-top to light the bridal lamp;<SUP>*</SUP><LB>
</BQ>
<P>but it is sad and ominous withal; and, to the auditor familiar with its import, as por-
tentous and melancholy as the fatal descant which, in poets' ears, preludes the
departure of the dying swan. The loves of Hero and Leander were (as we have
seen) presaged to an evil issue by the absence of the usual festive rites; a similar
defect forbodes to those of Romeo and Juliet a like unhappy destiny.
<P>What heart in the auditory but must have been smitten with compassion for the
bride? What eyes could have withheld the tribute of a flood of tears?
<P>To my mind this passage possesses, independently of its natural beauty, an artist-
ical charm worthy of the highest admiration: that consummate skill, I mean, with

and in Coriolanus IV, vi, 47, we have, &lquo;Go see this <I>rumourer</I> whipp'd.&rquo;
<P><SC>Blackwood's Maga.</SC> (vol. lxxiv, p. 455, 1853). <I>Who is a</I> &lquo;<I>Runaway?</I>&rquo; He is a
printer's (not devil but) blunder, says the old Corrector: we should read <I>enemies.</I>
Those may read <I>enemies</I> who choose. <I>We</I> certainly shall not&mdash;no, not even at the
bidding of Queen Victoria herself. We shall not turn ourselves into a goose to
please the ghost of an old amateur play-corrector, though he should keep <I>rapping</I>
at us till his knuckles are worn out. Read <I>Rumourers,</I> says Mr. Singer. No, Mr.
Singer, we will not read <I>Rumourers.</I> Read this thing, and read that thing, say
other wise authorities. No, gentlemen, we shall not read anything except what Sh.
wrote, and we <I>know for certain</I> that the word which he wrote was &lquo;Runaway's,&rquo; just
as it stands in the books, for we learnt this from a <I>medium;</I> yes, and the medium
was the Rev. Mr. Halpin, who has proved to our entire satisfaction that the text calls
for, and indeed admits of, no other alteration. There could not be a happier-chosen
or more expressive word than &lquo;Runaway's&rquo; as here employed.
<P><SC>Patrick Muirson</SC> (<I>N. and Q.,</I> vol. viii, Oct. 22, 1853). I interpret &lquo;runaways&rquo;
as signifying &lquo;persons going about on the watch.&rquo; Perhaps runagates, according to
modern usage, would come nearer to the proposed signification, but not to be quite
up to it.
<P><SC>Grant White</SC> [&lquo;<I>Sh.'s Scholar,</I>&rquo; p. 373, 1854]. The error will probably remain
for ever uncorrected, unless a word which I venture to suggest seems to others as
unexceptionable as it does to me. <I>Juliet</I> desires that somebody's eyes may wink,
so that <I>Romeo</I> may leap to her arms &lquo;<I>untalked of</I>&rquo; as well as &lquo;unseen.&rquo; She wishes
to avoid the scandal, the bruit, which would ensue upon the discovery of her new-
made husband's secret visit.
<P>I think, therefore, and also because the misprint is by no means improbable, that
Sh. wrote &lquo;<I>rumoures</I> eyes.&rquo; The absence of a long letter in <I>rumoures,</I> to correspond
with the <I>y</I> in &lquo;run-awayes,&rquo; does not trouble me. I have repeatedly found in my
proofs words containing long letters when the word which I wrote contained none,
and <I>vice vers&acirc;.</I> It should be noticed, too, that neither <I>unawares</I> nor <I>enemics</I> contains
a long letter. &lquo;Rumor&rquo; was spelt <I>rumoure</I> in Sh.'s day, and the possessive case
<I>rumoures,</I> of course.
<P>As to Rumor's eyes, they are as necessary to her office as are her ears or her
tongues. Virgil's <I>Fama</I> is but Rumor, and of her he says:
<BQ>
&lquo;Cui quot sunt corpore plum&aelig;<LB REND=RIGHT>
<I>Tot vigiles oculi</I> subter, mirabile dictu,<LB>
Tot lingu&aelig;, totidem ora sonant, tot subrigit aures.&rquo;&mdash;<LB>
<I>&AElig;neid,</I> Lib. IV, 181.<LB REND=RIGHT>
</BQ>
<P>And in Sh.'s day Rumor was represented with eyes as well as tongues, as we
know by the following description, evidently founded on Virgil's impersonation:
<P>&lquo;Directly under her in a cart by herselfe, Fame stood upright: a woman in a watchet roabe, thickly
set with <I>open eyes</I> and tongues, a payre of large golden winges at her backe, a trumpet in her hand, a
mantle of sundry cullours traversing her body: all these ensigns displaying but the propertie of her
swiftnesse and aptnesse to disperse <I>Rumoure.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<I>The whole magnificent Entertainement given to
King James and the queen his Wife,</I> &amp;c. 15 <I>March,</I> 1603. <I>By Thomas Decker,</I> 4to, 1604.
<P>Sh., however, had brought Rumour personally before his audience in the Induction
to 2 <I>Hen. IV,</I> where she is &lquo;painted full of tongues.&rquo; These quotations merely
show that the idea was sufficiently familiar to his auditors, learned and unlearned,
for him to use it in this manner.
<PB N=378>
<HE>378 <I>APPENDIX.</I></HE>
<P>But these considerations are not urged to gain acceptance for the reading which I
propose; their office is but to meet objections to it. If it do not commend itself at
once to the intelligent readers of Sh. with a favor which increases upon reflection,
no argument can, or should, fasten it upon the text.
<P>Mr. Collier's (MS.) furnishes &lquo;<I>enemies',</I>&rquo; a reading which is perhaps the worst that
has been offered.
<P>A correspondent from St. Louis suggested &lquo;<I>noonday's</I> eyes,&rquo; which is not without
some plausibility; and it resembles somewhat one of the readings proposed by
Dyce. But even if there were no objection, as to time, against the word &lquo;noonday,&rquo;
there is a literalness and particularity about it which are poetically out of place in
the passage for which it is proposed. But supposing such particularity not objec-
tionable on the higher grounds of criticism, the time specified in the term is incon-
sistent with the requirements of the scene; and therefore Sh. would have been
particular, only to be particularly wrong. This is evident from the fact, which a
short examination will bring to light, that <I>Juliet</I> was not married until after noon-
day, and that some hours elapsed between her marriage and the time of this solilo-
quy. [To prove that this soliloquy is spoken toward evening, Mr. White cites the
following lines: II, v, 1 and 2; II, iv, 163, and III, ii, 99.] But what need of this
comparison of hours and minutes? Is not the soliloquy itself steeped in the pas-
sion-breathing languor of a summer's afternoon just melting into twilight? Is it
not plain that <I>Juliet</I> has been watching the sun sink slowly down to the horizon,
and gazing pensively into the golden air, until her own imaginings have taken on its
glowing hue, and then she breaks out into her longing prayer for night and <I>Romeo?</I>
Facts and figures tell us that her soliloquy is spoken just before sunset; but what
reader of the whole soliloquy will not set aside the evidence of facts and figures as
superfluous&mdash;almost impertinent?
<P>[Mr. White here states that the same emendation, sustained by the same quotation
from Virgil, had been communicated to him by a friend&mdash;Mr. Hoppin of Provi-
dence, R. I.&mdash;but that both himself and his friend had been anticipated by Heath
and Singer, as he learned from the latter's communication to <I>N. and Qu.,</I> to which
his attention was first called by a correspondent in South Carolina. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>Here, then, we have three coincident conjectures from three persons, each ignorant
of the other's suggestion, which, if the word which they propose to substitute be
acceptable in itself, adds greatly to the probability that it restores the true reading.
Singer's independent conjecture that <I>rumourer's</I> is the word also affords collateral
support to the former, the idea being the same in both. But it should be remarked
that the line does not need a word of three syllables. The typographical error
which gave us <I>runaways,</I> and which Singer would correct by substituting <I>rumourers',</I>
almost certainly loaded the line with a redundant syllable. Notice also that the
addition of an <I>r</I> diminishes the chances for an error by the compositor. It would
be far more likely that &lquo;rumour<I>es</I>&rquo; should be mistaken for &lquo;runaway<I>es</I>&rquo; than that
&lquo;rumour<I>ers</I>&rquo; should cause the same error. Yet another objection against &lquo;rumour-
<I>ers</I>&rquo; is that its particularity is inconsistent with the poetical character of the passage,
in which <I>Juliet</I> uses only large and general terms.
<P>Collier claims, with reason, that the occurrence of the same conjectural emenda-
tion to two readers of Sh., without consultation, is cumulative evidence in its favor;
and here, in effect, is such a coincident conjecture on the part of four. But, what-
ever may be the decision between Singer on the one hand, and Heath, Mr. Hoppin
and myself on the other, I think it is quite evident that the word demanded by the
<PB N=379>
<HE><I>RUNAWAY'S EYES.</I> 379</HE>
<P>context is either <I>Rumour's</I> or <I>rumourers,</I> and I am quite willing to forego my claim
for the discovery in favor of Mr. Benjamin Heath, to whom the credit of first
&lquo;guessing&rquo; at the idea belongs; and I have no doubt that my Providence corre-
spondent is like-minded with me. Let those dispute or sneer about priority of con-
jecture whose minds and natures fit them to snarl over trifles,&mdash;the scraps and crumbs
of literary reputation: the object of all who have the true enthusiasm of Sh.'n stu-
dents is not personal credit, but the integrity of Sh.'s text.
<P>I had altogether passed by the theory advocated by the Rev. Mr. Halpin as carry-
ing its refutation on its face; but as it has recently found some favor with a few
whose judgments are entitled to respect, it is but proper that its claims to considera-
tion should be examined. His argument occupies nineteen octavo pages. [Mr.
White here gives Mr. Halpin's &lquo;positions and conclusions briefly&rquo; in fifteen lines. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
This argument is very learned and very ingenious, but far more learning and inge-
nuity have been displayed in the support of theories which, though more plausible,
were equally unsound. To examine it more properly we should have the entire
soliloquy before us as it appears in F<SUB>1</SUB>. . . . Is there anything here more than an
expression of the feelings of a newly married girl &lquo;many fathom deep in love?&rquo; Is
there not an utter absence of all formality and restraint in the construction of the
soliloquy? and is not the same freedom shown in the diction? It would be difficult
to point out in poetry a passage which has less the air of being constructed with
regard to a formula. Indeed, the poet seems to have been under no restraint but
that of versification; and not to have felt that. <I>Juliet</I> expresses her longing for the
coming of night several times; but that is evidently only because she wants night to
come. The approach of the time which will bring <I>Romeo</I> to her absorbs her whole
mind. There is no &lquo;intercalary principle,&rquo; or any other principle, evident in the
soliloquy. Even Mr. Halpin can only find that &lquo;four several invocations to Night,
<I>more or less</I> varied, occur at intervals <I>more or less</I> regular.&rquo; But the variation is
decidedly more, and the regularity decidedly less. With the same license, almost
any soliloquy might be said to be constructed on an intercalary principle. This
assumption of the hymeneal character of the soliloquy, which is the very key-stone
of Mr. Halpin's argument, is plainly but assumption; and, of course, the importance
of Cupid in the hymeneal masques, and the frequency of those masques in Sh.'s
day, are of no farther consequence.
<P>As to Cupid being called a runaway by Moschus, what did Sh. know about that?
It is not necessary to be of the Farmer school as to the no learning of Sh. to decide
at once that the supposition that he had read the ode of Moschus in the original is
entirely unwarranted; and in his day there was no translation of it. But even if he
had found Cupid called a runaway by some Greek or Latin authors, would he upon
that warrant have called him &lquo;runaway,&rquo; absolutely and without mitigation, not even
calling him &lquo;<I>a</I> runaway,&rquo; and having made no previous allusion to him? and this,
too, to a mixed audience, not one in fifty of whom had the tongues? Such was not
his way of writing for the audiences of the Blackfriars and the Globe.
<P>The fact that Ben Jonson, in his <I>Hue and Cry after Cupid,</I> calls Cupid &lquo;Venus's
Runaway,&rquo; is nothing to the purpose; because when the Masque opens Cupid <I>has run
away</I> from Venus, and it would be almost impossible to avoid speaking of him as
Venus's runaway. He is never spoken of simply as a runaway; much less is he
called absolutely &lquo;runaway,&rquo; even by Jonson. He is &lquo;Venus's runaway,&rquo; just as
Pompey, who runs away from Mr. Randolph of South Carolina, is Mr. Randolph's
runaway. But even were this not so, the occurrence of the epithet in Jonson's Masque
<PB N=380>
<HE>380 <I>APPENDIX.</I></HE>
<P>does not help Mr. Halpin, because that was not written until 1608; whereas, <I>Romeo
and Juliet</I> was written as early as 1596, and this soliloquy was printed in Q<SUB>2</SUB>.<SUP>*</SUP>
Mr. Halpin's eagerness in the defence of his theory probably blinded him to these
conclusive facts.
<P>That the andirons in <I>Imogen's</I> bed-chamber could have any acknowledged hyme-
neal significance, the very fact of her marriage, and the great dread which she had
of exposure, forbids us to believe. If winking Cupids had hymeneal symbolism so
universally recognized that it was only necessary for Sh. to write &lquo;that runaway's
eyes may wink&rquo; in order to have a promiscuous audience know that <I>Juliet</I> was
thinking of a winking Cupid as a part of a hymeneal pageant, <I>Imogen</I> would surely
have kept them out of her chamber at all hazards.
<P>Mr. Halpin's remark, that in the poem of <I>Romeus and Juliet</I> &lquo;Night and Cupid
are the only assistants at the spousal,&rquo; does not represent the passage in its true light.
It is merely narrative; the allusions to Night and Cupid are incidental and obvious,
and are made, not at the time when hymeneal allusions were appropriate, but when
<I>Romeo</I> and <I>Juliet</I> part at the Friar's cell:
<BQ>
&lquo;These said, they kisse, and then part to theyr father's house,<LB>
The joyfull bride vnto her home, to his eke goth the spouse;<LB>
Contented both, and yet both uncontented still,<LB>
Till Night and Venus child geve leave the wedding to fulfill.&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>How the perception of a clever and learned man may be perverted is shown by
the reference which Mr. Halpin makes to <I>Juliet's</I> supposition, &lquo;Or if love be <I>blind,</I>&rquo;
&amp;c., which he thinks &lquo;implies that she had already considered &ldquo;Love&rdquo; in the correla-
tive condition, and regarded him as <I>able to see.</I>&rquo; But <I>Juliet</I> does not make reference
here to the god of Love, but to a pair of lovers. Thus she says:
<BQ>
&lquo;<I>Lovers can see</I> to do their amorous rites<LB>
By their own beauties; <I>or</I> if love <I>be blind,</I>&rquo; &amp;c.<LB>
</BQ>
<P>The fact that &lquo;love&rquo; is spelled with a capital letter in no way confirms Mr. Hal-
pin's supposition; because the word is so spelled in every instance in which it
occurs in the soliloquy, as may be seen by reference to the passage as it is quoted
above from F<SUB>1</SUB>. Thus &lquo;Love-performing,&rquo; &lquo;strange Love grown bold,&rquo; &lquo;true Love
acted,&rquo; &lquo;in Love with night,&rquo; &lquo;the mansion of a Love.&rquo; Evidently no one of these
&lquo;Loves&rquo; has any more reference to Cupid than the other; and this is still further
shown, as far as the old typography can show it, by the fact that in the older quarto
the word is not spelled in this soliloquy with a capital letter in a single instance.
<P>To leave no part of Mr. Halpin's argument unanswered, his supposition that the
numberless works of ancient art, in which Cupid is represented as captured, impris-
oned, caged, fettered, and with his wings bound, are to be referred to &lquo;his notorious
propensity to <I>running away</I> from his mother,&rquo; is innocent indeed. He should have
consulted female counsel before venturing on such a plea. Women in classic days
were at heart much like women of now-a-days; and then, as now, they would see
Love bound, not for his mother's sake, but their own.
<P>There is, it seems to me, not the least shadow of a reason for believing that Sh.
would, without having so much as made an allusion to Cupid, speak of him abso-

<P>lutely as &lquo;runaway,&rquo; even supposing that he had any reason to expect that his audi-

that he would not have understood it himself.
<P>But besides this, there is one other consideration which is in itself conclusive upon
this point.
<P>Let it be remarked that the eyes in question were to close as the natural conse-
quence of a previous act. <I>Juliet</I> says, &lquo;spread thy close curtain, <I>love-performing</I>
Night,&rquo; in order that&mdash;what? That <I>Love's eyes</I> may wink? The absurdity of the
prayer is apparent. The argument for Cupid is worth absolutely nothing until it has
been shown that the coming of Night would as a matter of course put him to sleep.
But reason teaches and testimony establishes that night is exactly the time when that
interesting young gentleman is particularly wide awake. However much <I>Juliet</I>
might desire even Love's eyes to close on that occasion, it is ridiculous to make the
advent of &lquo;love-performing Night&rquo; <I>the cause</I> of his going to <I>sleep;</I> whereas it is
entirely consistent that she should wish Night to cause those prying or wandering
eyes which are personified in Rumor's, to close, that <I>Romeo</I> may come to her &lquo;un-
talked of and unseen.&rquo;
<P>When we remember the vital importance of the secresy of <I>Juliet's</I> nuptials, and
the desire which must have been almost uppermost in her heart, that <I>Romeo</I> might
be s<*>en entering her chamber window by no one who could talk of or rumor it, and
knowing, as we do, that Sh. and his audiences were in the habit of seeing such
people typified in the person of Rumor, covered with open eyes, and painted full of
tongues, can there be any doubt that &lquo;rumoures eyes&rquo; were the words written by the
poet?<SUP>*</SUP>

<P><SC>Delius.</SC> The eyes of such fugitives and vagabonds as tramp about at night.

<P>There is an older poem, called, <I>The Tragicall Hystory of Romeus and Juliet,</I>

<P>The quotations thus made will be sufficient to show the close attention paid by the
author of the play, both to the substance of the story and language of the old poem,
through this particular portion of the drama; for the remainder, not coming within
the present purpose, has not been examined and collated with the same scrupulous
and verbal minuteness.
<P>The <I>crux criticorum</I> in this passage is in the word &lquo;runaway,&rquo; which, being con-
sidered to be a corrupt reading, has been rejected, and many words by conjecture
substituted by ingenious persons,<SUP>*</SUP> much pleased and satisfied with their separate
offspring, and not wanting in due parental affection to recommend them to public
favour. From all such persons I am, however, obliged to differ, as I consider &lquo;run-
away&rquo; to be the true, authentic, and original expression of Sh., and that by him it is
here used in the sense of <I>Cupid</I> or <I>Love.</I>
<P>Now, there are two things which Juliet stands in need of, to secure the success of
her amorous projects and adventures&mdash;<I>i. e.,</I> that night should come and that Cupid
should be blind; or, in other words, that the deeds of love should be hidden in
darkness from the eyes and observation of the world. In a line that follows, she
says, what is explanatory of the former one: &lquo;If love be blind It best agrees with
Night.&rquo; Now, what says the elder poem?
<BQ>
&lquo;Contented both, and yet uncontented still,<LB>
Till <I>Night</I> and <I>Venus' child</I> give leave this wedding to fulfill.&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>Thus the success of Juliet's designs depended on the junction of Night and Cupid
in the poem as well as in the play. But then comes the question, Why is Love or
Cupid called <I>Runaway?</I> Now, Love is the <G>*)/epws dpare/ths</G> of the Greek poets; and
<FHL>
<NOTE>* I am more and more convinced of the truth of an observation made by a first-rate critic and scholar
of the last age,&mdash;&lquo;Pauci sunt, qui de <I>bonis correctionibus</I> bene judicare possint.&rquo; Nor is it a less rare
gift, &lquo;spuria discernere a germanis.&rquo;</NOTE>
<PB N=384>
<HE>384 <I>APPENDIX.</I></HE>
<P>what is the interpretation of <G>dpare/ths</G> in the dictionaries?&mdash;<I>Runaway.</I> Again, he is
the &lquo;amor <I>fugitivus</I>&rquo; of the Latin poets. How is that word explained?&mdash;<I>Runaway.</I>
What is Cotgrave's translation of <I>fugitve?</I>&mdash;Again, <I>Runaway.</I> It is the usual word.
&lquo;When <I>Cupid</I> with his smacking whip issueth forth to <I>runne.</I>&rquo;<SUP>*</SUP> It must also be
observed, that it was necessary that the term should be varied, as <I>Love</I> is mentioned
not less than <I>eight</I> times in this passage; and had he been designated here by his
name, <I>Cupid,</I> that mythological term, joined to Ph&oelig;bus and Phaeton, would have given
it an unnaturally stiff and learned air. It must be <I>especially observed,</I> that this speech
is made by Juliet in a very excited and elevated state of mind, absorbed entirely
with the hopes of possessing Romeo, and of gratifying her youthful and impetuous
passion for him. Full of impatient feelings, of rapid transitions of hope and fear,
hope of enjoyment and fear of discovery, strongly excited desires, gay voluptuous
thoughts, leading to wild extravagant fancies, she takes up with the first image and
expression that presented itself most forcibly, till, in the picture of &lquo;cutting Romeo
into little stars,&rquo; her fancy loses itself in its own hurried combinations, and gives
unrestrained scope and license to its wanderings. Under these circumstances, it
seems to me the very <I>characteristic</I> word which gives its effect to the whole passage,
and is most apt and beautiful in its wild expression of gaiety, which is emblematic
of the state of her mind, approaching, as she then believes, to the consummation of
all her desires; and at length, in the ardency of youth, only mentioning her doubts
and fears one moment, in order to forget them the next.
<P>It is perhaps unnecessary to say, that the word &lquo;runaway&rquo; is used elsewhere by Sh.
in the <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> and in <I>Mid. N. D.</I> I have somewhere read, that a passage has
been discovered in some poems, in which Cupid is called <I>Runaway.</I> This is well;
but I do not feel in want of any additional support to convince me that it is the very
identical word demanded,&mdash;that it sheds a pleasing and gay light which colours the
whole passage with its proper hue,&mdash;that no word could be substituted for it without
deeply impairing the poetical truth; and lastly, that Sh. himself placed it there.
<P>It may also be observed that this interpretation preserves the authentic reading of
the text&mdash;<I>Runawayes,</I> whereas many of the conjectural readings render it neces-
sary to alter it to <I>Runaway,</I> a license not without sufficient cause to be admitted. I
therefore, so far as my influence extends, cannot agree to this word being removed
for the substitution of any other that has been suggested, or for any reason hitherto
alleged.
<P>1. It is a word much more commonly in use in Sh.'s day than in ours.
<P>2. It is a familiar, playful, fanciful name, suited to moments, as these, of pleasing
excitement, hurried thought and joy.
<P>3. It is the English translation of <I>fugitivus,</I> by which Cupid is as well known as
Jupiter by the title of &lquo;The Thunderer,&rquo; Neptune &lquo;The Trident Bearer,&rquo; Diana &lquo;The
Huntress,&rquo; &amp;c., the &lquo;epitheton perpetuum&rquo; standing for the &lquo;nomen.&rquo;
<P>4. It is an epithet applied to him (<I>fugitivo</I>) by the Italian poets, and this is an
Italian story.
<P>5. It is used as an <I>emblem,</I> in which his history, and habits, and nature are
described.
<P>6. Lastly, it is the word established in the text of all the old editions.

<P><SC>Geo. Lunt</SC> (&lquo;<I>Three Eras of New England,</I>&rquo; &amp;c., Boston, 1857, p. 258). Now,
in order to explain this passage, if possible, let us resolve it into different language,
conveying precisely the same ideas throughout; and it may stand thus: Make your
best haste, O swift steeds of the sun, to be stalled for the night, at the mansion of
Ph&oelig;bus, in the West. If such a wagoner as Phaeton once of old was, only had the
reins, he would put you to your mettle, and, under the whip, would you dash through
heaven to your place of rest, and bring on night at once. Now, let it be so, love-
performing Night! Thus, now, as then, quickly spread thy close curtain that run-
aways eyes may wink! Such be the speed! Let this fiery charioteer,&mdash;this runaway
wagoner,&mdash;this Phaeton, runaway with by the steeds of the sun,&mdash;perform the same
feat now (successfully),&mdash;forthwith let him wink,&mdash;close his eyes&mdash;sleep&mdash;be it speed-
ily, night,&mdash;that under its shadow Romeo may&mdash;&lquo;Leap to these arms untalked of
and unseen.&rquo;
<P>This I conceive to have been the course of thought in Sh.'s mind. The metonomy
in the last line constitutes no objection to this explanation. &lquo;Unseen&rquo; would be the
ordinary consequence of darkness, and so, therefore, would be &lquo;untalked of;&rquo; and,
although observation in the natural course of events would precede discussion,&mdash;yet,
for poetical purposes, surely nothing can be more common than such a reversal of
the actual &lquo;order of their going.&rquo; The word &lquo;wink&rquo; of course is used for sleep, in
the common sense in which we employ it&mdash;<I>e. g.,</I> I have not slept a wink.
<P>And although I do not conceive, in regard to this or to any other passage of Sh.,
that it is essential for us to make it as precisely and consecutively consequential as
the propositions of a syllogism, yet, on the other hand, if it be objected that, whether
Ph&oelig;bus or Phaeton drive the chariot of heaven through its stages, it is the absence
of the sun which causes night,&mdash;and that, therefore, in the order of nature it is not
logically consecutive, to supplicate Night to spread her curtain in order that the eyes
of him may wink whose metaphorical retirement to repose is simultaneous and coin-
cident with the action prayed for, and who is, of himself, the potential cause of this
very effect of darkness, yet, figuratively speaking, and in reference to the personifi-
cation of the sun, as Ph&oelig;bus or Phaeton, it was sufficiently so, and indeed it was
strictly accurate for the poet so to form the imagination of it, and so to beseech Night
to draw her curtain over the face of things, after Heaven's charioteer had completed
his course and stabled his steeds; and especially as, in this instance, after his some-
what breakneck drive, he might, not unreasonably, be thought in need of his natural
rest.
<P>Although, therefore, in conceiving of the ordinary succession of day and night,
regarded as natural events, we are conscious that only upon the winking of &lquo;day's
garish eye&rquo; does night ensue,&mdash;and the obvious idea, in this aspect of the case, is,
not that the winking in question follows upon but accompanies the coming on of
night,&mdash;yet, otherwise, when we think of the sun as Ph&oelig;bus, or, as in this instance,
as Phaeton, driving his car to the west as his goal,&mdash;which presents the image of
&lquo;civil-suited Night&rquo; coming forward to spread her close curtain behind him, only
when the wagoner has arrived at his wonted mansion, and has disappeared within.
<P>The observation of Heath, therefore, on Warburton's note, though literally cor-
rect, is not poetically so. In fact, Juliet only hints at greater speed, rather than
complains of the tardiness of the sun. She addresses his coursers as fiery-footed
steeds; but rapid as is the movement of these flaming horses, still she would be glad
to hasten their speed. The regular flight of time, to be sure, is not fast enough for
her! In this consists the incompleteness and therefore the fallacy of Warburton's
<PB N=386>
<HE>386 <I>APPENDIX.</I></HE>
<P>theory. However swiftly the sun,&mdash;Ph&oelig;bus himself,&mdash;fulfills his ordinary course,
under his government the procession of the hours is uniform and orderly; and the
pace, though rapid, subject to strict guidance and control. In no proper sense, con-
sequently, can the sun itself be demonstrated a &lquo;runaway,&rquo; and <I>ergo,</I> as our friend
Launcelot Gobbo would say, Sh. did not thus offend against propriety and the nature
of things. But upon the fancy of Juliet, yearning as she was for the moment when
she was to be with her lover, flashed the idea of that irregular, meteoric race through
the skies which once called for the intervention of Jove's dread thunderbolt to stay
its progress; and if the unskillful charioteer on this occasion were not a &lquo;runaway,&rquo;
and, par excellence, the runaway, in this special connection when we are speaking
of the flight of time, and seeking to accelerate its progress, we know not where Sh.
could have looked for so fit an example; especially when this runaway sally is the
very subject of his fancy; and its chief actor is the very agent Juliet instances, and,
we presume, is wishing for, to hasten matters to the conclusion she so desired. For
in her fantastical imagination at the hint of the name, Ph&oelig;bus becomes Phaeton; this
idea fills her mind, and she thus pursues the chain of thought.
<P>The truth is, Warburton is the only one of the Sh. commentators who seems to
have had a glimpse of the poet's idea in this passage. But though it is strange that
what seems so obvious should not have occurred to a scholar like himself, apparently
his mind was not of a sufficiently poetical texture fully to apprehend the association
of thought in the text. Most other theories seem little better than ingenious trifling.
<P>The whole speech, in fact, is characteristically girlish, love-sick, extravagant,
erratic, Phaetonic. We must not here, then, require Sh. to produce in detail every
minute link in the chain of his earth-embracing and heaven-embracing associa-
tions, in order to enable inconsiderate eyes to follow the flight of his imagina-
tion; and he, we will suppose, imagined us capable of catching some flashes of his
meaning when his fancy touched into being those seeming wayward and intricate,
but still ever intermingling and harmonious, shapes of light.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 1). Mr. Grant White remarks that &lquo;&ldquo;Rumor&rdquo; was spelt <I>rumoure</I> in
Sh.'s day, and the possessive case <I>rumoures,</I> of course;&rquo; but F<SUB>1</SUB> is directly opposed to
such a conclusion; in it <I>the substantive</I> &lquo;rumour,&rquo; <I>which occurs twenty-one times,</I> <SC>is

yet proposed, not from any overweening fondness for my own conjecture, but because
it comes indisputably nearest to the <I>ductus literarum</I> of the old corruption. I must
not omit to add that it also occurred to a gentleman, who, not aware that it was

<P>ered as distinct from the lines which precede it. Again, Mr. Grant White is of

<P>The passages in our early poets about Night spreading her curtains, and Day
closing her eyes, are numerous; so in Drayton, <I>Baron's Warres</I> [cited p. 369].
(This stanza goes far to support the reading &lquo;<I>rude day's eyes</I>&rquo;.) Nor ought any one
to urge against the reading, &lquo;<I>That rude day's eyes may wink, and Romeo,</I>&rquo; &amp;c., that
it makes <I>Romeo</I> a trisyllable, while afterwards in this speech that name occurs as a

in the same speech.</I> So in III, i, 145, 146, <I>Romeo</I> is a dissyllable; in 157, a trisyl-

140, a dissyllable. In IV, iii, 27, 35, a dissyllable; in 31, a trisyllable.
<P><SC>Mary C. Clarke</SC> (&lquo;<I>N. and Q.,</I>&rquo; 2d ser., vol. v, p. 270, 1858). &lquo;Runnawayes&rquo; has
by all the commentators been pronounced to be a misprint, although by a forced and
far-fetched interpretation it might be supposed to refer to the &lquo;fiery-footed steeds,&rquo; the
horses of the sun alluded to in the first line of Juliet's speech. The reading which
has struck me is, &lquo;That <I>sunny day's</I> eyes,&rquo; &amp;c. This would give the same rhythm as the
old editions. It is nearest both in sound and appearance to &lquo;run-awayes&rquo;&mdash;sound,
if the transcriber from stage delivery made a mistake of ear; appearance, if the
printer made a mistake of sight. The epithet &lquo;sunny,&rquo; as applied to day, forms an
antithesis with the epithet &lquo;cloudy&rquo; as applied to night. &lquo;Sunny&rquo; also involves the
effect of glare, which suggests the verb to &lquo;wink.&rquo; And, moreover, the impersona-
tion of day, with its light and its sunshine, accords with the tenour of the speech
throughout, which deprecates all three, while invoking night and its opposite attri-
butes. To conclude, I cannot help thinking that &lquo;sunny-days,&rquo; as taken in connec-
tion with the whole speech, is most in the manner of Sh., who (especially in his
earlier plays, one of which Rom. &amp; Jul. is supposed to be) has shown fondness for
the poetical conceit, with antithetical style, maintained through entire passages.
<P><SC>Coll.</SC> (ed. 2). There have certainly been more suggestions than there are letters
in this word. It is generally admitted that <I>run-awayes</I> must be wrong. From
whom does Juliet wish that her proceedings with Romeo should be concealed?
From the members of the two hostile families&mdash;their &lquo;enemies;&rquo; and this word is
inserted by the (MS.), where it is spelt <I>enemyes:</I> if it had been spelt <I>ennemyes,</I> as it

(MS.), but because it is the very word required in the place. Nearly every com-
mentator has broached his own conjecture, some of them so unfortunate that it
seemed an exertion of at least equal courage and ingenuity to produce them. We
were formerly in favour of Jackson's <I>unawares,</I> which certainly comes nearest to
the letters, but the claims of &lquo;enemies,&rquo; suiting as it does both meaning and measure,
and reaching us on the authority of the (MS.), seem to us superior to all others.

<P><SC>Grant White</SC> (1861). No one of the many emendations that have been proposed
ever elicited my spontaneous recognition, and the best of them have equally failed
to satisfy my deliberate judgment. The efforts to explain the passage as it stands
are, with perhaps one exception, hardly less unsatisfactory. But I am inclined to think
that the true view of the passage was taken by the first editor who examined it&mdash;
Warburton. To Heath's much-approved censure of this explanation, the conclusive
reply is, that the previous address to the horses of the sun would naturally suggest
an allusion to the sun himself in this invocation, which is to Night; and that the
fact that the sun is <I>necessarily</I> absent as soon as night begins is the very reason
why <I>Juliet,</I> if she desired his absence, actual or potential, should invoke night's
presence.
<P>But there are other reasons than those suggested by Warburton for believing that
Ph&oelig;bus is the runaway meant by <I>Juliet.</I> For this closing of the eyes of watchful,
babbling day&mdash;typified by the god of day&mdash;would completely satisfy <I>Juliet's</I> earnest
wish that <I>Romeo</I> might come to her &lquo;untalked of and unseen.&rquo; She begs Night to
spread her curtains that sleep may fall upon the eyes of day&mdash;a fancy not uncommon
with the poets. See, for instance, this passage from Drayton's <I>Barons Warres:</I>
[See Dyce's note, p. 369. <SC>Ed.</SC>]. That &lquo;wink&rquo; was commonly used when Sh. wrote,

<P>There is, however, yet another reason, equally cogent with any of the foregoing,
and of a very different nature, for believing that Ph&oelig;bus is the runaway upon whose
eyes <I>Juliet</I> wishes the blindness of silence-bringing sleep to fall; and this is found
in the traces left of the augmentation and correction of the play before the printing
of Q<SUB>2</SUB>. For in (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) this invocation to Night does not appear, only the brief address
to Ph&oelig;bus's steeds with the allusion to cloudy Night in the last line. Now, in that
version <I>Juliet</I> calls upon the horses of the sun to hasten to &lquo;Ph&oelig;bus <I>mansion;</I>&rquo;
but with the addition of the invocation to Night, and the promptly-uttered wish that
the eyes of Day should close in sleep upon the spreading of her curtains, we find
&lquo;Ph&oelig;bus mansion&rquo; changed to &lquo;Ph&oelig;bus <I>lodging,</I>&rquo;&mdash;a variation so delicate, an adapta-
tion of the old fancy to the new so felicitous, the introduction of a leading thought
so subtle and yet so clear in purpose, that to believe it accidental would derogate
too much from Sh.'s skill, and tax too far the stretch of our credulity. And that the
invocation to Night was not accidentally omitted from (Q<SUB>1</SUB>), but was an addition to
the first version of the tragedy, seems very clear, because both in Brooke's poem and
Paynter's prose tale, which Sh. so closely followed, there are the following allusions
to that lover's desire for the quick setting of the sun and the spreading of night's
shadow which the four lines of <I>Juliet's</I> speech found in (Q<SUB>1</SUB>) so fully express:

<P>But in neither poem nor tale is there germ of the impassioned invocation to Night
which first appeared in the &lquo;augmented&rquo; Q<SUB>2</SUB>.
<P>Nevertheless, the designation of Ph&oelig;bus, or any other god or person, as runaway,
absolutely, and without any defining article, is so abrupt and strange that it is not
surprising that efforts have been made to find another meaning for the passage. The
most plausible of the many suggestions which have been made are&mdash;the Rev. Mr.
Halpin's; Mr. Robert Messinger's, of New York (in a letter to me), that &lquo;run-
aways&rquo; means &lquo;those who run in the way, runagates, vagabonds;&rquo; and Douce's. The
second of these explanations might perhaps be worthier of consideration, were it not
for the facts that, at the period when this tragedy was written, &lquo;runaway&rquo; appears to
have been used only to mean one who ran away, and that &lquo;runagate,&rquo; which had the
same meaning then that it has now, would have suited the verse quite as well as
&lquo;runaway;&rquo; while Douce's, although it suggests the view which <I>Juliet</I> would be
<PB N=390>
<HE>390 <I>APPENDIX.</I></HE>
<P>likely to take of her position towards her parents, is entirely inconsistent with the
passionful longing which this soliloquy expresses with such a singular union of direct-
ness and modesty, and which is its informing motive. For, as we have seen, &lquo;wink&rquo;
in this passage means (and in fact, as the winking was to be the consequence of the
spreading of night's close curtains, it can only mean) sleep; and that <I>Juliet should</I>
desire either <I>Romeo</I> or herself to be asleep at the time when she wishes that run-
away's eyes may wink, is a supposition not to be entertained for a moment.
<P><SC>Eugene J. Brady</SC> (&lquo;<I>N. and Q.,</I>&rquo; 2d series, vol. xii, p. 85, 1861). I have just dis-
covered the original reading of this passage. Juliet invokes Night instantly to come,
that the sun may be compelled to close his eyes. The poet's words were certainly
these: &lquo;sun-awake's eyes.&rquo;
<P><SC>F. A. Leo</SC> (&lquo;<I>N. and Q.,</I>&rquo; 3d ser., vol. i, p. 363, 1862). The Sh. scholars of three
centuries have published so many more or less ingenious notes about <I>Juliet's run-
away,</I> and yet the question is so far from getting a right answer, that it will do no
harm to any one if a very little and modest note tries to give it;&mdash;probably with the
same effect as the other notes did. If we take in view, the four last letters of &lquo;run-
awayes&rquo; are nearly the same as the letters of the next word, &lquo;eyes,&rquo; it will not be
throughout unjustified to suppose that the repetition of these four letters (for <I>a</I> and <I>e</I>
are very easily changed) results from an error of the compositor; and that the real
word in question, or rather the mutilated word only, is &lquo;runnawayes,&rquo; and not &lquo;run-
nawayes eyes.&rquo; Now, in reading Juliet's soliloquy we find that she wants not merely
&lquo;night,&rquo; but quite directly &lquo;cloudy' night;&rquo; she is of opinion that &lquo;Lovers can see to
do their amorous rites By their own beauties.&rquo; She calls the night a &lquo;Sober-suited
matron, all in black&rquo; and a &lquo;&mdash;&mdash; black-browed night.&rquo; In short, she wants all as
dark as possible, and probably will have nothing to do with the inquisitive, importu-
nate, and prating moonlight. The &lquo;close curtain&rquo; therefore are, as I suppose, the
clouds, which shall make wink the moon's eyes; and Juliet says: &lquo;Spread thy close
curtain, love-performing night&rquo; (and then lifting up her hand to the moon and the
stars), &lquo;That <I>yonder eyes</I> may wink.&rquo; If we now remember that the Qq generally
are published after some short-hand writing,&mdash;that, as Collier says, &lquo;The person or
persons who prepared the transcripts of the plays for the printer, wrote by the ear
and not by the eye: they heard the dialogue and wrote it down as it struck them,&rquo;&mdash;
the difference in some of the letters in the two words
<C><SD>runnawayes,</SD></C>
<C><SD>yondereyes,</SD></C>
</BQ>
<P>will not be of any importance; if we state the possibility that one could believe to
hear pronounced &lquo;runnawayes,&rquo; while the other said &lquo;yonder eyes.&rquo; (It is not to be
forgotten that many Englishmen pronounce <I>w</I> instead of <I>r&mdash;gweat</I> for <I>great!</I>) For
the rest let me say, without laying a great stress on it, that Sh. twice in <I>Rom. and
Jul.</I> uses the word &lquo;yonder&rquo; with regard to the moon and to the heaven, for &lquo;by
yonder blessed moon I swear.&rquo;
<P>One word more for those who mean that the sun is not yet gone: And that Juliet,
therefore, cannot lift up her hand to the moon. Well! she lifts up her hand to the
<I>cause of light,</I> may that be the sun or the moon, and &lquo;yonder eyes&rquo; is an epithet
quite as fit for the one as for the other. But it is to be understeod that, if Juliet
speaks of the <I>sun's</I> eyes, the &lquo;close curtain&rquo; can be as well (and even better) the
darkness as the clouds.
<P>And now let it go. You conceive that I believe my emendation to be the best,
for else I would not have published it; but that is not enough, and I am exceedingly
<PB N=391>
<HE><I>RUNAWAY'S EYES.</I> 391</HE>
<P>desirous to know whether the authorities of Sh. criticism laugh at my notes or accept
its contents.
<P><SC>Stylites</SC> (&lquo;<I>N. and Qu.,</I>&rquo; 3d ser., vol. ii, p. 92, 1862). It is impossible not to be
struck with the ingenuity of Mr. Leo's suggestion; but I would remark that if the
&lquo;eyes&rquo; of which Juliet speaks are to be referred to the sun, there is no need of any
alteration of the received text, a liberty always to be avoided as much as possible. . . .
Now, if Sh. calls night (in Mer. of Ven., II, vi, 47) a &lquo;runaway&rquo; in reference to
approaching day, he may well make Juliet call day, or the sun, a &lquo;run away&rquo; in
reference to approaching night. But I confess to have always doubted whether any
metaphor was ever intended here, and whether &lquo;runaways&rquo; is not the genitive <I>plural,</I>
and does not allude to mischievous spies. In London it was common enough,
formerly, before the establishment of the police force, for young lads (the Parisians
would call them <I>gamins</I>) to knock at a street door, or tie a cat or dog to the knocker,
and make their escape after having enjoyed the astonishment of the servant. These
boys were called &lquo;runaways,&rquo; and the servant would call their exploit &lquo;a runaway's
knock.&rquo; I have been told that in some country neighborhoods boys of a similar
character are fond of spying out sweethearts' assignations and playing a very unwel-
come third at their meetings, darting upon them at the most inopportune moments,
and running away to avoid the vengeance of the disappointed swain. If such a
practice prevailed at Stratford in Sh.'s time, he was quite capable of transferring it
to Italy, and of representing Juliet as fearful that her lover's steps might be watched
by these troublesome urchins and traced to her door.
<P><SC>Halliwell</SC>. This passage in the soliloquy of Juliet, in which her unlimited pas-
sion resolves itself into a storm of rapture, deserves to be viewed through this special
position&mdash;that Love is blind, and that Cupid himself would blush did lovers see &lquo;the
pretty follies that themselves commit.&rquo; So thought Jessica, when attired in the cos-
tume of the other sex, and Juliet's ardent and tumultuous expression of affection
must be referred to a somewhat more obscure delineation of the same belief. The
prayer of the lover is for secresy and rapidity, secresy during the celebration of their
rites, and the speedy approach of night to overshadow the eyes of Love. Her
desire is for the departure of day&mdash;&lquo;bring in cloudy night immediately;&rquo; for con-
cealment, <I>only a secondary wish</I>&mdash;&lquo;Spread thy close curtains, love-performing night.&rquo;
But why? There can only be one answer,&mdash;that the eyes of the god of Love may
be closed, and Romeo reach his love &lquo;untalked of and unseen.&rquo; Lovers can see by
their own beauties, or, <I>if Love be blind,</I> &lquo;It best agrees with night.&rquo; The &lquo;strange
love,&rquo; afterwards mentioned, is the generic idea, not the divinity here intended. Run-
away was a common pet name for Cupid, and the authenticity of the word is beyond
all doubt, and not one of the conjectural emendations can be adopted without de-
stroying the poetical beauty of the passage in which it occurs. But it could be sub-
stantiated by a <I>reductio ad absurdum,</I> for suppose that night, or Juliet, be intended,
and we at once arrive at an impossibility, or, to say the least, at a foolish tautology.
Let night spread her close curtains that night may sleep and Romeo find his Juliet!
Where is there in this the congruity so invariably observed by Sh. in similar flights
of his luxuriant fancy? The conjecture that Juliet is the Runaway implies a still
greater absurdity, no less than that of her desiring to slumber at the very time of the
approach of what she so eagerly desires.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2). The Rev. W. R. Arrowsmith, after alluding to &lquo;the prodigious
guesses at a substitute for &ldquo;runaways&rdquo; and the extravagant speculations touching the
persons to whom it refers,&rquo; writes thus: &lquo;It is supposed that to <I>wink</I> means only to
<PB N=392>
<HE>392 <I>APPENDIX.</I></HE>
<P><I>connive;</I> whereas, besides this its stricter sense, it also often signifies to close the eyes
in sleep, in sound sleep. But however that may be, whether ignorance of such
usage be at the bottom of their trouble with the recorded text or not, I defy the
queasiest objector of them all to produce one solid reason for questioning the pro-
priety of Sh.'s expressing the desired secresy of Romeo's visit by the darkness,
under cover of which runaways, <I>i. e.,</I> fugitives, may sleep secure from surprise, that
shall not tell with equal force against the propriety of his expressing the quickness
of a lover's hearing, by what is inaudible to the &ldquo;suspicious head of theft&rdquo; (Love's
L. L., IV, iii, 336). The conditions of secresy in that case, and of silence in this,
could not be exemplified by instances more happy in themselves, or more nearly
allied to each other.&rquo;&mdash;<I>The Editor of</I> &lquo;<I>Notes and Queries,</I>&rquo; <I>and his friend Mr.
Singer,</I> &amp;c., p. 11.&mdash;I have only to add that my conviction of &lquo;runnawayes&rquo; being a
gross corruption remains unshaken.
<P><SC>Knight</SC> (ed. 2) gives the substance of his note in (ed. 1), except that he does not
say that Zachary Jackson &lquo;set the matter straight.&rquo; He also states that Mr. Collier
adopted Zachary Jackson's emendation, and then quotes Dyce's objection thereto
and adds: There is much force in this objection. One more conjecture: <I>change a
